Regarding the benefit bestowed upon all bodhisattvas and sentient beings: this phrase refers to receiving instruction oneself. As for "listening in silence":
when the tranquil wisdom is held in profound stillness and the perfect hearing does not dwell [on objects], it is through such silence that one is able to listen in accordance with the truth.

This phrase refers to receiving instruction from others. This concludes the section on the response to the request for instruction, which combines with the preceding category. The previous combination [is now complete].
The section on "Praising and Requesting Instruction" concludes within the first part, the "Section on Praising and Granting Permission.

Next, the "Exposition of the Direct Answer" is divided into two parts. First, "Demonstrating the Causal Practice," which is further divided into two. First, "The Causal Practice of the Tathāgata," which is further divided into two. First, "The Fundamental Origination of Purity," which is further divided into two.
First, "Demonstrating the Fundamental Origination," which is further divided into two. First, "Designating that the Fundamental is Solely Awakening."
"Good son, the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gateway called 'Perfect Enlightenment' (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Regarding its textual structure, there are three phrases that indicate that the fundamental essence is solely enlightenment: the phrase 'good son,' the phrase 'Unsurpassed Dharma King,' and [the title] 'Perfect Enlightenment.'"
The phrase "There is a great cloud" refers to the Unsurpassed Dharma King, who is designated as the Tathāgata of the Fundamental Dharma-nature;

this phrase indicates the Teacher of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). The phrase "There is a great *dhāraṇī* gate" signifies that fundamental nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*) pervades both the internal and external;
it is "great" as distinguished from the partial and the small. *Dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "total retention. A "gate" (*mukha*) allows for both entry and exit.
It leaves nothing out, whether internal or external, and is fully endowed with the characteristics and functions of *dhāraṇī*. Yet, it is certainly not some peripheral or minor path;

there is nothing it does not encompass, for it penetrates all things. Therefore, it first designates "Great *Dhāraṇī*" to manifest its function, and subsequently designates the "Gate" to reveal its characteristic.
As for the name "Perfect Enlightenment" (*Yuanjue*), one should point to these characteristics and functions when invoking the name to summon the true essence.
This sentence demonstrates the characteristics of the dharma of Perfect Enlightenment.
Second, it indicates that from the sole state of Awakening flow forth all pure True Suchness (*tathatā*), Bodhi, Nirvana, and the *pāramitās*, which are taught to the Bodhisattvas.
The first two phrases of the prose section introduce "only awareness" (*vijñapti-mātra*). The phrase "flowing forth, etc. refers to the instruction for bodhisattvas. Regarding "all-purified":
there is no subject that cuts nor object to be cut; no subject that realizes nor object to be realized; and no causes or effects of defilement.

Regarding the phrase "Suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth": it refers to the fruits of the Buddha’s three virtues (*triguṇa*). It is the fruit of the *dharmakāya* of realized Suchness; the fruit of *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *prajñā* (wisdom);
and the fruit of *nirvāṇa*—the Sanskrit term for which, when translated here, is "perfect quiescence" (*yuanji*) or liberation.

Furthermore, regarding *pāramitā*: this is a Sanskrit term translated here as "reaching the other shore. The "other shore" is the Buddha-land; "reaching" means realization. It is the realization of Buddhahood.
The land adorns the Buddha-fruit, fulfilling and accomplishing it; because it contains immeasurable gates of pure Dharma within, the word "and" (*ji*) is used.
This phrase reveals that the nature from which all practices arise is fundamentally Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*). Regarding "instructing the Bodhisattvas":

the Tathāgata manifests the fruit and displays the land as a whole to instruct the Bodhisattvas, so that they may awaken to the fundamental purity of their own self-nature and attain the practice of enlightenment.

"The cause of that fruit. This phrase reveals that Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti) addresses those of the Bodhisattva nature. Together with the preceding section, this completes the "Exposition of the Fundamental Origin" (*shisuo benqi*).
Second, the "Exposition of the Purification of the Object" (*shisuo qingjing*) is divided into two parts. First, the heading for the severance of delusion, which is further divided into two.
First, the exposition of the illuminating power that effects severance.
When all Tathāgatas first established their stage of practice, they all relied upon the aspect of perfectly illuminating, pure awakening to eternally sever ignorance;
only then did they achieve the Buddha-way.
Regarding this passage, there are three phrases that demonstrate the capacity for severing and illuminating: "All... and so forth is one phrase; "all rely upon... and so forth is the second.

[The phrase] "Only then does one attain Buddhahood" constitutes a single sentence. Regarding "all Tathāgatas," this refers to tracing back from the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) to discuss the origin of the cause.

As for "originally arising in the ground of practice" (*mūla-pratipatti-bhūmi*), this "original arising" differs from the "original arising" mentioned above. The former speaks of the basis of the causal origin;
the latter refers to the time when the Bodhisattva first attained awakening and gave rise to the mind of pure causes during the stage of the Bodhisattva grounds (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*).
"Beginning with the initial cause": this phrase reveals the cause by way of the fruit. "All are based upon" means that the paths of all Buddhas are identical and without variation.

"Perfectly illuminating" means constant awakening without abiding. "The characteristic of pure awakening" means that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is devoid of the nature of subject and object.
"Permanently severing ignorance" means ultimate purity through quiescent non-duality. This phrase demonstrates...

"Only after thoroughly penetrating the causes does one attain the Buddha-way" means that through cultivation and realization, one achieves the perfect enlightened mind that is beyond cultivation and realization.
This phrase indicates the fruit attained. Within the text, the two characters "perfectly illuminating" (yuánzhào) point to the essential point for severing delusions.
It is not through effortful practice that the fundamental nature manifests as the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the perfect radiance.

When one does not lose this direct perceptual object, one attains the realm of pure awakening, wherein there is no locus for deluded awareness or luminosity. Therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) is forever severed.

Should the illumination fail to manifest perfectly, then based on that luminosity, objects are established; distinctions between identity and difference blaze forth, and ignorance is thus established. Ignorance...
This refers to the absence of the illumination of perfect reflection. It is impossible that one could sever that ignorance without relying on perfect reflection.
Second, showing what is severed, which opens into two parts: first, the interrogation and explanation, which opens into two; first, the interrogation.

What is ignorance (*avidyā*)? This first interrogative phrase at the beginning of the text asks: "What is it that is called ignorance? Although this is an inquiry into the name, its intent is actually to investigate its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the following section explains the characteristics and then concludes with the name. Next, there is an exposition consisting of two parts. First, the explanation [of the characteristics].

The nature and characteristics of delusion are opened into two. First, the nature of delusion is the delusion regarding the True; this is further opened into two. First, the emergence of all delusive natures:
"Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions."
The first phrase clarifies that all delusive natures are eliminated. "Good son" is one phrase. "All... and so forth is another phrase. "From" means "of its own accord.
"Beginningless" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); its essential nature is false and devoid of any origin or beginning.

This refers to those who come under the influence of the "karmic aspect" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). Due to this fundamental and beginningless false delusion, they give rise to further falsity, passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust until the present day.

This refers to the various inversions of the "evolving and manifesting aspects" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) of ignorance—where perception and appearance are confused, where delusive falsehood is woven into a murky turbidity, and where self and other, the environment and its inhabitants, are mistaken for one another; thus, deluded in themselves, they pursue external objects and cling to them.
Taking things as one's own; pointing to that lack of wisdom and the continuous grasping of names to create karma—these are the six coarse delusive natures of karma and suffering.
Two metaphors illustrate the delusion regarding reality.
It is like a person who has lost their way and confuses the four directions.
The phrase "like a person who has lost their way" serves as a metaphor to clarify the delusion regarding the Truth.
"Like a person who has lost their way" refers to one who is confused about the single Dharma-realm. "Confusing the four directions" means mistaking east for west and south for north. Constantly...
While dwelling in one's own original abode, one gives rise to the notion of being a stranger in a foreign land.

This metaphor illustrates how the luminous clarity of the nature of awareness, within its own fundamental mind, is deluded by its own appearances and falsely discriminates, grasping at and establishing the perceived object;

thus, the subject that perceives arises with distinctions, giving rise to love and hatred within the nature of the mind. This establishes the seeds and active manifestations of ignorance, just as a lost person becomes confused.
The original directions—east, south, west, and north—are transformed into the east, south, west, and north of a newly arisen location.

Together with the preceding section on the nature of delusion, this concludes the "Section on the Deluded Nature Obscuring Reality. Second, the "Section on the False Manifestations Being Fundamentally False," which opens into two parts:
first, the emergence of various false manifestations.
One falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind.

These two phrases from the text reveal various false appearances: the phrase "falsely identifying... and so forth, and the phrase "the six sense-objects... and so forth. Regarding "falsely identifying":

this refers to the false subjective nature that establishes what has been lost through illumination; it is precisely the state following the transformation of karma, manifestation, and subsequent [consciousness].

Regarding consciousness: as for the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—to take them as the characteristics of one's own body is to be deluded by their combination and establish the appearance of a self, thereby differentiating them into material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).
One fails to realize that the nature of the four great elements is fundamentally distinct from one another and lacks any real combination.

This phrase refers to the delusion of having a body. The "six objects" (ṣaḍviṣaya) are form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (dharma). "Conditioned reflections" refer to the cognitions produced by these objects;
that is, the mind-consciousness that engages in discursive thought by grasping at the shadows of objects as they fall away through the five sense-gates.

Regarding "taking them as the characteristics of one's own mind": delusion takes luminosity and establishes its own perceived division (svadṛṣṭibhāga), thereby differentiating it within the mental factors (caitta). It is not [the case that the object exists independently].
"Awakening to the fact that the reflected image is an attachment to delusion, one realizes that the radiance is not the original luminosity. This sentence refers to the deluded existence of the mind.

It constitutes the basis for the establishment of the dual phenomena of form and mind within the beginningless birth and death of sentient beings; in total, it demonstrates that these arise from the false recognition [of the self] and lack a truly existent nature.
Two metaphors clarify the distinction between the fundamental and the deluded.
It is like one with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky or a second moon.
Regarding the three phrases that illustrate the fundamental delusion through metaphors: "like one with diseased eyes," "seeing flowers in the sky," and "a second moon" constitute the metaphors.
"Like" (*pi*) means comparison; "that" (*bi*) refers to the person with diseased eyes. The "disease" refers to the ocular affliction.

"The eyes" refers to eyes afflicted by cataracts; this phrase is a metaphor for the karmic consciousness of ignorance (*avidyā*). "Seeing" refers to that deluded recognition by the cognitive consciousness (*vijñāna*);

"flowers in the sky" originally have no appearance of flowers, yet the appearance arises from diseased eyes—this phrase is a metaphor for grasping at the characteristics of the body, like seeing a second moon when there is only one true moon, and perceiving a double halo. This phrase is a metaphor for grasping at the characteristics of the mind.
Regarding the term "involvement" (*ji*): when one who has the eye disease of seeing empty flowers perceives two moons, they necessarily appear as a pair.
One who does not have the eye disease of seeing empty flowers cannot fail to see [the single moon]. Therefore, it is said "involvement.
This is a metaphor for the body-form that is falsely recognized; together with the mental characteristics and fundamental ignorance, these constitute the wheel of the three sufferings.

Regarding the cycle of birth and death: the reason the flower-like appearance is used as a metaphor for the body and the second moon as a metaphor for the mind is that the flower-like appearance is a phantom reflection arising from empty space.
When one’s diseased eyes encounter that eternally abiding empty space, the empty flowers vanish;

at that time, once the eyes are cleared of their defect, they become as clear and bright as before, yet they remain equal to those in a dark room or the blind in the night, all sharing the same condition.
The appearance of two moons is seen because the characteristic of the feet corresponds to the characteristic of the body.

There is no ground for relinquishing grasping except when a single lifetime’s lifespan is exhausted and one transcends the death-and-rebirth of the segmented realm. From the true moon, the illusory image of two moons arises;

due to a temporary ailment of the eyes, that true moon appears and disappears indeterminately, giving rise to the paired phenomenon of two moons. At times, when conditions converge, [the perception occurs].
One sees the double wheel. At times, when conditions depart, one enters silent contemplation (*mìngguān*). It is sufficient that the feet face the heart;

as objects arise, the nature of causes and conditions is indeterminate. This concludes the section on the "Intrinsically Delusive Nature" (the preceding section on the "Delusive Nature Confusing the Truth" is subsumed here), ending the section on the "Fundamental Delusion of Delusive Appearances. Second, the explanation of the causes of delusion.
The result is divided into two. First, the division of two based on delusion regarding the true cause. First, the cause of delusion regarding the real nature:
"Good son, space is truly without flowers; it is only the sick person who falsely clings to them."

The two phrases beginning with "When" constitute the cause for delusion regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*). "Good son," "one phrase," "emptiness and reality," and so forth—regarding the phrase "emptiness and reality have no flowers":
the characteristic of awakening is like space, pervasive and pure. The "sick person" is one whose eyes are diseased.
Those who hold false attachments do not realize that empty space has no such phenomenon as the arising of flowers.

Due to their own diseased eyes, they perceive within the pure void the phenomena of empty flowers arising and ceasing in disorder, and they cling to these as real, failing to realize the pure true reality (*dharmatā*).
This phrase refers to the cause of delusion regarding the truth. Regarding the absence of the moon analogy here, it is because sentient beings...

Regarding the mental characteristics perceived, one clings to them as being within the body; because the flower-like appearances are subsumed within the mind and body, they are not mentioned separately.
Second is the delusion regarding the fruit of true nature.
Due to false attachment, one is not only deluded regarding the intrinsic nature of this empty space, but is also confused about the source from which those real flowers arise.
In the text, two phrases concern being deluded regarding the fruit of true nature; the phrase "due to false [attachment]... and the subsequent phrase "also, furthermore...

[refer to this]. Regarding "due to false attachment": because one clings to false appearances, one becomes deluded regarding the true appearance. As for "not only": [it implies that there is further confusion beyond this].
"Only" (*wei du*) means "not alone. "The self-nature of empty space" refers to the nature of the pure, true reality (*dharmatā*).

This phrase concerns delusion regarding both phenomena and their nature. "Furthermore" (*yi fu*) implies inclusion. "The place where the flowers of reality grow" refers to the locus where the flowers of the mind of ultimate perfect enlightenment manifest.
This phrase concerns delusion regarding the mind; for it is through the pure nature that true reality is revealed.

The pure characteristics and nature are manifested by the awakening mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*). It goes without saying that if one is deluded regarding the characteristics, one is deluded regarding the nature.
Consequently, one loses the fundamental Buddha-enlightenment, which is all-pervading, pure, quiescent, and conforms to the equality of one's own mind.
Therefore, there is the phrase "not only... but also. The commentary states: "Those who are deluded regarding the fruit of true nature" refers to [those who lack] awakening.

The locus of accomplishment is the ultimate state of pure nature; therefore, it is called the "fruit. This concludes the preceding section on the text, which together completes the section on the causes and fruits of delusion regarding reality.
Second, the establishment of the causes and fruits of the false.
By this, there is the false existence of the cycle of birth and death.

A single phrase from the text establishes the causes and effects of delusion. "By this" means that because one is deluded regarding the causes and effects of the pure marks and nature, one instead undergoes the causes and effects of false marks and nature.
"Falsely existing" refers to flowers in the sky or a second moon. [The cycle of] birth and death...
Regarding "death": the seeds of fundamental ignorance give rise to active manifestations (*samudācāra*), and these active manifestations form new seeds;
as the old ones ripen, they function like a wheel revolving in a circle. Birth leads to death, and death leads to birth, continuing without interruption.

This concludes the section on the causes and effects of delusion regarding the True [Nature], which was combined with the preceding section. Now, this connects to the explanation of the false nature and characteristics.
The section on the subsumption under categories is concluded. Second, the conclusion of the name:
it is therefore called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
This single phrase concludes the name according to the text. As for the word "therefore" (*nam*), it is a term used to conclude and indicate the preceding passage. By means of this—

Therefore, this name is established. As for "ignorance" (*avidyā*): all sentient beings, in their entirety, have from beginningless time been deluded regarding the luminous nature [of mind], which is termed ignorance.

There are superior grades of ignorance, as well as its essential nature, characteristics, causes, and effects; these give rise to the two [categories of] sentient beings and Buddhas. For this reason, there are no sentient beings who do not possess ignorance.
When ignorance is completely severed, one immediately attains the Buddha-way. This concludes the preceding section on "Combined Interrogation and Explanation."

The section on collectively demonstrating what is to be severed—the delusion—is concluded. The section on connecting and demonstrating that which can sever and illuminate is subsumed under the initial heading;
thus, the section on severing delusion is finished. Next, the manifestation of purity is divided into two parts: first, the fundamental emptiness of ignorance is opened up into two.
First, regarding the fact that it does not have a real substantial entity, there are two parts.
First is the heading. "Good son, this ignorance has no real substantial entity.
This consists of two phrases in the text as a heading: the phrase "Good son" and the phrase "this [ignorance]... and so forth. This "no" [refers to the absence of a real entity].
"Clarifying" refers to the aforementioned nature, characteristics, causes, and effects of what is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Not having a real substance" means that since substance encompasses nature, characteristics, causes, and effects, and these four are not distinct from one another, one examines whether substance is truly real. Now, since all four are entirely empty, how could substance have any reality?
Second, clarifying through analogy has two parts: first, the analogy for the non-substantiality of arising.
Just as a person in a dream does not lack existence while dreaming, yet upon waking finds nothing at all to be obtained;
so it is with the two phrases regarding the metaphor for the non-substantiality of birth. The phrase "just as in a dream... and the subsequent phrase "and upon reaching... [illustrate this].
The word "just as" (*yathā*) is a term used for comparison. "A person in a dream" refers to a person manifested within the dream-objective realm, or oneself.
The body manifests differently from its original state, or the body itself remains unchanged while connecting with many other bodies—just like people within a dream.

This metaphor represents the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*). That "at the time of the dream it is not non-existent" means that the activities of those dreaming people are vividly present;
this metaphor represents the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of ignorance. "And reaching the awakening" refers to the characteristic of the arising of ignorance.

When the physical form opens and awakens to clarity, it is like the time when [the mind] again becomes perfectly luminous and illuminating. That which is utterly unobtainable is like a person in a dream and the events of that dream:
they are entirely without form, yet not non-existent, and ultimately non-existent. This serves as a metaphor for the fact that the states of abiding and proceeding are fundamentally empty.
This phrase is a metaphor for the lack of substance in ignorance; the second metaphor is for the lack of substance in cessation.
It is like various empty flowers vanishing into space; one cannot say there is a fixed place where they are extinguished.

The two phrases of the current passage serve as metaphors for the non-substantiality of extinction: "like various [flowers]" and so forth represents one phrase, while "cannot be said" and so forth represents the other.
"Like various empty flowers" refers to the manifold and non-uniform nature of self and other, the environment and its inhabitants, karmic actions, causes, and effects—their cessation.
Regarding "in empty space": it returns to its original state as empty space, which is all-pervasive and pure by nature.

This phrase is a metaphor for the cessation of ignorance. One cannot say there is a fixed place where cessation occurs; since space originally has no flowers, how could there be a place where flowers cease?

Just so, when such illusions cease, how can there be any characteristic of cessation? This phrase is a metaphor for the non-substantiality of cessation. This corresponds to the preceding section of the text.

The section on the joint establishment of the analogy is concluded. The preceding section on the correlation and manifestation, which subsumes [the argument] under the category of "not having a real substantial entity," is concluded.
Second, there is no place of arising.
Why? Because there is no place of arising.
The first two phrases state that there is originally no place of birth. Why is this? Because there is no place of birth.
The first phrase interrogates why ignorance is like a dream, a person, or flowers in the sky, lacking any real substance.
The second phrase explains that the self-nature of sentient beings is solely pure, perfect enlightenment, which, like the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, is all-pervasive and equal.

As for the place where real flowers arise—what other place could there be for that ignorance to arise? Therefore, it has no substantial reality, because from the beginning there has been no place of arising.
The preceding section on "The Non-Reality of the Combined" and the section on "The Fundamental Emptiness of Ignorance" are hereby completed.
Indeed, when one realizes that the essence of ignorance is not real, then all deluded body and mind cease to exist; one realizes that its arising has no locus.

Then, all delusive realms cease to exist; both the body and the objects of its delusive appearances are simultaneously absent. When ignorance is realized as being entirely void in its very essence, it becomes manifest.
Thus, the two kinds of birth and death exist merely as names.
All sentient beings falsely perceive arising and ceasing within that which is unborn; therefore, it is called "revolving in birth and death.
This passage consists of two phrases: "birth and death are merely names" and "all [sentient beings]," etc.

Regarding the phrase "all [sentient beings]," this refers to those born from the four modes of birth and existing within the nine realms of existence. Regarding the phrase "within that which is unborn," this is like a person in a dream or flowers in the sky.
"Those who perceive arising and ceasing through deluded vision" refers to the fact that the dreamer and the empty flowers are fundamentally without arising or ceasing;

yet sentient beings perceive arising and perceive ceasing—this is not a perception of actual existence. This phrase points to the birth and death of sentient beings. "Therefore" means because deluded vision is not real.
"Is called revolving in birth and death" refers to the unity of good and evil causes, suffering and pleasure results, and the defiled and pure aspects of the environment and its inhabitants.
All of saṃsāra is collectively and exclusively the object of the mental consciousness; together they are the objects of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
There is only verbal expression and no actual reality whatsoever. This phrase demonstrates that birth and death are merely names. These mere names reveal the purity of false cause and effect.

The preceding [passage] fundamentally revealed the purity of the nature and characteristics of falsity; thus, the purity of nature, characteristics, cause, and effect is itself the purity of all things.
Purity. The preceding section on the fundamental emptiness of ignorance combined with the subsequent section manifesting purity is concluded.

The initial heading on severing delusion is joined to the category of that which is purified, concluding that section. The section demonstrating the original arising is connected to the category of the purity of original arising, concluding that section.
Second, regarding the Dharma-practice of the Ground, there are two parts: first, the heading of the practices to be cultivated.

"Good son, regarding the Tathāgata’s cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment while on the causal ground, there are two phrases that mark the practice to be cultivated: the phrase 'Good son' and the phrase 'The Tathāgata... [etc.]'."
Regarding "the Tathāgata’s stage of causes" (*yīndì*): this refers to his own dwelling within the causal stage prior to attaining Buddhahood.
"Cultivating *yúanjué*" (perfect enlightenment) means cultivating the *yúanjué* of one's own nature so as to achieve its equality, purity, and pervasive fulfillment;

there is no other dharma to be cultivated. Second, showing the capacity for cultivation, which is divided into two parts: first, penetrating delusion and illuminating enlightenment, which is further divided into two.

First, realizing that the root of delusion is empty opens two [subsections]. First, the purification of the deluded subject and object opens two [subsections]. First, the purification of the delusion grasped by the subject:
knowing it to be a flower in the sky, there is immediately no cyclic existence.

Regarding the two phrases on the "delusory purity of the grasped": the phrase "knowing this to be a flower in the sky" refers to the first [of these two], which realizes the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing;
the phrase "there is no cyclic existence" refers to the second, which distances oneself from delusory objects. Regarding the "delusory purity of the grasper": [the same applies].
Furthermore, there is neither body nor mind that undergoes birth and death therein.
When a single phrase of the text can grasp the purity of delusion, this is to remain far removed from the nature of conjunction, constantly illuminating for oneself that the aggregates are empty.

One should contemplate that there is nothing capable of grasping, and thus one is forever freed from the bonds of karma. This concludes the preceding section on the combined refutation of the delusive subject and object of purification.
Second, the delusive nature is empty.
They do not exist because they are uncreated; they do not exist because their fundamental nature is non-existent.

Regarding the two phrases in the text, "delusive [phenomena] are empty by their fundamental nature": one phrase is "because they are uncreated," and the other is "because their fundamental nature is non-existent.
The first phrase means that through the application of effortful practice, there are no delusive subjects or objects. The second phrase means that ignorance has no self-...
In the nature of phenomena, subject and object cannot be established; from the very beginning they are entirely pure, ultimately without arising or ceasing.

The preceding section on the "Purification of the Deluded Subject and Object" together with the "Section on Realizing that Delusion is Fundamentally Empty" is hereby concluded. Second, "Illuminating Awareness as Being Like Space," which opens into two parts:
first, "Illuminating the True Mark."
That which knows is like empty space. That which knows empty space is the appearance of flowers in the sky.
In this passage, two phrases illuminate the realization of the true mark (*dharmatā*): the phrase "that which knows" and so forth, and the phrase "knowing emptiness" and so forth.
"That which knows" refers to the knowing that arises from the self-mind’s thorough understanding by one who practices *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*. As for "awakening" (*bodhi*), it is...

"Intrinsic awareness is like empty space" means that the nature of awareness is pure, like the characteristic of empty space; this phrase refers to the characteristic of pervasive illumination-awareness.
"Like empty space" means to thoroughly comprehend the true reality (*dharmatā*). "That which is like a flower in the sky" means to dissolve all delusive appearances;
this phrase refers to the realization and entry into true reality. These two [phrases] illustrate the purity of the nature of illuminating awareness.
Nor can it be said that there is no nature of awareness;
rather, a single phrase from the text illuminates the pure nature of awakening.

Regarding the statement "nor can it be said, etc.," one who cultivates perfect awakening knows for themselves that within the unspeakable there is nothing, thereby further advancing toward enlightenment and manifesting the ultimate, pervasive purity.
The nature of universal, equal enlightenment is fulfilled. This concludes the section on "The Union with the Text Above Completes the Section on Illuminating Enlightenment as Being Like Space.

The preceding union with the section on "Reaching the Fundamental Emptiness of Delusion" is subsumed under the section on "Reaching Delusion and Illuminating Enlightenment," which is now concluded. Second, "Conforming to Enlightenment to Accomplish Practice" is divided into two parts.
First, "Conforming to Enlightenment to Pervade and Fulfill" is divided into two parts. First, "Dispelling Delusions to Conform to Enlightenment."
Discarding both existence and non-existence is what is called "conforming to pure awakening.
In this passage, two phrases discard delusion and accord with awakening, while the phrase "discarding both existence and non-existence" is as follows:
"Discarding both existence and non-existence" means to penetrate the reality-mark (dharmatā), which is pure, and not to cling to empty flowers or illusory reflections.

By dispelling existence, one attains the pervasive nature of ultimate purity and dwells in right awakening; by this, one dispels non-existence. This phrase describes the perfect clarity of nature and characteristics.
"Is this" (*shì cǐ*) means "this is it. It points back to the preceding expression of simultaneous dispensation, as if saying: "If it is this, then it is this; if it is not this, then it is not this.
This is intended to make known that only through the simultaneous dispensation of both can one achieve compliance with the truth.

"Awakening is called 'pure awakening that accords' (*anuloma*)": this means that when one realizes that the nature and characteristics [of phenomena] are quiescent and manifest before one, such that there is no non-awakening, it is called "pure awakening.
When a single awakening pervades everywhere and perfectly unites with all things as a non-dual, identical nature, it is called "accordant awakening.
This phrase refers to the accomplishment through cultivation; the second explanation clarifies how [cultivation] accomplishes accord.

Why is this? Because it is the nature of empty space; because it is eternally unmoving; because within the Tathāgatagarbha there is neither arising nor ceasing; because there is neither cognition nor vision;
and because, like the nature of the Dharma-realm, it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions.
The first six phrases of the text explain the sequence of refutation and establishment. Why? Because [it is] one phrase: "because of the nature of space"; one phrase:
"because it is eternally unmoving"; one phrase: "the Tathāgata... and so forth; one phrase: "because there is no cognition or vision"; and one phrase: "according to the Dharma... and so forth.
Regarding the first phrase, it poses a question because it necessarily involves the simultaneous refutation of both [extremes], thereby establishing the sequence of the discourse. Second.

Regarding the phrase "because the nature of the sentence is like empty space": this explains that awakening is the nature of the true mark (*dharmatā*), and because it is not something that exists as impure, that [existence] must be discarded.
Regarding the third phrase, "because it is eternally immovable": this explains that awakening abides in equality and is ever-present before one; therefore, [non-existence] must be discarded.
By combining these two phrases, the explanation shows that awakening is free from existence and non-existence; thus, [the notion of its] existence must be discarded.
Both [existence and non-existence] are simultaneously discarded. "Within the Tathāgatagarbha" refers to pure awakening. "Without arising or ceasing" means there is no false subject-object duality;

this phrase signifies purity of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). "Without knowledge or vision" means there is no deluded cognitive clarity; this phrase signifies purity of the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*).
Combining these two phrases explains why awakening is pure and detached from existence and non-existence. Therefore, it should be understood as follows:
The simultaneous negation of both existence and non-existence is what is called "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*).

"Like the nature of the *dharmadhātu*" means it manifests as empty space that encompasses all without exterior. "Ultimately perfect" means the nature of wisdom is perfectly integrated with all things.
"Pervading the ten directions" means that this single realm of awakening is neither one nor many. This phrase explains the constant abiding of awakening.
Because it is free from existence and non-existence, the simultaneous elimination of both existence and non-existence is what is termed "conformity.

This concludes the preceding section on the text, which together completes the section on "Conforming to Awakening and Pervasive Fulfillment. Second, the conclusion of the name and the establishment of practice.
This is what is called the practice of the Dharma on the ground of cultivation (*yindi fangxing*).
The single phrase "this is" (*shi ze*) serves to conclude the name and establish the practice. "This is" refers to the term "conforming to pure awakening" (*jingjue suishun*);
only when one can be named as conforming to pure awakening can one be named as practicing the Dharma on the ground of cultivation. This is because one receives the name...
Pure awakening accords with reality by simultaneously discarding both existence and non-existence;

this is the characteristic of perfect illumination and awakening, and because it forever severs ignorance, it is called the practice of the Dharma on the causal ground. Yet, there is that which achieves the Buddha-way.

These two sections correspond respectively to the preceding ones. They indicate that the Dharma-practice of the Tathāgata’s causal stage consists solely of pure awakening, which harmoniously encompasses all ultimate, wondrous expedients.

This concludes the section on “Harmonizing with Awakening and Fulfilling Practice,” which was combined with the preceding section on “Harmonizing with Pervasive Awakening. It is now joined with the section on “Reaching Delusion and Illuminating Awakening.”

The section on "Demonstrating the Ability to Practice" is concluded. The section on "Connecting the Designation of the Methods to be Practiced" is subsumed under the section on "Dharma Practices of the Ground of Causality.
The section on "The Original Arising of Purity" is integrated into the section on "The Tathāgata’s Practices of Causality. Thus, it is concluded.
Second, the Bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind.
Because of this, the Bodhisattva arouses the pure mind within the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the single phrase "the Bodhisattva arouses the mind" in the text: "because of this" means because of the ground of practice that accords with pure awakening.

The Practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*). The explanation of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) in the Mahāyāna follows the previous [section]. The preceding section on the causal practices of the Tathāgata, combined with the present section on the causal practices of instruction, completes the exposition of the causal practices.
Second, showing the benefits for the末代 (final age).
Sentient beings of the final age who practice according to this will not fall into false views.
The phrase "according to this" indicates the benefit for those in the final age. "According to" (*yi*) means "by means of" (*yin*).
It refers to practicing by taking the Tathāgata’s pure awakening and the rules of Dharma-practice as one's standard. "Will not fall into false views" is explained as before. This and...
The Bodhisattva’s initial resolve is identical in its ultimate aim to that of the Tathāgata’s causal practice.

Therefore, by posing questions regarding the Tathāgata’s causal practice, he intends to instruct and guide Bodhisattvas for the benefit of sentient beings in the final age, enabling them to skillfully cultivate and study the Mahāyāna so as to penetrate the cause and encompass the fruit.
For this reason, this serves as a pointer; it is now integrated with the preceding section on "Instruction and Guidance on Causal Practice" and included within the general prose narrative.
The section-by-section presentation is concluded. Second, the summary verse in stanzas, which is divided into two parts. First, the introduction expressing the desire to proclaim [the meaning] again:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Now, wishing to restate the meaning of a single phrase from the introduction, I shall further clarify its essential significance through specific terminology.
This is done for the benefit of those who will come after, so that they may easily understand it. Second, the exposition of the verses is divided into two parts.

First, summarizing the intent to show the teaching based on the causes [of practice], which is divided into two. First, summarizing the intent regarding the Tathāgata’s causal practices, which is divided into two. First, summarizing the intent regarding the fundamental [nature].
The second part, "Arisen Purity," consists of two sections. First, summarizing the essential intent to show the original source from which it arose:
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that all Tathāgatas, from their original ground of practice, have all awakened through wisdom."
Second, the summary of the essential point to demonstrate what is purified:
To thoroughly understand ignorance Is to know it as being like flowers in the sky; Thus one can escape the cycle of transmigration.
Furthermore, it is like a person in a dream: Upon waking, it cannot be found.
Second, summarizing the intent regarding the practice of the Dharma according to the ground, which is divided into two parts: 1. Summarizing the intent to show the dharma to be practiced:
The Awakened One is like space, Equal, unmoving, and unchanging.
2. Summarizing the intent to show the one who is able to practice.
Awakening throughout the realms of the ten directions, one immediately attains the Way of the Buddha;
yet when all illusions have ceased and there is no place for them, the attainment of the Way is likewise non-existent, for the fundamental nature is already perfect.
Thus, the Bodhisattva who grasps the essential meaning of these two [verses] awakens the aspiration for enlightenment.
Within this, the Bodhisattva is able to give rise to the bodhicitta;
these two points summarize the essential intent and show the benefits for the final age.
All sentient beings of the final age who practice this will escape erroneous views.
The verse section is concluded. The preceding combined prose section, which comprises the introductory narration and the sub-section on the World-Honored One’s gracious response, is finished.
The combined introductory narration and the sub-section on the Bodhisattva’s posing of questions, leading into the total section on wisdom and abandonment that reveals true purity, is now complete.

This is because the realization of the Buddha-way depends upon the permanent severance of ignorance, and the permanent severance of ignorance depends upon awakening to the characteristics [of reality].
This is the perfect illumination; there is no illumination that is not perfect, and thus there is no aspect of awakening that is not pure.
By eternally severing ignorance, one accomplishes the Buddha-way. This is called "wisdom and severance manifesting true purity.
It means that by severing delusion through wisdom, the true purity is manifested. Furthermore, the original text states: "The Tathāgata cultivated [this] during the stage of the causal ground..."

Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti) means that knowing these [phenomena] to be like flowers in the sky, there is no further transmigration. This indicates that simply by knowing this, one realizes the purity of the True [Nature].

Being free from defilement belongs to the cessation through primordial wisdom (*jñāna-prahāṇa*). However, where there is cessation through wisdom, there must also be cessation through practice (*caryā-prahāṇa*).

If the cessation through wisdom has not yet manifested, how could the cessation through practice be established? Therefore, this chapter’s topical outline is titled "Cessation through Wisdom Manifesting the Truth. It remains.

The four chapters following [the preceding] constitute the section on severing delusive practices, collectively forming the "Dharma-practice of the Ground" (in-ting fa-hsing) wherein wisdom and practice are pure through such severance.
*The Commentary on the Words of the Mahāvaipulya Bodhimaṇḍala-lakṣaṇa-viniścaya-sūtra*, Fascicle Upper, Part One.
Commentary on the Words of the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta Sūtra of Definitive Meaning, Fascicle One, Part Two of the Upper Volume.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhatoṭara of Kaśmīra;
composed by the Śramaṇa Hongli of Luofeng in China.
The Śramaṇa Hongzan of Shenzhou at Qinzhou compares the two practices and opens two sections on severing delusion and attaining purity.
First, opening two sections on departing from illusion and severing delusion. First, opening two sections on resolving doubts and departing from illusion.
First, the preface describing the Bodhisattva’s posing of the question, which opens four sections. First, the preface to the question following the sequence.
Thus, this introduction reveals that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra attained conforming awakening through the causal practices of the Tathāgata.

He observed with compassion that sentient beings are deluded by non-attachment to existence and are unable to simultaneously dispel both existence and non-existence; consequently, they fail to attain conforming awakening and have no means to practice it.

The Tathāgata’s causal practice involves raising questions for the purpose of seeking the benefits of the Buddha’s teaching, so that one may not be deluded and thus avoid clinging, knowing what is to be abandoned, and thereby bringing about the cultivation of awakening in accordance with reality. This introduction consists of two parts: the threefold inquiry and the twofold opening.
First, the introduction describing the ritual sounds, which is divided into two parts. First, the introduction concerning the inquiry into dignified demeanor:
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, from within the great assembly, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha.

The interpretation of the phrasing follows the previous [section]. Second, the description of requesting instruction for the benefit [of others] is divided into two parts. First, requesting instruction on that which is to be practiced is divided into two parts.
First, he correctly asks about transcending illusion:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas in this gathering and for all sentient beings of the future age who practice the Mahāyāna,
we pray that you will explain how they should cultivate when they hear of this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment."
The three phrases of the introduction correctly inquire about the departure from illusion. The phrase "The World-Honored One of Great Compassion" [is one sentence].

The phrase "I pray that you will... [is one sentence]. The phrase "Having heard this... [is one sentence]. These are explained by analogy with what precedes. Regarding the pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment: it is perfectly free from existence and non-existence;
it pervasively abides and sustains the ten directions, conforming to the nature of empty space, eternally unmoving and unshakable.

There is no cognition or vision regarding arising and ceasing. How does one practice? Please resolve this: by being perfectly free from existence and non-existence, one attains the cultivation that accords with reality.
This phrase directly asks about what is practiced. Second, by way of contrast, it reveals the departure from illusion and the opening of the two [aspects].
First, regarding the difficulty of opening the two through the cessation of illusion: first, the objection is set forth that they are identical to illusion.
"Bhagavān, if those sentient beings know that both body and mind are like an illusion, how can they use an illusion to further cultivate an illusion?
[The text here sets forth a threefold objection based on the nature of illusion: Bhagavān, one sentence; 'If those [beings]... and so forth, one sentence; 'How...'"

Regarding the phrase "What is it that... and so forth: "If those sentient beings" refers to the person who understands [all things] to be like an illusion; here, the character *zhě* (者) is synonymous with the character *rén* (人).
Thus, it means "the person who knows [them] to be like an illusion. "Like an illusion" points to the objects of perception (*ālambana*).

"Body and mind are also like an illusion" means that the body and mind of the person who knows the illusion are likewise mere reflections of sensory conditions, lacking any real nature. This sentence...
"Pointing to body and mind as being identical to illusion": "How so? is a phrase of inquiry. "By means of illusion" means taking the illusory body and mind as the nature of the practitioner;

"further cultivating that which is illusory" means distancing oneself from the delusive objects that are like illusions. This sentence reveals the doubt that one cannot leave illusion by means of illusion.
I humbly request the World-Honored One to reveal the method for leaving behind the illusory delusions of body and mind. Thus [he spoke].

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that you will, for the sake of this assembly of bodhisattvas and for all sentient beings of the final age..."
He expounds the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice: how one should contemplate and how one should maintain [the practice].
Regarding the text, there are five phrases for requesting contemplative cultivation: one phrase for "The World-Honored One of Great Compassion," one phrase for "I pray that you...
and so forth, one phrase for "expound... and so forth, one phrase for "how should one contemplate," and one phrase for "how should one maintain."
The Bodhisattva practitioner cultivates by departing from illusion. Regarding "gradual progression," this refers to the beginning and end of departing from illusion;

this phrase constitutes a general inquiry. As for "how does one contemplate? it means to discern the departure from illusion. For if one cannot attain that which is to be discerned, one will fail to realize that all is illusion, and thus be unable to depart from illusion.
This sentence follows the Buddha's instruction that "knowing illusion is itself departure"; the character "know" (知) gives rise to the question.
What is meant by "abiding and maintaining"? It refers to the characteristic of the pervasive nature of awakening (*bodhi*).
For if one does not clearly understand this characteristic of the pervasive nature of awakening, how can one know that when all illusions are extinguished, awakening is manifested and perfected?

This phrase follows the Buddha’s instruction that "leaving illusion is awakening," and thus the character for "awakening" (*jue*) is used to pose the question. Because there is the knowledge of "leaving," there is the awakening of "entering. This is the Buddha’s teaching of Bodhi.
Regarding that upon which the Bodhisattva relies for practice, sentient beings may have fears arising from ignorance; therefore, they further pose specific questions.
Second, they request instruction on cultivation:
"Sentient beings have not yet attained realization; by what skillful means can you cause them all to attain universal awakening?"

In this passage, a single sentence requests instruction on awakening through practice. For sentient beings who have not yet awakened, "not yet awakened" means that by departing from illusory conceptualization, they immediately abide in enlightenment.

Regarding the question of what skillful means should be employed, this is a request for teaching on how one should contemplate so that all may universally awaken and attain the sustaining power of abiding in that very enlightenment.
Together with the preceding section, this constitutes the request for instruction on the capacity for awakening.
The section on cultivation is concluded. Second, the skillful means for requesting further instruction is divided into two parts.

As previously stated regarding delusion and confusion: "World-Honored One, if those sentient beings lack correct skillful means and correct reflection, they will become confused and distressed upon hearing the Buddha, the Tathāgata, speak of this samādhi, and will thus be unable to awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment."
Regarding the four phrases of the preceding section on delusion: "The World-Honored One" constitutes one phrase; "If he... constitutes one phrase; "Hearing the Buddha... constitutes one phrase;
and "Immediately regarding... constitutes one phrase. One who lacks correct skillful means regarding this last phrase lacks the detachment that is free from illusion.
One who lacks correct contemplation loses the awakening that is free from illusion. This phrase describes the state prior to birth.

"Delusion": regarding this samādhi, it means that while the awakened mind is immovable, the mind gives rise to delusion and distress. "Delusion" refers to a cognition that does not transcend illusion;
"distress" refers to the obstruction of phenomena and principle. This phrase describes the delusion arising within saṃsāra. "Unable to awaken and enter" means... [the inability to realize].
The awakening mind does not achieve manifestation. This phrase describes the delusion that arises subsequently. As for why it is so, regarding the prior delusion:
because one desires to obtain the Buddha’s demonstration of the correct expedient means, one reflects upon and discriminates between false cognition and erroneous thought;

thus, one realizes that the nature of thought belongs to the realm of the delusory, and its essence and characteristics are not the pure, awakened true nature. To employ this for cultivation is like drilling wood [to produce fire].

Fire depends on wood, awaiting its emergence until the wood is exhausted. If one does not understand this principle and merely exhausts the wood, one will achieve results that are eternally separated from all illusions;
thus, to seek the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing through causes of arising and ceasing is impossible.
The Bodhisattva Universal Eye, deeply fearing that sentient beings might become confused and bewildered by this and thus lose the ability to cultivate skillful means, requested further instruction.
He then entreated for compassionate teaching, saying:
"I pray that you will arouse compassion and, for our sake and for the sake of sentient beings in the final age, provisionally explain the skillful means."

The first part consists of two phrases for requesting compassionate instruction: "I pray you arouse compassion" (one phrase) and "for my sake, etc. (one phrase). Regarding "I pray you arouse compassion":

because sentient beings have been deluded regarding awakening since the very origin of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, one now requests the Buddha to arouse kindness and exercise pity toward those deluded beings.
This phrase seeks pity from one who is deluded regarding awakening; it is a provisional expression of skillful means.

This means that one knows the nature of thought and mind is ultimately like wood being exhausted. Now, it is simply by means of this that one leaves behind illusion, just as fire is produced by means of wood;

yet one does not grasp the wood itself as the ultimate reality. Therefore, it is called a "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*). This sentence serves to request further instruction for the benefit of the teaching.

Together with the preceding section, the "Section on the Expedient Means of Requesting Instruction" is concluded. This was previously combined with the "Section on the Ability to Practice the Requested Teaching."

The section on "Summarizing the Request for Instruction" is concluded. This is joined with the preceding section on "Inquiring about Dignified Conduct," which concludes the subsection on "Describing the Sounds of Ritual Protocol.
Second, the conclusion of the introduction regarding the beginning and end.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.

The interpretation of the phrases follows the previous examples. The preceding sections—combining the Preface, the Description of the Ritual, the Sounds, and the Categories—complete the three categories of the "Preface and Questions."
The section on the General Introduction, which follows the sequence of the questions posed by the Bodhisattvas, is concluded.

Second, the section on the General Introduction describing the World-Honored One’s response, which is divided into two parts. First, the long list of names indicating the opening [of the teaching], which is further divided into two.
First, the introduction praising and granting permission for the request, which is divided into two. First, praising the teaching as being capable of cultivation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, you are truly able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the gradual stages of cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance."
Regarding the four lines of the first section, they praise the teaching as being capable of cultivation; these two lines apply generally to both [the teaching and the practice]. The line "You all...

refers to reflection, and the line "abiding and maintaining" refers to upholding. The remaining explanations follow the previous pattern. Second is the praise of the skillful means for benefiting others.

"Up to employing various provisional means"—even a single phrase of praise within the text serves as a skillful means for benefit. The term "up to" (*yāvat*) is an expression indicating that which follows in succession.

With the intention of requesting instruction, the fundamental purpose lies in attaining right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) and thereby attaining right abiding (*samyak-sthiti*). [This is said] fearing that sentient beings might be unable to open [to the truth].
Because they have awakened through right reflection yet lost their correct maintenance of the state, they further request the teaching on skillful means;

for this reason, such praise is added. Regarding "various skillful means," it refers to the teaching that the body and mind are illusory defilements, as well as the teaching on being free from all such illusory defilements, which is revealed in manifold ways.
This concludes the section on Praise and Request for Instruction and Benefit, together with the preceding textual divisions. Second, the Promise to Respond.
The entrustment and reception are divided into two parts: first, the entrustment to listen attentively:
"Now you must listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
The interpretation of the phrasing follows the previous examples. Second, the reception of the teaching through silence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) joyfully accepted the instruction, and the great assembly listened in silence.

The commentary on the phrases follows the previous examples. This concludes the section on the granting of permission and the acceptance of the entrustment, which was combined with the preceding section on the praise and request for instruction.
Furthermore, this concludes the first part of the introductory sequence, the section on praise and permission. Next, the formal response is presented in two parts.

First, the instruction on the ability to practice is divided into two parts. First, the accomplishment of practice is divided into two parts. First, the designation of the fruit and the seeking of enlightenment:
"Good son, those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect *bodhicitta*..."

The first two phrases indicate the fruit and the seeking of enlightenment. "Good son" constitutes one phrase. "That beginner... and so forth constitute one phrase, referring to a newly initiated bodhisattva.
Since the intent of the request for instruction lies in the question, "By what kind of contemplation can one attain correct maintenance?
this is the inquiry raised by a beginner bodhisattva. Therefore, these phrases are used to indicate that he wishes to seek the purity of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the Perfect Enlightenment Mind (*pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*): one seeks the awakening of the original nature and does not long for the realization of differentiated fruits.
Second, showing that the cause is free from illusion, which opens into two parts: first, the gradual stages of practice, which opens into two parts; first, practice free from illusion.
One should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions.

One should practice by departing from illusion even with a single phrase. Regarding "one should maintain right mindfulness": this means rectifying one's mindfulness so that it does not rely upon or lean toward the crooked.
The firm and steadfast holding of the mind to remain detached, as described in the preceding chapter, constitutes right mindfulness. This refers to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.
When the mind is darkened yet its function remains unified, one is able to prevent the mind from arising in accordance with objects and from shifting as things change;
thus, one flows into the "middle of the middle" and possesses right mindfulness. To be "far removed from all illusions" means that both illusory objects and the illusory mind are entirely abandoned.
Because this encompasses the beginning and end of the causal practice, it is designated as "cultivation. Second is the gradual sequence for leaving illusion.
First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, settles the assembly, and sits in meditative seclusion in a quiet chamber.
Regarding the three phrases of the text, these constitute the gradual stages for departing from illusion: first, the phrase "relying on... and so forth; second, the phrase "settling the assembly";
and third, the phrase "sitting in meditative seclusion. As for "first relying," this is the fundamental beginning of the practice. *Śamatha* is a Sanskrit term...
The word "yu" (語) here is translated as "zhi" (止), which is the initial designation for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It carries the meaning of "quiescence," for it is capable of rendering the various evils and afflictions of the three karmas into a state of stillness. Therefore, the subsequent text explains that "extreme quiescence is the practice.

This teaches that one should first rely on this practice and subsequently maintain the precepts to consolidate it. However, since there are distinctions of great and small, as well as false and correct, regarding concentration, the term "Tathāgata" is specified.

To distinguish this: if one does not rely on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to maintain the precepts, one cannot establish the expedient means for Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

Furthermore, it is precisely because these [precepts] can accomplish the precepts concomitant with concentration (*samādhi-sahagata-śīla*). One who firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts has no transgressions of body or speech;

this is to prioritize the mind and subsequently the body and speech, causing the three karmas to be simultaneously stilled so that one enters and abides in concentration. This phrase is free from the characteristic of movement.
The gradual sequence for settling the assembly: each is taught to remain in quietude and composure, not forming pairs and having no attachments;

this is the gradual sequence for abandoning the mark of others (*pudgala-nimitta*). The gradual sequence for sitting in meditation in a quiet room: one does not trouble oneself with busy activities, stays far from noisy markets, and allows the body to be relaxed and forgotten;
this is the gradual sequence for abandoning the mark of self (*ātman-nimitta*). In all cases, one brings the conditions of perception to rest.

By restraining the body, one attains the restraint of the mind; by removing the obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), one gradually subdues the obstacles of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*) and is able to distance oneself from all illusions.
Because this is that upon which one must first rely when cultivating the Bodhi of the Buddha, it is called "gradual succession.

This concludes the preceding section on the text, completing the section on the Gradual Succession of Practice. Second, regarding "Contemplation and Abiding," there are two parts: first, "Leaving Illusion."
Contemplation is divided into two. First, contemplation of the bodilessness [of the self] is divided into two. First, discerning the union and separation is divided into two.
First, scrutinizing the attachment to the composite:
one constantly forms this thought, "This body of mine now is a composite of the four great elements."

When one carefully examines and firmly grasps a single phrase, constantly maintaining this reflection, one should scrutinize and contemplate it with such thoroughness that there is never a moment of forgetfulness.

"This body of mine" refers to the characteristics of one's own person. "The combination of the four great elements" refers to the basis upon which the characteristics of one's own person are established.
As for why they are called "great," it is because earth, water, fire, and wind each pervade everywhere. As for "combination," it means...
If one's own body were to consist of the earth element alone without the water element, it would lack the principle of cohesion, like dry flour or ash.
If it were to consist of the water element alone without the earth element, it would lack solidity, like oil or water.

If it were to consist of only the earth and water elements without the fire element, it would rot and decay on its own, like a mass of flesh in a limb. If it were to consist of only the earth, water, and fire elements...
That which is the great wind-element should not increase and should remain unmoving; yet now it is not so.
Therefore, one perceives one's own body as having the characteristic of being a composite of those four great elements. However, this is merely a locus of attachment formed by the deluded body.
Now, in order to dismantle these attachments, we shall first proceed through a thorough examination. This examination consists of two parts, each concerning the distinct elements.
That is to say: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these forms of matter belong to the earth element.
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, feces, and urine—all these belong to the water element. As for the warmth...
Fire returns to fire; movement returns to wind. When the four great elements separate from one another, there are five phrases in the text:
four phrases for each element returning to its own source, and one phrase for the separation of the four great elements.
As for what is called "that which is": it refers to that which, upon careful examination of one's own body, has its own specific name and fixed designation.
Regarding the fact that hair, body hair, and so forth all belong to earth: because they all possess the characteristic of resistance (*sapratigha*), they cannot be assigned to any other element.
This phrase establishes the earth element as distinct. Regarding the fact that saliva, mucus, and so forth all belong to water: because they all possess... [the characteristic of cohesion].
The mobile aspect cannot be attributed to any other element; this phrase establishes the water element as distinct. As for the statement that warmth belongs to fire:
because the manifest appearance of heat cannot be attributed to any other element, this phrase establishes the fire element as distinct.
That which moves and turns returns to wind: this clarifies that the appearance of fluttering cannot be attributed to the other elements.

This phrase establishes wind as a distinct element. As for the statement that "the four great elements are each separate": since they originally return to their own nature, what appearance could there be of their combining? Therefore, they are fundamentally separate.
This phrase generally summarizes the preceding four points to clarify that because they are each separate, the characteristics of the present body do not exist [as a unified whole].

Regarding their combination: among them, the two great elements of water and fire are called "essence" and "warmth" because these two elements manifest in the forms of the two great elements through the presence of the two characteristics of moisture and warmth; thus, they constitute a finger. Furthermore, the essence within the human body has no fixed location;
it arises when the warmth of the hundred limbs is moistened by the smoke and touch of the male and female fires of desire. Thus, it exists.
The seminal essence emerges. This seminal essence originally belongs to the category of *vāyu* (wind/energy). Within the human body, warm energy pervades the entire frame;
where it encounters friction or touch, it manifests as a sensation of heat. Since this warmth also belongs to the category of *vāyu*, it is called "energy" (*vāyu*).

However, although energy is fundamentally a state of integration, one can still observe signs of non-integration. It is truly clear that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not exist in a state of integration.
Decision. The combined text of the preceding section on "Harmony" (he) and "Examination" (shi) concludes the section on "Harmony and Separation.
Second, penetrating the illusory nature has two parts: first, knowing that the locus is empty.
One should now consider: where does this deluded body reside? Thus one knows that this body ultimately has no substance.

When one understands through two phrases that the locus and substance are empty, then the phrase "now" (jin zhe) indicates that this very phrase "now" refers to the manifestation of the current false body. "Where would it be located? asks where it is established.
This phrase seeks the body and finds no location; its meaning is identical to the intent of the two preceding phrases, "I and this present body."
Examine this: you have long held that the manifest form of the present body is established upon the combination of the four great elements as its locus.
Now, since each of the four great elements has departed from its characteristics and there is no longer a state of combination, this manifest body becomes devoid of any established basis.
"To know immediately" means to know that there is no place of establishment. "This body is ultimately without substance":

if there were substance, there would necessarily be a place of establishment; since there is no such place, it is therefore without substance. "Ultimately without substance" is a term signifying that it is utterly non-existent.
This phrase of knowing reveals that the substance is empty; the second point clarifies that its characteristics are identical to an illusion.
That which is characterized by combination is in reality identical to an illusion or a transformation.

When one understands even a single phrase of the text, one realizes that these characteristics are identical to illusions. Regarding "that which is characterized by combination," this refers to the manifest physical forms.

Regarding "in reality identical to an illusion or a transformation," although they exist, they are non-existent; since there is no location where they abide, they have no essence. Since they lack essence, it is appropriate that they lack characteristics.
The present body has no form or characteristic within its substance or location. What kind of characteristic is this?

It is no different from the illusory and transformative characteristics of the world, which appear as real despite having no substance or location. This is the realization that such characteristics are false and empty, whereby one attains freedom from the deluded attachment to the view of a self-body and its illusory defilements.
Together with the preceding section of the text, this completes the section on "Thoroughly Penetrating Illusory Phenomena."
The preceding section on "Contemplating the Absence of Body," which combined the truths and examined their synthesis and classification, is concluded.
Second, "Contemplating the Absence of Mind" is divided into two parts: first, examining the characteristics of the mind's objects.

The four conditions combine provisionally to give rise to the illusory existence of the six sense organs. The six organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally to produce an illusory vital energy that accumulates therein;
this resembles the appearance of a causal object and is metaphorically named "mind."

The text is divided into three sections for examination: the conditions of the mind’s object, the four conditions (one sentence), the six sense organs (one sentence), and that which appears as existence (one sentence).

Regarding the four conditions: the karmic consciousness proceeds toward rebirth, and through the flow of parental affection, it takes the four elements and the essence of blood as its causal condition to receive the mental conception and establish its own physical form. As for "provisional conjunction," it refers to the present manifestation of the four elements.
Each part, being separated from the aggregate of its constituent elements, is in reality identical to a magical illusion.

That which falsely exists as the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*)—since the organs are established based on the body and the conditions for the body are provisional—the characteristics of the organs lack true reality. This phrase examines the conditions for the arising of the organs.

Regarding the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*) of the six organs, this refers to both the ultimate sense organs (*paramārtha-indriya*) and the physical sense organs (*viṣaya-indriya*). As for the "intermediate," the ultimate sense organs refer to light and darkness.

The seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that arise from the delusive objects of motion and stillness while abiding in the midst [of the body]—as for the "external," these are the physical sense organs (*bu-chén gēn*), which are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) appearing like clusters of grapes or newly curled leaves.

As for their "synthesis," there are the physical sense organs composed of the four great elements, together with the transcendental sense organs (*shèng-yì gēn*) that reflect sound and reflect form. Through the mutual dependence of the internal and external, they flow outward and grasp at sensory objects.
Regarding those who possess the characteristics and functions of the six sense organs and falsely have the breath of conditions:
these are the dust-like reflections inhaled from within and without the gates of the senses, and the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that are stirred up.

That which accumulates therein—the consciousness that grasps the dust-reflections and cognitive perceptions of the sense-gates to establish the faculty of mental deliberation—is located within the hollow space of the physical mass of the body and within the five gates of the senses.

Regarding the conditions for the arising of discerning consciousness: that which appears to have the characteristics of an object-condition is the accumulated mental faculty (*manas*). From this, the discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises.

The mental faculty belongs to the category of the subjective perceiver; however, these objective conditions are fundamentally established through the gathering of the shadows and vapors of the sensory objects at the gateway of the root-faculties.
They are illusory transformations of a common nature and are not substantially real, but merely appear to exist. This is provisional.
That which is called "mind" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) that takes objects as its focus; it is what deluded sentiments falsely identify as the nature of the mind.
Since it exists only in a semblance, even its name is merely a provisional designation; not a single thing therein is real. It belongs entirely to false conditions.

This phrase points to the fundamental root-consciousness taking objective phenomena as its object, thereby revealing the emptiness and falsity of such objects. Second, resolving that the mind is without marks.
Good son, this deluded mind cannot exist without the six sense objects. When the four great elements are analyzed and dispersed, no sense objects can be found.
Within them, the conditions for the objects each return to their own place and dissolve; ultimately, no perceiving mind can be observed.
The five phrases of the main text resolve that there is no characteristic (*animitta*). "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "this emptiness... constitutes one phrase;
"the four great elements... constitutes one phrase; "within this... constitutes one phrase; and "ultimately... constitutes one phrase.

This "false and delusive mind" refers to the provisional designation of the sense-faculties, consciousnesses, and mind as if they were existent. If the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) do not exist, then [it] does not [exist].
Regarding that which "is able to have": the discernment of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the entirety of the perceived object as its condition.
