When there is no external dust (object) to trigger cognition, the illusory conditioning-vapor accumulated therein cannot produce a semblance of a condition; thus, one establishes the provisional name "mind."

This phrase elucidates that there is neither object nor mind. Regarding the "analysis of the four great elements": in their present state they are separated, and fundamentally there was no combination.
As for "no object can be obtained": if the combination of the four great elements does not exist, then there is no faculty capable of grasping;
how, then, could there be an object to be grasped? This phrase deduces that there is neither subject nor object. Within this, [it concerns] conditions...

"Dust" refers to the conditioning energies that accumulate therein. "Each returning to dispersal and extinction" means that while the conditions of dust originally deluded the faculties and the great elements were greedily grasped as falsely existent, now, through thorough and profound understanding, there is no faculty to grasp dust and no accumulation.
Returning to their source, each reverts to its origin, achieving dispersal and extinction. This phrase elucidates that there is nothing and no dust; ultimately, they do not exist at all.
Regarding the "object-condition mind that can be seen": this is a provisional designation established based on the appearance of what seems to exist.

Apart from the appearance of the object-condition that seems to exist, no separate object-condition mind can be found; therefore, it is said to be ultimately non-existent. This phrase decisively clarifies that there is neither object nor mind.
Together with the preceding section, this completes the "Contemplation of the Non-existence of Mind" chapter. The previous synthesis of contemplations is now concluded.

The section on the "Absence of Body" (amūrti-kāya), which concludes the section on "Contemplation Beyond Illusion" (māyā-vikalpa-vyatikrama), is finished. Second, the section on "Abiding Beyond Illusion" (māyā-vihāra) is divided into two parts.
First, demonstrating that there is no extinction in extinction:

"Good son, because the illusory body (*māyā-deha*) of those sentient beings is extinguished, the illusory mind (*māyā-citta*) is also extinguished; because the illusory mind is extinguished, the illusory..."
The dust also ceases. Because the illusory dust ceases, the cessation of the illusion also ceases. Because the cessation of the illusion ceases, that which is not an illusion does not cease.
In this passage, five phrases demonstrate cessation: "O son of good family, there is no cessation" constitutes one phrase; "as for those various [phenomena]" constitutes another phrase.
"An illusory mind," and so forth—this constitutes one phrase. "Illusory objects," and so forth—this constitutes one phrase. "The cessation of illusion," and so forth—this constitutes one phrase.
"Those sentient beings" refers to sentient beings who contemplate the absence of the characteristics of body and mind. "Because the illusory body has ceased" means:

"Immediately, as each of the four great elements is seen to be separate, one knows that the body has no substance; the illusory mind also ceases" means that as conditions and objects disperse and perish, there is no mind to be perceived.
This phrase indicates that the illusory mind, which acts as the subject of cognition, has no basis upon which to rely. "The illusory objects also cease" means that no objects can be apprehended.
This phrase indicates that the illusory forms, which serve as the objects of cognition, are the single path to Nirvana. "The cessation of the illusion" also... [is likewise].
"Cessation" means the destruction of the delusions of ignorance; this phrase indicates that both subject and object are like flowers in the sky, attaining neither arising nor ceasing.
"That which is not illusory does not cease" refers to the sustaining power of the true mark (*dharmatā*); this phrase indicates that the unmoving awakened mind is pure and present before one.

Within these phrases, there are four instances of the character *gu* (hence), all of which belong to tracing back to the source. Three instances of the character *yi* (also) and one instance of the character *bu* (not) all belong to the causal conditions. This is based upon the following:
The cessation that attains this cessation is fundamentally this cessation; it is not that this [cessation] attains non-cessation.

As for the cessation that attains the cessation of the mind, objects, and illusions within the body and mind: sentient beings have a central consciousness residing within the body. Objects arise because of the mind.
That which was established as illumination has vanished. Because the original marks were caused by delusion, one now attains understanding through the causal relationship of those marks.

It is not that illusion does not cease; rather, it is through the cessation of illusion that one attains its cessation. At the very beginning, there was non-awakening, a delusion regarding the True, whereby that which is non-illusion became the ignorance of illusion.
This ignorance of illusion is, in its essence, not illusion. These two metaphors—cessation and non-cessation—open up two aspects. The first metaphor clarifies this.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, its brilliance appears.

A single phrase from the text serves as an analogy to clarify this: "polishing" is a metaphor for being free from illusion; the "mirror" is a metaphor for Perfect Enlightenment (*vimalā-jñāna*); "the exhaustion of grime" is a metaphor for the cessation of all illusions;

and "the appearance of brilliance" is a metaphor for that which is non-illusory and thus does not cease. This is because the Great Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of one's own nature constantly illumines the Dharma-realm.

Hidden within the dust, yet not lost within the dust; thus, the illusory extinction is non-extinction—this is the meaning of the mirror’s luminosity appearing when the grime has been completely polished away.
This is the second combined clarification.
"Good son, you should know that both body and mind are illusory grime. When the characteristics of this grime are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure."
The three phrases should be explained together. "Good son" constitutes one phrase. "One should know... and so forth constitutes one phrase. "The marks of defilement...

and so forth constitutes one phrase. Regarding "one should know": it should be understood through the analogy of polishing a mirror to remove grime; one must recognize what constitutes the grime and then polish it away.
That both body and mind are illusory defilements means that obscured emptiness and darkened forms are intermingled with various delusive thoughts.

There is the characteristic of body and mind; this phrase indicates knowing the impurities upon which one grinds. "The characteristics of impurity are eternally extinguished" means that the characteristics of body and mind are extinguished, severing the root of ignorance.
"The ten directions are pure" means that the true reality (*dharmatā*) is revealed and maintained in equality.

This sentence demonstrates the knowledge of the luminosity that manifests. For if one does not recognize that the body and mind are defiled appearances, one will not know where to exhaust the polishing away of the mirror’s grime so that its luminosity may manifest.

It is impossible for the mirror’s luminosity to manifest if the grime has not been fully polished away. This concludes the preceding section on the analogy of extinguishing what is already extinguished.
The preceding synthesis of the "Manifesting Extinction as Non-extinction" section concludes its inclusion within the "Departing from Illusory Abiding" section.

The combined synthesis of the "Contemplating Departure from Illusion" section concludes its governance under the "Contemplating Abiding" section. The subsequent synthesis of the "Gradual Stages of Practice" section is encompassed within the "Manifesting Causes:
Departing from Illusion" section. The comprehensive synthesis of the "Designating the Result: Seeking Enlightenment" section is unified within the "Accomplishing Practice."
The topical outline is concluded. In response to the request, the principles for the bodhisattva’s gradual cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance are explained.

This section on the two skillful means for awakening is divided into two parts. First, the skillful means for departing from illusion is divided into two parts. First, showing [the nature of] illusion so that it may be known is divided into two parts.
First, reprimanding the ignorant and deluded regarding illusion is divided into two parts. First, identifying and clarifying the ignorant and deluded is divided into two parts. First, the analogy.
This reveals two points. First, it illustrates the fundamentally pure awakening:
"Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects the five colors, appearing differently according to the direction."
The first two phrases of the passage illustrate the metaphor of the originally pure awakening. The phrase "Good son" [is the address]. The phrase "For example... [introduces the analogy].
Taking the self-characteristic of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel as a metaphor for the characteristic of awakening: *maṇi* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "free from defilement.

Taking the self-nature of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel as a metaphor for the nature of awakening. Taking the circular function of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel—its reflecting colors according to their presence—as a metaphor for the function of awakening.
The five colors serve as a metaphor for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the various directions serve as a metaphor for the ten directions.

The intended meaning of this analogy is that because the pearl is fundamentally one and pure, it reflects and manifests accordingly; one should perceive the purity of the pearl within those reflections and manifestations.
These two metaphors illustrate the deluded attachment to existence.
That deluded person sees those *maṇi* jewels as truly possessing five colors.
This single phrase serves as a metaphor for the deluded attachment to existence. Because the *maṇi* is pure, it reflects colors; how could there truly be color?
To perceive them as truly existent is due to ignorance (*moha*). The term "that person" is a word used to distinguish [them] from those possessed of wisdom. This is because...
That the pearl has no five colors is something everyone understands; yet, deluded views perceive it as truly having them, and the masses of the ignorant believe this to be so.

Therefore, it is used as a metaphor for the lowest degree of ignorance. This concludes the section on the combined application of the text to the preceding categories, which together form the "Section on Manifesting through Metaphor.
Next, the combined explanation is divided into two parts: first, the combined metaphor that manifests awakening.
"Good son, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind.
This passage consists of two phrases that employ metaphors to reveal enlightenment: 'Good son' constitutes one phrase, and 'perfect enlightenment... constitutes the other."
The pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment is like a pure maṇi jewel. It manifests within the body and mind, merging with and reflecting the five colors;
it responds to each category according to its kind, merging with and appearing in each direction according to its place.
The intent of these "mergings" is to reveal that, as vast as the Dharma-realm, there is only this single pure awakening and no other thing. Second, the metaphor of merging resolves delusion.
That deluded person claims that the pure, perfect *bodhi* truly possesses such physical and mental self-characteristics; this is likewise the case here.
To resolve the confusion using the analogy, there are two phrases in the text: "that deluded one... and so forth, and "likewise... and so forth.
Since *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* manifests as body and mind because its nature is intrinsically pure, how could there truly be a body and mind? It is only through delusion that they claim it truly exists.
All belong to ignorance (*moha*). This phrase precisely reveals delusion. "It is also like this" refers to the ignorance of seeing the jewel as having color;
this phrase applies the analogy to ignorance. The application of the text and the preceding section together complete the "Section on Applying the Explanation.
The preceding "Section on Applying the Analogy to Reveal" is subsumed under the "Section on Marking and Revealing Delusion," which is now complete. Second, the Manifestation of Losses.
"Devoid of illusion.
Because of this, one cannot distance oneself from illusory transformations.

A single phrase from the text clarifies the failure to be devoid of illusion: "Because of this" means because of asserting that the body and mind possess real intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Failing to realize that [the world] is an illusion, one does not perceive the absence of bodily marks or mental marks, and thus fails to become detached from illusion.

The preceding section, which combined the headings for "Exposing the Delusion" and "Reproaching the Foolish and Deluded," concludes the section on "Reproaching the Foolish and Deluded regarding Illusion. Second, the explanation of "Illusion, Awakening, and Delusion."
Therefore, I speak of the illusory defilements of body and mind.
To explain "illusory awakening and delusion" according to each phrase of the text: "therefore" means because of this ignorance that cannot leave illusion behind.
When I say "illusory defilements of body and mind," I am refuting that delusion by teaching that body and mind do not truly exist, thereby causing [the listener] to realize this.

By knowing illusion, one attains liberation. The preceding section on "Charging the Foolish and Deluded with Illusion" together with the section on "Demonstrating How to Know Illusion" is hereby concluded.

Second, the conclusion that reveals the skillful means, which is divided into two parts: first, the actual revelation of the skillful means; second, [the subsequent exposition]. First, the actual revelation of the skillful means:
One who is free from the defilement of illusion is called a bodhisattva.
The single phrase in the text correctly reveals the skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding "one who is free from the defilement of illusion":

within the body and mind that possess the defilement of illusion, there is a purity that is free from illusion. Regarding "is called a bodhisattva": this refers to those assemblies who are pure and free from illusion.
One who does not share that delusion which asserts that body and mind are substantially real is called a Bodhisattva.

This is because within the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), there is only the single fruition of the Buddha, and no such designations as "sentient beings" or "Bodhisattvas.
Now, those who are deluded by illusory existence are termed "sentient beings," while those who have departed from the defilements of illusion are termed "Bodhisattvas."

This causes those deluded sentient beings to look up in admiration and abandon the name "delusion," while the Bodhisattva, through the single path of shared transcendence, attains that which is the very abandonment of delusion—namely, awakening.
Therefore, "Bodhisattva" is a designation for skillful means (upāya). Second, this serves as a counter-illustration of skillful means.
When defilements are exhausted and oppositions are eliminated, there is neither opposition nor that which is called "defilement.
These two phrases in the text serve as a reverse illustration of the skillful means. "Defilements are exhausted" refers to the quiescence of body and mind.
"Oppositions are eliminated" refers to the absence of sentient beings who are opposed to the Bodhisattva. This...
The first phrase indicates that there are no sentient beings; that is, there is no one who opposes defilement, and there is no one who departs from illusion by opposing delusive illusions.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of "names," there is no Bodhisattva who is to depart from illusion. This phrase demonstrates the non-existence of Bodhisattvas.

The two phrases together reveal that there is only the single, fundamental Buddha-enlightenment, in which the pure nature is perfectly manifest. This sufficiently shows that the designation "Bodhisattva" is established only as a provisional means.
This is the explanation of that. Therefore, it is said to be "revealed by contrast. This concludes the section on the combined text forming the conclusion of the "Expedient Means" (upāya) section.

The preceding combined demonstration of "Causing Knowledge of Illusion" is subsumed under the "Expedient Means for Leaving Illusion" section, which is now concluded. Second, the "Leaving Illusion and Opening Enlightenment," which has two parts:
first, opening enlightenment through the realization of cessation (nirodha).
Good son, because this bodhisattva and sentient beings of the final age have realized that all illusions are but the extinction of reflected images,
they then attain the manifestation of boundless, directionless, and pure space through their awakening.
The three phrases of the text serve as proof of the realization of cessation and awakening: "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "this Bodhisattva... constitutes one phrase;
and "at that time... constitutes one phrase. "This Bodhisattva" refers to the Bodhisattva Free from Defiled Illusion;
"sentient beings of the final age" refers to sentient beings who practice the removal of illusion; and "realization" refers to truly being free from illusion and dreams.
"At the time when awakening removes the obscuration," "the various illusory images are extinguished": the mind and its objects are illusory, like a person in a dream or flowers in the sky.
That all these are extinguished is merely the extinction of images; there is no extinction of a substantial nature.

The word "hence" (*gù*) is a term used to trace back to the origin, meaning that one attains awakening and manifestation precisely by realizing the extinction of illusions. This applies to the interpretation of the character *gù* throughout the entire passage. This sentence provides the proof.
"Extinction. "At that time" refers to the moment of realizing the extinction of illusion. "Attains immediately" means to obtain it at once.
"Pure and without direction" means being free from all delusive appearances. "Boundless space" reveals the true mark (*dharmatā*).
"That which is revealed by awakening" means knowing the fundamental self-awakening of the pure space. This phrase indicates that through the revelation of awakening, one penetrates reality.

One awakens to the realization of one's own fundamental nature, which is as pure as a mirror that has been opened to clarity. It is like the precious light within a mirror in empty space; awakening is like a precious mirror.
Yet, unless the defilements are polished away until they are exhausted, its luminous manifestation cannot occur. Therefore, it is attained through the realization of the extinction of illusions.
First, it speaks of "purity" (viśuddhi) to manifest awakening; next, it speaks of "empty space" (ākāśa) to manifest the emergence of awakening.
Fundamental purity and empty space are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of awakening, while awakening is the nature (*svabhāva*) of fundamental purity and empty space.
Since no characteristic can arise without a nature, one thereby knows that there is an awakening from which they proceed. Second, this reveals the opening of awakening.
Opening into two [sections]. First, opening into two regarding the perfect luminosity of awakening. First, opening into two regarding the true mark (*dharmatā*) of perfect luminosity.

First, opening into two regarding the suchness of defilement and purity. First, opening into two regarding the defilement and purity of ordinary phenomena. First, opening into two by enumerating the sequence of the causes of purity.
First, opening into two regarding the sequence of the causes capable of purifying. First, the purification of the mind-king (*cittarāja*).
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the purity of the mind is revealed.
In this passage, the phrase "the mind-king is pure" means that because awakening is perfectly luminous, one penetrates the true reality (*tathatā*) as a single, manifest awakening;
there are no two awakenings established as the locus for the clarity of various deluded cognitions. "Revealing the purity of the mind" refers to the state while still in delusion.

The mental characteristics grasped during the waking state are fundamentally illusory defilements. Now, with the single awakening of perfect luminosity, there are no longer two mental characteristics;
one clearly knows that the nature of consciousness illuminates the capacity produced by conditions.

There is only the true consciousness of awakened luminosity, which remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging—this is what constitutes purity. This manifestation of the pure mind is precisely the subduing and severing of the root.
Ignorance [is the obscuration of] the eight consciousnesses, the mind-kings, which are originally submerged within profound clarity.
When the two mental associates are purified, because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure; because the perceptions are pure, the eye-faculty is pure;
because the faculty is pure, the eye-consciousness is pure; because the consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure; and because the hearing is pure, the ear-faculty is pure.
Because the faculties are pure, auditory consciousness is pure; because consciousness is pure, the perception of objects is pure.
In this same way, it is likewise for the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
In the ninth section of the text, there are nine phrases concerning the purity of the mind:

one phrase on the purity of the mind (*citta-viśuddhi*), one phrase on the purity of vision (*darśana-viśuddhi*), one phrase on the purity of the faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi*), one phrase on the purity of consciousness (*vijñāna-viśuddhi*), one phrase on the purity of hearing (*śruta-viśuddhi*), one phrase on the purity of the faculties, and one phrase on the purity of consciousness. Thus, each pair of characters constitutes a single phrase. Now...
Regarding the phrase "the clouds disperse," when one sees that the dust is purified, it means that the visual faculty’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) simultaneously becomes clear and lucid;

this arises from detaching from clinging to objects. Now, because the mind is pure, one detaches from clinging and settles into stillness, whereby the fundamental luminosity of the nature is revealed.

This dispels the darkness of ignorance and the appearances of forms produced by the seeing-faculty. This is identical to the essence of the seeing-essence being limpid and primordial; it is the root of the seeing-faculty becoming pure.

Regarding "purity": there is the essential nature of the faculty of seeing abiding within. When this essence encounters the floating dust of the grape-cluster [the physical eye], it flows outward and chases after forms, forming the root and its deluded functioning.
Since the seeing has already been described as being "sticky," the pure essence remains latent within;
who else could then bind form to defile it? Therefore, it is identical to purity. This phrase means that the root is completely uprooted from its stickiness; it is the purity of the root.

Regarding the purity of visual consciousness: when seeing does not transcend the physical faculty and the faculty does not return to its source, consciousness follows the faculty and clings to objects to establish delusion.

When the faculty does not encounter the object and consciousness remains in profound non-discrimination, this is called knowing through consciousness that accords with the nature; this is what constitutes purity.

This phrase describes the perfect transcendence of the function of consciousness. Regarding "the purity of the auditory object (śrotaviṣaya) resulting from the purity of consciousness," this refers back to the purity of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Since the primary sovereign [consciousness] and the secondary derivative mental factors (*caitta*) are one, there is the illusory reflection of visual consciousness;
it is upon this that the illusory designation of the "auditory object" is established. If the reflection and the illusory consciousness are merged in darkness, [then...]

Why is it called "illusion"? Because it manifests [as such], it is identical with purity. Regarding the sequence of the meanings of "objects," "faculties," and "consciousness" as causes for purity, the three phrases are explained by analogy with what precedes.

As for the awakening to the purity of consciousness which renders objects pure: this refers to the perception that the nose, tongue, body, and mind all arise from the cause of the purity of consciousness;
subsequently, they are purified. This reveals that the delusions of consciousness alone constitute the illusory defilements of body and mind.
Because consciousness is pure and free from delusion, there is nothing that is not pure; this phrase cites purity as an example.
"In this manner" refers to the sequential purity of the three factors—the clarity and brilliance within seeing and hearing, the floating sense organs, and their cognitive discernment.
This phrase manifests purity through illustration. "Up to and including" means from the ear to the nose, from the nose to the tongue, and from the tongue to the body.

The body [is listed first] because it employs the most comprehensive terminology. This is because while the ear and nose both hear, the ear-consciousness is pervasive and detached, whereas the nose-consciousness is constant and immediate;

its function is not as extensive, yet even when detached from its function, it has no fixed location. Since the former is more extensive and the latter is more restricted, the nose-consciousness follows the ear-consciousness.
If it is the tongue, it always follows the nose; first distinguishing odors and subsequently taking in flavors, the tongue-consciousness therefore follows the nose-consciousness.
As for the body, because it experiences the sensations of hunger and satiety upon taking in flavors with the tongue, the body-consciousness follows the tongue-consciousness.

As for the mind, because it gathers the five sense faculties to establish a unified whole belonging to the bodily aggregate, the mental consciousness follows the body-consciousness. Although these belong to the category of manifest consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), they are nonetheless causes.
The seed-consciousness, through the sequence of causes produced by the perfuming of actualized states (*samudācāra*) without differentiation,
thus possesses the causal sequence from the ear-consciousness to the nose-consciousness, and even to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). By using the term "up to" (*yāvat*),
it is implied that the same applies to all within the nose, tongue, body, and mind— the clarity and brilliance of the sensitive faculties (*prasāda-indriya*) and their respective discernments.

Regarding the sequence of purification following seeing and hearing, there is nothing further to be manifested; within the body of deluded consciousness, there is only the single, pure, awakened, perfect, and luminous nature.

This phrase entirely exemplifies purification. Taken together with the nine phrases of the preceding text, they collectively constitute the causal sequence of that which is capable of purifying, all entering at once into the single, non-delusory sixth faculty of cognition (*ṣaṣṭha-āyatana*), which is purified in a single moment. Thus, combined with the preceding section, this completes the causal sequence of the purifier.
The section is concluded. Second, regarding the causes for purification, there are two parts. First, the purity of the objects of the senses (*viṣaya-rūpa*):
"Good son, because the faculties (*indriya*) are pure, the objects of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) are pure; because the objects of form are pure, the objects of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) are pure.
It is likewise for the objects of odor, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharma*)."

Regarding the four phrases of the text: "The objects of the senses are pure" constitutes one phrase; "The faculties are pure," and so forth, constitutes one phrase; "The forms are pure," and so forth, constitutes one phrase;
and "Fragrance and taste," and so forth, constitutes one phrase. As for the purity of the objects of the senses when the faculties are pure:

the six objects infect the faculties and give rise to consciousness. While the fundamental function of consciousness is universal, it establishes distinctions based on the faculties. To uproot [this infection]...
When the faculties (*indriya*) are pure, there is no separate consciousness established to absorb the defilement of sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

Since objects are neither bound nor liberated and are of the same source as the faculties, they are purified accordingly. Therefore, although previously one followed from the faculties to the consciousness, the reason for now not tracing back through the consciousness but rather tracing back to the faculties is significant. This phrase indicates that the characteristics of the objects are perfectly quiescent.
Regarding "the purity of form and the purity of sound-objects": since there are no characteristics of form whatsoever, from where could sounds arise?
This phrase first indicates the cause for the arising of form and sound, and subsequently shows the cause for their purity. "The same applies to fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena" means:
if it were not for the breath within the sphere of wind and sound, who would proclaim them? Apart from the breath that serves as the basis and condition, what would there be to perceive?

Being tranquil and detached, one has no attachment to flavors; what then clarifies the union and separation? If one were to merge with union and separation in darkness, who would be there to distinguish them?

This phrase illustrates the characteristic of arising through mutual dependence, which is fundamentally pure. That which is called "purity" means that each manifests the reality-mark (dharmatā) as equal and immovable.
There is no other than this detachment from the suchness of self-nature. As for why all six are called "objects" (*viṣaya*): [it is because they are the objects of the senses].
Because they possess the constituent parts of marks, the two great forms are pure.
Good son, because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure.
The fire element and the wind element are likewise.

Regarding the four phrases of the text, the first phrase concerns the purity of the great forms (*mahā-rūpa*). "Good son" constitutes one phrase. "The six sense objects," and so forth, constitutes one phrase.
"One phrase: 'The earth is pure,' etc. One phrase: 'The fire element,' etc. Regarding "the ground of the purity of the six sense-objects is the great purity":
the six sense-objects are collectively material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) that share the same source as the earth element; therefore, they follow in sequence with the aspect of purity.

This phrase has neither a separate nor a collective meaning. As for the earth element and the water element: earth and water are identical in their objective aspect (*dṛśya-bhāga*) and also in their subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
The earth element (pṛthivī-mahābhūta) of the individual is formed from the coagulation of the semen and blood of the parents;

the earth element of the world-system is established by water blown forth by the Anabilo wind. Therefore, the purity of the earth element is the purity of the water element. This statement is neither non-existent nor ineffective.
Following the water element is the fire element (tejo-mahābhūta); both the sentient realm and the insentient vessel-world of water possess the nature of transformation through fire.
From intense heat, moisture emerges. Following the element of fire is the element of wind. Fire and wind share similar characteristics:

within the realms of sentient beings and their physical environment (*bhājana-loka*), fire is the aspect of illumination arising from ignorance, while wind is the aspect of movement arising from ignorance.
That illumination emerges from movement; it is likewise so. Each category follows its own kind, and each returns to its own purity; this constitutes the sequence of causes. This...

Phrases have no intrinsic nature and no marks or functions. The pure explanation follows the previous section on the six sense objects. The reason the four are each called "great" is that they each pervade everywhere.
This concludes the second section, which combines the preceding and following parts to establish the causes for what is purified. The preceding section combined the causes that purify;
this section subsumes them under the enumeration of the sequence of the causes of purification. Second, a general manifestation of the causes of purification.
Good son, because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence are pure.
In this passage, two phrases collectively reveal the cause of purity: "Good son" constitutes one phrase, and "the four great elements... constitutes the other phrase.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The four great elements are pure," etc.: all phenomena within the realms and locations of the sentient and insentient worlds are manifested based upon the four great elements.

When these four great elements return to their source, they are as pure as space. Thus, the locations of the faculties and objects—the twelve bases of faculties and objects, the eighteen realms of faculties, objects, and consciousness;
the four continents, the four evil destinies, the Brahma kings, the six heavens of desire, and the five pure abodes of the non-conceptual—heaven—all become pure.
Residing within the four *ārūpyas* and the four *dhyānas*, there are twenty-five states that are not pure.

The preceding section, combined with the subsequent "Classification of the Causes of Purity" (*śuddhi-hetu-varga*), completes the "General Section on the Defilement and Purity of Mundane Dharmas. As for the subsequent "Classification of the Capabilities of the Cause," which generally manifests the causes based upon this section:
because it is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the fundamental capacity to give rise [to purity], when one thing is purified, all things are capable of being purified.
Purity shall be manifested in its totality. The specific characteristics of that which is able to emerge and establish what is to be established must first be shown;

once the capacity for purification is established, all that is to be purified shall be enumerated in sequence. Furthermore, if one necessarily enumerates both in their entirety, failing to list them in sequence, one does not see the ultimate purity of the capacity [to purify];
and if they are not manifested in their totality, one does not know the simultaneous purity of that which is to be purified.
Therefore, the defilements of both subject and object are here collectively enumerated.

Second, because the pure dharmas of the Sage are pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure; likewise, even up to the eighty-four thousand doors of *dhāraṇī* are pure.
All is pure. Regarding the two phrases "the noble dharmas are purified," there is one phrase beginning with "that purity... and another phrase beginning with "...thus...

As for the phrase "because of that purity," it refers generally to the defilement and purification of all mundane phenomena. As for the "ten powers": the first is the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible.

1. The power of the knowledge of what is possible and impossible; 2. the power of the knowledge of karma; 3. the power of meditative concentration; 4. the power of the faculties; 5. the power of aspirations;

6. the power of dispositions; 7. the power of the path leading to various destinations; 8. the power of recollecting past lives; 9. the power of the divine eye; and 10. the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
These constitute the Buddha’s attainment of the wisdom of reality as it is, which thoroughly penetrates all things and cannot be destroyed or surpassed by any other.

These are all termed "powers. Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): first, omniscience; second, the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); third, the proclamation of the obstacles to the path;

and fourth, the proclamation of the path leading to the end of suffering. These four are all termed "fearlessnesses" because, when the Tathāgata extensively proclaims his own and others' knowledge and abandonment amidst all assemblies, he is definitively free from error and thus possesses not even the slightest trace of fear or trepidation.

The marks [of the four analytical knowledges] are as follows: first, the knowledge of meaning (*artha*); second, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*); third, the knowledge of language (*nirukti*); and fourth, the knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
These four are all termed "unimpeded knowledges" (*pratisaṃvid*) because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is swift, discerning, and thoroughly penetrating without obstruction.
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): first, no failure in physical action; second, no failure in verbal action; third, no failure in mindfulness; fourth, no...
1. Absence of divergent thoughts; 2. No lack of concentration; 3. No lack of mindfulness; 4. No lack of clear comprehension; 5. No lack of equanimity; 6.
No lack of knowledge regarding equanimity; 7. No decline in zeal; 8. No decline in vigor; 9. No decline in mindfulness; 10. No decline in wisdom; 11.
No decline in liberation; 12. No decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation; 13. Bodily action follows wisdom; 14. Vocal action follows...
The practice of wisdom. Fifteenth, mental karma follows wisdom. Sixteenth, wisdom knows the past.
Seventeenth, wisdom knows the future. Eighteenth, wisdom knows the present. This is the dharma of the ultimate stage.

It is not shared with ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas; therefore, it is generally termed "unshared" (*āveṇika*). Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*):

within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the foundation of mindfulness of the body contemplates the impurity of the body; the foundation of mindfulness of sensation contemplates that sensation is suffering;
the foundation of mindfulness of the mind contemplates that the mind is impermanent; and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena contemplates that phenomena are without self.
The four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*): for the abandonment of unwholesome states that have already arisen; for the non-arising of unwholesome states not yet arisen;
for the increase of wholesome states that have already arisen; and for the cultivation and arising of wholesome states not yet arisen. The four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*):
the base of power of desire, the base of power of mindfulness, the base of power of energy, and the base of power of contemplation. These are the bases of power.

This refers to the fulfillment of the practice according to one's wishes. The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Regarding the term "faculty" (*indriya*), it is like a plant that possesses roots; by means of these roots, it is able to grow and flourish daily.

The five powers (*pañcabala*) are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Regarding the term "power," they are so called because they are capable of accomplishing wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*).
This refers to the destruction of all unwholesome dharmas. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*):

the factor of investigation of phenomena, the factor of energy, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquility, the factor of equanimity, the factor of concentration, and the factor of mindfulness. "Factor" (*aṅga*) means a constituent part;
it refers to the method cultivated as a constituent part, whether it be authentic or counterfeit. Regarding the eightfold noble path: right view and right intention.
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. "Right" means not relying on partiality or deviation;
"path" refers to that which leads through to nirvana. These seven categories—consisting of three, four, two, five, one, seven, and eight respectively—combine to form thirty-seven.
Because they assist those of various capacities in entering the path at shallow or deep levels, they are collectively named [the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment].

The Chapter on Aids to the Path (*Bodhipakṣa-varga*). This phrase refers to the noble dharmas that serve as the antidote to defiled phenomena. "In this way" indicates the purity employed by the various noble ones.

"Up to and including" encompasses numerous dharmas, such as the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and so forth.
The "eighty-four thousand dharanī-doors" is the name for the gateways to the Dharma attained by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

These meanings are not shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Although the dharma-gates are immeasurable, for now we shall limit ourselves to these as the remedies for all worldly defilements—the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). The *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra* explains the enumeration of these dharmas in detail.

This phrase refers to the noble dharmas that transform defilement into purity; it is by contrasting the fundamental state with the delusions of ordinary beings that the noble wisdom is revealed, thereby departing from defilement.
Dharmas accomplish pure dharmas, even unto various gateways of the Dharma. If one's own defiled dharmas are already pure, what further need is there to manifest them as pure dharmas?
There are no defiled dharmas and no pure dharmas; that which is the very nature of defiled dharmas is itself the nature of pure dharmas—this is purity.

This is identical purity. Furthermore, regarding this general manifestation of purity: taking ordinary phenomena (*pṛthagjana-dharma*) as the object to be purified and noble phenomena (*ārya-dharma*) as the means of purification, the single object of purification and the manifold means of purification are thus established by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).

The preceding section, which combined the categories of the defilement and purification of ordinary phenomena, concludes the section on the "Unity of Defilement and Purification. Second, the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanasattva-advaya*).
The opening has two parts. First, the direct penetration of self and others:
"Good son, because the nature of all real marks (*dharmatā*) is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, many bodies are pure;
because many bodies are pure, in this way it extends even to the perfect enlightenment of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions."
Purity. Regarding the four phrases of the text, they correctly penetrate both self and others. "Good son," one phrase; "all," etc., one phrase;
"one body," etc., one phrase; "many bodies," etc., one phrase. All real marks (dharmatā) are pure by nature.
This refers to the aforementioned ordinary and sagely, defiled and pure, states of complete purity.
For all phenomena—whether pure or defiled—are the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) of all things, like the nature of space. Without arising or ceasing, the wondrous marks manifest as pure.
As for "the purity of one body," it refers to the manifestation of the *dharmakāya*, the body of the true nature of all phenomena; this body is fundamentally...
There is no defilement; rather, it is only through delusion regarding characteristics and functions that there arises the defilement and purity of the dharmas of ordinary beings and sages.

Thus, one fails to realize the purity of this body. Now, since all dharmas—whether of ordinary beings or sages, defiled or pure—are returned to their fundamental reality, which is pure, one attains the purity of this body. Therefore, this phrase is explained next as revealing the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
"Purity. Regarding "the purity of one body and the purity of many bodies": the *dharmatā-kāya* is neither one nor dual with respect to self and other;
because it is not one, the single [self] manifests as many; because it is not dual, all are equally pure. This phrase refers to the purity of the *saṃbhoga-kāya*.
Regarding "the purity of many bodies is thus, and so forth," this means to see through to the *dharmatā*.
The body is neither one nor two, yet both return to the same purity. Furthermore, how could there exist any sentient beings with illusory, defiled bodies?
Therefore, the realm of sentient beings is exhausted within the realm of perfect enlightenment; the realm of perfect enlightenment is exhausted within the realm of ultimate purity.
This cannot be reached through mere inference; thus, it is expressed by such phrases as "even unto" to encompass it all. As for the "ten directions":
The Dharma-realm is the ten directions. This phrase refers to the purity of the Dharmakāya; it is said that this penetrates directly through both self and others.
Second, the support [the realm] fuses the one and the many.
Good son, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure; because many worlds are pure, [one world is pure].
Thus, it extends even to the exhaustion of empty space, perfectly encompassing all that is equal, pure, and immovable throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding the text, there are three phrases based on the fusion of the one and the many: "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "one world" and so forth constitute another phrase.
Regarding the phrase "many worlds" and so forth: "because one world is pure" refers precisely to the purity of *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (perfectly realized awareness).

Since it is fundamentally neither a world (*loka*) nor a realm (*dhātu*), there is only *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*. Sentient beings become deluded regarding the purity of this *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*, and thus the defilement of worlds arises.
Once one realizes the purity of the *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* within sentient beings, that is the [purity] of the world.
Pure. Therefore, it is manifested accordingly. Regarding the purity of many worlds: all worlds are the world of Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti);
all worlds are pure. This phrase refers to the nature-land being eternally quiescent. "In this manner" means, for example, the purity of one or many worlds.
"Up to and including" encompasses an infinite and inexhaustible multitude of worlds, extending to the very limits of space.
"Empty" means that it completely fills the worlds of empty space; this refers to the internal lack of anything impure.
"Perfectly encompassing the three periods of time" means that there is no space whatsoever throughout past, present, and future; this refers to the external lack of anything impure.
"All" is a term that combines the internal and the external, exhausting all possibilities. "Equal" means returning to the same source.

"Single characteristic" means being pure and devoid of all diverse characteristics. "Immovable" means eternally transcending arising and ceasing. This phrase refers to the permanence of the nature-land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
This concludes the section on the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants, which combines with the preceding category.

The previous combination of the sections on the identity of defilement and purity concludes the section on the Perfectly Illuminating True Reality (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*). Second, the Perfectly Illuminating Wondrous Nature is divided into two parts.

First, the perfect nature of wondrousness opens into two. First, penetrating the nature as it is identical to characteristics opens into two. First, penetrating the nature as it is identical to emptiness.
Good son, just as empty space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable.
When the three phrases of the text penetrate the nature, it is immediately emptiness. "Good son" is one phrase; "empty space, etc. is one phrase;
"you should know, etc. is one phrase. Regarding "empty space": it is the great general characteristic (*mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
This refers to the empty space that encompasses everything. What does this encompassing empty space encompass? It encompasses all things.

Because the pure empty space is the self-nature and phenomenal characteristic (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the three periods of time, which does not shift between the defilement and purity of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), there are such [expressions] as "and so forth. Regarding "such":

whether in a state of defilement or purity, all phenomena—the one and the many, the environment and its inhabitants—without exception, are fundamentally the characteristic of empty space. Regarding "equality": there is nothing that is not the characteristic of empty space; there is no phenomenon that is not [empty space].
Regarding "the emptiness": it is the emptiness that has no characteristic of arising and no characteristic of cessation. Regarding "immovable":
it is ultimately only characteristics and ultimately only emptiness, without any change. This phrase clarifies the characteristics;

one should know that the immovability of the equal nature of awakening is the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) that issues forth from boundless space, and within the characteristics of its issuing forth, there is...
This equality is immovable; the nature from which it is issued has always been equal and immovable.

Therefore, one should know that this phrase reveals the nature of essence. Now, this demonstrates the nature of the true emptiness of the single, universal reality; what follows demonstrates the nature of the wondrous existence of all phenomena.
Only when both emptiness and existence are thoroughly penetrated does the perfect identity become clear. This is the twofold penetration.
The nature is precisely existence.
Because the four great elements are immovable, one should know that the nature of awakening is equally immovable.
In this way, up to and including the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors being equally immovable, one should know that the nature of awakening is equally immovable.
Regarding the two phrases that penetrate the nature: "The four great elements (mahābhūta)... and so forth, and "In this way... and so forth.

As for "because the four great elements are immovable," it means that the four great elements are pure; thus, the Great [Element] is all-pervasive, the Great [Element] is eternally abiding, the Great [Element] does not encounter one another, and the Great [Element] does not know one another—this is what is meant by purity. These are the pure four great elements.
Since the fundamental nature is itself the mark of equality and immovability, it is here directly called "immovable. Regarding the phrase "one should know that the nature of awakening...
and so forth: this refers to what is manifested by the directionless, pure original awakening (*mūlābodhi*).
While the marks manifested therein possess this equality and immovability, one must know that the nature manifested is likewise equal and immovable. Therefore, one should know this...
Regarding the phrase "penetrating the nature of defilement": it is like the immovability of the four great elements. Regarding the phrase "and so forth":

this encompasses the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all pure dharmas. As for the instruction "it should be understood that... and so on: this is to be explained according to the preceding passage.
This phrase concerns the nature of purity and transparency. Combined with the preceding topical outline, it completes the section on "Transparency as Nature" (Chè-xìng jí-xiāng).
Second, "Transparency as Nature and Phenomenon" (Chè-xiāng jí-xìng):
"Good son, because the awakened nature is all-pervasive, pure, immovable, and perfectly boundless, you should know that the six sense faculties are likewise pervasive."
The faculties pervade the dharma-realm; because the faculties pervade it, one should know that the six sense objects pervade the dharma-realm.
Because the sense objects pervade it, one should know that the four great elements pervade the dharma-realm. In this manner, up to the gates of dhāraṇī, they all pervade the dharma-realm.
The five phrases of the text thoroughly clarify that phenomena are identical to nature. "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "the nature of awakening...
constitutes one phrase; "the faculties pervade... constitutes one phrase; "the objects pervade... constitutes one phrase; and "thus... constitutes one phrase.
Regarding "the nature of awakening pervades all": within the gate of the wondrous existence of true emptiness, all real marks are simultaneously awakened and manifested.
"Because it is pervasive, it is full. "Pure and immovable" refers to the various dharmas of true reality within the gate of the wondrous existence of true emptiness.
"Perfectly without bounds" means that the Dharma-nature is fundamentally both empty and existent; like a pearl rolling in all directions, it pervades and fills the dharma-realm.
The pervasion of the enlightened nature is likewise both empty and existent, without any admixture or distinction. The word "therefore" (故) traces back to the source.
Regarding the phrase "one should know": it means that one should understand how the pervasiveness of the nature leads to the knowledge of the pervasiveness of the characteristics.

As for "the faculties pervade the dharma-realm," this is because the faculty is itself awakening (*bodhi*). First is the phrase on the faculties, followed by the phrase on objects, then the phrase on the great elements, and finally the phrase on the *dhāraṇī* gates.

This is because the faculties, conjoined with seeing and characteristics, establish themselves as belonging to the immediate objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); [whereas] objects and the great elements...

The entirety of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is derived from the fundamental objective aspect. One should understand that the *dhāraṇīmukhas* and so forth belong to the noble, pure dharmas because they arise as the primary antidotes to defiled dharmas;
thus, their sequence should be known accordingly. Within a single aspect, one attains the pervasive presence of all aspects.

Regarding the meaning of the pervasiveness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): because the characteristic of partlessness is itself the characteristic of the totality of nature, and because each and every characteristic is the totality of nature, each characteristic is pervasive.
Other explanations follow the same principle. To explain the text in its combined form according to its sequence:
it says that one contemplates the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) as being unmoving like all emptiness and unmoving like all existence; in this way, it is pervasive.

Because all phenomena are perfectly pervasive and boundless within the pure and immovable state, one knows that all phenomenal marks originally manifest from awakening as a nature devoid of dualistic characteristics.
Now, how could a nature devoid of dualistic characteristics possess the marks of external natures?
One should understand that the entirety of marks is the entirety of nature, and the entirety of nature is the entirety of marks.

"Since the nature is all-pervasive, its characteristics are also all-pervasive," and so forth. The preceding section, "The Nature Penetrates the Characteristics," together with the section "The Wondrous Nature Perfectly Identifies with Characteristics," is hereby concluded.
Second, "The Wondrous Nature Perfectly Identifies with Characteristics" is divided into two parts. First, the explanation by means of the Dharma.
Good son, because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled.
Because the faculties and objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled, this extends even to the gates of dhāraṇī, which are likewise neither destroyed nor intermingled.
The first of the three phrases of the main text explains the Dharma: "Good son" (one phrase); "Because that wondrous cloud... (one phrase); "The faculties and objects...
(one phrase). Regarding the phrase "Because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervading," there is no nature that is not form, and no form that is not nature;
the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor mixed, being as non-existent as the nature itself.
"Arising and ceasing are conjoined and all-pervasive; this phrase indicates that defiled phenomena are unimpeded.
Regarding the phrase "the non-destruction of sense organs and objects," and so forth: all mundane phenomena are entirely suchness, and all supramundane phenomena are likewise entirely suchness.
It is not that some thing is destroyed or that various elements are mixed and combined to constitute supramundane phenomena. This is the meaning of this phrase.
The pure dharmas are unimpeded. This is because it is revealed that since nature and appearance are both total, the totality of appearance is the totality of nature;
thus, the mundane and defiled are identical to the sagely and pure. Each is individually pervasive and complete, each is individually pure, and there is no obstruction or hindrance.
Through the perfection of this non-mixture, one attains perfect detachment. Next, this is illustrated through a metaphor.
Just as the light from a hundred thousand lamps illuminates a single room, that light pervades it entirely without being impaired or mixed.
This is illustrated by two phrases in the text: the phrase "a hundred [thousand]... and so forth, and the phrase "its light... and so forth.

The metaphor of the hundred thousand lamps represents all phenomena (*dharma*); the light represents the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); and the illumination of the single room represents the pervasive filling of the Dharma.
The realm (*dhātu*). This phrase presents the metaphor. The phrase "its light" explains the intent of the metaphor, which lies in the pervasiveness of the light.

Because the characteristics of light encompass both the wondrous existence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the two gates [of appearance and reality], it is pervasive and thus free from destruction or confusion.

This causes one to attain the characteristics and the nature within wondrous existence and true emptiness, abiding securely in the realm of awakening. However, this must be illustrated by a metaphor for the sake of those who require clarification, because all...
The various phenomena of defilement and purity pervade the entire dharma-realm without any confusion or disorder.

Those who have not yet attained the state of entering, abiding, and emerging from samādhi to enjoy the nature of the objective realm cannot comprehend this. Therefore, it is illustrated by way of analogy: when the light of a thousand lamps illuminates a single room, each lamp pervades the room;
yet each remains in its own position without mutual obstruction, thereby manifesting the principle. This concludes the preceding section of the text.

The section on "Together Accomplishing the Wondrous Nature" is concluded. The preceding "Combining with the Wondrous Nature" is subsumed under the section "The Wondrous Nature of Perfect Clarity," which is now concluded.
This is joined to the section "Perfect Clarity of Reality," which is governed by the section "Awakening to Perfect Clarity," which is now concluded.
Second, regarding the accomplishment of awakening, there are two parts. First, regarding the cause that constitutes the practice of awakening, there are two parts.
First, the designation of pure conduct, which has two parts. First, the individual causes and effects.
Good son, because awakening is accomplished, you should know that a bodhisattva is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from dharmas;
they do not loathe birth-and-death, nor do they crave nirvana.
Regarding the four phrases of the first section on cause and effect: "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "because of the accomplishment of awakening" constitutes one phrase;
"it should be known that... constitutes one phrase; and "without weariness... constitutes one phrase. As for "the accomplishment of awakening":

it refers to the perfect clarity of nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), which is not a separate entity from anything else, but is solely the wondrous awakening that is all-pervasive, compliant, indestructible, and unmixed. Therefore [it is so called].
This phrase serves as a transition to what follows below. It indicates that while the Bodhisattva’s practice consists of conforming to awakening, it is not yet the accomplishment of pure awakening;
those who merely possess such conformity cannot yet achieve thorough penetration. Therefore, this is an original investigation. "That which must be known" means that it must certainly be known.
"Not bound by dharmas" means not being fettered by any dharmas of defilement or purity, thereby merging with the objective realm.
"One who does not seek liberation from dharmas" means that by not seeking liberation from any dharmas—whether defiled or pure—one merges with the mind;

this phrase demonstrates mastery over practice. "One who does not loathe saṃsāra" means there is no truth of suffering or its origin; "one who does not crave nirvāṇa" means there is no truth of cessation or the path;
this phrase demonstrates the contemplation of equality regarding retribution. These two [points] concern the dharmas of others.
Do not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor loathe those who violate them; do not value long-standing practice, nor disparage a beginner.
These two phrases concern the Dharma of others: "do not revere... constitutes one phrase, and "do not value... constitutes another.

To "not revere those who uphold the precepts" means to realize that there is no inherent nature in upholding them. To "not loathe those who violate the prohibitions" means to realize that there is no inherent nature in violating them.
This phrase refers to the profound principle of defilement and purity. "Not disparaging those who have long practiced" means one realizes there is no fixed nature of a bodhisattva;

"not belittling beginners" means one realizes there is no fixed nature of a sentient being. This phrase refers to the profound principle of the relationship between ordinary people and sages. Together with the preceding sections of the text, this completes the section on the heading of "Pure Conduct.
Second, the manifestation of accordance with awakening is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the practice of awakening through the Dharma.
Why is this? Because it is all-encompassing awakening (*sarva-bodha*).
Regarding the two phrases of the text, they explain awakening through the dharma of practice. Why is this so? The phrase "Why is this?

interrogates the reason why a bodhisattva is able to [practice] non-giving and non-seeking, and so forth. The phrase "Because it is all-encompassing awakening" explains and clarifies that the bodhisattva, by means of...
Following awakening to accomplish practice—this is precisely the pure dharma-practice of the aspect of perfect illumination-awakening.
There are two points regarding all awakening: first, that all dharmas are the aspect of awakening because their very nature is the aspect of awakening;
thus, the bodhisattva perceives only awakening and does not perceive dharmas. Second, that the bodhisattva is always awake and never deluded; therefore, there is nothing with which [to compare it].
Seeking among all dharmas, there are two analogies that clarify awakening and practice, opening up two aspects. First, the analogy is revealed:
It is like the light of the eyes clearly perceiving objects before one; that light is perfect and complete, such that it is free from both aversion and attachment.

The first analogy in this sentence clarifies the point: the "light of the eyes" refers to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the pure, bright, and clear essence of seeing, which serves as the metaphor for the Bodhisattva of Pure Conduct.
"Clearly understanding the objects before one" refers to simultaneous clarity, serving as the metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s compliance.
"The perfection of that light" refers to instantaneous, all-encompassing illumination; it distinguishes this from a conceptual clarity, as it is an instantaneous [cognition].

Because there is simultaneous clarity at the moment of perfect illumination, one clearly perceives the external object without yet giving rise to conceptual discrimination on the level of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Its light is "perfectly complete" (*yuanman*), which serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s perfect illumination. The meaning of this metaphor lies in these four characters.

Regarding "attaining freedom from hatred and love": it means casting one's gaze upon all things without avoiding the beautiful or the ugly; this serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva who does not [discriminate].
"Not seeking equality," etc. Next, the inquiry and the clarification: "For what reason? This consists of two sentences in the text:
one sentence for the inquiry, "For what reason? and one sentence for the clarification, "The essence of light... and so forth. Why? [Because...]
"Regarding 'the reason': it asks why one attains freedom from hatred and attachment through the light of perfect vision. As for 'the essence of the light being non-dual':
because a single light possesses perfection and is established as a non-dual illumination, it unifies the subject and object.

Regarding 'because there is no hatred or attachment': because there is non-duality, hatred and attachment do not arise; because there is non-duality, there is nothing that corresponds to hatred and attachment. This non-arising is due to..."

"Without capacity; there is nothing that should be, because there is nothing from which it arises"—this phrase explains the principle of using metaphors to fully illustrate all-encompassing awakening.
This section concludes the "Exemplifying Awakening Practice" (喻明覺行) chapter, together with the preceding textual divisions.

The preceding "Applying the Metaphor to the Teaching of Awakening Practice" (合法說覺行) is subsumed under the "Manifesting Accordance with Awakening" (顯隨順覺) chapter. This concludes the combined connection to the "Designating Pure Practice" (標清淨行) chapter, which governs the following.

The section on the Awakening of Causes and Practices is concluded. Second, the Awakening of the Resultant Mind, which has two parts. First, the realization of the cultivation of the result, which has two parts.
First, attaining the fundamental state where there is no cultivation, which has two parts. First, the pointing-out that there is no cultivation.
Good son, for this Bodhisattva and those sentient beings of the final age who practice this mind and achieve accomplishment,
there is herein neither cultivation nor accomplishment.
The three phrases beginning with "When" indicate that there is no cultivation. "Good son," one phrase; "this Bodhisattva," etc., one phrase; "regarding this," etc., one phrase.
"This Bodhisattva" refers to a Bodhisattva who accords with awakening. "And sentient beings of the final age" refers to those sentient beings who have achieved accord with awakening.
"Those who practice this mind" refers to those whose practice is perfected and complete. No [cultivation].
Second, when the awakened mind accords with all suchness and conforms to quiescence, the one who attains accomplishment achieves the perfection of non-dual accomplishment.
This phrase indicates the cultivation of accomplishment. "In this" refers to the perfection of attaining accomplishment.

"No cultivation" means that the cause of realization is identical to the fruit. "Nor is there one who accomplishes" means that the fruit of realization is identical to the cause. This is the phrase [of the commentary].

This demonstrates what has been accomplished. Since the cause and fruit of the perfectly awakened mind are identical and subject and object are darkly quiescent, there is nothing to cultivate and nothing to accomplish.
Therefore, one who attains accomplishment must do so within non-cultivation and non-accomplishment.

This pointing-out instruction is intended to ensure that Bodhisattvas and sentient beings who practice the awakened mind know what is accomplished, so that they do not become deluded regarding the Middle Way.
It should be understood as ultimate. Second, to manifest that there is no cultivation, two points are opened: first, abiding in the non-duality of the agent;
second, the universal illumination of Perfect Enlightenment is quiescent and non-dual.

Regarding the single phrase "abiding in the non-duality of the agent" from the text: "the universal illumination of Perfect Enlightenment" refers to the self-nature of the enlightened essence and its illuminating function.

The profound identity: through the perfect it is universal, and through the universal it is perfect. Regarding "quiescent extinction is non-dual": awakening is quiescence and illumination is extinction;
their own characteristics are one and the same. It is quiescent while being extinct, and extinct while being quiescent.
In this phrase, the first half contains the second half, and the second half reveals the first half. There must necessarily be the perfect and universal awakening-illumination.
This is the quiescence of the non-duality of existence and non-existence. The non-duality within that which is quiescent belongs to what follows, where it is revealed.
Here, it specifically designates the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) that has been accomplished—luminous, pure, and fundamentally wondrous. This non-duality of the two "in-what-is" opens into two:
first, the cessation of the measure of the world, which opens into two; first, the ultimate number merging with the measure.
Within this, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* unspeakable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding the phrase "within this": it refers to within the perfectly pervasive, awakened illumination.
"Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya*" and so forth—*asaṃkhyeya* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "innumerable. There are ten great [units]...

It is the first number among all numbers; it is called both "unspeakable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) and "number. It is the ninth of the ten great numbers, encompassing within itself the second, "immeasurable" (*aprameya*);
the third, "boundless" (*aparimāṇa*); the fourth, "unequaled" (*asamanta*); the fifth, "incalculable" (*agaṇeya*); the sixth, "inexpressible" (*anabhilāpya*);
the seventh, "inconceivable" (*acintya*); and the eighth, "unfathomable" (*atulya*). All these great numbers are contained therein.
Subsequently, taking the sands of the Ganges as a count, they correspond to the tenth great number, "unspeakable-unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*).
This reaches the limit of calculation and merges with the infinite. Indeed, the Ganges originally flows from the Elephant’s Mouth on the eastern side of Lake Anavatapta;
it circles forty *li* and flows mixed with golden sand, the grains of which are as fine as flour. Now, regarding its place in the numerical sequence...
Among gods and humans, those capable of calculation reach their limit at the number known as one *asaṃkhyeya*; they cannot know beyond this. For example: one and one is called two;
two and two is called four; three and three is called nine; ten tens are called a hundred; ten hundreds are called a thousand;
ten thousands are called ten thousand (*ayuta*); one hundred thousand is called a *koṭi*; ten million *koṭis* are called a *nayuta*. Ten million... [continued].
One *nayuta* is called a *bimba*. One thousand million *bimbas* is called a *katha*. Beyond a *katha* is an *asaṃkhyeya*. A multitude of *asaṃkhyeyas* is called "immeasurable" (*aprameya*).
A multitude of "immeasurables" is called "boundless" (*ananta*). A multitude of "boundless" is called "unequaled" (*atulya*).
A multitude of "unequaled" is called "incalculable" (*agaṇeya*). A multitude of "incalculables" is called "incomparable" (*asamkhyeya*). [Beyond] "incomparable" is...
That which is called "inconceivable" is immeasurable; that which is called "immeasurable" is ineffable;
and that which is called "ineffable" is as numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges River, constituting the number of worlds.
How is it that the worlds of all Buddhas are ultimately exhausted? The nature of the world is fundamentally the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

Since the nature of Perfect Enlightenment has no distinct seed-nature other than the nature of the Buddhas, there is only the realm of the Buddhas. Second, through metaphors, the realm is shown to be eternally quiescent.
It is like flowers in the sky: arising and ceasing in confusion, neither identical with nor separate from [the sky], neither bound nor liberated.
The first two phrases of the text serve as metaphors for the eternal quiescence of the realm (*dhātu*). "Like flowers in the sky" is one phrase;

"arising in confusion... and so forth is the other phrase. Regarding "like flowers in the sky": this metaphor signifies that the Buddha-world manifests within awakening, yet fundamentally possesses no arising or ceasing, being eternally [quiescent].

"Ever quiescent. This phrase provides a simile. "Arising and ceasing in disorder" is a metaphor for the various Buddha-worlds appearing and disappearing unpredictably—arising without real conditions and ceasing without real conditions. "Neither identical nor separate" is a metaphor for the various Buddha-worlds:

they constantly arise yet have nothing to which they are identical; they constantly cease yet have nothing from which they are separate. "Neither bound nor liberated" is a metaphor for the various Buddhas... [the text continues].
The world is not identical to all phenomena, yet it is eternally without bondage; it is not separate from all phenomena, yet it is eternally without liberation.
This phrase clarifies the analogy. Together with the preceding section, this completes the "Section on the Extinction of the World-Quantity.
Second, the purification of sentient beings' delusions is divided into two parts: first, the purification of the cause.
One first comes to know that sentient beings have been Buddha from the very beginning.
Regarding the phrase "one first comes to know": it arises because one’s illumination pervades all Buddha-worlds;

like the arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky, there is in reality no arising or ceasing, and thus one's knowledge begins. This "first knowing" is precisely *ādikṣaya-bodhi* (initial awakening). Sentient...

Regarding "beings are originally enlightened from the beginning": this simply means that not perceiving the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*) is itself original enlightenment from the beginning.
It is not that there is a Buddha existing externally who constitutes this original enlightenment. This original enlightenment is precisely *mūla-awakening* (*mūla-avabodha*).

Because one is deluded regarding *mūla-awakening*, there is a time of non-awakening (*an-avabodha*), wherein the world is falsely established and interwoven to form sentient beings. Therefore, it is now that the beginning is realized.
When awakening is unified, it illuminates the entire world like flowers in the sky, which have no reality;

arising and ceasing are devoid of both bondage and liberation, and there is nothing to be woven—the sentient beings of delusion. Thus, one attains Buddhahood, eternally severing ignorance at its source where delusion was established without cause, and the two fruits are purified.
Birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday.
When one sentence is realized, the fruit is pure. "Birth-and-death" refers to the suffering and its origin for sentient beings; "nirvana" refers to the cessation and the path for the Buddhas.
Sentient beings and Buddhas constitute the cause, while birth-and-death and nirvana constitute the fruit. That they are "like a dream from yesterday" means that [birth-and-death] arises...
Death is manifested through ignorance; Nirvana is realized through the cessation of ignorance.
Manifesting ignorance is like being in a dream; ceasing and realizing ignorance is like waking up. Yet, while one is dreaming, there is this awakening; once awakened, there is no further awakening.
Therefore, knowing now that sentient beings are originally enlightened, they are eternally awake and never dreamed; how could there be [any further awakening]?

Samsara and Nirvana are thus like a dream from yesterday, for one perceives that they are eternally non-existent in the present. This concludes the section on the Purification of Sentient Beings' Delusions, which combines with the preceding section.
This concludes the section on the Non-duality of "That Which Is" (the locus), which combines with the preceding section on the Extinction of the World's Dimensions.
This concludes the section on Manifesting Non-cultivation, which is governed by the section on the Non-duality of "That Which Can Be" (the capacity).

The section on "Joining the Mark-Point and the Non-Cultivation" concludes the sub-section on "Attaining the Original Non-Cultivation. Second, "Reaching the Original Non-Existence and Realizing the Opening" has two parts:
first, "Realizing that the Dharmas are Originally Non-Existent," which has two parts; first, "the Dharmas of the Fruit are Originally Non-Existent."
"Good son, because it is like a dream from yesterday, you should know that birth-and-death and nirvana are without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going.
Regarding the text, there are three phrases: 'the fruit-dharma is fundamentally non-existent,' 'good son,' and 'because it is like a dream from yesterday.'"
