Regarding the phrase "One should know that... and so forth, the statement "because it is like a dream from yesterday" points to a dream in order to bring about understanding. This sentence provides a detailed analysis. As for "One should know that... and so forth:
the person in the dream and the events of the dream do not exist within the dream; upon waking, they are found to have been fundamentally non-existent.
How could there be a birth-and-death that arises or ceases when it is fundamentally non-existent? How could there be a Nirvana that comes into being when it is fundamentally non-existent?
The phrase "the one who goes" clarifies the fruit. As for the two causal dharmas, they are fundamentally non-existent.
That which is realized is without gain or loss, without grasping or relinquishing. That which realizes it is without action, without cessation, without effort, and without extinction.
Regarding the two phrases concerning the cause, the dharmas are fundamentally non-existent.
As for the phrase "that which is spoken of" and the phrase "that which can speak," that which is realized resides within the dharma of realization.

There is no such thing as "speaking of attainment," for the dharma realized is not one where there is an attainment of nirvana through the loss of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), nor is it one where there is a grasping at nirvana through the abandonment of birth-and-death.

Regarding that which is capable of realization: it lies within the practice of realization. As for the phrase "non-action" (*anabhisamskāra*) and so forth, it does not mean that one attains *nirvāṇa* through active effort while ceasing [the cycle] by abandoning *saṃsāra*, nor that one attains *nirvāṇa* through passivity while losing *saṃsāra* through cessation. This is the mind capable of realization.

Regarding the term "cause" (*hetu*) in the relevant section, it is because gain and loss and so forth are distinguished according to the subjective (*grāhaka*) and the objective (*grāhya*). The subjective...

These are the causal dharmas. Regarding what was previously categorized as "fruits," these are established based on arising and ceasing within saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; thus, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are the resultant dharmas.
Combining these two sections of the text completes the proof that the fundamental nature of dharmas is originally non-existent. End of section.
Second, "Dharma as it is has no realization.
Within this realization, there is neither subject nor object; ultimately there is no realization, nor is there one who realizes.
Regarding the three phrases in the text, "Dharma as it is has no realization," and the phrase "within this... and so forth, [it means] "ultimately there is no realization" (1).
Phrase. Furthermore, there is no one who realizes—this is a single phrase. Regarding this "realizer," it refers to the realization of this very dharma of non-realization.
"The middle" refers to the entire totality of the dharma of non-realization. "No capacity" means that the capacity of the mind is fundamentally non-existent. "Nothing [to be] attained" means...
The fact that the Dharma is fundamentally non-existent is directly realized within the Middle Way and expressed through the Middle Word.
This phrase reiterates the previously indicated realization of the Dharma’s fundamental non-existence, thereby manifesting the principle of "non-realization.

The statement that there is ultimately no realization follows from the preceding sentence; for where there is subject and object, there is realization, yet when both subject and object are exhausted, how can there be realization?
Therefore, it is ultimately non-existent. This phrase refers to the non-existence of dharmas, and likewise there is no one who realizes them.
Following the statement regarding ultimate non-existence, it is because when there is a dharma to be realized, one establishes a mind that grasps at realization and designates it as the "realizer.
Since the dharmas to be realized are ultimately non-existent, upon what could a mind grasping at realization be established? Thus, there is also no such realizer. This phrase signifies non-self.
The section on the combined proof that the Dharma is fundamentally non-existent, which together establishes the realization of fundamental non-existence, is concluded.

The section on the continuous combination of attaining fundamental non-cultivation, which is subsumed under the section on the accomplishment of the fruit of cultivation and realization, is concluded. Second, the complete opening of the awakened mind.
The nature of all phenomena is equal and indestructible.
One should fully awaken the mind through every single word and phrase. As for "the nature of all phenomena," it is like the measure of the *dharmadhātu*:

whether conditioned or unconditioned, the four great elements, the sense organs, the sense objects, or any other phenomena whatsoever, they possess a nature that is neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding "equal and indestructible": it means that this nature is uniform and cannot be destroyed.
"Phenomena are all-pervasive, and phenomena abide eternally. This phrase is precisely what is meant by "mountains, rivers, and the great earth together fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
This is because, as stated in the preceding text, having attained non-cultivation and reached non-attainment constitutes the ultimate and permanent severance of ignorance;
it constitutes the ultimate fulfillment of the awakened mind. Therefore, this designation can be established.

This clearly demonstrates that "no cultivation and no realization" is not the same as annihilationism. The preceding sections on "Combining to Accomplish the Resultant Cultivation and Realization" and "Together Accomplishing the Resultant Section of Awakened Mind" are concluded.
The combined section on "Combining to Form the Causal Section of Awakening and Practice," which is subsumed under the "Section on the Achievement of Awakening," is concluded.
This connects to the "Section on the Perfect Clarity of Awakening," which is governed by the "Section on Revealing Awakening and Attaining Enlightenment," and is hereby concluded.
The section on "Synthesizing the Threads to Realize Extinction and Attain Enlightenment" concludes within the section on "Leaving Illusion to Attain Enlightenment.

The section on "Penetrating and Synthesizing the Expedient Means of Leaving Illusion" is collectively subsumed under the section on "Expedient Means for Attaining Enlightenment," concluding here. This answers the request to explain the expedient means for attaining enlightenment.
Furthermore, the section on "Synthesizing the Accomplishment of Practice" enters into the general demonstration of the capacity for cultivation, concluding here. (2)
This is the instruction on the skillful means for benefiting others. "Good son, those bodhisattvas who practice in this way, progress through these stages, contemplate in this manner,
maintain themselves in this way, employ these skillful means, and achieve awakening in this fashion, will seek such dharmas without becoming confused or distressed."
The nine phrases of the "When" section demonstrate the skillful means for benefiting others. These consist of: "Good son" (one phrase); "those bodhisattvas" (one phrase);
the six phrases beginning with "in this way" (*evam*); and the phrase "seeking suchness... and so forth. Regarding the six "in this way" phrases:
they refer to practicing by being free from illusion, up to awakening by being free from illusion. As for "seeking such a dharma," it refers to seeking...
The Dharma of the all-pervading enlightened nature, which awakens through practice free from illusion, is such that one does not become deluded or distressed.
By attaining the correct means of contemplation, one possesses the practice that achieves awakening within the state of equal enlightenment.
This takes the causal practice of conforming to awakening as the entirety of cultivation; thus, cause and effect are identical, and there is no separate means of action.
Because it is gradual, that which constitutes the practice and awakening is itself the Dharma; there is no realization apart from cultivation.

Therefore, this is resolved by means of these [principles]. First, the section on the combined demonstration of the teaching and the ability to cultivate has concluded, forming a continuous sequence of demonstrations.
Second, the summary verse in stanzas provides a general overview, divided into two parts: first, the introduction expressing the desire to proclaim [the teaching] once more.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
The method for explaining the verses follows the previous examples.

Second, the exposition of the verses is divided into two parts: first, summarizing the essential intent to show the teaching on the ability to practice, which is further divided into two; first, summarizing the essential intent.
The accomplishment of cultivation—O Puyan, you should know this: the bodies and minds of all sentient beings are like illusions;

their physical forms depend upon the four great elements, while their mental natures return to the six sense objects. Yet the essence of these four great elements is fundamentally separate [from one another].
Who is the one who brings about this harmony? By practicing in this way gradually, all things become entirely pure.
This is the opening of awakening through the two essential points of skillful means:
immovability pervading the Dharma-realm, and non-action, non-stopping, naturalness, and extinction; furthermore, there is no one who can realize it.
All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the void; the three periods of time are entirely equal, ultimately without coming or going.
(This second section provides the essential purport and demonstrates the skillful means for benefiting others.)
Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, as well as sentient beings of the final age, who wish to seek entry into the Buddha-way, should practice in this manner.
The verse summary (geya) is concluded. Together with the preceding prose (gadya), this completes the introductory section on the World-Honored One’s compassionate response. [The connection follows.]
The section on the Preface and the Exposition of the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry has concluded. Regarding the "Exposition of the Dharma":

the intent of the Bodhisattva’s question lies in attaining the correct expedient means of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). Through such attainment, one realizes that the mind abides in its own support.
In response, the World-Honored One teaches that one should constantly contemplate the body and mind, seeking the fundamental nature of the four great elements as each being devoid of characteristics.
The accumulation of conditions and vital energies returns to the mark of dispersion and extinction; there is nothing within body or mind.

Upon attaining this, one departs from illusion through the skillful means of awakening, whereby the awakened mind opens and is enlightened. Because sentient beings of the末代 (final age) are able to cultivate the causal practices of the Tathāgata, it is called "revealing the Dharma.

This concludes the section on "Receiving and Resolving Doubts" and the section on "Departing from Illusion," which together constitute the comprehensive section on "Departing from Illusion and Severing Delusion."
The pure void is manifested by awakening;
this corresponds to the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*. It is titled "Great Vaipulya" (*Mahāvaipulya*) to reveal the essence, attributes, and function of the Great Vaipulya awakening.
This is because, as stated in this chapter, "because awakening is perfectly luminous, it extends to the limits of space and perfectly encompasses the three periods of time. This section...
The scriptural text states: "This is what is called the awakening that manifests the boundless, directionless, and pure void.
Its purity is the vastness of its directionless function; the void is the directionality of its boundless appearance.
'Direction' refers to the immovable equality of the void. All these are the greatness of the essence manifested by awakening. This is one."
It is that which all sentient beings must realize and which is fully present before them.

The deluded, however, fail to take up this realization because they focus instead on the purity of the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) as set forth in the sutras, the purity of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradya*), and other dharani-gates, or the purity of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the nature of the single body and many bodies, and the single realm and many realms. Thus, they sink away from the point of actualizing it.

Consequently, you loftily extol the sacred realm as being entirely beyond your own capacity. Yet you have not considered that it is like hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room—a metaphor fully present in the sutras.
Why do you not take this up and realize it for yourself? The lamp-light is like the body; the emptiness of the room is like the realm (*dhātu*).
One lamp’s light reveals the emptiness of one room; a thousand lamps’ light reveals the emptiness of a thousand rooms. There is no limit to the number of lamps’ light that can reveal [emptiness].

If there were no emptiness of ten thousand chambers, or if only one chamber were empty, rather than being empty of a thousand chambers or empty of ten billion chambers, then a single chamber could not accommodate the light of a thousand lamps nor the light of ten billion lamps.

The principle regarding one body and one realm, as well as many bodies and many realms, is exactly like this. It is simply this very thing; there is no other thing. Great, Vast, Perfect, and Complete.
Awaken to the fact that external objects are nothing other than yourself. It depends solely on the person to recognize what is called the light of a lamp.
This light of a lamp is the *dhāraṇī* gate of all Buddhas; it is the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) of sentient beings.
Yet, the purity of these states of existence is the very purity of the gate; there are not two separate dharmas for sentient beings and Buddhas. In total, they are one reality.
This is the characteristic. It is the totality of one body; it is the totality of one realm. Many bodies and many realms do not transcend this.
Because sentient beings have not attained its purity, they lose the purity of the gate and the purity of the body and realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Nevertheless, all phenomena of form and mind, as well as the sentient and insentient worlds—the environment and its inhabitants—exist within the portion of sentient beings.
The twenty-five realms of existence are thus fully encompassed; therein one attains purity. This is what is called the lamp-light that completely illuminates the chamber.
It is the Great Vaipulya of Perfect Enlightenment that every person may receive. Consequently, this diagram has been constructed to assist in realizing Perfect Enlightenment.
While the sequence of elements listed in the sutra extends to the four great elements, here we do not include "Great" as a separate category.

Regarding the grasping of existence through the *dhāraṇī* gates: this refers to the broad category of "existence" (*bhava*), which encompasses both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Now, "the great" (*mahat*) refers to the general classification of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) without further distinction; since it already belongs to the realm of existence, it fully encompasses all mundane functions.

This is sufficient to illustrate how the *dhāraṇī* gates likewise encompass all noble functions (*ārya-vyāpāra*). Let the wise examine these matters in detail. If one were to represent them in a diagram: [Diagram description omitted as per instructions] (Note: The bracketed section indicates that the original text implies a visual representation, which has been translated descriptively.)

When the characters are written, the entire passage of the scripture is fully revealed. "Awakened" (jue) means that awakening is perfectly luminous. "Mind-consciousness" (xīnshí) means that the mind is pure and consciousness is pure.
"Perceiving the faculties, consciousness, and forms" (jiàn gēn shí sè děng) means that seeing is pure, the eye-faculty is pure, eye-consciousness is pure, and the form-object is pure, and so forth.
"Earth, water, fire, and wind" (dì shuǐ huǒ fēng) refers to the purity of the four great elements.

"Purity" refers to this. "Existences" refers to the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). That which does not possess the full complement of bases and elements is subsumed within the existences.
"Gates" refers to the *dhāraṇī*-gates. That which does not possess the full complement of powers and so forth is subsumed within the gates.

These are recorded in full because they are all set forth and revealed in the preceding sūtra passages on the various purities; the same applies to the subsequent sūtra passages on the various purities.

Since this passage belongs to the general exposition, it is inclusive. Regarding "characteristics and nature": this refers to the nature of ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Regarding "bodies": this refers to bodies that are both one and many.

Regarding "realms": this refers to realms that are both one and many. Since there is no difference between body and realm regarding oneness and multiplicity, they are not listed separately as "one" and "many."

"Emptiness" (*ākāśa*) means that empty space envelops [all things] in a perfect sphere. Regarding the presence of horizontal and vertical strokes in written characters: the vertical indicates sequential order, while the horizontal reveals the comprehensive detail. Regarding the distinction between inward and outward orientation:

mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are outward-oriented, while material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are inward-oriented; this signifies the meaning of the mutual correspondence between the fundamental seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
As for the "gate" having a "summit-connection": there is no difference in function between ordinary beings and sages; it is the summit of both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

As for "reception" (or "conjunction"), it is the dharma in which nature and characteristics are of one essence. Nevertheless, they exist in relation to one another. Regarding the gate of the relative nature:

the subtle manifestation fully reveals the function of the Sage, while ordinary function fully embodies the characteristic. There is no distinction between the extraordinary functions within these functions.

If one can truly realize that the ordinary and the sage share this same function, then this nature and characteristic will be perfectly luminous, entering the purity of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This is the sequence from which the diagram is composed.
This is the cause. May those who observe this not treat it with negligence.

Second, revealing awakening as the severance of delusion, which opens into two parts. First, resolving doubts to reveal awakening, which opens into two parts. First, the introductory narration of the Bodhisattva’s posing of the question, which opens into two parts.
First, the introduction to the question following the sequence.

Thus, this introduction clarifies that from the moment Vajragarbha Bodhisattva awakened by departing from illusion, he realized that he had been a Buddha from the beginning; it is the manifestation of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
He then felt compassion for sentient beings who have lost this original enlightenment due to the existence of non-enlightenment (*a-bodhi*). However...
If one does not realize that non-enlightenment (abodhi) does not exist externally, one is deluded regarding the existence of original enlightenment (mūlabodhi).

If one can be free from doubt and regret concerning original enlightenment, then there will be no non-enlightenment. By raising questions and hoping for the Buddha’s teaching and benefit, one ultimately manifests enlightenment;

thereby resolving doubts and attaining the realm of awakening. Part Two: The Preface and Questions, consisting of three sections and two openings. First, the Preface and Description of the Ritual, consisting of two openings.
First, the introduction concerning the inquiry into dignified deportment:
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

The explanation of the phrases follows the previous example. Second, the description of requesting instruction and receiving benefit is divided into two parts. First, rejoicing in hearing the present benefit is divided into two parts.
First, praising the arising of what was received:
"O Great Compassionate World-Honored One, you have skillfully proclaimed for the sake of all the assembly of Bodhisattvas the pure *Tathāgatagarbha* of perfect enlightenment."
The gradual expedient means of the practice for the ground of the Great Dhāraṇī serves to open up the ignorance of all sentient beings.

It consists of three phrases: the first phrase praises the generation of awakening; the second phrase, "The World-Honored One of Great Compassion," praises Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra who respond to the questions;

and the third phrase, "For the sake of all... and so forth, praises those whom the World-Honored One answers. The subsequent phrase universally praises the text of the World-Honored One’s responses to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Regarding the three chapters of the teachings and principles of the Universal Eye: as for "bestowing upon all sentient beings," this refers to the gradual skillful means of the causal practices of the Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas who have transmitted these instructions.
It was originally intended as a model for sentient beings of the final age to awaken those who are ignorant and deluded.

Upon hearing the dharma-practices of the causal stage that accord with pure awakening, one will not be obscured by cause and effect, and through a single realization, one will be free from all calculations.
When one hears that the delusion of falling into false views regarding subject and object is extinguished by all illusions, the awakened mind remains unmoved;
thus, one is no longer obscured by the delusion of the empty-flower-like false appearances of a body and mind that grasp at illusions through the practice of conforming to awakening.
When one hears the skillful means of dwelling in contemplation and maintaining the state of being free from illusion, one is no longer obscured by the capacity for cultivation and its accomplishment.

One shall attain freedom from confusion and delusion, avoiding the obscurity that fails to enter perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). This sentence establishes the fundamental basis for the arising of the inquiry;
it is specifically intended for those sentient beings who are still shrouded in the darkness of ignorance regarding the fundamentally wondrous enlightened mind.

Therefore, the preceding praise of the Buddha and proclamation of the source were aimed at opening up the mental obscurity of such beings. Now, those beings still possess within their inherently awakened mind (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa-citta*) that which has not yet been severed.
With these doubts, they returned to request the ultimate revelation and clarification. Second, regarding the purification of present wisdom:
the assembly of Dharma-practitioners, having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, found their illusory cataracts cleared away and their eyes of wisdom purified.
When a single phrase of the text briefly manifests the purity of wisdom: "The assembly of Dharma listeners" refers to those dwelling together in the Dharma assembly.
"The cataracts of illusion are cleared away" means that one has thoroughly realized that ignorance is like the vanishing shadow of flowers in the sky.

"The eye of wisdom is purified" means that once the cataracts are removed and the flowers have vanished, Perfect Enlightenment is revealed. This indicates that the entire assembly of Dharma listeners has already entered and abided in samādhi forever.
Having prostrated and severed ignorance, he realized his original Buddhahood and purified the cataracts of illusion.
This brief response to the questions posed is specifically intended to eliminate doubts and generate faith in sentient beings of the final age who have not yet escaped saṃsāra.

Together with the preceding topical outline, this completes the section on "Celebrating the Hearing for Immediate Benefit. Second, regarding the request for subsequent benefit, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the fundamental doubts.
The awakening [of the question] has two parts. First, doubting that there is delusive existence:
"World-Honored One, if all sentient beings have been enlightened from the beginning, for what reason do they still possess all ignorance?"

Regarding the three phrases at the beginning of the text, one first suspects that they are falsely existent. The World-Honored One says one phrase: "If all... and so forth. Then there is one phrase: "Why... and so forth.
If these various phrases were intended to be [affirmative], why would the subsequent phrase express doubt by saying "not"? It is as if it were said:
"If sentient beings were originally Buddhas, then there would be no ignorance (*avidyā*). Yet now, all sentient beings possess this ignorance; what then [is the cause]?"
Therefore, why is this so? By what cause does this being who has fundamentally attained Buddhahood also become a being possessed of ignorance?
This single question is precisely a doubt regarding the awakening of fundamental Buddhahood; it is merely a case of being deluded regarding the true source and clinging to the false.
Thus, one first gives rise to doubt from the false, and subsequently, that doubt turns toward the true.
If all sentient beings inherently possess ignorance, for what reason and by what causal conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been enlightened from the beginning?

This passage contains two sentences that resolve the doubt regarding the true attainment of Buddhahood: the first sentence, "If all... and so forth; and the second sentence, "For what reason... and so forth.
If the first sentence intends to establish [the truth], why would the second sentence raise a doubt as to its falsity? It is still said that ignorance arises because it was originally non-existent.
This would then belong to that which is primordially existent. A sentient being who possesses primordially existent ignorance is not a sentient being who is primordially enlightened.
For what reason, then, does the Tathāgata say that one is primordially enlightened? Because he seeks out the causal conditions [for enlightenment], he says one is primordially enlightened;
yet this immediately gives rise to the doubt that one is not primordially enlightened. This single doubt arises from the existence of delusive doubt.
Regarding that which is transformed and emerged: the three [stages] are completed, and doubt concerning the beginning and end is finalized.
Sentient beings throughout the ten directions originally attained the Buddha-way, yet later gave rise to ignorance; how could all Tathāgatas ever again give rise to any afflictions?
When the two phrases of the first section are concluded, the doubts regarding the beginning and end are exhausted. Regarding the phrase "the ten directions... and the phrase "all beings...":
those who are "ordinary beings of the ten directions" refer to all sentient beings who, within that which is neither identical nor different, blaze forth into difference and are born.
Furthermore, all sentient beings possess the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—which are differences; yet they fundamentally achieve the Buddha-way.
"Those" refers to the explicit teachings of the Buddha. "Subsequently arising ignorance" is based on what currently exists through birth.
This phrase concerns the ultimate end of true existence. "All Tathāgatas" refers to attaining the Buddha-way based on the root of future birth. "At what time," and so forth.
"Because after birth, ignorance arises. This phrase seeks the beginning of delusion. It is because there is no "non-birth" that the ignorance of existence arises.

Since the Tathāgata has no basis for delusion and thus attains Buddhahood, it is only when he has necessarily given rise to the Way of the Original Buddha that the Tathāgata can manifest its teaching.
Because ignorance exists, subsequent arising occurs; because of this, sentient beings possess afflictions.
This implies that the Buddha inherently accomplished by sentient beings is none other than all the Tathāgatas of the present.
If the inherently accomplished Buddha possesses subsequently arising ignorance, how could all the Tathāgatas be free from afflictions that arise again?
This single doubt arises because the two preceding doubts—regarding the false and the truly accomplished—are both difficult to resolve. Therefore, one seeks [an answer] in...

From beginning to end, these two stand established as a pair. When one investigates the root of doubt, it all originates from the state of ignorance; the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) undergoes successive false estimations, resulting in the three delusions.
These combine with the textual [analysis] of the falsely existent and the truly established, forming two sections that together constitute the "Exposition of Doubts Regarding Fundamental Awakening.
This concludes the section on Fundamental Awakening. Second, the Request for Further Instruction to Sever Doubts.

I only pray that you will not abandon your unimpeded great compassion; for the sake of all bodhisattvas, reveal the treasury of secrets, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, enable them to hear such a definitive dharma-gate of the Sūtra teachings so that they may forever sever doubt and regret.
The passage consists of two sentences requesting further instruction to resolve doubts: "I only pray that... and "...for the sake of all beings...
"I only pray" (*vīraṇa*) means to petition the Buddha. "Do not abandon [them]" refers to the World-Honored One’s manifest teaching that sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened;
this perfectly harmonious, abiding, and equal Dharma assembly is indeed an unobstructed great compassion. Therefore...
Now, I further entreat you not to abandon this great compassion. This phrase is a request for the Buddha to grant permission to speak. Regarding "opening the secret treasury":

the fundamental, originally accomplished awakening—the perfect, pure nature—is the treasury in which all phenomena abide and are maintained. Its indestructibility and non-confusion constitute its secrecy;
the removal of doubt and the generation of faith constitute its opening. "Thus" refers to the fundamental accomplishment that has been revealed and made manifest.
The Buddha’s awakening is as explained in the *Sūtra* and so forth, following the previous interpretation. Regarding the phrase "permanently severing doubt and regret":

it refers to definitively resolving the truth regarding the existence or non-existence of reality and delusion, and attaining the perfect clarity of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and pure faith. This sentence requests the severing of what is doubted.

The preceding section on "Presenting Doubts" and the section on "Original Enlightenment" together constitute the "Application for Request"; this concludes the subsequent section on "Benefits. This is now joined with the section on "Rejoicing at Hearing [the Teaching]" which concerns present benefits.

The section on "Summarizing the Request for Instruction" is concluded. This connects to the section on "The Inquiry Concerning Dignified Conduct," which concludes the subsection on "The Sequence of Describing the Sounds of Ritual.
Second, the conclusion of the sequence from beginning to end.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.

The explanation of the phrases follows the previous pattern. The preceding sections—the Preface, the Questions, the Ritual, and the Phonology—collectively complete the three sections of the Preface and Questions.

The section on the general introduction concluding the inquiry of the Bodhisattvas is finished. Second, the section on the general introduction describing the World-Honored One’s response, which is divided into two parts.
First, the long list of names showing the opening [of the teaching], which is divided into two. First, the introduction praising and granting permission, which is divided into two.
First, praising the request for instruction and benefit, which is divided into two. First, praising the fundamental awakening of the teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound secret, ultimate skillful means—the supreme instruction and definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna for these bodhisattvas."
The four phrases beginning with "When" praise the fundamental awakening (prakṛti-bodhi) that is the basis of the teaching. The two phrases beginning with "You all... serve as a general illustration.
The phrase "These various... refers to the following: "Profoundly secret" means that the awakening of original Buddhahood possesses a nature free from arising and ceasing;

"ultimate skillful means" means realizing that delusion has no beginning and knowing that the truth is perfect, constant, and eternal. This phrase praises the doubts and requests presented [in the preceding text].
The Teaching. Regarding the "supreme instruction": it is the perfectly luminous, pure awakening in which sentient beings and Buddhas are equal. Regarding the "definitive Mahāyāna":
it is the accomplishment of awakened mind wherein there is neither cultivation nor realization. This phrase praises the requested teaching and manifests its benefits.
Second, praising the benefits eliminates doubt.
This enables the Bodhisattvas training in the ten directions and all sentient beings of the final age to attain resolute faith and forever sever doubt and regret.
This section consists of two phrases: one praising the benefit and one severing doubt. "Is able to" and so forth constitutes the first; "forever sever doubt and regret" constitutes the second.

Regarding the phrase "Able to cause the ten directions... and so forth: when true and false delusions are shattered, pure faith is thereby established; this is the universal gateway for cultivation and study.
For one who attains decisive faith, awakening and fulfillment constitute the very foundation of Buddhahood.

This phrase refers to realizing the truth. Regarding "Permanently severing doubt and regret": permanently severing ignorance means no longer being deluded or distressed regarding enlightenment. This phrase refers to eliminating delusion. [These two] are conjoined.
The preceding section on the joint praise and request for instruction is concluded. Second, the granting of the answer and the entrustment of the reception, which is divided into two parts.
First, the entrustment to listen attentively:
"Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."
The explanation of the phrases follows the previous pattern. Second, having received the instruction, they remained silent.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, having received the command with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
The examples for the analysis of phrases are as before. The preceding combined section on the "Acceptance of the Request" (sūcanā-parigraha) is concluded.

The preceding combined section on the "Praise and Request for Instruction" (anuśāsana-prārthanā), which was subsumed under the initial section on "Praise and Acceptance," is also concluded. Next, the exposition of the "Direct Answer" (prativacana) is divided into two parts.

First, showing the instruction on fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi), which opens into two. First, manifesting the arising of delusion and the production of afflictions, which opens into two. First, delusion regarding the wheel [of saṃsāra] and the loss of awakening, which opens into two.
First, delusion regarding the nature and characteristics of the wheel, which opens into two. First, enumerating and demonstrating, which opens into two. First, all the characteristics of the wheel.

"Good son, all worlds—with their beginnings and ends, arising and ceasing, before and after, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, starting and stopping—these constitute two phrases of the 'All' (sarva) wheel-signs.
Good son, [the term] 'one phrase' refers to the 'All' (sarva), and the subsequent 'all... and so forth' (sarva-ādi) constitutes one phrase."
"All worlds" refers to both the sentient and the insentient realms. "Beginning and end" refers to the characteristic of temporal segmentation.

"Arising and ceasing" refers to the characteristic of the life-span. "Before and after" refers to the characteristic of temporal position. "Existence and non-existence" refers to the characteristic of concealment and manifestation. "Gathering and dispersing" refers to the characteristic of separation and union.
"Starting and stopping" refers to the characteristic of activity and rest. These twelve characteristics are present in all delusive phenomena whatsoever.
To not see the beginning and end is to see arising and ceasing; to not see arising and ceasing is to see before and after; to not see before and after is to see existence and non-existence;
to not see existence and non-existence is to see gathering and dispersing; to not see gathering and dispersing is to see starting and stopping;
to not see starting and stopping is to see the beginning and end. Thus, saṃsāra manifests, never having been transcended. This...
Because within doubt and delusion there is the formation of the three delusions of beginning and end as being real, these twelve [aspects] share the same characteristics.
Therefore, the entire title is intended to show that one is seeing the delusion of saṃsāra; it cannot yet be used to discern Perfect Enlightenment. Second, regarding the nature of all wheels:

Moment-to-moment continuity, revolving cycles, and various acts of grasping and rejecting constitute the nature of all wheels within every single phrase of the text. "Moment-to-moment" means that their essential nature is not permanent.

"Continuity" means that before a preceding thought has ceased, a succeeding thought arises in succession. "Revolving cycles" means that the objects of clinging are indeterminate. "Various grasping" refers to the diverse modes of apprehension.

As for "renunciation" (*śā*), it establishes the distinction between love and hatred; this is precisely the nature of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-vināśa*) of the saṃsāric mind.
The first four characters represent the nature of arising; the middle four characters represent the nature of abiding; and the final four characters represent the nature of changing and ceasing.

Possessing this saṃsāric nature, there exists the aforementioned saṃsāric characteristic. The former belongs to the characterized (*lakṣya*), while this belongs to the characterizing nature (*lakṣaṇa*). This is the saṃsāra of sentient beings.

The overall return [to the source] is established as belonging to this very nature. This is because the three delusions that arise wherever one may be are such that the mind of grasping and rejecting has not yet been forgotten;
thus, the distinction between the real and the false, existence and non-existence, and the fulfillment of the beginning and the end is made.
This concludes the section on "Collectively Displaying" (共成列示科) following the preceding section of the text. Second, the General Indication (總指).
"All these are saṃsāra.

This single phrase serves as a general summary. "All these" refers comprehensively to all phenomena—both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the defining nature (*lakṣaṇa*)—discussed above, indicating that they are all dharmas of saṃsāra.

This causes [the practitioner] to see that what is currently being questioned consists of delusions from which one has not yet emerged from saṃsāra. The preceding section should have been categorized as follows:

The section on the nature and characteristics of the wheel of delusion is hereby concluded. Second, regarding the loss of the realization of the Dharma, there are two parts; first, the explanation of the Dharma itself:
To discern Perfect Enlightenment while still remaining within saṃsāra means that one’s nature of Perfect Enlightenment is identical to the cycle of transmigration.
There is no possibility of escaping saṃsāra in such a state.

The three phrases of the text shall now be explained according to the Dharma. "Has not yet emerged from... and so forth is one phrase; "That perfection... and so forth is one phrase; "If one seeks to avoid... and so forth is one phrase.
Regarding "one who has not yet emerged from saṃsāra," this refers to the point where, within the delusory existence of the questioner, the true nature is established from beginning to end.
To "discern Perfect Enlightenment while not yet having departed from all superior natures and characteristics" means to seek the fundamental Buddha-enlightenment; this is the [third] phrase.
Delusion seeks the truth. That nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-gotra*) is the fundamental Buddha-nature of those caught in the wheel of delusion;

it is identical to that which undergoes transmigration. Failing to attain awakening and achieve abiding in equal purity and maintenance [of the Dharma], this phrase describes how one mistakes the truth for delusion.
If one were to escape saṃsāra, this would be a rhetorical device used by way of contrast; there is no such possibility, for such is the fundamental principle.
This is a correct refutation. This phrase cannot sever delusion; for it is only when the aspect of perfect illumination-awakening is present that ignorance is eternally severed.
If one still remains in the state of deluding the truth, how could one be able to refute delusion? It would simply be identical to continuing in the cycle of transmigration.
It is like a person who mistakes the south for the north: as long as the delusion has not been dispelled, they do not see the south, but see only the north.
"Direction. That which was originally the south now becomes the north in relation to one's current field of vision; this constitutes conformity with the process of saṃsāra.

There are two analogies that clarify this, each consisting of two parts. First, the analogy for the flow of sentient beings, which also consists of two parts. The first is the analogy for the flow of sentient beings.
For example, it is like moving one's eyes which can cause clear water to ripple; or again, it is like fixing one's gaze while spinning a firebrand, which creates the illusion of a circle of fire.

The two phrases beginning with "For example" illustrate the metaphor of the flow of mental states. The phrase beginning with "For example, like... and the phrase beginning with "Again, like... follow this. Regarding "moving one's eyes":
this refers to the eye that perceives objects. Regarding "can cause clear water to ripple": the clarity of the water is disturbed by the eye.
"Moving repeatedly like tossing waves. This phrase refers to the ability to transform that object. "The eye of one in meditative concentration" refers to the eye of clear vision.
"As if revolving a firebrand" means "even as"; the eye in concentration still revolves against that revolving firebrand.
For while a small firebrand circling inherently lacks the form of a wheel, when the eye of concentration confronts it, a red light is formed.

Regarding the "wheel" (*cakra*): this refers to the visual rays revolving and continuing as a circle of fire; hence it is said, "as if revolving. This phrase indicates the causal factor by which [the wheel] is turned.

To examine the meaning of these two metaphors: they are established upon the capacity for cognition and vision inherent in the eyes, which constitutes the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of the world of sentient beings.
Thus, one loses the pure self-nature and its sustaining power of *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. Next is the metaphor for the revolution of the two receptacles (*bhājana-loka*).
"The clouds move and the moon travels; the boat moves and the shore shifts. It is also like this.
Regarding the three phrases of the textual analysis, the analogy of the vessel’s transmigration consists of:

"the clouds move and the moon travels" as one phrase, "the boat moves and the shore shifts" as one phrase, and "it is also like this" as one phrase. "The clouds move" refers to the appearance of the clouds rushing along. "The moon travels" is due to...

The clouds rush about while the moon’s movement is revealed. Although the sun and moon revolve around Mount Sumeru and possess their own natural circulation, this is not a phenomenon of deluded motion.
Now, when the clouds move north, the moon appears to move south; when the clouds move west, the moon appears to flow east.
This is due to the movement of the clouds, not a movement inherent to the moon itself. This sentence...
"Turning that capacity": regarding "the boat moves and the shore shifts," because the boat does not remain stationary, one perceives the shifting of the shore.
This sentence indicates that the cause by which [perception] is turned is likewise so. "The clouds race and the moon moves, as when the eyes flicker at still water;
the boat moves and the shore shifts, as when fire revolves before a fixed gaze. This sentence combines the previous metaphors to clarify the capacity of seeing and its object.
In detail, the meaning of these two metaphors is established as the characteristics of the cloud and the shore within non-discrimination;

this refers to the flow and transformation of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) as its dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), whereby one loses the pure self-nature that sustains *pariniṣpanna-jñāna*.

Within this context, the moon and the boat should serve as metaphors for the subjective perceiver (*grāhaka-citta*), because the brightness of the moon and the capacity of the boat both possess the nature of being capable [of perception]. Thus, the preceding sections of the text together constitute the first section on the primary metaphor.
[The preceding section] concludes. Next, the opening of the two [analyses] is clarified. First, the analogy for the process of transmigration is explained:
"Good son, when the various rotations have not yet ceased, that object which supposedly abides beforehand cannot even be found."
The first two phrases clarify the metaphor of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). "Good son" constitutes one phrase. Regarding the phrase "all whirling... and so forth:
as for those whose whirling has not yet ceased, their eyes move and their vision is unsettled, such that they are unable to distinguish between the clouds and the shore, which appear to be shifting.
Regarding those objects that previously existed: even the rocking of water and fire or the movement of the moon and a boat cannot be found;

how much less could one ever find the absence of those various signs of rocking? This sentence clarifies that while the objects are hidden and manifest as distinct, the nature of awareness is equal and accordant.
Furthermore, these revolutions are not the fundamental saṃsāra; this is still [the case].

If even that [ordinary mind] revolves, how much more so when one awakens to the equality of all phenomena and accords with it? Furthermore, the defiled mind of birth and death is the very root of saṃsāra;

its being identical to the process of transmigration is sufficient for clear determination. Therefore, the preceding and following passages employ the terms "yet" (shàng) and "how much more so" (huàng shèng hé yuē) to mutually illuminate one another. Second, the explanation of the transmigration of phenomena.

How much more so for one whose mind revolves in the defilements of birth and death and has never been purified; such a person may contemplate the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) yet fail to transcend the cycle of rebirth.
This section contains two sentences clarifying the flow of phenomena: the phrase "how much more so... and the phrase "contemplating the Buddha...

The term "how much more so" (*kaihe*) is not used here in the same sense as the expressions regarding the revolving nature of delusion. As for "the mind defiled by birth and death," it refers to the faculties...

Regarding "fundamentally ignorant" and "never having been purified": if there is still the dualistic discrimination of grasping and rejecting, or of the real and the false, this phrase has not yet emerged from saṃsāra.
Regarding "contemplating the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment" and "originally achieving Buddhahood without returning": if one does so, one is identical to those who flow through cyclic existence;
this phrase provides no place for avoiding the wheel [of rebirth]. This is because the real and the false are not correlative phenomena; therefore, they do not exist as a duality.

Established. If one establishes that there is delusion, then truth is necessarily negated; thus, through successive errors and confusions, one seeks from beginning to end and actually achieves only the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).

This concludes the section on the combined textual analysis, which together with the preceding section completes the sequential explanation. The previous combined section on the initial metaphor concludes the categorization under the section explaining the illustration.

The continuous combination of the section on the Dharma-explanation concludes the section on the loss of awareness regarding the Dharma and its illustration. [The following] connects the combination...

The section on the nature and characteristics of the wheel of delusion concludes within the section on the loss of awakening in the wheel of delusion. Second, the conclusion reveals the arising of delusions:
"Therefore, you give rise to the three delusions.
This single sentence from the text concludes by revealing the arising of delusions. As for "therefore": because the mind of saṃsāra revolves within Perfect Awakening (vimala-bodhi).
For this reason, that which arises does so because of conditions; it is precisely through these causal conditions that the mind of saṃsāra gives rise to the three delusions.
As for these three delusions: the first delusion is false existence; the second delusion is the formation of the real; the third delusion is the beginning and end.
This is intended to demonstrate that the three delusions arise fundamentally from losing awareness due to confusion regarding the wheel [of saṃsāra].

It causes one to purify the defiled mind of birth and death so as to emerge from saṃsāra and enter Perfect Awareness (pariniṣpanna-jñāna). The preceding section on "The Confusion Regarding the Wheel and the Loss of Awareness" concludes the chapter on "Revealing How Delusion Gives Rise to the Three Delusions.
Second, "Revealing Awareness, Severing the Wheel, and Opening [to the Truth]" has two parts: first, a detailed revelation of the fundamental nature.

The awakening that opens [the gates] has two parts. First, the enumeration of metaphors to clarify the opening has two parts. First, the realization of reality as being without delusion has two parts.
First, the metaphorical clarification has two parts. First, the metaphor for the purity of nature has two parts. First, the removal of cataracts so that nothing arises.

Good son, it is like the illusory cataracts that cause one to falsely perceive flowers in the sky. If these illusory cataracts are removed, one cannot say that these cataracts have been extinguished and will ever arise again at some time. All such cataracts are likewise.
When the four phrases of the text are considered, there is no arising once the cataract is removed. Good son, one phrase is as follows: "For example... (one phrase).

"If the cataract of illusion is removed" (one phrase). "One cannot say... (one phrase). The cataract of illusion is a metaphor for the nature of delusion; the flowers in the sky are a metaphor for the appearances of delusion.
Because of the presence of the cataract of illusion, one perceives the flowers in the sky; therefore, once the cataract is removed, they will never arise again.
The "characteristic of the flower" (*puṣpalakṣaṇa*). This phrase traces the origin [of the delusion] so that one may know what is to be eliminated.

"If the illusory cataract is removed," refers to the capacity to sever delusion; this is the primary metaphor. One cannot say that "this cataract has already been extinguished," for this cataract is precisely an illusory cataract.
When will all various cataracts ever arise again? These various cataracts are precisely empty flowers; the flowers emerge from the cataracts.
This is a false perception; therefore, it is called "all cataracts. This phrase serves as a summary and clarification. Second, the inquiry and explanation regarding the absence of arising:
Why is this so? Because the two phenomena—the cataract and the flower—do not exist in mutual dependence.

The text consists of two phrases to interrogate and explain the absence of arising. The phrase "For what reason? [is the interrogation]. The phrase "Because of the cataract-flower," and so forth, [is the explanation]. As for "For what reason":
by virtue of what cause does the flower cease to exist once the cataract is removed? This phrase constitutes the interrogation. Regarding the two phenomena of "cataract" and "flower":
they are the nature and characteristics of the subject and the object. "Because they are not mutually dependent" means that the flower, as the object, arises from the cataract, as the subject.
It is not established through mutual dependence upon distinct intrinsic natures that there is a separate arising and ceasing; therefore, when the cataract is removed, the flower vanishes.

This sentence explains and clarifies this. Together with the preceding section, the "Analogy of the Purity of Nature" is completed. Second, the "Analogy of the Purity of Characteristics" is divided into two parts:
first, the extinction of the flower and the absence of its arising.
It is also like the case of flowers in the sky: when they vanish into the sky, one cannot say that the sky will ever again give rise to flowers.

Regarding the two phrases in the text, "the flowers vanish and do not arise," this corresponds to the phrase "as it is said" (*yathā... tathā*). One cannot say [that they arise again], as indicated by the phrase "as it is said.

The metaphor of flowers in the sky represents delusive appearances; their vanishing into the sky represents the realization of the fundamental true nature (*dharmatā*). This phrase serves as the primary metaphor.

Regarding the phrase "it cannot be said that... and so forth: when one is deluded regarding the fundamental true reality (*dharmatā*), illusory appearances arise; once the true reality is realized, how could there be any further illusory appearances?
This sentence serves as a conclusion to clarify this point. Second, the inquiry and explanation concerning the absence of arising.
Why is this? Because emptiness is fundamentally without flowers, as they neither arise nor cease.

Regarding the text, there are two phrases that interrogate and explain the absence of arising: "Why is this? constitutes one phrase, and "Emptiness is fundamentally... and so forth constitutes the other phrase.
As for the phrase "For what reason": this interrogative asks why no flowers arise further within space. Regarding the statement "Space is fundamentally without flowers":
flowers arise from illusory cataracts; they do not arise from space. As for the phrase "Because there is neither arising nor ceasing": where there are flowers, there is arising and ceasing.
Since flowers are fundamentally non-existent, how could there be arising or ceasing? Thus, one realizes that fundamental space is eternally...
"There is no arising or ceasing. This phrase explains and clarifies [the preceding]. Together with the previous section, the "Section on the Metaphor of Purity of Characteristics" is completed.
The previous "Section on the Metaphor of Purity of Nature," which was subsumed under the "Section on Manifestation through Metaphor," is now concluded. Second, the combined explanation.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are identical in their arising and ceasing; the wondrous enlightenment of perfect illumination is free from the cataracts of delusion.
These two lines of text clarify this together: one line concerning "birth-and-death" and so forth, and one line concerning "wondrous enlightenment" and so forth.

"Birth-and-death" refers to that which is falsely existent; "nirvāṇa" refers to that which is truly established. "Identical in their arising and ceasing" means explaining the falsely existent and explaining the truly established.
This is established. In general, the arising and ceasing of empty flowers is not yet the realization of the fundamental reality-mark (dharmatā) of purity.
Since the reality-mark is fundamentally without flowers, how could there be the arising and ceasing of birth-and-death or nirvana? This phrase clarifies the analogy of the purity of characteristics.
As for "wondrous enlightenment’s perfect illumination," it is the nature wherein no object of illumination is established and deluded agency has perished; it is free from the cataract of flowers.
This means: ignorance is forever severed, and all oppositions are transcended. It is because of the cataract of existence that there is arising and ceasing;
apart from the nature of the cataract, what could arise and what could cease? This sentence clarifies the analogy of the pure nature.

The preceding section on "Correlating the Analogy to Reveal" and the section on "Together Establishing Reality and the Absence of Delusion" are hereby concluded. This clearly demonstrates the fundamental attainment of Buddhahood and awakening, which cannot [be otherwise].
It cannot be said that they exist within the delusive, nor can it be said that they are established within the real. Second, the purification of the two delusions reveals the original reality.
First, the designation of the dharma reveals two aspects. First, pointing to the permanence of the characteristics.
Good son, you should know that space is neither temporarily existent nor temporarily non-existent.
Within this passage, two phrases point to its characteristic of eternal abiding: "Good son" constitutes one phrase, and "you should know... and so forth constitutes the other phrase.
"Should be known" means that one should immediately realize through the analogy of empty space; "not something temporarily existent" means that empty space has no beginning;

"not something temporarily non-existent" means that empty space has no end. This is to take up the preceding point regarding the empty space in which the arising and ceasing of the flower-appearance do not exist, and to decisively cause [the practitioner] to know it. Second, this demonstrates the pervasive nature [of the mind].
How much more so, then, is the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-avabodha), which accords with [all things] and constitutes the equal nature of empty space.

In this single phrase of the text, the pervasiveness of the nature is revealed. "How much more so" (*jùfù*) is a term denoting supreme excellence. "Tathāgata" refers to one who has fundamentally attained Buddhahood and awakening;
it is the wondrous enlightenment that is the essence of the fruit (*phala*). "Perfect Enlightenment accords with [all things]" means it pervades the ten directions non-dually.
"Conforming to it, one takes as the equal nature of space. This refers to the non-directional space manifested by awakening;
because its nature is without beginning or end, it is pervasive and equal, difficult to point out or designate.

It is not a space that is merely temporarily existent or nonexistent, which is used here as a metaphor to bring about understanding. This concludes the section on "Designating the Dharma," together with the preceding category.
Second, the illustration through analogy is divided into two parts. First, the analogy that clarifies original perfection:
"Good son, it is like smelting gold ore; the gold does not exist because of the smelting. Once it has already become gold, it cannot again become ore.
Even after an infinite period of time, the nature of the gold is not destroyed. One should not say that it was originally unperfected."
The five phrases of the main text are illustrated by the following metaphors: "Good son" (one phrase); "just as when melting... and so forth (one phrase); "since it has already been said...
and so forth (one phrase); "the sutra does not say... and so forth (one phrase); and "it should not be said... and so forth (one phrase). Regarding the metaphor "like melting gold ore":
this illustrates the removal of defilements from illusion. The statement "gold is not produced by the melting" means that the melting merely removes the ore to reveal the gold.

It is not that the gold was newly produced by smelting; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s awakening being fundamentally established. This phrase is a metaphor for destroying doubt and cultivating the awakened mind.

That it has already become gold is a metaphor for the extinction of illusion and the manifestation of awakening. That it does not again become ore is a metaphor for being forever free from all illusions.
This phrase is a metaphor for destroying doubt and delusion to give rise to the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). "Passing through infinite time" is a metaphor for having no beginning or end.
"The nature of gold does not decay" is a metaphor for being subject to no change or transition. This phrase is a metaphor for destroying delusion regarding the eternally abiding awakened mind.
One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished; nor should one say that by smelting away the ore, it cannot become ore again.
Gold is not gold that was accomplished from the beginning. This phrase serves as a concluding metaphor to clarify that the Buddha’s awakening is fundamentally accomplished.
The second part clarifies this fundamental accomplishment together:
the Tathāgata’s Perfect Awakening is likewise thus.

When a single phrase is properly explained, it clarifies the fundamental accomplishment. Regarding the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi): its being fundamentally the Buddha-enlightenment is also like this;
it is like the indestructible nature of gold—it is merely the removal of the ore, not the destruction of the gold itself.
It cannot be said that it is not originally accomplished gold. This concludes the section on the combined textual analysis of the illustrative metaphor.
This concludes the preceding section on the integration of the indicated dharma, which is subsumed under the category of the delusory and the pure as being fundamentally true.

This clearly demonstrates that the Buddha-enlightenment of the fundamental state is ineffable regarding its beginning or end. This concludes the section on the continuous integration of the true as being free from delusion, which governs the subsequent enumeration.

The section on the Manifestation of the Analogy is concluded. Second, the Manifestation of Ultimate Emptiness is divided into two parts. First, the Manifestation of Original Purity is divided into two parts.
First, the Twofold Emptiness of Phenomena and Self is divided into two parts. First, the Emptiness of Phenomena.
"Good son, the wondrous, perfect, and complete awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) of all Tathāgatas is fundamentally devoid of both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
[This consists of] three phrases: 'the emptiness of dharmas' (one phrase), 'all' (one phrase), and 'fundamentally non-existent' (one phrase).
The phrase 'all' indicates awakening; *bodhi* refers to the Truth of the Path; and *nirvāṇa* refers to the Truth of Cessation."

These two belong to phenomena (*dharma*). Now, by revealing that they were originally non-existent, it clearly demonstrates the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Second is the emptiness of self (*pudgalasūnyatā*):
there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood.

A single phrase from the text [states] the emptiness of self; the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished through *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, while the non-attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished through [the absence of these].
Enlightenment and nirvana are not established. Since the very essence of enlightenment and nirvana is non-existent, how could there be one who attains them?
Because enlightenment and nirvana do not exist as such, there is no Buddha who either establishes or fails to establish them.

That there would be a Buddha who either establishes or fails to establish them is to posit a self based on dharmas. Now, that there is no Buddha who either establishes or fails to establish them is precisely [the truth].
The non-existence of phenomena and the non-existence of self. This concludes the preceding section on the two voids of phenomena and self.
Second, the non-arising of cause and effect:
there is neither deluded saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra.
When a single phrase states that cause and effect are unborn, those who falsely perceive cyclic existence refer to the cause and effect of the six classes of ordinary beings;

those who do not perceive cyclic existence refer to the cause and effect of the four types of noble ones. Now, all of these are fundamentally non-existent. This is because where there is a dharma and a self, there are ordinary beings and noble ones;

but where there is no dharma and no self, what ordinary being or noble one could there be? That the dharmas and the self of both ordinary beings and noble ones are all absent is what constitutes purity.
The section on the joint establishment of the emptiness of both phenomena and self, which concludes the section on manifesting original purity, is finished.
Second, showing the delusion of defilement, which is divided into two parts: first, the delusion of annihilationism.
However, the perfected realm of the śrāvakas— in which body, mind, and speech are all utterly extinguished—
can never reach that nirvāṇa manifested through direct personal realization.

The three phrases [of the text] should be severed to eliminate confusion and delusion: "But all... constitutes one phrase; "body and mind... constitutes one phrase; and "never... constitutes one phrase.
As for "but all" (*dàn zhū*), this refers to ordinary beings (*pǎn*). The term "all" is a collective designation that encompasses all śrāvakas.
Regarding the "perfectly complete realm" of the śrāvakas, their realms are not actually perfect; this is entirely due to what they have established.

The light fails to reach the deceased, and they lose their perfectly clear nature. If ignorance is suppressed and severed, and a portion of the afflictions is purified, then a corresponding portion of the realms becomes perfect.
Those of the Two Vehicles realize the emptiness of persons and enter the perfectly luminous Dharma of the nature of emptiness;
they escape birth-and-death through segmentation and free themselves from the bonds of the triple world. Regarding the subtle, pure, and turbulent life-forces of all worldly beings, in an instant—

However, [the state] where [these] are shattered and split apart constitutes the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) that is perfected. This phrase refers to the dharma that is realized. Regarding the expression "body, mind, and speech," and so forth:

the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) consider the destruction of the seven consciousnesses and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to be the cessation of the body; they consider the severing of the discrimination of the six consciousnesses to be the cessation of the mind.
These two types of consciousness are the objects of names and conventions (*nāma-vyañjana*) and lack substantial reality. By severing these two consciousnesses, one is liberated.
"The cessation of linguistic conceptualization is what can realize me; one can never reach [the ultimate] through mere words," and so forth.

This refers to the fundamentally wondrous and perfect awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) that is the source of delusion. As for its direct realization, it emerges from the originally present, perfectly wondrous awakened mind of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This is because the practitioners of the two vehicles have not yet forgotten their realization of the non-existence of a self (*dharmanairātmya*), and thus still maintain a sense of a subject who realizes.

It is not that which was previously personally realized. That which exists in its own state—the wondrous awakening where there is neither dharma nor self, and both subject and object are empty—this is true personal realization.
The realization of those of the Two Vehicles does not reach this point. As for what is manifested as nirvana, it is the manifestation of quiescent extinction;
for all things are revealed as awakening, all things are the pure reality-mark (dharmatā), and all things...
All possess the nature of neither arising nor ceasing. Whatever is manifested is entirely *nirvāṇa*. There is no arising and no Buddha; both are unimpeded and accordant with reality.
Those followers of the Two Vehicles, however, are addicted to emptiness and rest in quiescence; they regard accumulation as suffering and cessation as bliss.
Therefore, they ultimately cannot reach that *nirvāṇa* which is personally realized and manifested by him. This sentence refers to the following passage.

The Tathāgata’s phrase regarding the realm of Perfect Enlightenment is without difference or sameness; yet, by manifesting the existence of cultivation and realization, one loses the fundamental principle of Buddhahood as Perfect Enlightenment, which is beyond cultivation and realization.
This leads to two types of delusion through attachment to existence. First, the manifestation of this loss.
How much less can one use a mind characterized by discursive thought (*vitarka*) to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*)?
The phrase "how much less" serves to manifest the fault; it is an expression used to highlight inferiority.

This is because the discursive mind possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is the very root of saṃsāra and the nature of the Truths of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*); these are what the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyānika*) distance themselves from.

If one has already lost the realization of the Truth of Cessation by means of the Truth of Suffering and its Origin—having failed even to attain the Buddha-awakening that is one's own original nature—how much less could one hope to realize Perfect Enlightenment through the conceptualizing mind that contemplates this Truth of Suffering and its Origin?

Here, the "measuring" of the conceptualizing mind refers to the three delusions regarding the beginning and end of the falsely perceived existence of the truth, which constitute the core of the inquiry. (2)
The explanation through analogy is divided into two parts. First, the analogy:
it is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly; one could never set it ablaze.

This refers to the first phrase of the current passage. A firefly lacks the nature of incineration; this serves as an analogy for the fact that the "mind-only" (cittamātra) contemplated here has no substantial reality.

Regarding the term *Sumeru*: it is a Sanskrit word translated here as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). Mount Sumeru is composed entirely of the four precious substances, serving as a metaphor for the majestic abiding of the light of Perfect Enlightenment (*Pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). As for the statement that "in the end, nothing can adhere to it":

just as a firefly cannot burn anything, much less burn Mount Sumeru, this most clearly demonstrates that the conceptualizing mind is incapable of fathoming the realm of Perfect Enlightenment. Next, [the text] clarifies:
If one enters the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s perfect quiescence with a saṃsāric mind and saṃsāric views, one will ultimately never reach it.

This shall be clarified in the following passage. A "saṃsāric mind" refers to the discursive mind—that is, the mind that continuously flows from moment to moment, revolving in a cycle of grasping and rejecting.
A "saṃsāric view" refers to the false notion of existence sought after, which begins by falsely establishing what is real.
"Finally ending the three delusions and entering [the state]" means entering it by means of the mind of saṃsāra.
"The Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction" refers to the fact that sentient beings are fundamentally awakened as Buddhas;
this is the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, yet in reality there is not a single sentient being who attains extinction—this is ultimate awakening. "Ultimately unable to reach it" is like a firefly.
That it cannot be burned by Mount Sumeru. This concludes the section on the combined textual analysis forming the analogy for clarification.
The preceding section on the combined exposition of loss concludes its inclusion within the section on the delusion of clinging to existence.

The continuous combination of the section on the delusion of annihilation concludes its governance of the section showing the delusion of defilement. The subsequent connection with the section revealing original purity is encompassed within the ultimate emptiness.

The section on Manifestation is concluded. Regarding the phrase "extreme emptiness" (*jìkōng*): it reveals that in the section on Manifestation, the two types of emptiness—the self and phenomena—and their causes and effects are non-arising;

and it demonstrates that in the section on Defilement, the simultaneous loss of both emptiness and existence constitutes the ultimate perfection (*jíyuán*). Thus, the realization of emptiness is perfected within Manifestation.

This causes the three delusions to be eliminated. Furthermore, the combined and arranged metaphors have been clearly presented; the section on the comprehensive summary returning to the detailed manifestation of Original Enlightenment is now complete.
Second, the conclusion on severing the cycle of rebirth:
"Therefore, I say that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra."
The main text concludes the essential point by severing the cycle with a single phrase. "Therefore" is a term that承接 (receives and follows from) what precedes it.

It refers to the section on the analogy of awakening to the removal of cataracts from the flower, wherein the nature of space is neither momentarily existent nor non-existent; this is the fundamental non-existence of the section on ultimate emptiness.

Dharmas are selfless and unarisen; because all that is grasped by both the noble and the ordinary—whether as empty or as existent—cannot reach the ocean of great quiescent extinction, one must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.

This means severing the mind of saṃsāra, which is the fundamental wheel of ignorance that acts as the sovereign master. By not giving rise to views of saṃsāra, one then eternally eliminates the three delusions and achieves [enlightenment].

Regarding the pure faith in original enlightenment (*prakṛti-viśuddha-bodhi*): the preceding section on the detailed exposition of original enlightenment, together with the section on manifesting the severance of the wheel [of delusion], is hereby concluded.
The combined section on revealing the arising of delusion and the production of afflictions, leading into the general demonstration of the teaching on original enlightenment, is also concluded.

Second, the demonstration of benefits and the severance of doubts is divided into two parts. First, the delusion regarding the cause that results in affliction is divided into two parts. First, the illusory and non-illusory fruits are divided into two parts.
First, the causes are indicated and divided into two parts. First, the fundamental illusory mind is shown:
"Good son, whatever thoughts arise from the existence of a mind are all the illusory vapors of the six sense-objects;
they are not the true essence of the mind."
The three phrases beginning with "When" demonstrate the fundamental illusory mind. "Good son," "there is activity," and so forth; and "all these are 'and so forth,'" and so forth.
Regarding those who engage in conceptualization: the discriminating false consciousness, through the union of sense organs and objects, takes on a nature that is neither existent nor non-existent.
That which arises from the mind originates from the deluded nature of ignorance, which is fundamentally luminous clarity.
That which is established in a single thought-moment is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). This phrase points to all the minds of saṃsāra;

"all such as these" refers generally to the nature and characteristics of deluded mind, which do not transcend the conditions of sensory objects and mental conceptions. "Sensory objects" (*viṣaya*) are the locus from which perception arises;

"conception" (*saṃjñā*) is the faculty that produces what is produced. Furthermore, the cognition triggered by sensory objects is the deluded consciousness of discrimination (*vikalpa-vijñāna*); conception...
The dust that is inhaled is ignorance, which deludes one regarding existence. The revolving and recurring deluded mind consists entirely of these two factors;

therefore, it is said that "all are. The explanation of "conditioned breath" follows the previous [analysis]. As for "not the true essence of the mind": this is not the fundamentally wondrous enlightened mind that is free from arising and ceasing;
it is entirely a phantom image of conditioned breath, lacking any substantial reality or nature. This phrase refutes and clarifies all...
The phrase "the mind is illusory and false" introduces the meaning of the following metaphors. Two metaphors establish the cause of illusion;
it is already like flowers in the sky.
The single phrase in the current passage establishes the cause of illusion. This clarifies that the various deluded minds lack any real substantial essence.
Just as flowers in the sky are not real, they lack the nature of a cause. This concludes the preceding section on the collective establishment of the initial indication of the cause.
