Next, the demonstration that there is no fruit is divided into two parts. First, it demonstrates the fundamental contradiction with the fruit.

Using this contemplation to discern the realm of the Buddha, a single phrase from the text shows that the fundamental [nature] contradicts the fruit. Contemplation is entirely illusory, while the realm of the Buddha is entirely real.
Using the illusory to seek the real results in the real not becoming illusory; this is what is meant by "fundamentally contradicting. Second, the two metaphors establish that there is no fruit.
It is like empty flowers further producing empty fruits; such a succession of deluded imaginings has no basis in reality.
The passage consists of two sentences that establish the metaphor of the absence of fruit: "It is just as... and so forth, and "Successively... and so forth.
"It is just as empty flowers" is a metaphor for the mind of discursive thought (*vikalpa-citta*). "Further producing empty fruits" is a metaphor for [discerning]...
"Buddha-realm. This phrase reveals a contradiction. Regarding "successive false imaginings": empty flowers originally arise from false imagination;

now, seeking to produce a fruit of emptiness by binding them, is yet another false imagination. "There is no such possibility" clarifies that there is no such thing as a fruit of emptiness produced by binding empty flowers.
This sentence concludes the explanation. The intended meaning of this analogy is to clarify that using the conceptualizing mind—
Discerning the Buddha-realm: it is because one mistakes the Buddha-realm for a fruit of delusion that one seeks it among empty flowers.

Yet, how many have become entangled in the empty fruit of these empty flowers! This concludes the section on "Demonstrating the Absence of Fruit," which together with the preceding section forms the second part.
Previously, the section on "Identifying the Cause" was subsumed under the section on "The Illusory and Non-illusory Fruits. (2)
Illusion is not the true cause.
Good son, the deluded and floating mind, with its many clever views, cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment.
This passage consists of two sentences: "Illusion is not the true cause" and "Good son. The phrase "The deluded... and so forth constitutes one sentence.
Those with many clever views engage in successive false conceptualizations and are unable to accomplish the skillful means (*upāya*) of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

This failure is due to losing the skillful means of mental cultivation; thus, this section concludes by showing that the fruit arises from the cause. Failing to see the absence of the fruit, they do not realize the cause of delusion.
Therefore, while the previous section demonstrated the absence of the fruit, this section determines that there is no cause. This corresponds to the heading: "The Illusory Nature of Illusory Fruits."
The section on the delusion regarding the cause that produces the fruit of affliction is concluded. Second, the refutation of the question to reveal the benefit.
Such a distinction is not a correct question;
a single phrase from the text refutes the question and reveals the benefit. "Such a distinction" refers to this aforementioned delusion regarding the fruit.
Because there is conceptual differentiation, this is not a correct question. A correct question clarifies the cause and demonstrates the accomplishment of the cultivation of the fruit.
What is currently being asked concerns confusion regarding cause and fruit; it cannot serve as a standard for practitioners.

Rather, it is a supplementary inquiry intended to provide further clarification and benefit. However, because it does indeed provide such benefit, it was previously praised as excellent. It belongs solely to—

Because it is supported by the ancillary [sections], it is now set aside for clarification. The preceding sections on the "Combining Delusions and Their Fruits" and the "Delusion Regarding Causes" have together completed the demonstration of benefits and the resolution of doubts.
This concludes the section on the "Continuous Combination Demonstrating the Teaching of Original Enlightenment," which entered into the general long-range arrangement of the sequence.
Second, the summary verse provides a general overview in two parts: first, the introduction expressing the desire to proclaim [the teaching] again.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

The method for explaining the verses follows the previous examples. Part Two: The Exposition of the Verses is divided into two sections. First: Summarizing the Essential Meaning to Reveal the Teaching on Original Enlightenment (benjue), which is further divided into two.
First: Summarizing the Essential Meaning to Manifest the Delusion and Arising of Ignorance.
Vajragarbha, you should know that the nature of the Tathāgata’s quiescence has never had beginning or end.
If one contemplates it with a mind of saṃsāra, one immediately turns back; merely reaching the limit of saṃsāra, one cannot enter the ocean of the Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "there has never been a beginning or an end": this decisively resolves the third doubt concerning the true end and the false beginning.

Once this single doubt is resolved, all doubts regarding the manifestation of the false and the perfection of the true are simultaneously settled. Because one is deluded about the true beginning and end, one fails to attain the eternally abiding awakened mind;
consequently, the false views of saṃsāra arise. The entire body of teaching and principle presented in the long prose section is summarized herein.
Therefore, the verse reiterates this point. Second, it reiterates the essential meaning to reveal the wheel of awakening and severance.
It is like refining gold ore: The gold does not exist because of the refining;
Although it is gold from the very beginning, it is ultimately accomplished through refining. Once it has become the substance of pure gold, It will never again become ore.
Birth-and-death and nirvana, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are equally like the appearance of flowers in the sky.
This couplet sets forth the essential meaning to provide benefit and sever doubt.
Since even contemplation is like a magical illusion, how much more so the pursuit of what is false? If one can thoroughly understand this mind...
Thereafter, one seeks perfect enlightenment to realize this mind—that is, to realize this deluded mind. The verse commentary is concluded.

Together with the preceding prose, the section on the sequential narration of the World-Honored One’s response is finished. Combined with the preceding section on the Bodhisattvas’ inquiry, we enter the general summary.

The section on "Resolving Doubts to Reveal Enlightenment" concludes. Regarding the phrase "resolving doubts": there are three persistent doubts concerning whether the false exists, whether the true is established, and whether [enlightenment] has a beginning or end.

If these are not clearly resolved, one will continue to cycle through analytical distinctions regarding the original Buddhahood and enlightenment, becoming increasingly bewildered and unable to subdue or sever ignorance to reveal the original enlightenment (*mūla-jñāna*).
Now, with this chapter of questions and answers, the nature [of reality] is fully revealed.
Awakening is eternally abiding, without beginning or end. It cannot even be said to exist as reality, much less that it exists as delusion.

To know that delusion has no existence is itself quiescence; when the nature and characteristics of body and mind manifest before one, one eternally abides in nirvana—the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Awakening.
Second, showing the Dharma to reveal awakening is divided into two parts: first, the introductory narration by the Bodhisattva.
Xing asked Kai two questions. First, regarding the introductory inquiry that follows the sequence:
therein, this introduction reveals that Maitreya Bodhisattva, from the perspective of the mind of saṃsāra, was unable to enter into the Tathāgata.
In the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction, the Buddha commanded that one must first sever the root of saṃsāra.
This is to cause the overturning of non-awakening so that initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) may manifest the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

Out of compassion for sentient beings of the final age, fearing they may not yet know how to ultimately sever the deluded nature of saṃsāra and thus ultimately manifest the awakened mind, I have raised these questions; I hope for the benefit of the Buddha’s teaching.

To cause universal understanding: resolving the will to sever the cycle of existence and accomplishing initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*). Part Two: The Introduction, consisting of three sections and two divisions. First:
The Introduction, describing the ritual protocols, consisting of two parts. First: The introduction asking about dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

The explanation of the phrases follows the previous example. Second, the description of the request for instruction and the resulting benefit is divided into two parts. First, the celebration of hearing the present benefit:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, you have extensively opened the secret treasury for the sake of the bodhisattvas, causing the great assembly to deeply awaken to the discrimination between samsara and the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox.
You are able to bestow upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Way regarding Mahāparinirvāṇa."
One gives rise to resolute faith; no longer following the realms of saṃsāra, one does not give rise to views of cyclic existence.
Regarding the text, there are six phrases celebrating the present benefit of hearing [the teaching]: "The World-Honored One of Great Compassion" (one phrase);
"extensively for... (one phrase); "causing all... (one phrase); "able to bestow... (one phrase); "regarding the great... (one phrase).
The phrase "no more such talk" refers extensively to the Buddha’s unobstructed great compassion. This phrase celebrates the manifestation of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*).

"Deeply awakening to saṃsāra" means thoroughly penetrating the nature and characteristics of cyclic existence. "Discriminating between the heterodox and the orthodox" means not being deluded regarding the causes and effects of the true and the false.
This phrase celebrates the overturning of non-awakening (*a-bodhi*). "The fearless eye of the Way" means knowing...

"In attaining samādhi, one fundamentally achieves Buddhahood"—this phrase celebrates the initial realization of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Those who give rise to decisive faith" forever eliminate the three delusions of reality and falsehood;
this phrase celebrates the awakening to pure enlightenment. "The realms of saṃsāra" refers to the characteristics of arising and ceasing from beginning to end.
"Those who perceive them cyclically" engage in conceptualization, grasping, rejecting, and discrimination; this phrase celebrates the entry into *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*. (2)

After the request, [the Buddha] further explained two points. First, he explained the beginning of the teaching on initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*), which itself comprises two parts. First, regarding the accomplishment of the practice:

"World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to roam within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction (*mahā-nirvāṇa-samudra*), how should they sever the root of saṃsāra?"
The three phrases beginning with "When" describe the accomplishment of cultivation; the phrase "World-Honored One" [is the response]. The phrase "If there are...
and so forth marks the cultivation; the phrase "How... and so forth asks about the abandonment. Regarding "How should it be abandoned?":
this asks for what reason one desires to roam the ocean of awakening, and states that one must first abandon the root of saṃsāra. This refers to saṃsāra...

The fundamental nature belongs to the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*). To achieve initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), one must necessarily eliminate this non-awakening; as long as non-awakening has not been eliminated, there can be no initial awakening.
Fearing that [the practitioner] might give rise to further ignorance, I pose this question in order to bring about initial awakening so that there may be something capable of being cultivated.

The second [section], the differentiation of what is cultivated, is divided into two. First, the differentiation of the dharmatā of delusion and awakening is divided into two. First, the nature of the wheel of delusion:
regarding all saṃsāra, how many kinds of natures are there?
When a single phrase of the text resides within the nature of the wheel of delusion, for those wandering in saṃsāra through the birth and death of the three realms,
as to how many kinds of natures constitute the causal conditions for the formation of karma: since the distinctions within the cycles of the three realms are manifold,
if one does not request an exposition of these distinct natures, there will be no way to know what differs and what is the same, and thus no means to realize the fundamental basis.

Since there is an initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*) that must be severed regarding the attainment of one's place within saṃsāra, this question is posed to clarify it. Second, regarding the nature of awakening and cultivation:
how many distinctions are there in the cultivation of the Buddha’s bodhi?
When a single phrase of the text pertains to the nature of awakening and cultivation, those who cultivate the bodhi of the Buddha are, in fact, cultivating the awakened mind.

As for the various distinctions, these refer to the degrees of depth in one's realization; herein, through the severing of delusions and the opening of awakening, there is progressive advancement through the stages of the initial, middle, and final minds.
Without clarifying these distinctions, one will be unable to know the ultimate state. Thus, there is no duality between ordinary beings and Buddhas.
Since there is its "initial awakening" (ādi-bodhi), this question is posed to clarify it. This concludes the preceding section on the Dharma-nature of delusion and enlightenment.
Second, regarding the skillful means of teaching and transformation:
when returning to enter the realm of worldly toil, how many kinds of skillful means for teaching and transforming should be established to deliver all sentient beings?
Regarding the skillful means of teaching through a single phrase that lead one back into the midst of worldly toil:

manifesting bodies according to the various types of beings to gather and transform them through shared activities—when it is asked how many such kinds should be established, and so forth—it is because there is a distinction between delusion and awakening.
Although the gates of teaching are manifold, there must necessarily be a certain number of skillful means of teaching to be established that bring about ultimate perfection.

The Point of Return. Had he not requested instruction, there would have been no way to know what skillful means would cause all sentient beings to sever the root of saṃsāra and roam within the great ocean of quiescent extinction; therefore, he poses this question.

The preceding section on the "Dharmatā of Delusion and Enlightenment" together with the section on "the Differences in What is Cultivated" are now complete. This [section] clarifies that one does not become confused regarding the differences in what is cultivated.
Because the ultimate accomplishment of the practice of *bieyi* (distinctive benefit) is the initial awakening (*shijue*), they jointly pose the question.

This concludes the section on the combined inquiry regarding the attainment of the practice, which belongs to the category of requesting instruction on initial awakening. Second, the request for instruction on perfect enlightenment (*yuanwu*).
I only pray that you will not abandon your great compassion for the world,

so that all practicing bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age may have their eye of wisdom purified and their mirror-like minds illuminated, thereby attaining the perfect realization of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.
When Wén requested instruction from Yuánwù in four lines of verse, there were four sections: "I only wish... and so forth; "May all beings... and so forth;
"The eye of wisdom... and so forth; and Yuánwù’s response, "...I only wish not to abandon you... and so forth.

This [verse] reveals that the bitter fruits of saṃsāra are what the Buddha compassionately seeks to save; it thus opens up and manifests the originally wondrous enlightened mind, thereby accomplishing the initial awakening.
"Awakening. Now, because he requests further instruction on initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), it is said "without abandoning. This phrase is a request for the Buddha’s permission to speak.
"The eye of wisdom is solemnly purified" means to be reverent and pure; it refers to the clear and bright eye being free from the cataracts of flowers and the delusive marks of arising and ceasing.
"Illuminating the mirror of the mind" means that the great, perfect mirror of wisdom is equal, pure, and pervades all of space.

When one looks at it with cataracts, the appearance of arising flowers is produced, and the original luminosity is lost. When the clear and bright eyes illuminate it, the pure, circular light of the original radiance is revealed.

This passage requests an exposition of the non-dual, quiescent, and universally illuminating nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), which accomplishes initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
Regarding the phrase "perfectly awakening to the Tathāgata," and so forth: it refers to the ultimate initial enlightenment merging with the fundamental wondrous enlightenment (*mūla-pratibodha*).

"The Buddha of non-dual birth possesses all-knowing vision. This phrase signifies that the accomplishment of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*) brings about the manifestation of original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*).
The preceding section on the combined request for instruction regarding initial enlightenment, together with the subsequent section on the resulting benefits, is hereby concluded.

Furthermore, the combined section on the celebration of hearing [the teaching] and the present benefits is subsumed under the section on the description of the request for instruction and its benefits; this is now complete. This is followed by the section on the inquiry regarding the majestic demeanor of the introduction.
The section on the sequence of the ritual music and its categories is hereby concluded. Second, the conclusion of the introductory sequence:
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning and ending the cycle.

The examples for the commentary on the phrases are as before. The preceding sections—combining the introduction, the description of the ritual, the sounds, and the categories—complete the three categories of the introductory inquiry.
Connecting the introduction and inquiry, one proceeds to the subsequent section; this completes the general introduction describing the Bodhisattva’s formulation of the question.

Second, the introduction describing the World-Honored One’s response is divided into two parts. First, the long list of names showing the opening [of the teaching] is divided into two. First, the introduction praising and granting permission.
The opening section has two parts. First, the praise and request for instruction, which itself has two parts. First, praising the beginning of the teaching and initial awakening:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, you are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound, secret, subtle, and wondrous [Dharma]."
Regarding the meaning of this:

the three phrases within the text praise the beginning of the *pratyavekṣaṇā-abhisambodhi* (initial awakening) according to the specific passage; the two general examples refer to the phrase "you all," and so forth;

"profound" (*gambhīra*) means reaching the ultimate source of both the true and the false, exhausting the limits of conceptual thought; "secret" (*guhya*) refers to the [relationship between] the true and the false...

That the nature and its characteristics are both identical and distinct can only be known by the Buddha. "Subtle" refers to the nature of the limit of consciousness, which is neither empty nor existent.
"Wondrous" refers to the nature of pervasive awakening, which is both empty and existent.

This is the meaning of initial awakening, which is the meaning of the total realization of the true when delusion is exhausted. It is a profound, secret, and wondrous meaning; therefore, this is shown as praise.
Second, to praise the perfection of his realization:
it causes the wisdom-eyes of all bodhisattvas to be purified, and enables all sentient beings of the final age to forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra,
awakening their minds to the true nature of reality and attaining the patience of non-arising.
The three phrases of the first section praise and benefit Complete Enlightenment (Yuanwu). The phrase "causing all... and the phrase "causing [them] to... refer to the awakening of the mind.

Regarding the phrase "cleansing the eye of wisdom": "cleansing" means purification; it refers to the state of the pure, illuminating mark of enlightenment being free from the cataracts of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
This phrase signifies the brilliance of wisdom. The phrase "permanently severing saṃsāra" refers to the destruction of the fundamental...
Ignorance (*avidyā*). This phrase is the false purity. When the mind awakens to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) is accomplished;

when one possesses the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is maintained. This phrase is the realization of awakening. Together with the preceding sections, this concludes the section on Praising and Requesting for Instruction and Benefit.
Second, the granting of the answer and the entrustment of acceptance, which is divided into two parts: first, the entrustment to listen attentively.
"Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
The explanation of the phrases follows the previous pattern. The two disciples accepted the instruction and remained silent.
Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

The explanation of the phrases follows the previous examples. The preceding section on the combined text, which together completes the section on the response of granting permission and the entrustment of the teaching, is finished.

The preceding combined section on the praise of the request for instruction and benefit, which is subsumed under the initial section of the preface praising the granting of permission, is also finished. Next, the exposition of the formal response is divided into two parts.

First, decisively severing [delusion] to open the way for the wheel; second, manifesting the wheel to cause its severance to open the way. First, providing a detailed exposition of saṃsāra, which opens into two parts.
First, listing the delusions of the wheel:
"Good son, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, because of various forms of affectionate attachment and greedy desire..."
There is saṃsāra. This passage consists of two sections. First, the delusions of saṃsāra are listed: "Good son" (one phrase); "All... and so forth (one phrase).

Regarding "from the beginningless limit": this refers to the initial limit of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding "due to the existence of various [phenomena]": this refers to the eight aspects of primordial ignorance.
The essence of consciousness is deluded by its own mental states; when thoughts stir, grasping arises, establishing the nature of knowing and seeing.

Thus, the essence of consciousness within the six faculties confronts the six external objects, becoming deluded by their appearances and giving rise to grasping, which triggers a mind of攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging and seeking).

Its coarse and subtle cravings are too numerous to calculate, hence they are called "various. "Affection" refers to the internal mind, while "desire" refers to external objects; therefore, [this state] exists.
Regarding "saṃsāra": taking saṃsāra as a whole, it is established through karma arising from craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Thus, the four characters "you" (有), "you" (有), "si" (四), and "zi" (字) correspond closely with one another, clearly revealing the person. Next, the lineage (*gotra*) is explained in two parts: first, to manifest the root of craving.
If all beings in all worlds— whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—
all come into existence through sexual desire, one should know that in saṃsāra, craving is the root.
The first two phrases clarify the root of craving. The phrase "If there are... and the phrase "It should be known that... are as follows:

"If there are" is an expression used to provide analogies for the sake of understanding. "World" refers to the environmental world (*pratyaya-loka*), which is the locus where all four types of birth take refuge.
"All lineages" refers to the mental consciousnesses through which all four types of birth establish their lives.

This refers precisely to the nature and destiny (xing-ming) discussed below: the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—encompass the entire cycle of rebirth within the six realms.

Beings in the heavens and those in hell are born by transformation; ghosts may be born either from a womb or by transformation; and the "sons of ghosts" (*pūtana*) as well as terrestrial *rākṣasas* are born from a womb.

All others are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Humans possess all four modes of birth. The mother Viśākhā gave birth to thirty sons from an egg. Ordinary humans are born from a womb (*jarāyuja*).
The maiden Āmra was born from the moist interior of a withered old mango tree. At the beginning of the eon, humans were born by transformation.
Animals also possess all four modes of birth. The *garuḍa* and nāgas possess all four modes of birth. All other beasts are born from a womb. As for other birds...
Regarding those born from eggs, those born from moisture, and those born through transformation: all arise due to sexual desire. "Sexual" refers to sexual passion, attachment, and craving;

it is any defilement of emotion that is collectively termed "sexual. Even in the case of transformation birth, this is based on karmic defilement. To observe this according to the gravity of afflictions in the Desire Realm: for those dwelling on earth, there is physical union;
in the Yāma Heaven, there is embracing; in the Tuṣita Heaven, there is holding hands; and in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, [there is mutual gazing].
Laughing together at the signs of others' transformations, the Four Heavenly Kings and the inhabitants of the four continents are alike.

As for the other various classes of beings—those born from eggs, moisture, or wombs—who among them can be free from lustful desire when their minds are defiled and their vital energy is transmitted? Therefore, all are included within this cause.

Regarding the term "zheng" (正) in the phrase "zhèng xìngmìng" (正性命): the character "zheng" signifies the meaning of the fundamental root, which corresponds with the character "zhu" (助) in "zhu fā" (助發) below, forming a complementary pair. That is to say:
"Correct" (*zhèng*) refers to the designation for that which abides in the center as the sovereign master of the essential causes and conditions that bring all things to completion.
This character "correct" (*zhèng*) manifests the mind capable of cognition (*nényuán xīn*). Lust is the objective field (*suǒyuán jìng*) upon which it depends.

Indeed, for all types of sentient beings taking birth and receiving life, there is no instance where the three conditions do not harmonize: the father, the mother, and the subjective state of the self.
Emotion and perception envelop one simultaneously, neither preceding nor following; this constitutes the cause and effect of establishing one's physical life.
Although parents exist, if the emotional context lacks the recipient’s own emotion and perception to receive it, then the cause and effect will not be accomplished.
It can be seen that the birth of life and nature occurs precisely at the time of the parents' sexual desire, for it is therein that life and nature are established. Life and nature.
This refers to the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) being clearly manifest in daily life and its connection to the duration of a single lifetime.

However, this is merely the delusive conditioning-vapor resulting from the conjunction of the three conditions. One’s own portion of affective ideation constitutes the nature, while the parents’ portion of affective emotion constitutes the life-force.
The sharpness or dullness of human nature is simply the clarity or turbidity of this conditioning-vapor; it is the affective state of the parents that one receives and assimilates.

At that time, both the sentient being and the parents possess consciousness. When one receives the objective conditions of the parents' thoughts through the medium of one's own thoughts, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) is clear.

When one receives the objective conditions of the parents' emotions through the medium of one's own emotions, the vital energy becomes turbid. The length of a person's life depends upon the abundance or deficiency of this vital energy.
At the moment of receiving the parents' emotional and mental states, if one maintains a state of quiet mindfulness and does not immediately [succumb to them], [the resulting life will be long].
When one establishes the subject and object and exerts them, the vital energy (qi) gathers and becomes full.

If there is no silent mindfulness with which to maintain oneself, and one instead establishes the subject and object and exerts them, the vital energy disperses and becomes empty. Therefore, the life and nature of all beings fundamentally belong to the root and trunk of one's own thoughts.

If, during one's ordinary life, one realizes that all phenomena are illusory and does not falsely harbor greed and desire, then wherever one directs the mind toward rebirth and enters a womb, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) received will invariably be pure and full.

If one clings to appearances, is bound by attachments, and harbors much false greed and desire, then wherever one directs the mind toward rebirth and enters a womb, the vital energy received will invariably be turbid and empty. This is called "correct. This phrase points to the present.

Regarding the principle that "for all sentient beings, one should know that the root of saṃsāra is craving," this means one should understand that it is precisely because of lustful desire that their lives and natures are established.
This phrase is intended to provide clarification: if lustful desire is the cause, who could rightly establish their life and nature?
For apart from that which is fundamentally cherished, what else could possess the power to establish them? Therefore, it points [to this].
First, causing them to understand so as to perceive the root of saṃsāra; second, manifesting the desire to assist in continuing the opening [of understanding]. This has two parts:
first, opening [the discussion on] the causes and effects of body and life; within this, first, tracing back to the origin to reveal the arising of craving.
Because the various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
In this passage, there are two sentences that trace back to the origin of the arousal of craving: the sentence beginning with "Because there are... and the sentence beginning with "Therefore...".

Regarding the phrase "because there are various desires": it refers to the sexual desire of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), the contagion of emotional thoughts, and the engagement with sense objects (*viṣaya*).
All that gives rise to greed consists of various illusory and false objects that assist in triggering the nature of craving.
This triggers the arising of a craving mind, which produces thoughts of conceptual grasping and defiled attachment; when these mental states manifest, one establishes a physical life based on desire.
This phrase traces the cause of craving. Therefore, because of this assistance in triggering the nature of craving, there is the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings.
The uninterrupted cycle of saṃsāra constitutes a continuous succession; this phrase establishes craving as the fruit. These two explanations clarify cause and effect:
desire arises from craving, and existence arises from desire. Sentient beings cherish their lives, yet they remain dependent upon the root of desire; thus, craving and desire serve as the causes.
Craving is the cause and existence is the fruit.
To clarify this cause and effect through six phrases: first, the phrase "craving arises from desire" means that when there is a mind of craving and grasping, one perceives desirable objects;
this is the cause. Second, the phrase "existence arises from desire" refers to the reception of thoughts regarding one's parents and the resulting emotional defilement.

Now, there is the life-span of a single existence; this refers to the fruit. The phrase "sentient beings cherish their lives" encompasses the conceptualization of taking birth, as well as all emotional views that desire longevity;
this refers to attachment to the fruit. This, in turn, relies on the fundamental source of desire.
The fundamental source of desire is precisely the loving heart that gives rise to craving. Since the cherished life is entirely an object of desire, whenever desire exists—
Regarding the statement that "it is established through mutual dependence on craving," it is therefore said to "rely [upon itself]. This phrase serves as the basis for the cause;
the phrase "craving as the cause" means that craving gives rise to desire as its cause. This sentence clarifies that craving itself is the cause, and there is no other separate cause.

"Craving for life" constitutes the phrase regarding the fruit. Herein, "life" is established upon craving as the fruit. This phrase explains and clarifies that craving itself is the fruit, and that there is no separate fruit.
Taken together, this demonstrates that nothing other than the single mind of craving, circling and revolving, constitutes the seed-nature of saṃsāra.
This concludes the preceding section on the text, completing the section on the cause and effect of body and life.

Second, the suffering of the objective realm of retribution is divided into two. First, the specific presentation of the objective realm of retribution is divided into three. First, the karmic retribution of hatred and envy:

because various conditions of opposition and conformity arise regarding objects of desire, when those objects turn away from the heart’s affection, one gives rise to hatred and envy and creates various kinds of karma.
Therefore, one is reborn again in the realms of hell and hungry ghosts.

Regarding the three phrases concerning the karmic retribution of hatred and envy: the first phrase, "due to [the causes]... refers to the objective conditions; the second phrase, "[the result]... refers to the objective outcome; and the third phrase, "therefore...
refers to the arising of various states of opposition and compliance. "Arising" refers to the conceptualization of the mind of attachment. "Opposition" [refers to...]
This is not an object of one's cherished desires; that which accords with it is indeed an object of one's cherished desires. This phrase indicates that the mind arises based on objects.
When an object runs counter to the mind’s affection—that is, when it contradicts the object of one’s own cherished love—one gives rise to hatred and jealousy.
Because the object of non-affection appears before the mind, one first seeks to become weary of and detached from it, and thus feels hatred. Subsequently—
Envy arises from the desire to cause harm. Regarding the performance of various karmas:
all evil conduct—such as contempt, arrogance, provocation, destruction, humiliation, deceit, injury, and plunder—is established by a mind of hatred and envy.
This phrase indicates that karma is formed through the mind; therefore, it is said that one undergoes the retribution of the evil realms due to such hateful karma.

Because there is no distinction in the causes that bring about this state, "rebirth" occurs; having previously escaped, one now returns once more. This demonstrates that the cycle of *saṃsāra* involves repeated journeys back and forth.
This phrase refers to the experience of retribution according to one's karma within the three evil destinies: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Specifically, those who possess the highest degree of the ten non-virtuous actions receive their retribution in hell; those with the middle degree [receive it] as hungry ghosts; and those with the lowest...

This is the section on animals. As for those animals whose names are now obscured in the text, they are included within the category of hell-beings and hungry ghosts because their wording follows a concise style.
Second, the abandonment of the retribution of evil karma.
One knows that desire is to be reviled. Through revulsion for the path of karma born of craving, one abandons evil and delights in the good.
Furthermore, one manifests as a deva or human. This consists of three phrases: "abandoning the retribution of evil karma," "knowing that desire is to be reviled," and "craving and revulsion...

and so forth, ending with "furthermore manifesting as a deva or human. Regarding "knowing that desire is to be reviled": it means knowing that from the arising of greed, anger is subsequently opened [i.e., produced].
The gateway of hindrances leads to the three miserable realms (*durgati*), which are to be loathed. This phrase gives rise to the mind that seeks to sever desire.
Regarding "one who loves and loathes the paths of karma" (*karmapatha*): this means loving [the cessation] while loathing those paths of karma.

It refers to the mind delighting in liberation from the fruits of suffering and finding satisfaction in loathing the causes and conditions of evil karma. This is precisely the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā-mūla*) that lies latent; it must be abandoned.
Those who delight in the good abandon the ten unwholesome actions: the three of body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
the four of speech—falsehood, frivolous talk, harsh speech, and double-tongued speech; and the three of mind—greed, anger, and delusion.

They take pleasure in the ten wholesome actions, such as non-killing and non-stealing, along with the various lay precepts and codes of discipline. Thus, they completely cease all evils and uphold all virtues.

This phrase refers to the diligent severing of the practice of desire. "Manifesting again" indicates that after appearing, it again disappears; and after disappearing, it again appears—this is the realm of retributive results within saṃsāra.
"Devas and humans" refers to the various celestial beings and human beings. If one is endowed with the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions, one receives the retribution of the desire heavens.

If one is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one receives the retribution of the form heavens. By cultivating the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one attains the formless [heavens].

The retribution of the heavens: if one possesses the middle grade of the ten wholesome actions, one receives the retribution of the human realm; if the lower grade, one receives the retribution of an asura.

That the asuras are not mentioned here is due to the brevity of the text; they are also included within the phrase "humans and devas. This phrase concerns receiving retribution according to one's karma.
Second is the abandonment of the karma of craving and its retribution.

Furthermore, because one knows that all cravings are to be loathed, one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*), yet this still nourishes the root of craving. Consequently, there appear superior conditioned fruits (*saṃskṛta-phala*).

Regarding the text, there are three phrases concerning the abandonment of the karmic retribution of craving, and one phrase each for "furthermore, knowing... and "abandoning craving... [and so forth].

[This is] a phrase. Then he manifested [the teaching], saying: "A single phrase: because all craving is to be loathed. This means that since craving gives rise to desire, it is the root from which greed originates.
That craving which arises in the realm of desire is something to be loathed; this phrase inspires the mind to abandon craving.

"Discarding craving and delighting in relinquishment" means discarding that craving-mind and delighting in the Dharma of relinquishment; this is precisely the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the four dhyānas. Four.

In the sphere of infinite space, one becomes weary of form and takes space as the object; having relinquished space, one takes consciousness as the object; having relinquished consciousness, one relies on the sphere of nothingness;

having relinquished the sphere of nothingness, one takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the object. That which causes the root of craving to flourish again is this: there is no difference between relinquishing and grasping.
In total ignorance, one perceives that ignorance is the root from which craving arises; yet now, one treats relinquishing itself as [the cause].

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is that which perfumes ignorance, causing it to grow, be sustained, and flourish. This phrase establishes the proliferation of the formations of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃskāra*). Regarding "that which manifests":

this refers to the manifestation of the retribution of pleasure and equanimity, which possesses no separate functional capacity; it is simply the non-dual nature of the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), wherein cause and effect are entirely one, rooted in craving.
As for "the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*): in the realms of form and formlessness, consciousness constitutes the essential nature of the realm; this is existence (*bhava*).

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): as for "superior wholesome fruits," this refers to the excellence of the environments and inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) in the form and formless realms, which are obtained from the retribution of meditative concentration and surpass those of the desire heavens;
these are the fruits of superior wholesome karma. This phrase concerns the receiving of retribution according to karma.
This concludes the section on the distinct presentation of the objects of retribution, which together with the two preceding categories forms the [third] division. Second, the summary of saṃsāra.
Because all are within saṃsāra, they do not constitute the Noble Path.
The single phrase "all are within saṃsāra" serves as a summary of saṃsāra. Regarding the phrase "because all are within saṃsāra":

this refers to the superior wholesome fruits of conditioned phenomena, which are identical to the realms of retributive experiences of suffering and pleasure; these are all manifestations of ignorance, belonging to a single class of seed-nature characterized by craving and desire.
Regarding cause and effect: that which does not establish the Noble Path is not the expedient means of Perfect Enlightenment; therefore, it must be severed, for it is the root of saṃsāra.

By cultivating Perfect Enlightenment, the preceding section on "The Realm of Retribution" (Baojing) has been fully presented, completing the subsection on "Suffering and Joy within the Realm of Retribution.

Furthermore, the subsection on "The Causes and Effects of Body and Life" has been integrated and subsumed under the section on "Manifesting Desire to Assist Continuity," thus concluding the connection. [End of Section]
The section on "Manifesting the Root of Affection" concludes the subsection on "Clarifying the Spiritual Lineage.

The section on "Synthesizing the Initial Enumeration of the Wheel of Delusion" concludes the subsection on "Detailed Demonstration of Saṃsāra. Second, the clarification of that which is to be severed.
Therefore, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and avoid the cycle of saṃsāra, they must first sever greed and eliminate craving and thirst.
Herein, two phrases clarify what ought to be severed: the phrase "therefore... and the phrase "first sever...". Regarding "therefore":
all causes and effects of the arising and nourishing of craving belong to saṃsāra and do not constitute the state of a sage.
This is because of the Way. Those who wish to escape birth and death awaken to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

those who seek to avoid the various cycles of rebirth abide in and maintain the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This phrase indicates the fruit sought. "First severing greedy desire" cuts off the cause of continuous succession;
"furthermore removing craving and thirst" excavates the fundamental nature. This phrase shows the causes to be severed. For if greedy desire is not severed, then...

If one gives rise to craving without ceasing, one cannot escape birth and death. If the thirst of craving is not eliminated, then the fundamental underlying delusions cannot be permanently stilled and the cycle of saṃsāra will persist.
This is the state of total non-awakening; how then could there be initial awakening?

Only by attaining the ability to free oneself from the bonds of the three realms and departing from the laws of arising and ceasing can one realize the perfect enlightenment of the equal self-nature. Therefore:

That which must be severed in its respective place is called "thirst" (tṛṣṇā). Because of the root of craving from beginningless time, one follows ignorance to grasp at the ocean of conditioned existence and mistake it for a bubble;
perceiving oneself as insufficient, one gives rise to craving and greed. It is like a person suffering from exhaustion and thirst who longs for a drink to sustain life.
The preceding section has provided a detailed exposition on the "Section on Severing the Wheel," completing the "Section on Manifesting the Wheel to Enable its Severance. Part Two.
Chapter Two: The Benefit of Changhua. First, the Severing of the Wheel of Saṃsāra in Changhua.
"Good son, the transformations and manifestations of Bodhisattvas in the world are not rooted in non-love. Rather, through compassion, they cause others to relinquish their attachments;
thus, while appearing to rely on various forms of craving, they enter into birth and death."
The three phrases clarify the severance of the wheel [of samsara]. "Good son" is one phrase; "Bodhisattva... and so forth is one phrase; and "merely...

and so forth is one phrase. Regarding "the transformations of a bodhisattva," this refers to a bodhisattva who enters into the realm of afflictions, assuming various forms according to the species [to be saved].
Regarding "manifesting in the world," this refers to manifesting within the world with a body identical to that of all sentient beings.
Life and its support (the physical body) are not distinct; that which is not based on craving is the root.

Craving is the very foundation of saṃsāra, yet the Bodhisattva has long since eternally severed it through teaching. Therefore, he does not enter into the defilements of the world with craving as his root.
This phrase demonstrates that the Bodhisattva has severed the root of saṃsāra; rather, by means of compassion, he gives rise to the function of illusory wisdom to cause those [beings]...
"Abandoning craving" means teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they may understand the root of saṃsāra and abandon all thirst for craving.
"Provisionally employing greed and desire" refers to parents; "greed and desire" indicates the emotional defilement of the parents' two drops of semen and blood.
This is because when a Bodhisattva enters the womb to receive a body, he merely borrows the semen and blood of the parents as the causal conditions for the four great elements to establish his form.
The physical body has no self-conceptualization or emotional attachment; it is sustained by the life-faculty through the defiled consciousness of sexual desire.

It departs when it wishes to depart and arrives when it wishes to arrive, exercising mastery over birth and death. Yet those who enter into birth and death do so because the four great elements of the physical body are impermanent;

their true nature is fundamentally one of arising and ceasing, being a combination of causes and conditions. The Bodhisattva, knowing this, enters [the world] intentionally in order to act in concert with others.
"Comprehensively transforming and guiding. This phrase indicates that the Bodhisattva’s illusory wisdom, which accords with conditions, possesses this capacity for manifesting and revealing.

This is because the original inquiry concerned the skillful means of teaching and transforming sentient beings—specifically the skillful means to be established for severing saṃsāra and cultivating bodhi.
Therefore, following the demonstration of severance and cultivation, it now demonstrates [this] by means of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding those whom he teaches and transforms: if one cuts them off, it is solely the root of craving; if one cultivates them, it is solely the Bodhi of the Buddha.
This demonstrates that the cause and fruit of the single nature are non-dual in terms of cutting off and cultivation. Second, the benefit of the wheel of cutting off.
If all sentient beings in the final age are able to renounce all desires, eliminate hatred and attachment, and forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra,
diligently seeking the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, they will immediately attain awakening within their pure mind.
The four lines of the verse conclude by describing the benefits of severing the wheel [of saṃsāra]: "If one... and so forth; "is able to relinquish...

and so forth; "diligently seeks... and so forth; and "in the pure... and so forth. One who is able to relinquish all desires will not give rise to craving and will sever the wheel of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, one who removes both hatred and attachment will eliminate the source that nourishes craving and sever its root.
This is saṃsāra; this is that which can sever it. The eternal severance of saṃsāra is that which is to be severed.

The logical synthesis of these phrases is the accomplishment of the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) that severs delusion. Those who diligently seek the Tathāgata remain far removed from the realization attained by the Śrāvakas.

The explanation of the "state of Perfect Enlightenment" follows the previous [section]. This phrase refers to the ultimate *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (始覺) being identical with the fundamental *tathatā-jñāna* (本覺).
Regarding the "pure mind," it is the original Buddha-enlightenment whose nature is devoid of subject and object, pervading all things with equality; thus, one attains awakening.
When the initial and fundamental enlightenments merge, the pure nature is perfected. This phrase signifies the attainment of non-cultivation and non-realization. Therein lies...

Regarding the "benefit of the resolution": within the context of the inquiry, one requests instruction on the perfect realization of all practices, which is the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

This knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata is inherently possessed by sentient beings; it is not realized through external verification. Being able to sever the wheel of delusion is the ultimate realization of truth.
Thus, both severance and realization may be manifested together, or severance and realization may be emphasized individually; yet it is not merely severance.
Furthermore, there is another distinct purpose for providing this proof. Therefore, we now provide a summary of the benefits regarding both abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
This causes one to see that what is abandoned is precisely what is cultivated, and what is cultivated is precisely the abandonment itself. These benefits are identical;
they are not two separate principles. Thus, those who wish to traverse the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescence must first abandon the very root of saṃsāra.

This is because there is no place for entering awakening apart from the state of severing delusion. This concludes the section on the "Concluding Benefits" which, together with the preceding textual divisions, completes the chapter on Manifesting the Wheel to Cause Severance.
This concludes the section on "Determining the Essential Wheel of Severance," which subsumes the preceding combined exposition on manifesting the wheel to cause severance.

Second, regarding the teaching on the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment, it is divided into two parts. First, revealing the distinctions of the nature (dharmatā), which is divided into two. First, a general clarification of these distinctions, which is divided into two.
First, revealing them by way of what is falsely imagined.
Good son, all sentient beings, due to fundamental craving, manifest ignorance, thereby revealing the five natures with their various inequalities.
Of these, three phrases are manifested through delusion; one phrase, "Good son," is [the teacher's address]; and one phrase, "all" and so forth, is [the subject matter].
Regarding the phrase "it manifests as... and so forth: "by means of fundamental greed" refers to the root of affectionate attachment, which is the characteristic of the mark of non-wisdom (*avidyā*).
"Manifesting non-wisdom" means that "fā" (發) signifies bringing it forth into revelation, while "huī" (揮) signifies spreading it out and distributing it.
This is because when non-wisdom deludes the true nature, the three subtle states of karma, transformation, and manifestation arise latently; at this stage, the mark of wisdom has not yet arisen.

The essence and nature [of ignorance] are profound and hidden, difficult to know. Because one continues to grasp at the marks of wisdom through fundamental craving and attachment, ignorance subsequently manifests as having an object;

thus it is said to be "elaborated. This phrase demonstrates that there is deluded function and reveals the existence of a deluded essence, which constitutes the defiled nature of the delusion to be severed. This brings forth the five phrases of nature; these constitute the delusion to be severed.
The nature of defilement exists as the nature of purity through abandonment and cultivation; this is for the purpose of manifesting their distinct differences, which will be fully detailed later.
Since all sentient beings equally realize Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), how could there be any difference in the nature of cultivating Bodhi?
Therefore, these delusions are shown to manifest the distinctions, so that one may know how to cultivate the Bodhi of the Buddhas.
First, it is to eliminate the severance of delusion. Second, it is to cause one to know that although there is cultivation of bodhi, one has not yet eliminated delusion;

if all delusions are purified and ultimate awakening is attained, then one realizes that sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning, and there is no longer any need for cultivation or realization. Second, this is based on the manifestation of the capacity for delusion.
Based on two kinds of obstacles, there is the manifestation of depth and shallowness.

According to a single phrase in the text, these two kinds of obstacles manifest through the power of false conceptualization; the details are fully provided in the passage below. Regarding the manifestation of depth and shallowness:
if the two obstacles that are currently active are deep, then the cultivation of bodhi is shallow. As for the two obstacles that are currently active...
If [the former] is shallow, then the cultivation of bodhi is deep. This arises from the manifestation of the subduing and severing of fundamental ignorance and craving;
it is the functional activity of the nature of delusion. This concludes the section on the general clarification of distinctions, together with the preceding textual division.

Because there is the nature of defiled conditions, there is the nature of pure conditions. Without the nature of defiled conditions, there would be no basis for establishing the nature of pure conditions. Therefore, from...
The false nature of subject and object is shown as the differentiation of manifestation. Second, the detailed enumeration of these differentiations is divided into two parts.
First, the differentiation based on the characteristics of manifest karma is divided into two. The first is the inquiry.
What are the two obstacles?

This initial interrogative phrase at the beginning of the text serves to clarify that, without understanding the two obstacles, one cannot know whether they are suppressed or abandoned, nor the depth of their suppression or abandonment;
therefore, this interrogation is made manifest. Next follows the explanation.
The first is the obstacle of principle (*li-zhang*), which obstructs right knowledge and vision; the second is the obstacle of phenomena (*shi-zhang*), which continues the cycle of birth and death.
These two points shall now be explained in sequence. First: [as stated in] the first phrase, "the obstacle of principle.

This refers to delusion regarding the true nature, which is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Second: [as stated in] the second phrase, "right knowledge and vision. This refers to the original enlightenment that is inherently perfected from the beginning.

"Brilliant and wondrous awakening. As for "obstruction," the portion of ignorance is manifest while the portion of wondrous brilliance is hidden; it is like a cataract on a flower, not a phenomenon that exists through mutual dependence.

This phrase refers to delusion regarding wisdom (*jñāna*). Regarding "obstruction of phenomena," "delusion" refers to the branch-and-leaf ignorance of the true reality (*dharmatā*), namely the various objects of desire involving attraction and aversion toward the favorable and the unfavorable, which continue the cycle of birth and death.
"Continuing birth and death" means transmigrating within the three realms. This phrase refers to delusion regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The combined textual analysis above completes the section on the characteristics of present karma based on the categories.

Based on these two obstacles—whether they have been suppressed and severed or not yet suppressed and severed—one relies upon the distinctions in the characteristics of karma according to the five natures in the present. This results in two distinct categories of nature and characteristics, which are further divided into two parts.
First, the interrogation and explanation, which is itself divided into two; first, the interrogation.
What are the five natures?

At the beginning of the first sentence of the text, there is an inquiry that does not clarify the characteristics of the natures being differentiated, nor does it manifest the latent afflictions to be severed.

Therefore, this inquiry must be made explicit. Next, the explanation unfolds in two parts. First, regarding the differentiation of the four natures within the true cause (*tathāgatagarbha*), one is... [in] existence.
The causes and effects of the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are divided into two. First, the nature of not yet having attained fruition.
"Good son, if these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, it is called 'not yet becoming a Buddha.'"

When the three phrases of the text have not yet realized the nature of fruition, there is one phrase of the "Good Son. If this [phrase] is repeated, it is called the "one phrase of not yet becoming a Buddha.
The term "if this" is a direct pointer to the delusions of principle—the cognitive obscuration—and the delusions of phenomena—the obscuration of birth and death.
Those who have not yet attained the severance of these two obscurations are, in their entirety, ordinary beings fully possessed of ignorance.
"Afflictions. This phrase indicates the practice. Those called "not yet Buddhas" are sentient beings who are fundamentally Buddhas;

they fail to achieve awakening due to obstacles of phenomena and principle. It is like gold in ore: as long as the ore has not been smelted away, it is called "unrefined gold," yet it is not that gold was originally absent.
If the ore is smelted away, the pure gold appears in its entirety. Likewise, if one subdues and severs the obstacles, the Buddha-nature is realized as originally perfected. Therefore...

This is established as a designation to manifest that the nature of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical, thereby distinguishing it from the externalist lineages that are fundamentally non-existent.
This phrase concludes the naming. Second, the causal nature has not yet been revealed.

If sentient beings have forever abandoned craving and first eliminated the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), yet have not severed the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), they are only able to awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
they are not yet able to manifestly abide in the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
When the four phrases have not yet manifested the nature of the cause; when the phrase "if all... has not yet severed the obstacle of principle;

when the phrase "but can... has not yet been able to [accomplish]...; and when the phrase "if all..."—where "if all" is a hypothetical expression—has not yet permanently abandoned desire, severed the delusions of views and thought, and realized that objects are illusory and devoid of a mind of craving or grasping. First...

"Those who eliminate the obstacle of phenomena" are those who have escaped the bonds of the triple world and departed from the death and rebirth of the segmented realm; this phrase refers to the shallow practice.

"Those who have not yet severed the obstacle of principle" are those who have not yet severed fundamental ignorance and are unable to attain quiescent conformity; this phrase refers to the profound obstacle.

Regarding the phrase "merely being able to awaken and enter," etc.: because one eternally abandons craving, there is no cause for accumulation; by removing the obstacle of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), one is freed from the fruit of suffering.
By cultivating the path, one realizes cessation (*nirodha*). Thus, the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is accomplished thereby; hence it is called "awakening and entering.
However, taking suffering and its accumulation as that which is to be severed, and the path and cessation as that which is to be realized, this still falls within [the realm of dualistic grasping].
This is accomplished through cultivation; it is not the nature of the original Buddha’s realization, which is beyond cultivation or proof.

Therefore, this [text] merely serves to distinguish [the two vehicles] by highlighting their failure in the causal-ground practice of the perfect enlightenment of one's own nature. The terms "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha" are both designations for the Two Vehicles.
Those who attain understanding based on words are called *śrāvakas*. Those who achieve awakening through causes and conditions are called *pratyekabuddhas*.
Regarding the phrase "this stage is inferior and has not yet manifested," it means that the perfected realm of the two vehicles has not yet reached the fundamental source;

because they have not personally realized the *nirvāṇa* that manifests and achieved the presence of quiescence (*śamatha*), it is said that it has not yet been manifested. Furthermore, this is stated to distinguish [the stage of the Bodhisattva] from the positions of the two vehicles.

Within this assembly, many bodhisattvas manifest through skillful means (*upāya*) to provide teachings according to the various types of beings. Because they conceal their sublime practices within, it is said that they have not yet revealed themselves.

Regarding the "bodhisattva realm": it is the state where one perceives all phenomena of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa with the perfect illumination of the eye, free from hatred or attachment, acting with spontaneous mastery and accordance with reality.
That one has not yet been able to manifest and abide therein indicates that the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) has not yet been severed. Thus...
"Abiding in the realm of ignorance"—this phrase negates the "Great. Together with the preceding section, this completes the section on the causes and effects while remaining entangled.
Second, the causes and effects of emerging from entanglement are divided into two parts: first, the accomplishment of the nature of the cause of awakening.
"Good son, if all sentient beings in the final age wish to float upon the Tathāgata’s great ocean of perfect enlightenment, they should first make a vow to diligently sever the two obstacles.
Once these two obstacles have been suppressed, they will be able to awaken to and enter the realm of the Bodhisattvas."
The five phrases of the main text constitute the nature of the cause for awakening. "Good son" is one phrase; "if all... and so forth is one phrase; "first one should... and so forth is one phrase;
"the two obstacles have already been subdued" is one phrase; and "then one can... and so forth is one phrase.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to roam freely," "roaming freely" refers to an empty boat drifting and tossing upon the waves, following the current without the dangers of wind and surf.

When obstructing the palisades and laboring with oars, this serves as a metaphor for attaining the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, which accords with the Tathāgata’s fundamental nature—tranquil, unobstructed, and sovereign.

This phrase indicates the aspiration; "one should first make a vow" means one should generate the pure great vows of a Bodhisattva, seeking the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment and establishing right knowledge and vision, thereby avoiding the error of falling into those peripheral and inferior calculations.

"Taking up diligence to sever the two obstacles": this means that by eliminating the obstacles of phenomena and principle and completely severing fundamental and derivative ignorance, one realizes that both the self of persons and the self of dharmas are empty.
Because the pure vows of a Bodhisattva are accomplished through this, one makes a vow to sever the obstacles;

this is followed by the pointing out of the goal. One should resolve to sever the obstacles and establish the practice to accomplish them. This phrase demonstrates the cultivation of the two obstacles.
Regarding "already subdued": because the root has been severed, the branches and twigs wither first;

the manifestation of the characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the subtle characteristics of nescience (*avidyā*) lose their nourishing moisture and are gradually extinguished, becoming profoundly hidden and without trace.

Thus, once birth and death have ceased, the state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) shall manifest before one. Because this state of quiescent extinction has not yet manifested, it is called "subdued. This phrase reveals...
Regarding the phrase "one can immediately awaken and enter," etc.: once birth-and-death has been extinguished, one is no longer deluded regarding quiescent extinction;
the returning light illuminates quiescence, and ultimate initial awakening merges with wondrous fundamental awakening to constitute the practice of conforming awakening.

As for the "Bodhisattva realm," it means that within the realm of all-encompassing awakening, there is no duality of aversion or attachment. This sentence constitutes the realization of the second [aspect]: the nature of the fruit of fulfillment.

If the obstacles of phenomena and principles have been eternally severed and extinguished, one immediately enters the subtle and wondrous perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata and the great *nirvāṇa*.

In this passage, there are two phrases concerning the fulfillment of the nature of the fruit: "if phenomena... and so forth, and "immediately enters... and so forth. The first phrase refers to the fulfillment of the causal nature, while the second phrase refers to the entry into the fruition.
"Sentences. Regarding 'the obstacles of phenomena and principle have been eternally severed and extinguished': Universal Enlightenment shines everywhere, quiescent and non-dual;

this phrase clarifies the practice. Regarding 'immediately entering the Tathāgata': this is the realization of total severance without further effort. This differs from the Bodhisattvas, who still possess a mind that seeks awakening.
This refers to the distinction between having already severed the obstacles and merely having suppressed them; that which has been suppressed remains [as a latent tendency]."

Because what has been severed has not yet been forgotten, the capacity to illuminate can still arise. When there is eternal severance, that which was severed is entirely quiescent, and thus the capacity to illuminate is non-arising.

Therefore, they are distinct. Regarding "subtle and wondrous perfect enlightenment" (*sūkṣma-adbhuta-pūrṇa-bodhi*): "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) refers to all phenomena; "wondrous" (*adbhuta*) means being free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
The combination of these two terms clearly manifests the pure nature of perfect enlightenment within the totality of phenomena—both their total immanence and their total transcendence.
"Fulfilling Bodhi" refers to the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm; "Great Nirvana" refers to the great samādhi of intrinsic nature.

This phrase fully reveals that the three virtues of the secret treasury are thoroughly realized from the cause through to their fulfillment. "Subtle and Perfect Enlightenment" is the thorough realization of the Dharmakāya from the cause;
"Fulfilling Bodhi" is the thorough realization of Prajñā from the cause; and "Great Nirvana" is the thorough realization of Vimukti from the cause.

The combined section on the causes and effects of emerging from entanglement (*niṣkrānta-saṃyojana*) is completed. The preceding combined section on the causes and effects while in entangment (*saṃyojana*) was subsumed under the section on the four natures of the primary cause (*hetu*);
that section is now complete. Second, the single nature of the false cause (*mithyā-hetu*) is divided into two. First, the manifestation of the fundamental correct nature is divided into two.
First, the absence of distinct causes is divided into two. First, the non-distinct cause of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-hetu*).
"Good son, all sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
Regarding this, there are two phrases that do not differ in their cause for realization: 'Good son' constitutes one phrase, and 'all [sentient beings]' and so forth constitutes the other."
Regarding "all have realized perfect enlightenment": sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas; how could there be any perfect enlightenment that has not been realized?
It is only that sentient beings possess the nature of realization—the realization of perfect enlightenment—whereas the Tathāgata lacks the nature of realizing perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is precisely the sentient being. Since they have fundamentally all realized it, what further realization could there be? This is...
Therefore, the nature of the fruit of fulfillment consists solely in the permanent severance and extinction of the two obstacles; that is, "severance" is synonymous with "realization.
This is what is meant by "non-realization," and this is what is meant by "universal realization. There are two distinct ways of cultivating the causes.

"Encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and following the practices for the stage of the cause (hetu-bhūmi) performed by that [friend]": at that time, the cultivation [of the path] may be either sudden or gradual.
Regarding the text, there are two distinct phrases concerning the cultivation of the cause: the phrase "encountering a spiritual friend... and so forth, and the phrase "at that time... and so forth.
"Encountering a spiritual friend" refers to one's own preceptor (upādhyāya). "Following the practices for the stage of the cause performed by that [friend]" means...
The Dharma practiced by the Master is the extraordinary cause for this. As for "at that time," it refers to the period when one has completed the cultivation under the Master.
Regarding the fact that there are both sudden and gradual modes of cultivation: gradual cultivation consists of the Three Vehicles, while sudden cultivation pertains solely to the One Vehicle.

However, it is precisely because gradual cultivation exists that sudden cultivation is revealed; otherwise, if there were only the One Vehicle, what would be sudden and what would be gradual? Now, regarding those who [practice] the sudden...
The gradual approach is that from which distinct causes originate; it exists due to a teacher and is not inherently present by nature.
This refers to the distinct fruit, which originally seeks the Buddha’s bodhi through the ultimate purification of one's own obstructions;
it is not something produced by dependence on others. Because cultivation based on others constitutes a distinct path, sudden and gradual differ. Therefore, in the sutra texts, based on that—

At that time, what has been accomplished is immediately designated as the "Manifestation of Names and Phrases. This concludes the section on the "Common Foundation of the Original Non-differentiation," following the preceding analysis of the textual structure.
One should understand that while there is no difference in the *hetu* (cause) of realization (*pratyāyana-hetu*), there is a difference in the *hetu* of cultivation (*bhāvanā-hetu*).
If one knows that all differences are illusory, then the nature of the fundamental non-differentiated *samyag-hetu* (correct cause) will be fully realized right before one. II.
Together they shall achieve the same fruition.
If one encounters the path of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi and practices correctly, regardless of whether one's faculties are great or small, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding the two phrases "together they shall achieve the same fruition," the phrase "if one encounters... and so forth refers to the fact that regardless of whether one's faculties are [great or small], and so forth.
This phrase means: To encounter a Tathāgata is a cause for celebration and fortune. "Unsurpassed Bodhi" refers to entering ultimate awakening and the perfection of the self-nature.
"The path of correct practice" refers to making vows to sever hindrances and achieve enlightenment; this phrase represents the fulfillment of the causes.
Regarding the statement that "the capacity of the root has no magnitude," it means that both person and phenomena are empty, being equal and pure; furthermore, there is no such thing as a "root."
How could there be distinctions of great or small? All attain the fruit of Buddhahood by awakening to the ocean-like wisdom of their own original mind, which is quiescent and extinguished.

This phrase refers to the perfect fruit. The preceding sections—“Conforming to the Original” (本) and “No Distinct Cause” (無殊因)—together complete the section on “Manifesting the Original Right Nature” (彰本正性).
Here, the right nature is used to manifest the false nature; this can be understood through error. Otherwise, the false nature would inherently exist.
Regarding "sentient beings," one cannot say they are all sentient beings who have fundamentally attained Buddhahood. Therefore, the World-Honored One first provides this indication.
Second, it is revealed that through erroneous views, two [categories] are opened up: first, those who fall into externalism based on their views.
If sentient beings, though seeking virtuous friends, encounter those with false views and fail to attain correct awakening, this is termed the lineage of external paths (*tīrthika-gotra*).
This section consists of three phrases: "If [sentient beings]... and so forth constitutes one phrase; "encounter those with false views... and so forth constitutes another.
This phrase—this so-called "one phrase"—is as follows: although one seeks a virtuous friend, it is actually a search for a true guide.

This phrase serves to distinguish those whose fundamental cause of birth is correct from those who encounter false views; those who cling to and grasp at the duality of subject and object regarding cause and effect;

and those who, failing to attain right awakening, give rise to false knowledge and views that deviate from the path to Nirvana. This phrase shows how reliance on such a teacher leads to delusion. Thus:
The word "this" (*ce*) is a term used to point to reality. Since those outside the Way (non-Buddhists) lack the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), their adherence to views results in perversion;
therefore, this points to reality to make known the source from which such perverse natures arise. This phrase concludes the naming [of the first section]. Second, it assigns blame to false teachers.
The errors and faults of false teachers are not the fault of sentient beings.

One should attribute every single word of the text to the false teacher. Sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened; it is by mistakenly encountering a false teacher that they lose what they should cultivate and realize, thereby becoming heterodox and externalist.
This is not a heterodox or externalist nature inherent in the original self-nature of sentient beings. Therefore, the fault lies with the teacher.

The error lies with the teacher and not with sentient beings. This attribution of blame serves only to further reveal that sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened from the beginning and possess no nature of delusion; they merely practice erroneously.

Once one knows how to seek a good teacher and attain the path of correct practice, then from the fruit back through the cause, there are no sentient beings who are not Buddhas. (This concludes the combined text of the preceding section.)

The section on "Establishing and Manifesting through Erroneous Misclassification" concludes. The preceding section on "Unifying to Reveal the Original Correct Nature," which subsumes the category of "Belonging to the Single Nature of Erroneous Causes," concludes.
