The continuous unification of the "Correct Cause and Four Natures" section, which governs the subsequent "Explanatory" section, concludes.
The connection to the initial "Inquiry" section, which is encompassed within the "Inquiry and Explanation" section, concludes. Second, the conclusion is manifested.
This is called the differentiation of the five natures of sentient beings.

The phrase "this is called" serves as a concluding summary for the preceding text. Regarding "this": it refers back to the five natures that have been explained above. Regarding "sentient beings": [it refers to those who possess these natures].
The designation for the fruit of ignorance is manifested through the five natures as they are developed by fundamental craving; it does not exist inherently from the beginning.

Therefore, what is now pointed out as the differentiation among sentient beings is none other than the ignorance of sentient beings, and thus none other than the differentiated nature of sentient beings.

Consequently, one attains the three non-differentiations, namely: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a philosophical commentary (likely on the *Awakening of Faith*), and the final portion of the sentence is incomplete.*
Thus, when there was no Buddha-nature, it was established as a designation; now that Buddha-nature exists, it is designated in relation to the existence of sentient beings.

Therefore, the five natures in their entirety belong to the fundamental category of sentient beings. The preceding combination of the sections on "Investigation and Explanation" completes the section on "Establishing the Distinct Characteristics of Natures.

The subsequent connection with the section on "The Characteristics of Present Karmic Activity" completes the detailed listing of the section on "Categorizing and Belonging to Specific Differences. [This concludes] the conjunction.

The section on "General Clarification of Distinctions" concludes the subsection on "Manifesting the Distinctions of Nature. Second, "Revealing the Merit of the Conclusion," which opens into two parts.
First, "Revealing the Achievement of Manifestation," which opens into two parts. First, "Becoming a Buddha through Compassionate Transformation."
Good son, bodhisattvas enter all worlds solely through the skillful means of great compassion to awaken those who have not yet realized the truth.
They even manifest various forms and appearances, confronting or conforming to circumstances, and by working alongside others, they transform them so that they may attain Buddhahood.
The three phrases of the main text describe the transformation through compassion into Buddhahood. "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "Bodhisattva," and so forth, constitutes one phrase;

and even "and so forth," and so forth, constitutes one phrase. "Only" (*kevala*) means solitary. To say that he alone uses the Great Compassion as a skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings through the One Vehicle refers to the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and his skillful instruction for those who have not yet awakened, thereby dispelling their delusions.

"All sentient beings who have not yet shattered ignorance within their fundamentally wondrous enlightenment"—this phrase transforms those who are deluded. "Up to and including" (*yāvat*) is a term of comprehensive inclusion.
"Manifesting various forms and appearances" means that one follows the categories and conforms to the physical forms of the four modes of birth and the nine realms of existence;

there is no form that does not receive [the teaching], and no signless state in which [the Buddha] does not appear. Regarding "circumstances of compliance and resistance," appearing as pure upon entering the state of sainthood is "compliance."

Entering among ordinary beings to manifest defilement is the "contrary" [method]. Those who share the same activities as them—whether ordinary or sage, whether defiled or pure—accord with them without distinction in order to gather and transform them.
To transform them so that they attain Buddhahood means to cause them all to enter ultimate, pure awakening and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This phrase is the realization of awakening; it thus demonstrates the knowledge of the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation. Regarding...
All sentient beings follow but a single Buddha-way, with no divergent paths of cultivation.

Therefore, [the text] encompasses the various manifestations above by means of inclusive phrasing, and below it concludes by manifesting the ultimate goal: transforming all beings to lead them to Buddhahood.
Second, this is entirely based on pure vows.
All are based upon the pure vow-power from time immemorial;

each single phrase of this text relies entirely upon that pure vow. Regarding "all are based upon": assuming physical forms and manifesting appearances—whether through contrary conduct, compliant conduct, or the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather and transform beings throughout all paths—none of these fall outside of this.
As for "pure vow-power from time immemorial": [it refers to the power of vows made by the Buddhas since beginningless time].

When a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind, they immediately vow to lead all sentient beings into ultimate awakening, free from the conceptual perceptions of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. This mind generated by the Bodhisattva is the mind of original enlightenment itself;
it is not of the nature of causes and conditions. Therefore, it is said to be "beginningless. This demonstrates the practice maintained by the Bodhisattva according to the teaching.
Among those who guide through transformation, it is the teacher who, having severed and exhausted ignorance, gives rise to causal formations.
For were ignorance not severed and exhausted, there could be no pure power of aspiration capable of eliminating the four marks of arising.
Were one not to enter into all things by relying on this power of aspiration, one would be unable to remain unimpeded and sovereign amidst circumstances both adverse and favorable.
It is not that there is no falling into error due to self-doubt and fear; rather, the Bodhisattvas of Great Resolve enter birth and death repeatedly and attain freedom from doubt and fear.

Furthermore, they do not fall into error because of the power of accomplishing their pure vows. This concludes the section on the accomplishment of the manifestation of virtue, which together with the preceding section forms the whole.
Second, the accomplishment of the conclusion of benefits is divided into two parts: first, making vows to seek Buddhahood.
If all sentient beings in the final age should give rise to a superior resolve regarding Great Perfect Enlightenment, they should make the pure great vows of a Bodhisattva, speaking thus:
"May I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and seek out spiritual friends."
Do not encounter non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles.
One should issue five phrases of vows to seek Buddhahood: one phrase for "if there are various... (諸云云), one phrase for "one should issue... (當發云云), one phrase for "should act...
(應作云云), one phrase for "seeking a spiritual friend" (求善知識), and one phrase for "do not encounter... (莫值云云).

"Those who give rise to the superior mind" refers to the generation of the mind that accomplishes awakening—the attainment of a mind that is directionless, pure, boundless like space, and free from grasping.
This phrase indicates the aspiration (*chanda*). "Should generate" means it ought to be generated.
Regarding "the Bodhisattva’s pure great vow," the explanation follows the previous [section]. Because one generates the Bodhisattva’s pure great vow, this is ultimate pure awakening.
Sever ignorance; only by permanently severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way. Therefore, one should resolve [to do so]. This phrase indicates the vow.

The expression "one should speak as follows" and so forth serves to clearly set forth the vow being made so that it may be fully understood. Regarding "abiding in the Perfect Enlightenment of the Buddhas":
through the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, which is perfectly illuminating and pure, one realizes that all sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened.
"May I fulfill the pure great vows of a bodhisattva. This phrase is a vow to attain the dharma of non-apprehension, which serves as the basis for what is sought.
"Seeking a spiritual friend" means seeking a guide of great compassion; this phrase is a vow to find a teacher who possesses correct knowledge and vision. "May I not encounter...
[refers to] avoiding those whose practice is inferior and who do not enter the ocean of awakening; it does not refer to those lacking a resolute mind (*adhyāśaya*).
That which is sought after is twofold: first, the severing of hindrances and the realization of awakening;

second, practicing according to one's vows to gradually eliminate all hindrances. When the hindrances are exhausted and the vows fulfilled, one ascends the pure Dharma-palace of liberation and realizes the wondrously adorned realm of Great Perfect Awakening.

The first section has two phrases concerning the severing of hindrances and the realization of awakening: one phrase beginning with "In accordance with his vow... and one phrase beginning with "When hindrances are exhausted...".
Regarding those who practice in accordance with their vows, they distance themselves from the four marks and realize knowledge and vision; as for those who gradually sever all hindrances...
The two obstacles—those of phenomena and of principle—are successively suppressed and severed. This phrase describes the entry into the bodhisattva realm.
"Obstacles exhausted and vows fulfilled" means that ignorance is eternally severed and one becomes universally pure; thus, one ascends the pure Dharma-palace of liberation.

First, regarding the purity of the Buddha-dharmadhātu’s body and land: those who realize the wondrously adorned realm of Great Perfect Enlightenment possess the universal purity of the Buddhas’ dharmadhātu body and land;
this is the perfection of purity and the accomplishment of the awakened mind. This phrase constitutes entry into the realm of the Tathāgata.
Together with the preceding section, this completes the "Section on the Accomplishment of the Concluding Benefits. The preceding [sections] have been combined.

The section on "Accomplishing [the Path]" within the Changhua [Prefecture] concludes its inclusion under the section on "Benefiting through Bonds. Regarding the establishment of these two sections as belonging to one category:
it is because when Bodhisattvas enter the mundane world to teach and transform others, their primary purpose is to awaken sentient beings;

and when sentient beings resolve to practice the path, this is entirely due to the Bodhisattvas' teaching and transformation. Since these two aspects mutually support one another, the tone of the scriptural text naturally [reflects this].

Connected and linked together. Having concluded the section on the classification and management of the teachings for manifesting the distinctions of nature and the cultivation of *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda*), this connects to the section on the determination of essentials for severing the wheel [of suffering], concluding the entry into the general long arrangement. Second, the summary verse provides a general overview in two parts:
first, the introduction expressing the desire to proclaim it again.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse.

The method for explaining the lines is as before. Second, the exposition of the verses is divided into two parts: first, summarizing the essential purport to manifest the definitive wheel of decision.
Maitreya, you should know that all sentient beings fail to attain great liberation solely because of their craving;
thus they fall into the cycle of birth and death. If one can sever both hatred and love, as well as greed, anger, and delusion—not through any partiality—one shall all attain the path of Buddhahood.
Hatred and love belong to the active manifestations (*samudācāra*); greed, anger, and delusion belong to the seeds (*bīja*). However, without love there is no greed; without hatred there is no anger;
and without greed and anger there is no delusion. Delusion belongs to fundamental ignorance (*mūlavidyā*).
Fundamental ignorance, through the active manifestations of love and hatred, triggers the karma of greed and anger, nourishing and perfuming [the continuum] so that the seeds are not severed. If...
There is no manifestation of craving or aversion that gives rise to the karma of greed and hatred; once their nourishment is removed, they are immediately severed and extinguished.
Therefore, the preceding verse speaks of severing aversion and love, while the subsequent verse speaks of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Regarding the phrase "and with" (*ca*), it means that by severing aversion and love, one reaches [the severance of] greed and so forth. As for the expression "not due to distinctions, etc.," this is because the two lines beginning with "if able" constitute permanence.
One severs the characteristic of ignorance; when ignorance is eternally severed, one attains the Buddha-way. What further differentiated nature could there be to rely upon?
The prose section demonstrates that the differentiation of the five natures fundamentally arises from the manifestation of ignorance.
Since there is nothing within ignorance itself, there is nothing to be manifested, and thus nothing to rely upon. The intent of this verse fully reveals that severance itself is realization.

There is no other witness. Second, by grasping the essential meaning of the teachings to cultivate perfect enlightenment, the two obstacles are forever extinguished. By seeking a teacher, one attains correct awakening;
following the vows of Bodhi, one relies upon Great Nirvana. All the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions do so through their vows of great compassion.

Manifesting entry into birth and death for those currently practicing, as well as for sentient beings of the final age who diligently sever all attachments and views, they shall return to Great Perfect Enlightenment.

The section on the introduction and the exposition of the Bodhisattva’s inquiry is concluded. Regarding the "Exposition of the Dharma" (*dharma-nirdeśa*):

by knowing and severing the root of saṃsāra, ignorance is subdued and eliminated; by knowing the distinctions between the nature (*prakṛti*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which manifest from the beginningless clarity, one realizes that original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is entirely devoid of cultivation or realization, and thus remains undeluded regarding original enlightenment.
By subduing and severing ignorance, one attains what is called "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*), for there is no such thing as non-awakening.
When non-awakening is absent, fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is revealed and manifested, achieving perfect purity.

This concludes the section on "Revealing Awakening" within the structural outline of "Joining and Resolving Doubts to Manifest Awakening," specifically the subsection "Severing Delusion. Regarding the term "severing delusion": because there is the resolution of doubts concerning fundamental awakening, [delusion is severed].

If there were no initial non-awakening (*abodha*) to establish ignorance (*avidyā*), then with the presence of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) as the revealed principle, there would be no subsequent non-awakening from which ignorance could suddenly arise.
When the anterior and posterior limits of ignorance are severed, this is the accomplishment of pure awakening;
through this, one attains compliance in cultivation, manifesting awakening to cut off delusion. This is the integration of the warp and weft to dissolve illusion.

The section on "Severing Delusion" concludes within the section on "Practicing the Severance of Delusion and Purification. However, it must first be preceded by the severance of delusion that is free from illusion, after which awakening is revealed.

Because sentient beings are deluded regarding their nature due to being deluded regarding appearances, one must first resolve doubts and demonstrate the Dharma so that they may leave behind all illusions;
only then can they distance themselves from all appearances and achieve the perfect illumination of pure awakening.
[The] characteristics. Only afterwards does one realize that they can be opened and revealed to eternally sever ignorance and accomplish the dharmic practices of the Tathāgata’s causal stage.
Therefore, these four chapters are combined and unified. The topical outline states: "Practices that Sever Delusion and Purify.

Regarding "practices that sever," it means that while nature possesses all [aspects] and characteristics possess all [aspects], one is not deluded regarding any nature or any characteristic; this is the general [principle].
The single awakened mind manifests itself; there are no two, nor three, such as the illusory duality of subject and object.
This is the thorough penetration of the self-nature and the path of correct practice through awakening. It integrates wisdom and severance to manifest true purity.

This concludes the section on the general integration within the category of the purity of the practice of severance and wisdom. For indeed, there is no aspect of the wisdom that severs, the objects severed, or the practice that is not pure.
This constitutes the Dharma-practice of the Tathāgata’s causal ground. It eternally severs ignorance and ultimately severs the cause [of suffering].
Now, if the severing of the cause is not clarified, it will be difficult to proclaim the realization of the fruit. Therefore, there are these five chapters above;

and herein lie the following five chapters, which concern the purity of cultivation for realizing the nature, serving as the thorough severance and realization of the cause. Thus it is said. So be it.

"Only the conditions of dust-shadows and breath. This phrase describes the Buddha’s manifestation of the truth. The first two phrases constitute the request for instruction on the sublime realization: "May [the Tathāgata] explain...

because both the state of severance and the state of realization are, from the outset, non-dual within the awakened mind, the ultimate perfection of that which is severed is precisely that which is realized.
Ultimate. Previously, through hearing the teachings and principles, the most supreme definitive meaning has already been fully revealed, wherein delusions are ultimately severed without remainder.

Now, for the sake of severing the non-ultimate [delusions] of the assembled multitude who have come, so that they may avoid the confusion of clinging to what is not realization as realization and the confusion of mistaking cessation for the ultimate purity, and because they have lost the ultimate purity of realization, I further request you to proclaim the distinctions of realization.
This causes them to know what it is that is realized and what it is that is attained; it enables them to know what it is that is abandoned and what it is that is severed.

Because they no longer have dualistic confusion regarding ultimate purity, it is said that [the Buddha] "repeatedly proclaimed" [the teaching]. The Dharma King explains this according to the previous [passage]:

"The nature of perfect enlightenment" refers to the absence of grasping or rejecting, gain or loss, abandonment or realization, and cause or effect. This phrase is the request for the repeated proclamation of the perfection [of the teaching].
This is for the purpose of knowing the distinctions between what is realized and what is attained. That which is realized is the subjective mind; that which is attained is the objective phenomena.
As for the distinction: what constitutes the realization of sentient beings, and what constitutes the realization of bodhisattvas?
"What is the realization attained by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One? This sentence is a formal request to restate the specific distinctions [of that realization].
It is because one is not deluded regarding the perfection of the awakened mind. Second, it concludes by benefiting those who hear the teaching.
This is intended so that sentient beings in the final age, upon hearing this sacred teaching, may attain awakening in accordance with it and gradually enter [the path].

Each phrase of the text concludes by summarizing the benefit of hearing the teaching. "This sacred teaching" refers to the distinctions in the realization attained through the request for its further proclamation.
"In accordance with" means to practice in accord with the distinctions of what has been realized, thereby following toward the enlightenment of perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

"Those who have attained awakening" refers to those who are not deluded regarding what has not yet been realized, and who do not cling to or begrudge what has already been realized, thereby attaining the primordial perfection of *bodhi*. "Gradual" means sequential;

it refers to the sequence from the realization of sentient beings to the realization of Bodhisattvas, and from the realization of Bodhisattvas to the realization of Tathāgatas. "Able to enter" refers to [entering] by way of the Tathāgata...
The realization attained upon arrival allows for entry into the ocean of Great Perfect Enlightenment and the accomplishment of complete Bodhi.

First, the single nature is all-pervading.

"Good son, the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a nature that exists as a nature; it arises in accordance with all natures. It is without grasping and without realization. This passage contains six phrases:
first, 'the nature is all-pervasive' (one phrase); second, 'good son' (one phrase); third, 'the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment' (one phrase)."

The phrase "the nature of non-nature" constitutes one sentence. "Arising in accordance with all natures" constitutes one sentence. "Non-appropriation" constitutes one sentence. "Non-realization" constitutes one sentence.

Regarding the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālaya-vijñāna*): it is the inherent nature that is not a dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); this sentence marks the fundamental principle. As for "the existence of the nature of non-nature":
it means that there exists the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment apart from the nature of the natures belonging to bodhisattvas and sentient beings. This...

The phrase "manifesting through differentiation" (*ju-zhang-li*) refers to the meaning of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of intrinsic emptiness as being unchanging. "Following the various natures and arising" (*xun-zhu-xing-qi*) means to conform to or follow.

It signifies that [the Buddha-nature] arises and manifests according to the differences between the natures of sentient beings and the nature of the Bodhisattva. This phrase reveals "identity" (*ji*).

This identity refers to the meaning of the true suchness of intrinsic existence as following conditions (*sui-yuan*). However, because it only follows conditions, it is unchanging; and because it only remains unchanging, it follows conditions.
Regarding conditions: if they were subject to change, they would have an end; how then could they pervade all things in accordance with conditions?

Since they exist in accordance with conditions, they are presently manifest; this is sufficient evidence that they are beginningless and unchanging. Therefore, the nature of self-awakening does not belong to another.

Regarding conditions, it is entirely neither separate from nor identical to the other. There is no grasper and no agent; this phrase refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). There is no witness.

"Nothing exists. This phrase refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, these five phrases may be combined into one, because the four phrases—non-nature, nature, and so forth—all manifest based upon the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Alternatively, these five phrases may be combined into three: the phrase on "Perfect Enlightenment" serves as the fundamental phrase;
the two phrases concerning "non-nature" serve as the causal phrase; and the two phrases concerning "no grasping" serve as the resultant phrase. This is because...

The fruit is that which arrives by means of causes. When there is a complete detachment from causes that are not of the nature [of reality], there is the fruit of emptiness of person, wherein there is nothing to be grasped.
When there is a complete conformity with all things such that they are identical to the cause, there is the fruit of emptiness of phenomena, wherein there is nothing to be realized.
Whether divided or unified, neither deviates from the meaning of the single nature being universally pervasive. This is the opening of the two-in-one aspect of quiescent extinction.
2. First, tracing back to fundamental quiescence:
within the true mark (*dharmatā*), there are in reality neither bodhisattvas nor sentient beings.
Regarding the text, there are two phrases that trace back to fundamental quiescence; "within the true mark" is one phrase, followed by "in reality there are none," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "within the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): within the nature of perfect enlightenment, there is the equality and non-duality of the boundless, pure, and directionless void.
This phrase indicates that it is a single mark. Regarding "in reality there is none": to speak of reality, there is nothing to rely upon, as it excludes illusory existence.

Regarding "Bodhisattvas and sentient beings": these are the names and marks of the noble and the ordinary; since they exist because of their dependence on the nature, they are not, in themselves, Bodhisattvas.
The nature of all sentient beings is the perfectly enlightened nature (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi-citta*).

Within this nature, how could there be the characteristics of those various sentient beings and bodhisattvas? Therefore, they truly do not exist. This phrase demonstrates quiescence; it is because it is solely quiescent.
This constitutes a single characteristic. Therefore, tracing back to the root, the second [section] elucidates quiescent extinction (*śānti*) by opening into two parts.

First, the interrogation and explanation: "For what reason? Both bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations. Because illusory transformations cease, there is no one who attains realization."
The text is divided into three sections consisting of three sentences: "For what reason? (one sentence); "Bodhisattvas... (one sentence);
and "Illusory transformations... (one sentence). Regarding "For what reason?": this phrase poses a question.

Since there currently exist bodhisattvas and sentient beings with names and characteristics, yet it is now said that they truly do not exist, it is necessary to inquire into and clarify the reason why they do not exist; [the answer is that] they are all illusory.

Regarding "transformations" (*nirmāṇa*): Bodhisattvas and sentient beings emerge from ignorance (*avidyā*). That which emerges by virtue of ignorance being fundamentally illusory is itself a transformation produced by illusion;
therefore, it is said that "all are [transformations]. This phrase explains why the names and characteristics of Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are not real, and thus do not exist in reality.
As for "because illusory transformations cease": when the delusions of ignorance are destroyed, the Bodhisattva...
When the names and characteristics of sentient beings are not established, there is no one who attains realization. Illusory appearances have no intrinsic nature;
as for dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, when they cease, they cease completely, and there is nothing that does not cease.
This phrase explains that bodhisattvas and sentient beings who are not real are entirely returned to quiescent extinction, and thus truly do not exist. Next is the analogy and its application.
For example, the visual faculty does not see itself. Its nature is inherently equal, yet there is no "equality" [to be found therein].
This consists of two phrases: the analogy and its application. The phrase "for example... and so forth represents the analogy; the phrase "its nature is inherently...

and so forth represents the application. "For example, the visual faculty" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*). "Does not see itself" refers to the fact that true reality is non-dual, without grasping, and without realization.
Because only the true mark (*dharmatā*) is non-dual and there is nothing further to be grasped or realized, in reality there are no bodhisattvas or sentient beings;

all are but illusory transformations. This phrase metaphorically clarifies that bodhisattvas and sentient beings, who have fully returned to quiescent extinction, are fundamentally one in their true mark.
"The nature is inherently equal" refers to the single mark of true nature (*ekalakṣaṇa-bhūtatā*). "There is no one who is equal" means there is no one capable of realizing it.

*Nature*. This phrase combines the explanation that because there is but one nature, there is but one characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Thus, in reality, there is no nature capable of being realized by either Bodhisattvas or sentient beings;
rather, all returns to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). This concludes the combined section above, which together completes the elucidation of the section on Quiescent Extinction.

The preceding combined section on Tracing Back to the Fundamental Quiescent Extinction is subsumed under the section on the Single Characteristic of Quiescent Extinction. [This concludes] the continuous combination.
The section on "The Single Nature Pervading All" concludes the section on "The Fundamental Equality of Dharmas. Second, the section on "Seeking Practice through Accordance" is divided into two parts.
First, "Differences Arising from Delusion":
sentient beings are deluded and inverted, unable to eliminate all illusory transformations; thus, they remain within the false effort of [striving for] extinction or non-extinction.
This clearly reveals the distinction.

Regarding the two phrases of the text: the phrase "sentient beings... and so forth refers to how differences arise due to delusion; the phrase "at cessation... and so forth refers to [the state of] extinction.

As for "sentient beings who are deluded," this refers to the fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*)—which is the root of delusion regarding direction and changing locations—and it is not something that can be suddenly destroyed.

Ignorance is identical [to the state of] the Tathāgata in that both obstacles are eternally severed; yet, insofar as one has not yet been able to eliminate all illusory transformations, this phrase refers to the impurity of illusory defilements.
Regarding "not yet extinguished within extinction," this concerns the depth of the subduing and severing of the two obstacles—of phenomena and principle—within the midst of false effort.
As for "the existence of subject and object in cultivation and realization," this immediately manifests differentiation, which constitutes [the stage of] *bhūmi*.
The phrase "establishing bodhisattvas among sentient beings" refers to a state where quiescence has not yet manifested. The two fruits accord with non-duality;
if one attains the quiescence that accords with the Tathāgata, in reality there is neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent.
The two phrases of the first section correspond to non-duality as the fruit. If one attains [the state], there is the phrase "and so forth";
if it is not attained, there is the phrase "in reality, there is none. "If one attains" is a term used for anticipation. Regarding "the Tathāgata’s quiescence is in accord with":

within the ocean-like wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, all things are perfectly integrated, such that there are no births and deaths, nor nirvana and samsara. This phrase represents the ultimate severance of delusion; in reality, there is no quiescence.

As for "extinction," there is nothing to be realized or awakened to; as for "quiescence," there is no one capable of realizing or awakening to it. This phrase signifies the perfection of the awakened mind.
This concludes the section on "Seeking Accordance with Practice" when combined with the preceding category.

This concludes the section on "The Equality of the Fundamental Dharma" when subsumed under the category of "Perfectly Awakened Nature. This is the response to the request for a restatement of the Perfectly Awakened [Nature].

Regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*): there are two distinctions that accord with nature, which open into two. First, abiding in obstruction and accords with nature, which opens into two. First, resolving obstruction, which for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) opens into two.
First, designating conduct, which opens into two. First, departing from delusion to open to awakening, which opens into two. First, deluded ignorance and indulgence in desire.
Good son, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been deluded by the notion of a self and by those who love this self;
they have never known for themselves that their thoughts arise and perish from moment to moment, and thus they give rise to hatred and attachment, becoming immersed in the five desires.

Regarding the four phrases of the text: "deludedly indulging in desire" constitutes one phrase; "all things, O son of good family" constitutes one phrase; "never [having spoken] such-and-such" constitutes one phrase;
and "therefore arising such-and-such" constitutes one phrase. The "delusory self" refers to the ignorance that initiates karma (*karmābhisamskāra-avidyā*).

The "attachment to self" refers to the ignorance that continues karma (*bhavābhisamskāra-avidyā*). These phrases are fundamentally endowed with forgetfulness and delusion, such that one has never known them for oneself.

To awaken without cause, yet for every thought-moment there is arising and ceasing, means that the illusory mind is impermanent. If one realizes the impermanence of the mind, one will not follow it in transmigration.
Not knowing this arising and ceasing is itself the grasping at existence and the craving for birth—this phrase refers to the lack of the illumination of wisdom.
Thus, when hatred and love arise, the deluded mind follows the cycle, giving rise to calculations and attachments toward favorable and adverse conditions.
Delusion: Those who are addicted to the five desires pursue the objects of the five sensory realms with such intensity that they forget their way back home.
This phrase refers to the active manifestation of defiled conditions. Second, awakening to the realization of weariness.

If one encounters a virtuous friend who instructs them to awaken to the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment and clarifies its arising and ceasing, they will immediately realize that the nature of this life is inherently subject to toil and anxiety.

This corresponds to the four lines of text where one awakens to the realization that awareness itself is laborious. If one encounters a single line of instruction from a virtuous friend, it is as follows: "One... [and so forth].

The phrase "revealing arising and ceasing" means that by understanding this single phrase, one understands all subsequent phrases. "If one encounters [this]" is a term used to express the hope for such an opportunity.
"A virtuous friend" refers to a Bodhisattva who enters the mundane world to teach and transform others. This phrase reveals the causal conditions for awakening;

"teaching and causing them to attain enlightenment" means that the Bodhisattva teaches and transforms others so that they may achieve realization. "The pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment" is the true mark (dharmatā), which is like empty space.
"Equally abiding and immovable, free from the illusory defilements of body and mind, as well as subject and object"—this phrase indicates the Real.

"To clarify that which arises and ceases refers to the realms of saṃsāra, ignorance, and the consciousness-mind"—this phrase indicates the delusory. "Thus one knows this arising" [is the realization].

"Manifesting before one's eyes, body, mind, and life-span—by nature they are weary toil. This means that the nature of the body and the seeds of life are inherently free. "Toil" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and their ego-clinging;

"concern" refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) and their grasping at objects. For the nature of the six organs is identical to the *bodhi* of the Tathāgata, yet it manifests as a state of weary toil due to staring into emptiness.
Because these weary organs exist, there arises the deluded consciousness of discrimination, which constitutes the nature of the wheel of continuity of karmic actions. It is not [inherently] so.
"Severing birth and death, one receives this body and life as its retribution. This phrase awakens the understanding of arising and ceasing.
Together with the preceding section, this completes the "Section on Opening Awakening from Delusion. Second is "Resting Labor and Resolving Purity."
Furthermore, if there is a person who has forever severed weariness and anxiety and attained the purity of the dharma-realm, yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstacle to themselves,
they will consequently lack mastery over Perfect Enlightenment.
The three phrases of the "When" (*yadā*) section serve to rest from fatigue and bring about liberation and purity. As for the subsequent "If" (*yadi*) phrase, it refers back to that same "If" phrase;

thus, regarding that "If" phrase: "If" (*yadi*) indicates uncertainty or non-existence, while "Furthermore" (*punaḥ*) indicates a transition. By means of the instruction of a virtuous friend, one is led to awakening;
once the laborious anxieties regarding the nature of birth are understood, one can directly sever ignorance and enter [the path].
The nature of pure awakening—now one understands this as "pure" while taking "obstruction" as "awakening. This is yet another point of delusion. Therefore, it is said:

"If, furthermore, weary toil is forever severed," this refers to the extinction of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). "Attaining the purity of the Dharma-realm" refers to the purification of the turbidity of sentient beings.
The cause for the understanding produced by this phrase is precisely that "pure understanding"; that is, the superior [realization] arises from the purity of the Dharma-realm thus attained.

To give rise to a conceptual understanding that grasps at realization and views as an obstacle to oneself means that one cannot directly sever ignorance to enter the ultimate purity of self-awakened nature.
This phrase refers to the formation of an obstacle based on understanding; it belongs to the delusion regarding objects of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the principle of ignorance.
"Hence" means because this understanding itself acts as an obstacle, one lacks mastery over Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

This refers to the meaning of sovereign non-obstruction. To lose it is to fail to attain the light of wisdom that perfectly illuminates without obstruction. This phrase contradicts the *prajñā* of the causal stage.
The preceding section on "Opening Enlightenment from Delusion" together with the section on "Establishing the Marked Practice" is now complete. Second, the conclusion of the title.
This is called the ordinary person’s conformity with the nature of awakening (*bodhi*).
A single phrase from the text serves as the conclusion for this title. "This" refers to the purity attained and the obstacles resolved.

It is called "the ordinary person" because that which is purified and resolved consists of the limits of practice; they have not yet exhausted the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and remain entirely within ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because they possess the noble lineage of wisdom (*āryavaṃśa*), they are called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). As for those who accord with the nature of awakening (*bodhātman*):

all distinctions between the severance and realization of ordinary beings and sages arise and cease within awakening; awakening neither arises nor ceases within anything. Awakening is the host, and all else are guests.
Whether arising, ceasing, or in a state of quiescent extinction, none can shake the Awakened One.
Therefore, from ordinary beings up to the Tathāgata, all are one in their conformity (*anuloma*).

As for the distinctions within this conformity, they arise from differences in persons and not from differences in the Dharma. Ordinary beings conform as ordinary beings, and so on, up to the Tathāgata.

This is naturally in accordance with the Tathāgata. It is like the five colors reflecting upon the light of a pearl; the light of the pearl is inherently one, while the reflected colors are inherently distinct.
Nevertheless, these colors appear within the light; it is not that the light enters into the colors—this constitutes "accordance.

The preceding section on the combined headings and sub-sections, which together form the "Section on Resolving the Obstructions of Ordinary Beings," is concluded. Second, regarding the "Awakening to the Obstructions of Bodhisattvas," two parts are opened.
First, the indication of practice:
"Good son, all bodhisattvas take views as an obstruction. Although they have severed the obstruction of views, they still abide in the awakening to those views.
Taking this awakening to obstructions as an obstruction itself, they lack mastery."
The four lines of the verse are as follows: "Good son" constitutes one line; "all... and so forth, constitutes one line; "although severed...
and so forth, constitutes one line; and "perceiving hindrance... and so forth, constitutes one line. Regarding "perceiving views and understandings as hindrances":

this means that when one perceives various pure understandings as being attached to the mind of deluded thought and discrimination, one fails to achieve the unimpeded light of Prajñā-wisdom. This line illuminates the increase of the intrinsic nature.

"Clarity": although one has severed the obstacles to understanding, even if one is able to distance oneself from all conceptual grasping so that there is no longer an obstacle of non-understanding, yet one still dwells in the perception of awakening;
the mind of discernment that perceives and understands these obstacles remains strong in its luminous illumination and has not yet returned to perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*).

This phrase indicates that awakening is not yet fully perfected. "Obstacles to awakening": the luminous illumination of awakening itself becomes an obstacle because there is still this luminous illumination of awakening.
There is no non-establishment of the objective; the hidden and concealed subjective mind is not the realm of the Buddha.

It is not that the nature of identity and difference is extinguished, nor is it something that cannot be reached by all identities and differences. Therefore, the obstruction of awakening is itself an obstruction.
Thus, those who lack mastery lose the tranquil extinction of unobstructed, compliant practice. This phrase refers to the extraordinary fruit of liberation. Second, the conclusion of the name.
This is called the bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening (*bodhita*).
This single phrase from the text serves as a summary title. "This" refers to the conceptual understanding (*vikalpa*) that is to be severed and the awakening in which one abides.

"Named a bodhisattva" means that one has already severed the obstruction of conceptual understanding regarding the purity of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is precisely the cessation of the measure of the dharma-realm. By means of the Buddha—

One who takes awakening as their own mind is therefore called a Bodhisattva. Those who have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*)—while practicing the mind at the stage of "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) amidst delusion regarding awakening—have no specific designation for the Middle Way. Because they still abide in awakening, they have not yet entered the stages. This follows the nature of awakening;

the explanation is analogous to what precedes it. This concludes the section on the Bodhisattva obstructed by awakening, which combines the textual headings and the classification of practice to form this whole.
Second, the cessation of hindrances is explained by opening it into two parts. First, the Bodhisattva of Quiescence opens it into two. First, the designation of practice opens it into two.
First, a general manifestation of quiescence:
"Good son, where there is illumination and where there is awareness, both are termed hindrances. Therefore, the Bodhisattva constantly maintains awareness and does not abide in illumination."
It is simultaneously extinguished together with that which illuminates.
In the text, three phrases collectively manifest this extinction: "Good son" (one phrase), and "There is illumination... and so forth (one phrase).

Therefore, regarding the phrase "there is illumination" (*yǎozhào*) and so forth: "having illumination" means to know with clear and lucid awareness; "having awareness" (*jué*) means that awareness is luminously aware.

Taken together, this refers to an awareness that has not yet realized the wondrous [nature], which establishes itself within the realm of luminosity. Consequently, the manifestation of both illumination and awareness is termed an "obstruction.

Where there is awareness, there must be luminosity; where there is luminosity, a locus is established. Thus, one loses the fundamental perfect enlightenment (*yuánjué*), which is universally illuminating and quiescent.
"Non-dual equality and conformity. This phrase reveals the obstacles to the awakening that abides. "Therefore" means because of these obstacles to the awakening that abides.
"Constantly awakened and not abiding": when awakening abides, it becomes non-awakening and constitutes deluded awakening;
by turning the light back toward awakening, one does not abide in luminous awakening. When there is no non-awakening, this is constant awakening. [This is] what is desired.
To attain constant awakening is precisely to not abide. How does one not abide? It is precisely through constant awakening. To state the essential point:

when there is no [clinging to] luminous awareness, this is called constant awakening; this is called non-abiding. This is because it overturns the previous state of abiding in awareness, thereby resulting in non-abiding.
Regarding "the illumination" and "the illuminator": illumination itself is that which possesses illumination, which is the objective dharma (*dharmin*); the illuminator is...
Thus, that which possesses awareness is the active self (*kartṛ-ātman*). That which is simultaneously quiescent means: when illumination ceases, the illuminator also ceases;
when the illuminator ceases, the illumination also ceases. Fundamentally, there is no duality of subject and object; therefore, cessation and wondrousness are simultaneous.

As for what is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirvāṇa*): awareness is utterly perfect and luminous, such that there is neither subject nor object. Thus, it is not the extinction of arising and ceasing, but rather the extinction of quiescence.
"Extinction. This reverses the preceding state of abiding awareness. Having lost the perfect clarity of that [abiding] awareness, one advances toward the constant awareness that does not abide.
Because of the perfect clarity of ultimate awareness, the illumination and the illuminator undergo simultaneous quiescent extinction.
The functional efficacy lies in the non-abiding of constant awareness; the extinction of subject and object is merely its manifest result. This phrase reveals the non-...
Abiding in the cessation of awakening. Second, the detailed demonstration of cessation is divided into two parts. First, the cessation of the sphere of mental activity is divided into two.
Initially, it is illustrated through a simile:
"For example, if a person were to cut off their own head, because the head has already been severed, there would be no one capable of cutting."
This shall be illustrated by two sentences of analogy: first, "For example... and second, "...as previously stated. Regarding the phrase "to cut off one's own head":

the "head" is a metaphor for the luminous illumination of awakening (*bodhi*). Because this luminous illumination gives rise to objects of perception, it serves as the basis for delusion and falsehood.
Just as the head is the support for the life of the body, so too is the cessation of the head a metaphor for departing from luminous illumination.

"Self-severance" is a metaphor for the non-abiding of constant awareness (*buddhi*). When awareness abides, luminous illumination is established; when awareness does not abide, luminous illumination is quiescent.

This luminous illumination is, in its original source, none other than awareness; there is no separate or distinct dharma. It is simply through the non-abiding of awareness that one is able to achieve eternal departure. This is...
It is to be abandoned by oneself and severed by oneself; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for self-severance. This phrase establishes the analogy.
Regarding the phrase "because the head has already been severed": because the head has already been severed, there is no one capable of severing it—there is no person who severs their own head.
This phrase clarifies the analogy. Human life is entrusted to the head, yet life is not the head itself. Although life is not the head, once [the head] is severed, [life is lost].
As for its head: there is no person who can regenerate it. This demonstrates that the fundamental nature of awakening is not "illumination"; illumination is a manifestation.

Since there is no illumination, there is no enlightened awareness. It is like a person whose head has been severed; there is no longer a person who can sever themselves. Next, this clarifies the point.
"Then, by means of the obstructing mind, one extinguishes all obstructions oneself. Once obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no one who extinguishes the obstructions.
These two phrases should be explained together: "Then, by means of... and so forth, and "Once obstructions have been severed... and so forth.

"Obstructing mind" refers to the illuminating awareness that is being explained; it corresponds to the "person" in the analogy. "Extinguishing all obstructions oneself" refers to the awareness that eliminates them.

"Brilliant illumination. This corresponds to the metaphor of severing one's own head. This phrase demonstrates that by awakening to and subduing the primordial clarity (*ādi-prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), one is able to achieve quiescent extinction.

"The obstructions having been severed and extinguished" means that the nature of the clarified primordial illumination is forever free from subject and object; this corresponds to the metaphor of the head having already been severed.
"Without extinction or obstruction" means there is no cessation, illumination, or cognition. This corresponds to the metaphor of "one who is incapable of severing.

This phrase demonstrates that awakening and illumination are darkly one, fully manifesting quiescent extinction. Together with the preceding section, this completes the section on "the cessation of the sphere of mental activity.
For indeed, the luminosity of awakening is the flow of true permanence; by extinguishing this luminous awakening, one enters the pervasive, perfect, and equal permanence.
Abiding in the cause of immovable purity and the absence of outflows, this is the attainment of the state where mental activity ceases;
it is the twofold severance of the path of language. First, the metaphor is revealed.
The teaching of the *sūtras* is like a finger pointing at the moon. If one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
This is illustrated by two phrases in the text: "The *sūtra* says... and "If one sees the moon...".
The explanation of the *sūtra* follows the previous pattern. As for "teaching" (*śāsana*), it refers to all the words and principles of the various *sūtras*, which bring about awakening.

"When a Bodhisattva enters into the awakening to self-nature (svabhāva-bodha), it is like the finger pointing at the moon. The finger pointing at the moon represents the awakening to self-nature; the moon represents that very nature;
and the pointing finger represents the teaching of the scriptures. This phrase provides the analogy. "If one then sees the moon," means seeing the moon that was pointed out by the finger.
When the Bodhisattva enters into the awakening to self-nature, they fully comprehend that which is pointed out and clearly recognize the finger pointing at the moon.

Regarding the meaning of this: when a Bodhisattva penetrates the names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) used in the teaching, they realize that these are ultimately not the moon itself.

While the moon is luminous and the finger is dark, the finger pointed out is entirely not of the substance of the moon. Likewise, the names, phrases, and phonemes belong to the realm of sounds and linguistic conventions;
as phenomena produced by causes and conditions, they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are free from dependence on others (*paratantra*), being non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The nature of reality is utterly distinct from both the true and the false; this phrase provides the analogy. Next, it is applied to clarify the meaning:
all the various verbal teachings and demonstrations of the Tathāgatas for the sake of bodhisattvas are likewise thus.

"When a single phrase of the text is clearly explained, it is likewise so" means that verbal explanation and instruction are intended to lead one to awaken to self-realization (*svapratyātma-vedya*), like pointing toward the moon above.
However, the words, phrases, and principles of the teaching are not themselves self-realization; they are like the finger, which ultimately is not the moon.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva who has awakened to the mind abandons the Dharma-body expressed through words. This completes the preceding section on the textual structure.

The section on "The Cessation of the Path of Language" is concluded. The preceding section on "The Cessation of the Sphere of Mental Activity," which was subsumed under the detailed exposition of the section on "Manifesting Quiescence," is now concluded.
The combined section on "Comprehensively Manifesting Quiescence," which governed the section on "Designating the Practice," is now concluded. Second, the conclusion of the title.
This is called the Bodhisattva who has already entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening (*bodhisaṃvitti*).

A single phrase from the text serves as the concluding title; the detailed explanation follows the previous pattern. The preceding section, which combined the headings for the practices, completes the chapter on the Bodhisattva of Quiescent Extinction (*śāntinirvāṇa*).
Second, the "Pervasive Fulfillment of the Tathāgata" opens into two parts. First, the heading for the practices opens into two parts. First, a general demonstration of pervasive fulfillment.
"Good son, all obstacles are ultimate enlightenment.
This first phrase generally demonstrates pervasive fulfillment. "Good son," one phrase, is an address and a call.
"All," and so forth, one phrase, refers to the perfectly luminous *dharmatā*; there is no delusion to be severed. All is enlightenment; enlightenment is one.

All things are ultimately non-dual. This is detailed in two parts: the universal pervasiveness and the opening of the two. Within each of these, there is the universal pervasiveness of each realm, which is further divided into two.
First is the universal pervasiveness of self-awakening, which is divided into two: first, the cause and fruit of the three virtues.
Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation. Whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all termed nirvana.
Wisdom and folly are both collectively designated as prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are equally bodhi.
Ignorance and suchness are no different in their realm. All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and delusion, are together the brahma-conduct.
The six phrases of the main text concern the causes and effects of the three virtues:

one phrase beginning with "attaining mindfulness," one phrase beginning with "accomplishing the Dharma," one phrase beginning with "wisdom," one phrase beginning with "bodhisattva," and one phrase beginning with "ignorance."
Regarding the phrase "all precepts," and so forth: those who possess mindfulness take true suchness (*tathatā*) as their object; those who lose mindfulness take sensory objects as their object.

There is nothing that is not liberation because mindfulness has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Mindfulness is constantly arising and ceasing. One may contemplate true suchness yet be unable to abide in true suchness;
one may contemplate sensory objects yet be unable to reach those sensory objects. Therefore, it is liberated through a single cause.

"Liberation. This phrase refers to the definitive cause. "The establishment of dharmas" means the perfection of pure awakening; "the destruction of dharmas" means the illusory extinction of birth and death.
Both are called *nirvāṇa* because pure awakening is equal and immovable, while birth and death are false and non-arising;
thus, they share the same fruit, which is *nirvāṇa*. This phrase refers to the definitive fruit. "Wisdom" means perfect, illuminating purity; "delusion" means conceptual discrimination.
As for the subject and object being universally the Prajñā: they are perfectly illuminated as non-dual in essence, constituting a single, total awareness and clarity.
Therefore, they share the same cause, which is Prajñā; this phrase refers to the cause of wisdom. Regarding the dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and external paths:
Bodhisattvas achieve purity through the wisdom of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa-jñāna*); non-Buddhists achieve defilement through the grasping of views.
Although both share the same *bodhi*, the wisdom of transcendence clarifies the insight of true emptiness, while the grasping of views illuminates the light of illusory existence;
thus, they both converge upon the fruit of *bodhi*. This phrase refers to the fruit of wisdom. "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) is the nature of sentient beings; "Suchness" (*tathatā*) is...
"Buddha-nature" refers to the realm of non-differentiation, which is the realm of Perfect Enlightenment; this phrase constitutes the cause of the body.

"All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms" refer to bodily activities that have emerged from the entanglements. "Lust, anger, and ignorance" refer to bodily activities while still within the entanglements. Both are the practice of Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).
All are of the nature of non-action and are identical in essence and pure. This refers to the fruit of the body [of the Dharma]. Second, regarding the cause and fruit of a single land:
the sentient beings and their lands share the same single dharma-nature; thus, even the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands.
The first section contains two phrases concerning the cause and effect of a single land: "sentient beings... (one phrase), and "the hells... (one phrase).
Regarding "sentient beings," this refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*). Regarding "land," this refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

"Sharing the same *dharmatā*" means that all which arises through the toil of mutual dependence within the universal clarity of awakening is established by the four great elements; they possess no separate intrinsic nature. This phrase constitutes the cause of the land.
Regarding the mention of "lands" as including sentient beings: this refers to the shared karma of self and others that constitutes the environment of reliance (*pariṇāmanirmita*).

Because the purity of sentient beings is not manifested, one does not perceive the purity of a single land. As for the hells, they are the realms of retribution for the ten non-virtues; as for the celestial palaces, they are the realms of retribution for the ten virtues.

That these are all considered "pure lands" is because the suffering and pleasure of dream-visions, and the sorrow and joy of illusory persons, are all collectively empty and false experiences. They do not exist.

Substantiality. Therefore, this phrase "entirely pure" constitutes the fruit of the land. Together with the preceding section of the text, the chapter on "Self-Awakening Pervasion" is hereby concluded.
Second is "Awakening Others' Pervasion."
Those with nature and those without nature equally attain the Buddha-way; all afflictions are ultimately liberated.
Regarding the text, there are two phrases concerning awakening others that are all-pervasive: the phrase "those with nature," etc., and the phrase "all," etc.
Those with nature are the beings of the single Dharma-realm; those without nature are the land of the single Dharma-realm. They equally attain the Buddha-way.
There is not a single sentient being who does not enter ultimate enlightenment; there is not a single land that is not fundamentally the light of eternal quiescence (*nitya-prabhāsvara*).

This phrase perfects the cause for the awakening of others. "All afflictions" refers to the defiled and pure perceptions of sages and ordinary beings, as well as good and evil, suffering and pleasure, and the realms of karmic retribution.
"Ultimate liberation" means being identical with the bodies, lands, causes, and fruits of all Tathāgatas. This...

The phrase "perfecting the fruit of awakening others" concludes the preceding section on the pervasive fulfillment of self-awakening, together forming the section on the pervasive fulfillment of the single realm.
Second is the pervasive fulfillment of the many realms:
the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm illuminates and comprehends all phenomena as being like empty space.

When a single phrase of the text pervades many realms, the "ocean of the dharma-realm" refers to the ocean of Great Perfect Enlightenment, and "wisdom" refers to the wisdom of Great Perfect Enlightenment.
Regarding the measure and number of the ocean of Perfect Enlightenment, this is fully explained in the "Chapter on the Universal Eye.

As for "illuminating all marks," it means that by means of the wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment, one illuminates and realizes all the marks of the various dharma-realms within the ocean of Perfect Enlightenment, just as [the sky illuminates] space.
"Emptiness" refers to the pure, true reality (*dharmatā*) of the self-characteristic of Perfect Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*).

The preceding combined section on the "Pervasive Fulfillment" (*vyāpti*) has been completed in its detailed enumeration. The combined section that collectively demonstrates the "Pervasive Fulfillment" and its inclusion within the "Headline Section" (*pratijñā*) is now concluded.
Second, the conclusion of the title.
This is called the Tathāgata’s conformity with the nature of awakening (*bodhita*).

A single phrase from the text serves as the concluding title; the detailed explanation follows the previous pattern. The preceding section, which combined the headings for practice and attainment to form the "Pervasive Fulfillment of the Tathāgata," is now complete.
This is followed by the integration of the "Silent Extinction Bodhisattva" section, which is subsumed under the heading of "Conformity through the Severing of Obstructions"; this is now complete.

Having completed the section on the classification of the accordant nature according to the distinctions of the "junction, abiding, obstruction, and accord" (jiejhezhu'ai suishun ke), one now answers the request by restating the distinctions of the realization attained (zhengde).

This concludes the section on the comprehensive demonstration of the entry into the category of the "perfectly integrated awakened nature" (lunhe yuanman juesing) and the section on the specific distinctions of the teachings.
Second, the demonstration of the benefits for the末代 (final age) is divided into two parts: first, the direct pointing to sudden realization, which is further divided into two.
First, the heading indicates two parts; first, being like the mind which is non-arising.
"Good son, it is simply that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts."

One does not extinguish the various deluded minds; one dwells within the realm of false conceptualization without applying further discernment, and in this lack of discernment, one does not distinguish what is real.
Regarding the text, there are six phrases: "As with the mind being without arising," "Good son" (one phrase), and "But as for all... (one phrase).
"Abiding in one," etc.—one phrase. "Regarding all," etc.—one phrase. "Dwelling in delusion," etc.—one phrase. "Regarding the non-existent," etc.—one phrase.

"Abiding at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts" means constantly abiding within the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of perfect luminosity, not falling into the realm of conceptual understanding or cognitive awareness. This phrase marks the initial severance of delusion. Regarding "all":
Regarding the statement that "deluded mind also does not cease": the deluded mind forms a continuous cycle through the successive arising and ceasing of every thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).

If for even a single thought there is no arising, the continuity is severed, and it immediately subsides into total cessation. Since it originally has no place of abiding, what further thing could there be to cease?
Therefore, it also does not cease. If one gives rise to a mind that seeks to cease the deluded mind, this—this [very act]...
The mind turns into a basis for delusion; though mind and mind cease and extinguish one another in continuous succession, there is nothing capable of extinguishing them.
Even the knowing itself does not cease or extinguish. This is what is meant by the subtlety of cessation. It is precisely what is called "the function of non-action.

That this function is not in vain means that this phrase cuts off delusion at its source and brings it to its ultimate end. Having realized this cutting-off of delusion from beginning to end, one can directly [subdue] all delusions.
"Permanently severing [delusions] and accomplishing initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi): dwelling in the realm of delusive thought without applying cognitive discernment.

This means that when perceiving objects through direct perception (pratyakṣa), there is fundamentally no discrimination; being as it originally was, without discrimination, is called "not applying. Because this non-application exists, one is eternally quiescent in the face of objects.
Although dwelling in the realm of delusive thought, it is no different from residing in a pure land (śuddha-kṣetra). This phrase attests to the realization of truth.
Originally, for one who lacks realization and fails to discern reality, the luminous manifestation of objects is devoid of a knowing nature;
this is the root of non-abiding, equal to the ocean-like expanse of the *dharmadhātu*, and without a second head.
Just as one's own eye faculty cannot see itself, if one further seeks that which is real and attempts to discern it, this is precisely "losing one's head."
Frantic running—endless delusion and confusion—establishes its root from this point. Therefore, it is directly revealed without discrimination.

If one can abide in patience regarding this non-discrimination, one will penetrate the source of the fundamentally awakened, pure, and ultimate mind, possessing the power of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This phrase penetrates the ultimate truth. By thoroughly understanding this original source, one naturally realizes that the single true reality is eternally identical to the perfectly luminous fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), such that one enters the samādhi of the momentary limit (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*) together with all Tathāgatas and attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) without any difference.
Second, hearing and understanding this without doubt.
When those sentient beings hear this Dharma-gate, they believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without giving rise to alarm or fear.
This consists of two phrases: "Hearing and understanding without doubt" (one phrase) and "They believe and understand...

(one phrase). In the first phrase, they realize the Dharma instantaneously upon hearing it; in the second phrase, they realize it instantaneously through belief and understanding. "Belief" means practicing without doubt.
"Understanding" means practicing with clear comprehension. "Receiving" means practicing by taking up the burden. "Maintaining" means practicing for a long duration.
"Not giving rise to alarm" means no sense of strangeness arises. "Not giving rise to fear" means no thought of difficulty arises.

This refers to practitioners who have long practiced the Mahāyāna and obtain the opportunity to hear the characteristics of this fundamental Dharma. Together with the preceding section, this constitutes the heading.
The section on practice is concluded. Second, the naming [of the stage]:
this is called "conforming to the nature of awakening.

A single phrase from the text concludes the name: "This sudden realization conforms [to the nature]; it directly coincides with the conduct of fruition; it is not a gradual cultivation and realization."
Regarding the "function" (功用): because it does not deviate from the distinct stages [of practice], it is designated simply as "conforming to the nature of awakening" (隨順覺性).

The preceding section on "Directly Pointing to and Sudden Realization" (直指頓證), together with the heading for "Conduct" (行), is hereby concluded. Second, "Manifesting and Exhorting" (彰顯勸誘) is divided into two parts.
First, it demonstrates that causes have been planted for a long time.
"Good sons, you should know that such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
as well as to great Bodhisattvas, thereby planting the roots of all virtues."
The first two phrases clarify that the causes have been planted for a long time. "Good sons" constitutes one phrase. "You all... constitutes one phrase.

"Sentient beings such as these" refers to those sentient beings who, through faith, understanding, upholding, and compliance, awaken to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). "Those who have already made offerings to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
and so forth, refers to the Great Perfectly Round Awakened Mind (*mahāpariniṣpanna-avabodha-citta*), which is like the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers.

In these Buddha-lands of sand, which are collectively adorned by great Bodhisattvas, how could anyone who has not previously made offerings to these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma-gate for the sudden realization of the awakened mind without giving rise to alarm and fear? As for those who have made offerings:
their inner minds are constantly pure throughout the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), and they do not give rise to the three poisons.

Not being obscured regarding the Three Jewels, one enters the gateway of principle and phenomena; with wisdom, one illuminates emptiness, and with meditative concentration, one maintains it, thereby attaining the pervasive, perfect enlightenment of equal adornment.

As for "planting the roots of all virtues," this means making offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas to plant immeasurable fruits of virtue, and making offerings to immeasurable Bodhisattvas to plant immeasurable causal virtues. Because cause and effect are thoroughly interpenetrating, it is said:
The multitude of virtues. Second, the direct realization of the fruit.

When the Buddha says, "This person is called one who has accomplished all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*)," this single phrase from the text reveals the direct realization of the fruit. Regarding the Buddha’s statement, "This person": only a Buddha can know and can certify [this].

The "attainment of all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā) refers to the resultant wisdom of the Tathāgata. Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) constitutes the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm;
this is all-encompassing wisdom. Now, by suddenly realizing [this] in accordance with the nature of awakening, it is called "attainment.

This concludes the section on "Manifesting Exhortation," which, together with the preceding sections, completes the exposition. The previous section on "Directly Pointing to Sudden Realization" is subsumed under the heading of "Instruction."

The section on "Further [Explanations] in the Final Age" concludes. This is joined with the section on "Manifesting the Teaching and Extraordinary Realization," which is governed by the subsequent section on "Providing the Correct Answer.
This concludes. Next, this is joined with the initial section on "Preface, Praise, and Permission," leading into the general section on "Arranging the Long Rows.
This concludes. Second, the verse summary provides a general overview in two parts: first, the preface expressing the desire to proclaim again.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse.

The four phrases of the opening section celebrate the hearing [of the teaching] and its present benefits: "The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One" (one phrase);

World-Honored One, it is like a great city that has four gates; those who come from various directions do not arrive by only one path.
This should be understood through two phrases of the text as a metaphorical illustration: "World-Honored One" constitutes one phrase, and "it is like... and so forth constitutes another.

The "great city" is a metaphor for the Great Perfectly Round Awakened Mind (*mahā-vartula-bodhicitta*); the "four gates" are a metaphor for conforming to the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*); and "those who come from various directions" is a metaphor for the conformity of these four natures.
"Awakening is not limited to a single path. There are many routes through every gate; this is a metaphor for how nature conforms to nature, each being more than a single phenomenon.

The adornment of Buddha-lands by all Bodhisattvas and the attainment of Bodhi do not rely on a single expedient means.
This shall be clarified by combining the phrases according to the text. Regarding "Bodhisattvas adorning Buddha-lands," this accords with the causal practice;

"City. "Not a single expedient" refers to the various dharma-gates of cultivation and study; this corresponds to the metaphor that there is not merely one path.

The first phrase of the text provides the basis for the response. "I only pray that the World-Honored One [will speak]" constitutes one phrase;
