First, showing and teaching the practice to be undertaken, which opens into two; first, skillfully discerning the practice of the Dharma, which opens into two; first, investigating the fundamental distinctions, which opens into two;
first, original enlightenment is non-dual.
"Good son, supreme and wondrous enlightenment pervades all the ten directions; it gives birth to the Tathāgatas and is equal in essence with all phenomena.
Regarding all practices, there is truly no duality."
Regarding the four phrases of the text, fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is non-dual. "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "unsurpassed," etc., constitutes one phrase;
"giving birth," etc., constitutes one phrase; and "among all," etc., constitutes one phrase. The phrase "unsurpassed" demonstrates that awakening is pervasive and non-dual.
"The Tathāgata giving birth" refers to the original arising of the fruition-virtue. "Bestowing upon all dharmas" refers to the original state of causal practice.
"Arising. Being equal in essence" means that cause, fruit, awakening, and practice are non-differentiated. This phrase shows that awakening accords with non-duality.
For all practitioners, throughout the cultivation that penetrates the cause and encompasses the fruit, there is truly no duality;
for in reality, there are not two. This is because the pervasive accord is solely awakening. This phrase...
It demonstrates that cultivation and realization are truly non-dual.

Second, regarding the three types of comprehensive inclusion, there are immeasurable enumerations of skillful means that accord with them. As for the comprehensive inclusion of the ultimate destination, there should be three kinds according to the distinctions in the nature of the sequence.
Regarding the two phrases for the "when," there are three types of inclusive gathering (*saṃgraha*): the phrase beginning with "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth;

the phrase beginning with "perfect inclusion" (*pari-saṃgraha*) and so forth; and the phrase on "immeasurable expedient means. These demonstrate that [the former] resides within the gathering of practice. As for "perfect inclusion," it refers to the perfect inclusion of immeasurable expedient means.

"Those to whom one returns" refers to the subsuming of distinct practices into the perfect practice. "Following nature" means following the nature of the practices as they are subsumed within that which is returned to.

"Distinctions" refers to establishing distinctions by subsuming the distinct. "That which ought to exist" refers to the inclusion of all that ought to exist in accordance with the infinite natures of various practices.
"The three kinds" refers to the three gates of skillful means. This phrase indicates the practices that are subsumed; it corresponds to the preceding section of the text.
The section on the distinctions of tracing back to the source is completed. Second, the distinctions of practice are revealed in three parts.
First, śamatha-concentration is revealed in two parts. First, concentration arising from pure awakening is revealed in two parts. First, the practice of pure awakening.
"Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment and take the stillness of the pure enlightened mind as their practice—this shall be explained in three sentences.
'Good son' is one sentence; 'if all... and so forth is one sentence."

The phrase "with a pure [mind]," and so forth, refers to one who awakens to the purity of Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi). To awaken means to realize the luminous clarity of perfect illumination, free from a mind of grasping or rejecting;
this phrase is rooted in the awakening to Perfect Enlightenment. "With a pure awakened mind" means to be detached from the deluded thoughts of dualistic discrimination between subject and object.
Taking stillness as the practice means taking the state free from the movement of subject-object discrimination as the practice of awakening and concentration.
This phrase clarifies the practice of being able to concentrate; next, it brings forth the characteristics of concentration.

By clarifying all thoughts, one awakens to the agitation of consciousness, and tranquil wisdom arises; the adventitious defilements of body and mind are thereby extinguished forever, and one is able to inwardly give rise to serene pliancy.
The three phrases beginning with "By means of clarifying... constitute the characteristics for the arousal of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The phrase "By means of clarifying the various thoughts," refers to the aforementioned attainment of stillness;

by taking the state of detachment from the movement of conceptualization—which is devoid of subject and object—as one’s practice, the various thoughts naturally become clarified and tranquil. Thus it is said, "by means of..."

This refers to the cause for the arising of the agitation of lower-level consciousness. Regarding "the agitation of consciousness," it means to clearly perceive the subtle arising and ceasing of the agitation within consciousness so as not to follow its流转 (transmigration/flow).
This is not the stilling of thought; since there would be no one capable of such clear perception, it is said to be "by means of" [this].
"The generation of tranquil wisdom" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-prajñā*). For consciousness functions through conceptualization and agitation.
Movement. Now, one awakens to the agitation of consciousness; because one does not follow after discrimination, [true nature] arises.

This phrase shows that concentration arises from this awakening. Regarding the "adventitious dust" of body and mind: earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, belong to the deluded capacity of clarity (*vidyā*).
They arise through mutual dependence and fluctuation; they are illusory phenomena and do not possess the nature of permanence. Therefore, they are called "adventitious dust. From...

"This" refers to the ground from which tranquil wisdom arises. "Permanently extinguished" means the transcendence of the turbidity of life through the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*);
this phrase demonstrates the establishment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Capable" means that from cessation, one attains capability, which is non-dual in its essential nature.
"Internally arising" means being manifested through awakening, rather than grasping external objects. "Quiescent" means being free from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Moving and shaking, one attains the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the nature of self-peaceful extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). Regarding "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*): it is the ultimate immovability within the equality of empty space;
this phrase explains the opening of concentration. Together with the preceding section, this completes the section on the arising of pure awakening and concentration.
Second, the manifestation of the fixed name and the opening of the two [aspects]. First, the manifestation of the fixed [state] and the illustration by means of a metaphor:
because of its tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear within it, like reflections in a mirror.
The three phrases clarify the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and manifest the metaphor. The phrase "by virtue of tranquility" [indicates the nature];
the phrase "the worlds of the ten directions," and so forth; and the phrase "like an image in a mirror. The first phrase traces back to the accomplishment of awakened absorption.

"The worlds of the ten directions" refers to the full manifestation of the *pariṇāmanirmita* (environmental) retribution. "The minds of all Tathāgatas" comprehensively cites the *upapattideha* (physical) retribution. "Within this" refers to within the state of tranquility.

"Manifesting within stillness" means that the environment and its inhabitants are manifested through clarity; this phrase reveals the samādhi of Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahāpariniṣpanna-bodhi*), in which the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), both the environment and its inhabitants, is encompassed by perfection.
"Like an image in a mirror": the mirror is a metaphor for the samādhi of awakening, and the image is a metaphor for the environment and its inhabitants;
this phrase uses a simile to reveal the meaning. This concludes the definition of the two types of samādhi.
This "skillful means" is called *śamatha*.
The two phrases of the text specify and conclude the name: the phrase "this skillful means" specifies it, and the phrase "is called *śamatha*" concludes the name.
*Śamatha* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "cessation" (*zhi*), which is another name for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This corresponds to the preceding section.

The section on the collective formation of the designated name is concluded. The preceding section on the convergence of pure awakening giving rise to concentration is subsumed under the category of *śamatha* (calm abiding);
this section is now concluded. II. The opening of the wisdom of *samāpatti* has two parts: 1. The opening of the wisdom arising from pure awakening, which further has two parts;
first, the practice of pure awakening.
Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they use their mind of pure awakening to know that the nature of the mind,

as well as the sense organs and objects, are all produced by illusion. They then give rise to various illusions to eliminate the illusory self, and transform these illusions to open the way for the illusory multitude.
The five phrases clarify the practice of pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*). "Good son" constitutes one phrase. "If all... and so forth constitutes one phrase. "By means of purity...
and so forth constitutes one phrase. "Immediately arising... and so forth constitutes one phrase. "Transforming... and so forth constitutes one phrase.

As for the root of these various phrases, the interpretation follows the previous [explanation]. Regarding the phrase "one who knows the nature of the mind," the character *zhī* (know) arises from pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*). That is to say—
The preceding "grasping at stillness" and "grasping at characters" have the same meaning; it is as if saying one knows the nature of the mind that cognizes and perceives.
This "nature of awakening" refers to the internal mind, while "roots and objects" refer to external conditions.

"All arise from illusory transformation" means that within the pure awakened mind, these various mental states and objective realms fundamentally lack any substantial essence. Therefore, one knows that all present appearances are entirely illusory transformations. This...

The phrase "knowing illusion" means that one who gives rise to various illusions initiates the contemplation of transcending illusion in order to eliminate the illusionist; this transcends the mind that creates illusion.
The phrase "transforming various illusions" refers to the opening and closing of the sense organs and their objects, manifesting bodies and lands, and opening up for the illusory multitudes;
this refers to the nirvana of oneself and other sentient beings. This phrase transcends that which is created by illusion.
Next is the characteristic of generating wisdom.
Because of the arising of illusion, one is able to internally generate great compassion and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
In the text, there are two phrases that constitute the characteristic of generating wisdom: "because of the arising of illusion" and "one is able to... and so forth.
[Verse] The first line traces the origin of compassion and wisdom from their point of inception. The second line reveals the manifestation of compassion and wisdom. Regarding "Great Compassion":

since the pure nature of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment) is fundamentally devoid of the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas, how could there truly be a wisdom born of compassion?
Therefore, the wisdom born of compassion that the Buddha possesses is originally manifested as an illusion in response to illusory sentient beings; it now arises by means of [the power of] illusion.

Free from illusion, their wisdom is identical to that of all Buddhas; thus it arises spontaneously. As for "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*): although illusory compassion arises and ceases, in reality there is no arising or ceasing at all;
it is ultimately like space, equal and immovable. This concludes the preceding section on the text, which together completes the section on the Arising of Wisdom through Pure Enlightenment.
Second, manifesting wisdom and concluding the title, which opens into two parts: first, manifesting wisdom by illustrating it with a metaphor.
All Bodhisattvas arise from this and progress through gradual stages of advancement.

Because those who contemplate illusions are not identical to the illusions themselves, yet their contemplation of them as non-identical is itself entirely illusory, they are forever free from the marks of illusion. These perfected and wondrous practices of the Bodhisattvas are like seeds growing in the soil.
The four phrases beginning with "When" clarify wisdom and manifest the metaphor. "All... (one phrase), "That contemplation... (one phrase), "Permanently free from illusory signs...
(one phrase), and "These various... (one phrase). For the practitioner who arises from this, it means arising in conduct that is free from illusion;
for one who gradually progresses, it means gradually attaining freedom from all illusions. This phrase demonstrates the departure from illusion.
Regarding the statement, "The one who contemplates that illusion is able to be free from the wisdom of illusion because they are not identical to the illusion":

this means that wisdom belongs to the subject who is free [from illusion], and is therefore not identical to the illusory object that is to be abandoned. Regarding the statement, "not identical to the contemplation of illusion": this means it is not identical to the wisdom that contemplates the illusion.
"Because all are illusion" means that the very wisdom capable of observation is itself entirely illusion; this phrase indicates that which is to be abandoned.

This clarifies that there is a gradual progression in the explanation of the preceding phrase, namely, progressing toward the abandonment of the observing wisdom. Regarding "the illusory appearances are forever abandoned":

while the illusory observation has not yet been abandoned, the illusory appearances still remain latent; only when the observing wisdom becomes profoundly tranquil are the illusory appearances forever [abandoned].

"Detachment. This phrase indicates detachment from illusion. Regarding "the wondrous practice that is perfected": when illusion is extinguished, awakening is revealed. "Like sprouts growing from soil":
soil is a metaphor for the function of detaching from illusion; sprouts are a metaphor for the awakening mind being opened and revealed.

For awakening is accomplished by means of detaching from illusion, just as sprouts grow by emerging from the soil. This phrase is a metaphorical clarification. The second finger signifies the name of the Wisdom-knot.
This "skillful means" (*upāya*) is called *samāpatti*. In this passage, two phrases are used:
one to indicate wisdom (*prajñā*) and one to provide its name. The phrase "this skillful means" indicates wisdom, while the phrase "called *samāpatti*" provides the name.
*Samāpatti* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "equipoise" (*tingzhì*). It is simply another name for wisdom.
"Perfect enlightenment shines universally. This concludes the section on the combined text above, which together points to wisdom and completes the section on the naming of the result.

The preceding section on "Pure Enlightenment Giving Birth to Wisdom" was subsumed under the section on the wisdom of *samāpatti*; this concludes that section. Within the three types of *dhyāna*, the Middle Way opens into two.
First, "Pure Enlightenment Manifesting the Middle" opens into two: first, the practice of pure enlightenment.
Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they do not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness with their mind of pure awakening.
They clearly understand that both body and mind are hindrances; they possess the luminosity of non-cognitive awareness that does not rely upon any such hindrances.
The five phrases of the passage clarify the practice of pure awakening. "Good son," one phrase; "If all... and so forth, one phrase; "By means of purity...
and so forth, one phrase; "To fully know... and so forth, one phrase; "Without knowledge... and so forth, one phrase.

Regarding these phrases, the fundamental realization is explained according to the preceding [section]. "Not grasping at illusory transformations" excludes both the illumination of illusory existence and all forms of quiescence.

"Phenomena" refers to that which obstructs and illuminates emptiness and stillness; this phrase signifies the perfect clarity of pure awakening. "Thoroughly knowing" refers to the knowledge of penetrating realization.

"Body and mind" refers to the domain of the sense organs and consciousness. "All being hindrances" means that when there is attachment to the sense organs and consciousness, quiescence is not manifested.
This phrase issues forth the illumination of perfect clarity. "Lacking the clarity of conscious awareness" means there is no established object for conscious awareness to clarify.
"Nature does not rely on any obstructions" means that the nature of mind is eternally free from the duality of subject and object in conceptualization; this phrase cuts off fundamental ignorance.
Next is the characteristic of the Middle Way.

They shall forever transcend the realms of the obstructed and the unobstructed. They will experience the world as well as their own bodies and minds within the sphere of sensory objects, like the sound of a bell within a vessel resonating outward.
Thus, afflictions and nirvana will not hinder one another, and they will be able to internally give rise to the light ease of tranquil extinction.
The four phrases beginning with "When" constitute the characteristics of the Middle Way: the phrase "permanently attains... and so forth; the phrase "enjoys...
and so forth; the phrase "afflictions... and so forth; and the phrase "is able to... and so forth. Regarding "transcending those who are obstructed": this means not abiding in afflictions.
Regarding "transcending those who are unobstructed": this means not abiding in nirvana. Through these phrases, the Middle Way is established as enjoyment.
"Zhè" (者) means "to transcend. Because one attains transcendence, one is able to enjoy [the state]. As for "the marks residing within the realm of dust": "yù" (域) refers to a boundary or domain.
The marks of the world, body, and mind reside within the realm of sensory objects; thus, it is by not leaving the triple world that one truly leaves the triple world.
This is precisely the obstacle and non-obstacle of what has been transcended. It is like the resonance within a musical vessel.
The analogy refers to the characteristics of body and mind within the world of the sensory realm.

"Vessels" refers to vessels made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or clay—anything that produces sound when struck, such as bells and chimes. "Huang" (鍠) is the resonant *huang-huang* sound emitted from within the vessel at the moment it is struck.
That the sound issues forth externally is a metaphor for manifesting transcendence beyond the body and mind of the world.

"By attaining it, one enjoys its use. This phrase metaphorically clarifies the Middle Way. The phrase regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) clarifies, in conjunction with the former, that one does not fall into either extreme;
thus, one attains enjoyment within the body, mind, and world. For to retain afflictions is to obstruct *nirvāṇa*, which results in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
it cannot be said that one attains enjoyment by merely obtaining the body and mind within the world.

If one retains nirvāṇa, it obstructs afflictions; this would mean that having realized cessation and attained restful quiescence, one would not return to the world, and thus the body and mind would lack their functional utility.
Only by now neither retaining nor obstructing can one attain such utility, thereby enabling the manifestation of the Middle Way within the very midst of phenomena.

As for "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*), it refers to the equality of all dharmas, devoid of the characteristics of increase or decrease. As for "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*), it is in accordance with the Dharma.
"Equally like empty space, it is immovable. This concludes the preceding section on the text, completing the section on the Middle Way within Dhyāna.
Second, manifesting the Middle and concluding the title, which opens into two parts: first, the doctrinal exposition manifesting the Middle.

The wondrous enlightenment accords with the realm of quiescent extinction; it is beyond the reach of one's own or others' body and mind, and sentient beings and their lifespans are all but floating thoughts.

This is explained through two phrases of the text to clarify the Middle Way: the phrase "wondrous enlightenment... and so forth constitutes one [section], while the phrase "one's own or others'... and so forth constitutes the other.
"Phrase: 'Subtle Awakening. This refers to the nature of awakening on the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). This phrase demonstrates the quiescence (*śānti*) that has internally arisen;
it is the Tathāgata’s conformity with the realm of quiescence to manifest the Middle Way.

The 'Self and Others' phrase demonstrates that the four marks—the self, person, sentient being, and life-span—are ultimately pure, thereby clarifying the realm of quiescence. [It refutes] the view of a self and persons."

Because they are distinguished by their subordinate characteristics (*anu-lakṣaṇa*), it is said that [the primary characteristic] cannot reach them. Because the views of sentient beings and life-span are distinguished by their subordinate views, it is called "floating thought" (*pluta-saṃjñā*).
This is the name for the *mudrā* formed between the two middle fingers.
This "skillful means" (upāya) is called *dhyāna*.
In this text, two phrases are used to indicate the middle and conclude with the name: the phrase "this skillful means" indicates the Middle Way, and the phrase "called *dhyāna*" concludes the name.

The phrase "If [there are] various... and so forth is the first phrase, which indicates wisdom. The phrase "because they have severed the afflictions" is the middle phrase.
In this phrase, the word "because" (*hi*) takes up the aforementioned "unimpeded activity" as the reason for the severing of the afflictions.

Furthermore, because one gives rise to [the practice of] "dwelling in ultimate stillness" (śamatha) from below in order to sever afflictions, the phrase "dwelling in ultimate stillness" follows the fixed sequence.
This is the second summary of the names.
This Bodhisattva is one who first practices *samāpatti* (trance attainment), then practices *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), and subsequently practices *śamatha*.
The example for the phrase-commentary is as before. This concludes the section on concentration within the gradual development of wisdom (*prajñā-krama*) according to the preceding textual analysis.

This concludes the section on the sequential inclusion of the three dharmas within the aforementioned synthesis of the gradual development of wisdom and concentration. Regarding the threefold equalization of the three dharmas, there are three parts;
first, the equalization of wisdom within concentration, which opens into two sections. The first is the heading of the practice.

If bodhisattvas, through the skillful application of the power of transformation, reach both quiescence and cessation while remaining in accord with them, this constitutes the two phrases of the text that mark the practice.
The first phrase, "If [bodhisattvas]... and so forth, first establishes the state; the second phrase, "Reaching quiescence...
and so forth, integrates and identifies that state within meditative concentration. These two constitute the summary of the name.
As for this Bodhisattva, he is named "One Who First Cultivated Samāpatti and Simultaneously Cultivated Śamatha and Dhyāna.
The interpretation of the phrasing follows the previous examples. This combined section above completes the "Wisdom Equal to Concentration" portion;
the second part, "Wisdom and Concentration Equal," is divided into two: first, the heading of the practice.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, employ various manifestations to support ultimate stillness, they subsequently sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the text, there are two phrases that indicate the practice: "If [various]... and so forth, which is the single phrase on the fusion of wisdom and concentration;
and "subsequently severing the afflictions," which is the single phrase on attaining entry therein. Second is the conclusion of the name.
This Bodhisattva is named "Simultaneous Cultivation of Samāpatti and Śamatha, Followed by Cultivation of Dhyāna. The explanation of the terms follows the previous pattern.
This combined text, according to the preceding classification, completes the section on the simultaneous cultivation of wisdom and concentration.
Within the three types of wisdom, the simultaneous cultivation of concentration is divided into two parts: first, the designation of the practice.
If bodhisattvas support their state of quiescence through the power of transformation, they subsequently abide in the pure, unconditioned meditative concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-dhyāna*).

This section consists of two sentences indicating the practice: the first sentence, "If [bodhisattvas]... and so forth, integrates [the elements] within wisdom; the second sentence, "Subsequently abiding...
and so forth, indicates that the concentration is actually generated upon attainment. Second, this concludes the name.
This Bodhisattva is named "Simultaneous Cultivation of Samāpatti and Dhyāna, Followed by Cultivation of Śamatha. The interpretation of the phrasing follows the previous examples.
This combined text, together with the preceding section, completes the subsection on "Equalizing Concentration" within the Middle Section on Wisdom.

The two subsections—Wisdom and Concentration Equalized, and Concentration Equalized—within the preceding combined section on Wisdom and Concentration Equalized, are subsumed under the three dharmas; this concludes the subsection on Gradual Equalization. [The sections] are now joined in sequence.

The three dharmas and two categories governing the cultivation of wisdom and the section on unimpededness are concluded. Within the three [sections], the cultivation of unimpededness is divided into three.
First, the two dharmas of gradual progression are divided into two. First, the sequence of the middle and then meditative concentration is divided into two. First, the indication of practice.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*śānti*), give rise to supreme tranquility and abide in purity—this consists of two phrases indicating the practice:

the phrase "if [there are] all... and so forth represents the concentration included within the middle [dhyāna], while the phrase "abiding in purity" clearly indicates the concentration itself; these two constitute the summary of the name.
This Bodhisattva is one who first cultivates *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and subsequently cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding).

The explanation of the phrasing follows the previous pattern. This completes the section on the sequence of first [cultivating] the middle [concentration] and then fixed concentration. Second, regarding the sequence of first [cultivating] the middle [wisdom] and then wisdom, there are two parts:
first, the designation of the practice; second, the detailed explanation. First, the designation of the practice.
If bodhisattvas initiate activity through the power of quiescence (*śamatha*), they accord with quiescent function regarding all objects.
In the text, two phrases indicate this practice: the phrase "If [there are] various... and so forth, which subsumes wisdom within the middle [of the path];
and the phrase "Regarding one... and so forth, which manifests wisdom. The second [part] concludes the name.
This Bodhisattva first cultivates *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) and subsequently cultivates *samāpatti* (attainment).
The explanation of these terms follows the previous pattern. This completes the section on "First Middle and Subsequent Wisdom" when combined with the preceding category.

The preceding combination of "First Middle and Subsequent Samādhi" concludes the categorization under the two dharmas of the gradual sequence. [The text] opens the second [section]: The Two Dharmas of the Gradual Sequence.
2. Within the first [section], the gradual opening of concentration and wisdom has two parts: 1. Indicating the practice.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*) and the various intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), abide in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and give rise to transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
The three phrases of the main body are marked as follows: the phrase "If [the Bodhisattvas]... and so forth first establishes the middle [section];
the phrase "abiding in meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*) follows next; and the phrase "arising transformations" (*nirmāṇa*) is placed last as wisdom (*prajñā*). Second, the names are concluded.

As for this Bodhisattva, he is one who first cultivates *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), then cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding), and subsequently cultivates *samāpatti* (attainment). The explanation of these terms follows the previous pattern. This completes the section on the gradual development of concentration and wisdom within the upper division of the text. Second, regarding the gradual development of wisdom and concentration, there are two parts: first, the designation of the practice; second, the detailed exposition. First, the designation of the practice: The Buddha addressed Mahāmati: "If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to enter the Tathāgata’s inner realization of the Dharma-realm, he must first cultivate the three kinds of samādhi. What are the three? They are: 1) the samādhi of the light of the mind; 2) the samādhi of the light of the mind and its objects; and 3) the samādhi of the extinction of the mind and its objects. What is meant by the samādhi of the light of the mind? It means that when the Bodhisattva practices meditation, he first observes the internal mind, perceiving it as like a phantom, like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, like a reflection in water, like a mirage, like an echo, like the moon in the water, like a transformed body, and like a manifested image. He contemplates that all dharmas are likewise like phantoms, illusions, dreams, shadows, reflections, mirages, echoes, the moon in the water, transformed bodies, and manifested images. Having contemplated them thus, he realizes that the nature of the mind is originally empty and quiescent. Because he has realized the emptiness and quiescence of the mind, he does not perceive the external objects of the mind. Because he does not perceive external objects, he attains the samādhi of the light of the mind. This is called the samādhi of the light of the mind. What is meant by the samādhi of the light of the mind and its objects? It means that when the Bodhisattva practices meditation, he further observes both the internal mind and the external objects, perceiving them as like phantoms, illusions, dreams, shadows, reflections, mirages, echoes, the moon in the water, transformed bodies, and manifested images. He contemplates that all dharmas are likewise like phantoms, illusions, dreams, shadows, reflections, mirages, echoes, the moon in the water, transformed bodies, and manifested images. Having contemplated them thus, he realizes that the nature of both mind and objects is originally empty and quiescent. Because he has realized the emptiness and quiescence of both mind and objects, he transcends the duality of subject and object. Because he transcends the duality of subject and object, he attains the samādhi of the light of the mind and its objects. This is called the samādhi of the light of the mind and its objects. What is meant by the samādhi of the extinction of the mind and its objects? It means that when the Bodhisattva practices meditation, he further observes the internal mind and the external objects, perceiving them as like phantoms, illusions, dreams, shadows, reflections, mirages, echoes, the moon in the water, transformed bodies, and manifested images. He contemplates that all dharmas are likewise like phantoms, illusions, dreams, shadows, reflections, mirages, echoes, the moon in the water, transformed bodies, and manifested images. Having contemplated them thus, he realizes that the nature of both mind and objects is originally empty and quiescent. Because he has realized the emptiness and quiescence of both mind and objects, he transcends the duality of subject and object. Because he transcends the duality of subject and object, he enters a state where there is neither mind nor object. Because there is neither mind nor object, he attains the samādhi of the extinction of the mind and its objects. This is called the samādhi of the extinction of the mind and its objects. Mahāmati, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can enter these three samādhis, he will immediately attain the Tathāgata’s inner realization of the Dharma-realm. If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation and the unconditioned nature, give rise to activity within the pure sphere and return to meditative concentration—this is marked by three phrases in the text: "If [they]...
and so forth constitutes one phrase indicating the beginning and middle; "give rise to... and so forth constitutes one [phrase].
The wisdom within the phrase refers to the single phrase "subsequently entering meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*). This is the second part of the title.
This Bodhisattva is one who first practiced *dhyāna* (meditation), then practiced *samāpatti* (attainment), and subsequently practiced *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The examples for the phrase-commentary are as before. This concludes the section on the gradual cultivation of wisdom and concentration within the combined text.

This concludes the section on the sequential inclusion of the three dharmas within the preceding combined section on the gradual cultivation of concentration and wisdom. Within the three sequential cultivations of the three dharmas, there are three parts;
here, the first part concerns the simultaneous cultivation of concentration and wisdom, which opens into two sections. The first is the heading of the practice.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of cessation and various forms of purity, abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and give rise to emanations (*nirmāṇa*), this is explained in two parts:
first, the phrase "if [all] bodhisattvas... and so forth indicates the practice; second, the phrase "abide in... and so forth indicates the integration of concentration and wisdom.
The second part concludes by stating the name.
As for this Bodhisattva, he is named "One Who First Cultivated Dhyāna and Simultaneously Cultivated Śamatha and Samāpatti. The explanation of the phrasing follows the previous examples.

Combined with the preceding section, this completes the middle section on the Equalization of Concentration and Wisdom. Within the second [section], the Equalization of Concentration and Wisdom is divided into two parts:
first, the designation of the practice; second, the detailed exposition. Regarding the first, the designation of the practice:
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), support ultimate stillness and thereby give rise to transformations, this is indicated by two phrases in the text.
The phrase "If all [Bodhisattvas]... and so forth establishes the definitive fusion of the provisional and the ultimate within a single sentence;
the phrase "and thereby give rise to transformations" indicates that wisdom has been activated. Second, the names are summarized.
This Bodhisattva is named "Simultaneous Cultivation of Dhyāna and Śamatha, Followed by Cultivation of Samāpatti. The explanation of the terms follows the previous pattern.
Combined with the preceding section of the text, this completes the middle division on "Equilibrium of Samādhi and Wisdom" (Zhìdìng Qíhuì).
Within the three divisions, the section on "Wisdom Equal to Samādhi" (Zhìdìng Qíhuì) is further divided into two parts: first, the designation of the practice.

If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), support their transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) and give rise to the wisdom of the most tranquil, pure, and luminous realm, this should be understood through two phrases in the text.
The phrase "If all... and so forth indicates that within a single moment of wisdom, there is integration; the phrase "and gives rise to...
and so forth indicates that concentration is thereby attained and manifested. Second is the summary of the name.
This Bodhisattva is one who first practices *dhyāna* and *samāpatti*, and subsequently practices *śamatha*.
The explanation of the phrasing follows the previous pattern. Combining the text with the preceding section, this completes the middle category of "Equalizing Wisdom and Concentration" (*zhì-dìng*).
The preceding combination of the middle concentration and equalized wisdom concludes the sub-section on the "Gradual Equalization of the Three Dharmas. This connects and combines the two.

The section on the three dharmas within the discipline of cultivation without obstruction is completed. This connects to the section on the combined cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom without obstruction;

this is included within the section on the comprehensive cultivation without obstruction, which is now concluded. The synthesis of the separate cultivation of accomplishments is unified under the section on the comprehensive inclusion of the gradual wheel, which is now concluded.
Second, the combination of the two perfect wheels opens into two parts: first, the designation of practice.

If all bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), perfectly unify with all things, such that regarding all natures and characteristics there is no departure from the nature of enlightenment—this section contains two phrases indicating the practice: "If all... and so forth, and "regarding all... and so forth.

"By means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment" refers to the ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). "Perfectly unifying with all things" means universally illuminating the dharma-realm; this is the first phrase.
"Constantly quiescent yet illuminating": for those who do not depart from the awakened nature within all phenomena and their characteristics, they constantly realize the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This does not mean that illumination arises from a place of non-illumination; this phrase means "constantly illuminating while quiescent. These two lines conclude the names [of the two gates].
This Bodhisattva is named "One Who Perfectly Cultivates the Threefold Nature of Purity in Accordance.
Regarding the two phrases that conclude this passage: the phrase "this Bodhisattva" reveals the excellence of the person;
the phrase "is named [so-and-so]" reveals the excellence of the dharma. As for the "threefold nature," it is total awakening and total contemplation, which are simultaneously one and...
Third, regarding "the purity that accords with non-duality": this does not refer to cultivation based on the power of unreal illusion through unawakened perception;
rather, it is the accord of pure awakening, and is thus called "pure. This is stated to demonstrate that the foundation of perfect cultivation is fundamentally without cultivation or realization.

The combined text above, together with the preceding section, completes the *Dunlun ke* (Sudden Wheel Section). The prior combination of the individual subsumption of the *Jianlun ke* (Gradual Wheel Section) within the *Shixiang ke* (Section on Indicating Characteristics) is completed. Second: The Cultivation of the Teachings.
"Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva. All bodhisattvas practice in this manner.
Regarding the textual structure, there are three phrases that teach the practice: 'Good son' is one phrase; 'these are called...

and so forth is one phrase; and 'all... and so forth is one phrase. As for the term 'these are called,' it refers back to what was previously named. This phrase definitively names the dharmas. Practice..."
"Thus" is a term used to point directly [to the subject], indicating that there is nothing distinct from the practice itself. This phrase is definitively applied to the person who practices.
The preceding section on "Combining and Indicating the Characteristics" (相科), which comprised the sub-section on "Listing and Displaying the Wheel Characteristics" (列示輪相科), is concluded.

The subsequent section on "Connecting and Manifesting the Total Number of Wheels" (輪數科), which entered into the sub-section on "Entering the General Demonstration of the Teacher’s Ability to Practice" (總示教能修科), is also concluded. Second, the demonstration of the benefits and the skillful means.
If Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this wheel, they should maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and engage in tranquil reflection.

For twenty-one days, they should seek compassion and repent; then, having placed markers for each of the twenty-five wheels, they should single-mindedly seek compassion and take whichever wheel their hand first grasps.

By following the instructions revealed by that binding, they will immediately know whether the path is sudden or gradual. If even a single thought of doubt or regret arises, [the practice] shall not succeed.

Accomplishment. The seven phrases within the text demonstrate the skillful means for benefiting others: the phrase beginning with "If there are... (one phrase); the phrase beginning with "One should maintain...

(one phrase); the phrase beginning with "Seeking compassion... (one phrase); the phrase beginning with "Regarding these two... (one phrase); and the phrase beginning with "With a sincere heart... (one phrase).
The phrase "relying on the fetters," and so forth; the phrase "in a single thought-moment," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "one who relies on this wheel":

it means practicing in accordance with the Dharma. This phrase is stated first as a heading. "One who maintains the holy life" refers to the purity of bodily conduct. "One who reflects in tranquility" refers to...
Gathering the mind in purity, tranquility is the cessation of delusion, and contemplation is the discernment of dharmas.
By means of untainted, tranquil wisdom, one distinguishes between the true and the false, discarding the false and retaining the true. This phrase eliminates the active manifestation of ignorance.

To "seek compassion and repent" means to seek the Buddha’s great compassion and pity for one's inclusion and protection, thereby removing past transgressions, afflictions, karma, and karmic obstacles. Thus one repents.

This is a matter of the Chinese and Indian traditions being preserved in varying degrees of detail. In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *kṣamā*; its meaning is "tolerance. This refers to the request for others to tolerate and forgive one's offenses.

To explain the terms individually: "confession" (*chàn*) means to lay bare one’s prior transgressions; "repentance" (*huì*) means to reform the past and cultivate the future. Regarding the "thirty-five days":
this refers to the initial thirty-five days of receiving a physical body, which is the stage prior to the formation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This is the former...

The *ādāna-vijñāna* establishes the duration and timing of karmic retribution; therefore, the present repentance for past offenses must likewise undergo a transformation over a period of twenty-one days.
This phrase eliminates the seeds of ignorance, and as for "placing markers at each stage of the wheel":
The sequence of the twenty-five wheels, from first to last, is revealed by this phrase. "Sincerely seeking compassion" means to single-mindedly seek the Buddha’s compassionate bestowal.
"Taking them as they arise while forming mudrās" means that for these twenty-five wheels, there are only three single [mudrās], while the remaining ones all possess two or three;
thus, the twenty-five wheels correspond to twenty-five knots, which one takes up as they arise during the formation of the mudrās. This...
When phrases are extinguished and the private biases of the mind are severed, one seeks the Buddha to reveal the Dharma.

Regarding those who rely on the knots for instruction, by examining whether the knots are single or multiple, uniform or circular, and their sequence of priority and gradualness, one immediately knows the sudden and the gradual: the distinct inclusion of the gradual wheel and the perfect synthesis of the sudden wheel.

This passage clarifies the method of cultivation and resolves doubts in the mind. "If one harbors doubt or regret for even a single thought, the cause one has cultivated will be lost and thus not accomplished" means that the fruit of realization will be forfeited.
"Seeking refuge with a sincere heart" refers to possessing the various capacities for entry [into the path].
Because delusion obstructs pure awakening, it is not accomplished. This phrase indicates that when precepts give rise to conceptual discrimination, one loses what has been cultivated and maintained.

This is because accomplishment is achieved through practicing in accordance with awakening. The preceding section, which combined the instruction on the capacity for cultivation and its categorization, is concluded.

Following this, the section providing the formal response is completed. Finally, the initial section of the introduction—which includes the praise and permission—is joined to the general long-format structural outline, and the entire arrangement is hereby concluded.
The second section, the verses in *geya* style, provides a general summary in two parts. First, the introduction expressing the desire to re-proclaim [the meaning]:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to re-proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses.

The explanation of the phrasing follows the previous example. Second, the narration of the spoken verses in two parts. First, summarizing the essential intent to demonstrate the teaching on how to practice.
The opening has two parts. First, the essential point is presented to reveal the total number of wheels:
"Vimalakīrti, you should know that the unimpeded and pure wisdom of all bodhisattvas arises entirely from meditative concentration."
II. Summarizing the Essential Meaning and Enumerating the Number of Cycles, divided into two parts: 1. Summarizing the Essential Meaning and Indicating the Characteristics.
That which is called *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*—these three dharmas have twenty-five types of cultivation, categorized as sudden and gradual.
Second, summarizing the essential teaching for cultivation:
Among all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all practitioners of the three periods of time,
there are none who have attained Bodhi without relying on this Dharma— except for those of sudden enlightenment and those whose natures do not accord with the Dharma.

This excludes only those of sudden enlightenment and those whose nature is not in accord with the Dharma; this is intended to manifest that the fruition-awakening is without cultivation or realization.
Furthermore, it shows by contrast that the causal practices must necessarily rely on this wheel for their cultivation, such that there is no difference between them.
Second, this section provides the essential points and the benefits of the expedient means.

All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should always uphold this wheel and practice it with diligent application, following it in accordance with the power of the Buddha’s great compassion.
By relying on the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, they will before long realize Nirvana.
"Relying on the power of the Buddha’s great compassion" means seeking his mercy through repentance and seeking his mercy for instruction in the sudden and gradual methods of cultivation.
The verse section is concluded. The preceding combination with the prose (gadya) to complete the introductory exposition on the World-Honored One’s response is finished.
The connection with the introductory exposition on the Bodhisattva’s inquiry to include it within the section showing the perfection of cultivation is completed.

Regarding the term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), that which is capable of cultivating is the twenty-five wheels of practice described in this chapter, which serve as the skillful means of cultivation. This connects [to the following].
The section on the Perfect Inclusion of the Upper Chapter, which subsumes all into the Total Perfect Inclusion without obstruction, is completed.
Regarding the twenty-five diagrams of the Twenty-five Wheels, these are established through the practice of the three dharmas—sudden and gradual. First, the single dharma...
First, one practices a single method alone. Next, one gradually practices two methods. Next, one gradually practices three methods.

Furthermore, one practices one method simultaneously with two methods, and two methods simultaneously with one method. In this way, these four stages of application pass through all three methods, forming twenty-four cycles that constitute the culmination of gradual practice.
Thereafter, the three methods are perfectly integrated and practiced as a whole, forming the wheel of sudden realization. Thus, [the total is]...
There are twenty-five [sections]. These are the fundamental aspects of the Dharma that fully encompass the three dharmas;
if these are not clearly revealed, one will not understand the gradual progression of the three dharmas, nor will one understand their sudden perfection.

Furthermore, this would obscure the sequential order of the inquiries posed by the two Bodhisattvas, Vīryaśrī and Prabhāsa: one [inquiry] was to request the general teaching on what is to be cultivated, and the other...

To request that you specifically bestow instruction on how to cultivate [this practice], I have provided a diagram to illustrate the rhythmic patterns that must not be confused, using the hand-pioba as a model.
In the diagram, there is one large circular form, which represents the Great Perfectly Awakened Mind (*mahā-vajra-citta*). Within it are three smaller circular forms.

The wheel of the sudden realization of the three dharmas in perfect union: within each circular form, the eight circular forms arranged in four tiers represent the four stages of gradual progression through the single, the double, and the triple-combinations.

Regarding the distinctions among the eight circular forms—such as being solitary, having one layer, two layers, or three layers with thick black borders—the "solitary" refers to a single dharma alone.
The wheels: two layers represent the integration of two dharmas; three layers represent the integration of three dharmas.
The deep black represents the aspect of the mutual integration of two dharmas. The medium black represents the integration of one dharma as equal to two dharmas.
The peripheral black represents the integration of two dharmas as equal to one dharma. This is merely a provisional illustration of the principles of the phrases in the root sūtra.
