Body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent; how much more so are the sense organs, objects, and illusory realms? All are eternally quiescent.
Yet, if one seeks perfect enlightenment while that nature of perfect enlightenment is not itself a state of quiescence, this is called a "sickness."
There are six phrases for extinguishing the seeking of awakening within the illness: "fourth, extinguishing the illness" (one phrase);
"if again... (one phrase); "body and mind... (one phrase); "how much more... (one phrase); and "all... (one phrase).
Regarding the phrase "That roundness... and so forth: the first clause identifies the name of the affliction. "Permanently severing all afflictions" means entering the fundamental, clear nature;
it is like the subsiding of waves, wherein the root-source of all arising and ceasing is extinguished. This clause shows that person how to abandon the mind of self-clinging.
Regarding the phrase "Body and mind... and so forth: this describes exiting the domain of the *skandha* of form (*rūpaskandha*), where the generative impulses of the common lot suddenly...

However, it is shattered and torn asunder. This phrase indicates that the person demonstrates the characteristic of severing afflictions and attains the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The term "how much more so" is a word used for emphasis. Regarding "the false objects of the sense organs and their fields": this refers to the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) produced in dependence upon the sense organs and their fields.

Indeed, the dharmas that give rise to consciousness are the sense organs and their fields; the organs are established based on the body, while the fields arise from the mind. Since both body and mind—
Ultimate emptiness: what sense faculties and objects could give rise to consciousness?
Therefore, this phrase is used to demonstrate how those who have received instruction and attained the realization of the emptiness of persons abandon their own false conceptualizations.

These two phrases together collectively demonstrate the thorough manifestation of the permanent cessation of all afflictions, the accomplishment of purity, and the characteristic of extinction. "All are eternally quiescent" means:
That person, having realized through their body, mind, and consciousness that delusion is ultimately empty, seeks to attain *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment) and achieve purity.
This phrase means that when that person illuminates the attainment of cessation, they seek *yuanjue*; yet because it is not a state of quiescent form, it is said [as follows]:

the quiescence of the nature of awakening universally illumines perfect stillness (*yuanji*), and there is no separate characteristic. As for "the characteristic of form... [it refers to the following].

"Quiescence" refers to the obscured ignorance (*avidyā*) that fully establishes the characterized (*lakṣya*). Therefore, it is not pure awakening. This phrase explains the illness of extinguishing [delusion];
because one seeks awakening by investigating the extinction of that which is deluded, the manas within the seeds abandons its grasping and returns to its proper station.
When the seven types of self-clinging within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are exhausted, all afflictions are forever severed.
Body and mind become ultimately empty; the seven [consciousnesses] are reduced to the six sense bases, wherein the delusions of consciousness are eternally stilled.

The entire being abides in its true state, and the ignorance that was delusion becomes pure awakening. Therefore, one sees that the notion of truly existing phenomena that can be extinguished is forever rendered obscure.
Thus, one achieves pure awakening. Not realizing that the delusive nature of ignorance is not the profound and luminous nature of awakening—how then can one attain awakening?

This concludes the section on the three illnesses associated with the combined "objective phenomena" (所法), which follows the previous section on the two illnesses associated with the "subjective capacity" (能法).

This concludes the sequential explanation following the combined section. This concludes the detailed enumeration of the characteristics of the illnesses, which is governed by the initial section of inquiry.
Second is the manifestation of the proof of purity.
One who is free from the four maladies knows purity.
A single phrase in the text manifests this proof of purity: namely, having attained freedom from the four maladies, ignorance will certainly be eternally extinguished.
Only by severing [delusion] can one refrain from engaging in the errors of "clinging" and "rejecting" regarding the six [objects], and allow the seven delusions to cease naturally.

Yet, one takes the delusion of abiding ignorance as the very nature of realization. Thus, one knows that the purity of what is realized is the knower. This refers to the definitive instruction for sentient beings of the final age regarding the four maladies of the Dharma;
through the distinction between being free or not free [from these maladies], one may verify whether a teacher has realized the Dharma. As stated previously:
The detailed enumeration of the categories of the symptoms of illness, which together constitute the category of "separation from illness" as a dharma, is hereby concluded.

The integration of the categories of "evidence of the dharma" and "separation from illness," which are subsumed under the category of "demonstration of the purity of the dharma," is likewise concluded. Second, the separate contemplation of the deviant and the correct.
"One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice wrong contemplation.

Regarding this passage, there are two distinct sentences that differentiate between the wrong and the right: "One who practices this... and so forth, and "If one contemplates otherwise... and so forth.
"One who practices this contemplation" refers to contemplating the Teacher’s Dharma by way of being free from the four maladies; this is what is meant by "right contemplation. It is as follows:

"Skillfully seeking the teacher’s correct knowledge and vision": this phrase indicates what is correct. If one observes otherwise, being ignorant of how to observe the Dharma so as to remain free from affliction, allowing the mind to wander recklessly according to likes and dislikes and attachments and aversions, such a person is called one of "erroneous observation. This refers to the evil knowledge and vision of one who deludedly seeks a teacher.
This phrase excludes what is erroneous. The preceding sections, taken together with the section on purity, complete the perfection of the selection of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*).

The section on "Separation" concludes. The section on "Union and Seeking a Teacher for Sudden Realization" is subsumed under the section on "Humanity and Dharma and Right Contemplation," which concludes.
Second, "Entering Awakening through One’s Own Practice" is divided into two parts. First, "Accomplishing Practice by Following a Teacher" is divided into two parts.
First, "Physical and Mental Accordance" is divided into two parts. First, "Life-long Devotion."
"Good son, those living beings in the final age who wish to practice should, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual benefactors.
They should complete two phrases: 'Good son' as one phrase, and 'In the final age... and so forth as the second phrase. Throughout their entire lives, they should take refuge in them."
Those who wish to practice and desire to achieve the cultivation that accords with awakening should, for as long as life lasts, not draw near to false teachers;

rather, they should take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One for the remainder of their lives. As for making offerings, one should provide the four requisites at the proper times with a pure mind and devotion.
"Virtuous friends" refers to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); the explanation follows the previous pattern. This sentence indicates reliance [upon these supports].
Perfect Enlightenment. Second, regarding the mind descending like a bird from the sky:
if that spiritual friend wishes to come near and approach you, you should sever pride; if they instead distance themselves, you should sever resentment.
Manifesting favorable and adverse conditions as being like empty space.
Regarding the text, there are three phrases: "As clouds descend upon the mind," "If again... (one phrase), and "Manifesting favorability...
(one phrase). As for the first phrase, because one does not perceive the Tathāgata through the aspect of coming, it is [included] within knowledge.
When one encounters those who are wise and intimate, one should sever the mind of pride (*māna*). Regarding "pride," the explanation follows the previous [section].
Second, because one does not perceive the Tathāgata through the aspect of departure, one should remain distant from those who are wise;

one should sever the mind of resentment and harbor no sense of grievance, thinking that they have abandoned me. Third, because one realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, regarding the virtuous...

Regarding objects that accord with one’s own inclinations as manifested by consciousness, and those that oppose one’s own inclinations, one views them all as being like space—ultimately pure and free from the arising of divergent thoughts.
This concludes the section on "The Body and Mind Following Accordance," which together with the preceding section forms the first part. Second:
"Equality of Self and Others."
To thoroughly understand that body and mind are ultimately equal, being of the same essence as all sentient beings without distinction.

This section on "the equality of self and others" consists of two phrases: the first phrase establishes that one does not posit the characteristics of body and mind for oneself, which constitutes ultimate equality;
the second phrase establishes that one does not posit the characteristics of body and mind for others, which constitutes being of the same essence without distinction. This is derived from...

One subdues the mind and takes refuge in the teacher, making offerings and drawing near to them. This opens up correct knowledge and vision, resulting in the pure wisdom of awakening that is perfectly free from the four marks.
Thus concludes the preceding section on "Harmonizing Body and Mind" in accordance with the ritual, which together completes the section on "Accomplishing the Service and Practice of the Teacher."
Second, distinguishing between delusion and awakening.
Only through such cultivation does one enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
In this passage, a single sentence distinguishes between delusion and awakening. "One who cultivates in this manner" refers to the aforementioned subduing of the mind and taking refuge.

The teacher of right knowledge and vision accomplishes pure awakened wisdom through practice; only then does one enter Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa), whereupon there is no longer defilement or delusion.
If one instead approaches another teacher and establishes a separate practice, one will become lost and fail to enter awakening.

The preceding sections on serving the teacher and accomplishing practice together to complete the section on entering awakening through one's own practice are concluded. This concludes the continuous synthesis of person and dharma. Correct.
The section on Contemplation regarding the classification of practice based on awakening is concluded. This answers the request of those seeking the Dharma to practice according to the teachings.
Second, the section on Severing Delusion and Accomplishing Realization is divided into two parts. First, the section on Eliminating Illness and Continuing Delusion is divided into two parts.
First, investigating the source of deluded awakening.
"Good son, sentient beings in the final age cannot achieve the Way because they have not yet attained liberation due to the presence of all seeds of beginningless self and other, hatred and love."
The three phrases beginning with "When... investigate the confusion of awakening. The phrase "Good son" is one sentence. The phrase "In the final age...
and so forth is one sentence pointing out delusion. Because of the phrase "Due to [the existence of]... and so forth, there is the beginningless self and other, as well as hatred and love;
these are the ignorance of root and branch. "All seeds" refers to both newly perfumed and formerly matured [seeds]. Therefore, those who are not yet liberated [are so] because of this.
Therefore, liberation has not yet been achieved, and the pure conduct of liberation is not manifested; this means that the practice of the Path has not yet been perfected.
Second, the manifestation of practice eliminates illness and opens two aspects: first, the manifestation of the emptiness of persons in practice.
Furthermore, if there is a person who views an enemy as their own parent with a mind free of duality, all illnesses will be eliminated.

This single phrase from the text manifests the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). An "enemy" is an object that gives rise to hatred; a "parent" is an object that gives rise to love.
A person's hateful mind arises simply because it has been transformed from love; it is because something is no longer loved that one consequently comes to hate it.

The mind that faces an object of aversion is not dualistic; the mind that faces an object of attachment is likewise not dualistic. This is not merely the absence of aversion, but also the absence of attachment.
When both aversion and attachment are forgotten, present activity becomes pure, the perfuming of ignorance is severed, and the seeds lose their moisture.
Thus, one attains the ability to purify delusion, and all illnesses are immediately eliminated. As for "all illnesses," these are all the delusions of ignorance.

This is the nature [of the teaching]. Second, regarding the manifestation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*): among all phenomena, the self and other, as well as aversion and attachment, are likewise so.

When it says in the text, "a single phrase of the manifestation of the emptiness of phenomena is likewise so," this combines with the aforementioned manifestation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Recently, I have observed that the practice of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) is being manifested. It is further stated:

"If there is a person who contemplates birth-and-death as if entering nirvāṇa, with a mind free of duality, they will immediately eliminate all ailments. This concludes the section on "Manifesting Practice to Eliminate Ailments," which, together with the preceding sections, completes the synthesis.

Since the previous section was analyzed through inference, the section on "Delusion and Awakening" is subsumed under "Eliminating Ailments"; this concludes the section on "The Continuation of Delusion."
Second, regarding the arousal of the mind and the departure from views, there are two parts. First, the arousal of the mind as taught by the instruction:
"Good son, sentient beings in the final age who wish to seek Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) should arouse the mind by making this declaration:
'I shall cause all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space to enter ultimate Perfect Enlightenment. Within that Perfect Enlightenment, there is no..."
The "Awakened One who takes up" eliminates all marks of self, other, and person;
this refers to the fourfold teaching on the mind generated according to the text. "Good son," is one phrase. "In the final age," and so forth, is another phrase.
Regarding the phrase "as for 'like clouds'... and the phrase "regarding 'the perfect'...": one who seeks Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue) seeks the mind of perfect awakening.

One who should resolve to generate the aspiration must give rise to the mind that delivers sentient beings. This is because within the ocean of Perfect Enlightenment, worlds are infinite and sentient beings are infinite;
all are established by the mind of Perfect Enlightenment. If one does not resolve to deliver these various worlds...
The sentient beings within the realms dwell together in purity; this is none other than the ultimate, perfect purity of the awakened mind.

This phrase serves as an instruction to generate the bodhicitta. Regarding the statement "speaking thus," the subsequent text clarifies that it is through explicit words that the teaching can be manifested.
As for the reason for generating the mind, the passage beginning with "extending to the limits of space" and so forth refers to the *Dharmadhātu* of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).
"May I cause them all to enter... and so forth means causing them all to attain Buddhahood and perfect the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). This phrase indicates the mind that is generated.

"Within Great Perfect Enlightenment" refers to within the Great Perfect Enlightenment; "there being no one who grasps at enlightenment" means there is no fourfold mind of realizing, awakening, understanding, or comprehending enlightenment, as one enters the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatāprajñā*).
"Eliminating self, other, person," and so forth, means merging with the non-duality of self and others.

The illusory objects of hatred and love become the practice of liberation. This phrase indicates the virtuous conduct by which the beings to be saved enter into pure awakening, thereby fulfilling those who have generated the resolve for enlightenment. Second, they are definitively able to transcend views.
Thus, one who has resolved their mind in this way does not fall into false views;
even a single phrase of the text is sufficient to decisively bring about freedom from such views. "In this way" refers to the generation of the resolve as taught.

"Does not fall into false views" means that one does not achieve the partial or limited realizations of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, but is able to achieve perfect enlightenment. This concludes the preceding section of the text.

The section on "Together Accomplishing the Arising of the Mind and Departing from Views" is concluded. The preceding combined section on "Eliminating Illness and Continuing Delusion" is subsumed under the section on "Severing Delusion and Achieving Accomplishment," which is now concluded.
This answers the inquiry regarding the elimination of illness, the arising of the mind, and departing from views.
The combined section on "Relying on Awakening for Cultivation" and its entry into the general long arrangement of the sequence is now concluded. Second, the verses in summary provide the overview.
2. First, the introduction: wishing to restate this meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
The method for explaining the lines is as before. 2. Second, the narration of the verses, which opens into two parts: first, summarizing the essential intent based on awakening and cultivation.
Opening the Two: First, the Correct Contemplation of the Essential Meaning Regarding Persons and Dharmas.
Pujue, you should know: If those sentient beings in the末世 (final age) Desire to seek a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), They should seek one who possesses correct vision.
One whose mind is far removed from the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), And who eliminates the four maladies within the Dharma.

This refers to the exposition of the maladies through the sequence of *zuo* (activity), *ren* (reliance), *zhi* (stopping), and *mie* (extinguishing). The first, second, third, and fourth—namely, activity, reliance, stopping, and extinguishing—are based on the posteriority and priority of consciousness.

Now, in this verse, the sequence of activity, stopping, reliance, and extinguishing is based on the arising and ceasing of consciousness. One seeks awakening through activity, yet thereby clings to the clarity of the six consciousnesses.
This involves calculating the arising of the six consciousnesses; by seeking awakening through cessation, one abandons the external half of the manas.
This involves calculating the cessation of the six consciousnesses; as a single category of arising and ceasing, by seeking awakening through naturalness, one clings to the entire body of the manas.
This involves calculating the arising of the seven consciousnesses and seeking awakening through their cessation; thus, one abandons the internal half of the *manas*.

This involves calculating the cessation of the seven consciousnesses as a single category of arising and ceasing. Therefore, these are combined in verse. The second [section] extracts the essential meaning for self-cultivation and entry into awakening.

Associate with those free from pride; remain far removed from anger and resentment. Upon encountering various sensory realms, the mind should give rise to a sense of wonder, as if the Buddha had appeared in the world.

This second section provides the essential purport for severing delusion and accomplishing enlightenment. The first part provides the essential purport for eliminating afflictions and eradicating delusions.
Not transgressing what is non-discipline, the root of the precepts is eternally pure;

there is no further manifestation of hatred or attachment, and ignorance is forever severed. Because one abides in the pure precepts of the Buddha, this is the summary verse. Second, the summary of the essential meaning:
generating the mind of enlightenment while remaining free from views.
Deliver all sentient beings so that they ultimately enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Without the conceptual distinctions of self, other, person, or counterpart, and by relying upon correct wisdom, one immediately transcends false views and realizes awakening and *parinirvāṇa*.
"Realizing awakening and *parinirvāṇa*" refers to the wondrous perfection of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The Sanskrit term *parinirvāṇa* is translated here as "entering."
Nirvāṇa. Awakening is the Dharma-body; cessation is liberation; and crossing over is Prajñā. The verse section is concluded.
The preceding integration with the prose, which categorized the introduction as the section on the World-Honored One’s gracious response, is finished.

The combined integration with the introduction, which categorized the Bodhisattvas’ posing of questions, leading into the general demonstration of the complete transcendence of phenomena, is concluded. As for what is called "phenomena" (dharma), it refers to the correctness or deviation of persons.
One distinguishes one's own practice by means of the Dharma realized; one achieves perfection by making offerings to those who uphold the True Dharma.

Thus, one may eliminate illness and be able to give rise to the Bodhicitta, entering the ocean of pure awakening. Therefore, this section specifically points to the Dharma to clarify its scope, thereby encompassing the entire body of teaching and principle.
Furthermore, it does not overlap with the purport of the preceding chapter. Previously, it was shown that the Perfect [Teaching] transcends the mind.

The section on "The Mutual Completion of Categories and the Unobstructed Separation" concludes. The section on "The Continuous Union and Perfect Inclusion of the Unobstructed" concludes by being subsumed under the section on "The Unobstructed Cultivation and Realization.
The section on "The Connection between Nature and Realization as Being Like Space" governs the section on "The Purity of Nature and Cultivation During Realization," which now concludes.
This, in essence, is the ultimate purity wherein nature is luminous, cultivation is perfected, the mind is detached from phenomena, and all is wondrous.

The section on the purity of the practice of discernment and wisdom within the "Synthesis of the Threads" concludes the general clarification of the causes for the purity of abandonment and realization.

Now that the causes have been clarified, the fruit may be realized. May this be granted so that sentient beings of the末代 (final age) whose roots of virtue have long been planted may together encounter this teaching. Thus it is stated.
Commentary on the Words of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment: The Definitive Meaning, Scroll Lower-Middle and Scroll Lower-Lower,
translated by the Kasmirian Śramaṇa Buddhatoṭara.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Hongli of Luofeng in Zhendan;
collated by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Zaiqu in the Divine Land. This work contains two sections:

[1] the Pure Contemplation of the Two Kinds of Fruits, and [2] the Expedient Means for Opening the Two. The first section, "Preface and Narration of the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry," is further divided into two parts. The first part: [The text continues with the specific doctrinal content.]
The introduction follows the sequence of the inquiry.
Thus, this introduction reveals the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment’s skillful means for purifying awakening through causal practice, severance, and realization. The Bodhisattva of the World...
"World-Honored One, your questions and my responses have been fully explained. Sentient beings of the final age can directly rely on these teachings to practice and achieve the perfection of *bodhi*.
However, regarding the initial expedient means for practicing contemplation while dwelling in retreat at a *bodhimanda*, we have not yet heard the Sage’s instructions."
Fearing that sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age might become confused and distressed by this, thereby failing to obtain its benefits,

they have raised questions regarding the definitive (*nītārtha*) Dharma-gates revealed in this assembly, hoping for the Buddha’s instruction and benefit so that sentient beings of the末法 age may know the skillful means of former cultivation,
attain the ultimate completion of practice, and realize the fruit within the causal source within the ocean of self-nature awakening.

Part Two: The Preface and Questions, Divided into Three Sections, Each Further Divided into Two. First, the Preface Describing the Ritual Protocol, Divided into Two. First, the Preface on Questioning Regarding Dignified Conduct:
The Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, the phrasing and interpretation of which follow the previous examples.
Second, the description of the request for instruction and benefit is divided into two parts. First, the celebration of hearing the present benefit:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes you have extensively expounded the various skillful means of Pure Awakening, enabling the multitudes of the final age..."
There is great benefit in being born [into this teaching].

The text should be divided into three sections to celebrate the present benefits of hearing [the Dharma]: one section for "The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One," one section for "For my sake...
and so forth, and one section for "Causing the end... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "various skillful means," it encompasses the ten bodhisattvas who were previously answered in their inquiries.
Regarding the doctrine and principles shown: this phrase praises the teaching. "Greatly increasing benefit" refers to the accomplishment of the skillful means for practicing the Mahāyāna;
this phrase demonstrates the benefit. Following the formal request, the subsequent benefits are divided into two parts: first, the request for the initial skillful means.

“World-Honored One, we have now attained awakening. However, for those sentient beings in the future age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa who have not yet attained awakening, how should they dwell in retreat and cultivate this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment?
Within this Perfect Enlightenment, which of the three kinds of pure contemplations should be taken as primary?”

The five phrases of the introduction request the initial expedient means: one phrase for the World-Honored One, one phrase for "we," one phrase for "if the Buddha," one phrase for "how," and one phrase for "this circle.

The phrase "we" manifests long-standing practice; the phrase "the Buddha" expresses compassionate concern for those who have newly begun; and the phrase "how" inquires regarding the method of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
This "Perfect Sentence" asks about the skillful means for cultivating contemplation. Regarding the questions required for these two skillful means:

because the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment requires being free from the marks of self, person, and so forth, as well as not clinging to the realms of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, it is necessary for the Buddha to demonstrate that his dwelling is not tied to a following of disciples, and to request the presence of the Tathāgatas and Great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.

As for Bodhisattvas acting as companions: by means of the three contemplations of Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue san guan*), they fundamentally encompass all phenomena within their perfection, such that there is neither beginning nor end.

Fearing that sentient beings of the末代 (final age) might become confused regarding the point of entry, it is necessary for the Buddha to reveal the preliminary expedient means (*upāya*) of the three contemplations to serve as a guiding rule.
Second, the response of the two benefactors concludes with the benefits.
I only pray that the Great Compassionate One will bestow great benefit upon the great assembly and sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age.
A single phrase from the text shall serve as the response to conclude the benefits. This concludes the section on the subsequent benefits, combined with the preceding section on the formal petition.

This concludes the section on the description of the request for instruction and benefits, which subsumes the preceding section on the celebration of hearing the present benefits. This concludes the combined introduction.
Question: Regarding the section on Dignified Conduct (*īryāpatha*), the explanation of the sequence of rites has concluded. Second, the conclusion of the introductory sequence:
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning from the end and returning to the start.

The examples for the phrase-by-phrase commentary are as before. The preceding section, which includes the introduction, the description of the ritual, the phonology, the categorization, and the inclusion within the introduction, concludes with the three sections on the inquiry.
This connects the inquiry from the introduction to the subsequent section on entering the general introduction, concluding the section on the Bodhisattva’s raising of the inquiry.

Second, the introduction describing the World-Honored One’s response is divided into two parts. First, the long list of names indicating the opening is divided into two. The first is the introductory praise and permission.
The opening has two parts. First, the praise and request for instruction:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, you are indeed able to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means, thereby bestowing great benefit upon all sentient beings."
The four-line verse of praise for requesting instruction consists of two general lines: "You all... (one line) and "...with the Great [Vehicle]...
(one line). Second, the granting of the answer and the entrustment for reception is divided into two parts: first, the entrustment to listen attentively.
"Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
The explanation of the phrases follows the previous pattern. The two [disciples] received the instruction and remained silent.
Then, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

The example for the word-by-word commentary is as before. The preceding section on the combined text, which together completes the section on the granting of permission, the response, and the entrustment, is finished.

The preceding combined section on the praise and request for instruction, which was subsumed under the initial section on the praise and permission of the prologue, is also finished. Next, the presentation of the formal response is divided into two parts.

First, the instruction on the skillful means for opening [the gates], which has two parts. First, the skillful means for the summer retreat (varṣā), which has two parts. First, the cultivation of the awakening to self-nature, which has two parts.
First, the constant cultivation based on analogical insight.
"Good son, whether the Buddha remains in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, even during the final age of the Dharma,
there may be sentient beings who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna and, having faith in the Buddha’s secret, great, perfectly enlightened mind, desire to practice it.
If they dwell within a monastery with a community of followers, they may, due to various circumstantial matters, reflect and investigate according to their capacity, as I have already explained."
The seven phrases of the "When" section follow the pattern seen in the "Constant Practice" [section]: "Good son" (one phrase), "all sentient beings" (one phrase), "if the Buddha...
and so forth (one phrase), "there being various... and so forth (one phrase), "if he were in... and so forth (one phrase), "having conditions...
and so forth (one phrase), "as I... and so forth (one phrase). "If the Buddha were to remain in the world," [his] transformative conditions would not yet...

"Completed. If it refers to after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is the proclamation of stillness at the Twin Śāla Trees; if it refers to the age of the Dharma’s decline, it is after two thousand years. These phrases are all cultivated simultaneously.
There are certain phrases that distinguish the nature of one’s inclination toward cultivation. If one dwells in the silence of these phrases, there is no further attachment.
"Gārāma" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Monastic Garden" (Saṅghārāma). Phrases involving conditions are active and not detached, such as the phrase "like me."

The preceding example is indicated as an illustration. Second, the detailed exposition of the limits of practice is divided into two parts. First, the designation of the method is divided into two parts.

First, the establishment of the period for *an-guo* (summer retreat) is divided into two parts. First, the cultivation of the period of mindfulness of the Buddha is divided into two parts. First, the number of days for the period of cultivation.
If there are no other circumstances or causes, one should establish a site for the practice of the Way (bodhimaṇḍa) and set a time limit.
If a long period is established, it shall be one hundred and twenty days; a medium period, one hundred days; and a short period, eighty days. One should then settle in a pure dwelling.
The three phrases regarding the period of cultivation for the text; if it says "furthermore" (若復), it is one phrase; if it establishes "furthermore" (若立), it is one phrase;
and the placement of the Pure Abodes (淨居) is one phrase. Regarding "conditions of other matters" (他事因緣): this refers to the Bodhisattva’s work of benefiting others.

That is to say, when establishing a site of practice (道場), if there are no conditions for benefiting others, one performs self-benefit by establishing the site of practice in order to transform impurity.
The earth becomes the cause for the Pure Land. Regarding the establishment of a time limit: by exerting oneself with punctuality, one shall shatter the deluded perceptions of billions of kalpas.
This phrase refers to the cause and fruit within the world of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).

As for the mention of a long period of one hundred and twenty days and so forth, this refers to the periods for the three stages of cultivation and realization—initial, middle, and final. The initial stage lasts many [days], while the middle stage lasts twenty.

The middle period consists of twenty days, mostly occurring in the latter half. This is because during the initial period, one performs repentance for the first three weeks, seeking instruction on the sudden and gradual cultivation of the wheel of concentration (*samādhi-cakra*).
Only thereafter does one formally enter the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) to repent and seek compassion, thereby encountering favorable conditions.
During the middle period, one engages solely in formal repentance for three weeks, without further seeking the wheel of concentration.

Because of this repentance, twenty days are subtracted. During the subsequent period, since the obstacles of both fact and principle have already been removed by the two previous rounds of repentance, one simply focuses on mindfulness directly; there are no further days of repentance for the three weeks, so another twenty days are subtracted.
Generally, the formal practice of these three periods consists of eighty days each; thus, [the total] is thirty-eight times twenty.

Regarding the fourth, the gradual sequence of the wheel-counts: "one wheel per ten days" means that one wheel encompasses the dharma-realm of the ten directions, and one day constitutes one such dharma-realm;
therefore, one wheel comprises ten days of cultivation. This phrase refers to the duration of the samādhi-wheel of Perfect Enlightenment.
"Establishing" means abiding securely without departing. "Pure Abode" refers to the very site of the bodhimanda that has been established.
This phrase indicates sitting in meditation within the bodhimanda without leaving it, thereby gathering the mind through mindfulness. Second is the correct contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha.

If the Buddha is currently present, one should practice right reflection; if after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should fashion images and maintain mental focus and visual contemplation to give rise to right mindfulness.
This is equivalent to the days when the Tathāgata was alive and various banners and flowers were suspended [as offerings].

When practicing the threefold contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha, one should contemplate as follows: "The Buddha...," "The Buddha...," and "Returning to..."; these three phrases are identical.
One who practices correct reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*) does not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, nor does one seek him in sound or form.
This phrase serves as a warning that the Buddha exists in the state of non-arising and permanence.
"Visualizing" (xiǎng) refers to manifesting the physical form and appearance of the Buddha. "Mental focus" (xīn cún) refers to the turning of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
"Visualizing with the eyes" (mù xiǎng) refers to the turning of the mental factors (*caitta*). Because the eye is itself the mind, one speaks of "visualizing" rather than "seeing.

One should engage in correct contemplation (*samyak-samādhi*); one should not seek the Tathāgata by means of the mark of quiescence, thereby sinking into emptiness or becoming stagnant in stillness. This...

The phrase "admonishing that after the Buddha's extinction there is no arising and severing the notion [of cessation], returning to the same as the Tathāgata’s day of eternal abiding" means that one realizes the nature of the image [of the Buddha] is equal to empty space, identical to both the living and the Buddha. "Hanging various banners and flowers":

the banner serves to ward off dust, and the flower serves to manifest awakening; these represent the accomplishment of the two functions of exclusion and illumination, thereby adorning [the practice]. This phrase darkly eliminates the view of annihilationism.

The Dharma-offering. Together with the preceding section on the textual arrangement, this completes the section on the Period of Cultivating Recollection of the Buddha. Second, the Section on Repentance and Gathering the Mind, which is divided into two parts:
first, repentance for purification; second, [the practice of] gathering the mind.

After twenty-one days, he prostrated before the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeking their compassion and repenting. He encountered auspicious signs and attained mental ease (*praśrabdhi*).

Regarding the text, there are two phrases for "repenting and becoming pure" (*kṣamāpanā-viśuddhi*); following this, there are three instances of "after [a period of]... and so forth, and one instance of "encountering auspicious [signs]... and so forth.
[This] phrase: for twenty-one days, the explanation follows the previous [instruction]. "Bowing one's head" means to touch the head to the ground and then rise slowly and deliberately.

"The ten directions" refers to the Dharmadhātu of Perfect Enlightenment (*Samantabhadra*). "The names of the Buddhas" means to recite their names as if beholding them, while concentrating the mind on pure awakening, seeking compassion and repenting;
the explanation follows the previous [instruction]. This phrase removes defilement. "Encountering a wholesome state" means liberation.

Regarding the signs of response: for one who has attained mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the afflictions are subdued; this phrase signifies the attainment of purity. Second, regarding the gathering of mindfulness toward non-arising:
for twenty-one days, one should exclusively gather the mind in mindfulness.
The three phrases of the first section encompass the mindfulness of non-arising. "After twenty-one days" refers to the eightieth day of formal cultivation.

"Exclusively gathering mindfulness" is the preparatory practice (*pūrvayoga*) prior to attaining the pure awakened mind by withdrawing from delusive objects of perception and distancing oneself from illusory falsehoods.
This phrase demonstrates the pure mind of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It establishes the non-existence of the three contemplations.

The practice of removing hindrances is the primary cultivation within the *bodhimaṇḍa*. This concludes the section on Repentance and Mindfulness, which together with the preceding section, completes the entire text.

The previous section on the Cultivation of Reciting the Buddha’s Name during the Period of Practice is subsumed under the section on Establishing the Period for Summer Retreat; this concludes that section.
Second, regarding the opening of the summer retreat (*varṣā-vāsa*), there are two parts: first, showing the distance from the Two Vehicles; second, [showing the distance from] the Small Vehicle.
If one observes the three-month summer retreat at the beginning of the year, one should dwell as a pure bodhisattva with a mind detached from the śrāvakas and without relying on a retinue;
this first phrase indicates the distancing from the two vehicles. If the scripture says "and so forth" (yún yún), this single phrase should be understood as "and so forth" (yún yún) [one].

"Phrase. "If it is a sūtra," means even if one encounters it. "At the beginning of summer" refers to the fact that, according to monastic custom, the *anvārambha* (rainy-season retreat) takes place in the first month of summer.
"Three months" refers to the ninety-day period of observing the *śīla* (restraint). This phrase indicates the time and month for the *anvārambha* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Since the practices of Bodhisattvas, though differing [in scope], must necessarily conform to the same regulations, they are aligned with the summer months; thus it should be stated as such.

The term "cloud" (*yun*) indicates the knowledge of distinct practices. "The mind is detached from that of the *śrāvakas*" means the mind is detached from the realization expected by the *śrāvakas* and enters the unimpeded *dharmadhātu* of reality.

"Without relying on a retinue" means without borrowing; whereas the *śrāvaka* retreat (*an-gu*) relies on others to perform the ritual procedures and thus requires a retinue, the Bodhisattva is not like this. For the sake of cultivating unsurpassed wondrous enlightenment, they enter...
Because the dharma-realm is unimpeded in phenomena, one performs rites before the Buddha, taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as the monastery (*ārāma*).

This is precisely what constitutes the purity of a bodhisattva. This phrase demonstrates that there is no confusion with the practices of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), which would result in the loss of the bodhisattva’s realization of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmadhātu-pratītyasamutpāda*). Second, it reveals the cultivation of wondrous enlightenment, which opens into two parts. First:
The words were manifest and the Dharma revealed.
On the day of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), he spoke these words before the Buddha:

"I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā] named so-and-so, who has mounted the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivates the practice of quiescence, together enter the pure true reality (*bhūtatathatā*)."
Abbot: To take Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, with body and mind dwelling in the wisdom of equality, for the self-nature of nirvana is without attachment or dependence.

The eight phrases of the opening section clarify the terminology and manifest the Dharma. The phrase "on the day of the *varṣā* retreat" [is one phrase]. The phrase "as for the following... [is one phrase].

The phrase "dwelling in the Bodhisattva vehicle" [is one phrase]. The phrase "cultivating the practice of quiescence" [is one phrase]. The phrase "entering together into the following... [is one phrase].
"By means of the great cloud... (one phrase). "Body and mind... (one phrase). "Nirvana... (one phrase).
Regarding the day of entering the retreat (*an-gu-jil*), it is the sixteenth day of the fourth month; this phrase marks the time and is identical to the prohibitions.
"Directly before the Buddha" refers to directly receiving the fruit of realization. "Distinct from the two vehicles and relying on the Saṃgha" means to speak these words while [in that state]. In...
Regarding the term "bhikṣu" (biqiu): it is a Sanskrit word that encompasses three meanings. First, "one who destroys evil":

through the completion of the three *karmavācanās* of receiving the precepts, one generates the wholesome restraint (*śīla*) and thereby destroys the unwholesome restraint. Second, "one who terrifies Māra":
because he is able to destroy evil, Māra becomes terrified, leaves his own realm, transforms his retinue, and vacates his palace. Third, "one who begs for sustenance": begging for wealth.

One who provides for the body achieves personal purity and virtue, becoming a field of merit for the world. One who begs for the Dharma to cultivate the mind achieves personal wisdom and conduct, becoming a guide for the world.
As for *bhikṣuṇī*, it means a female renunciant; specifically, a woman who has received full ordination.
*Upāsaka* and *upāsikā* are Sanskrit terms; here they are translated as "male lay follower" and "female lay follower," referring to those who have received the three refuges and the five precepts.
Because men and women capable of approaching bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs may serve as attendants, [the text] says "so-and-so," each calling their own name.
Because their practice differs from that of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), the laity are included. This phrase indicates the perfect identity of cause and fruit;

those who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle enter the causal practice of awakening, which is distinct from the two vehicles' delusion regarding the realization of the fruit of awakening. Thus, they cultivate the practice of quiescent extinction.
"Perfect enlightenment shines universally, distinguishing it from the non-awakening of ignorance of the two vehicles. These two phrases refer to the cultivation of the awakened mind.

"Entering together" means there is no distinction in the blazing establishment of an objective realm. "Pure real mark" means that the sense organs and their objects are all-pervasive, lacking any nature of destruction or confusion.
"Abiding and maintaining" means that the perfectly shining pure light is held in total retention without movement. By means of the great cloud...
The term "Cloud" refers to that from which the abiding of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is established.

These two phrases refer to the transformation of the fifth and eighth consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishment and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, whereby the body and mind rest securely within the ocean of fruition.

When the formations of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) are exhausted, the foundation of birth becomes clear and undisturbed; the nature enters the primordial clarity, like waves subsiding and transforming into still water, becoming level and calm.
The "wisdom of equality" (*samatā-jñāna*) refers to the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). The "intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is unconditioned": because it is non-conceptual, it transcends all objective referents (*ālambana*).

These two lines refer to the transformation of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses into the wisdom of equality and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). By penetrating the fundamental cause, these four lines taken together constitute the [complete] realization.
Regarding the awakening of the mind, secondly, he proclaims his words to request a companion:
"I now respectfully request not to rely on the Śrāvakas, but rather to enter the three-month summer retreat together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of cultivating the supreme and wondrous cause of Bodhisattva awakening, I shall not be bound by a retinue."
This passage consists of three phrases that clarify the request for a companion. "Not relying on the śrāvakas" means not sharing the same causal conditions as those of the two vehicles;

this phrase distinguishes [the practitioner] from the Lesser Vehicle. "I shall certainly grant it" means a definitive granting. Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas... and so forth:
it signifies that within the assembly of the Dharma of equality, the principal and its associates, cause and effect, self and other, constitute a single path of resonance and response.

This phrase reveals the "Great. Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva practices," etc., it refers to the perfection of the qualities of the fruit. Regarding "because of the great causal conditions," it refers to the cultivation and realization of wondrous enlightenment;

that is, through the causal conditions of ultimate, pure awakening, one causes all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm to enter together into the great ocean of quiescent extinction.
This is the most magnificent of causal conditions. Regarding "not being bound by a retinue," [it refers to] the retinue...
The designation "assembly" refers to the followers of the Śrāvaka-dharma. In the Dharma-assembly of Perfect Enlightenment, all sentient beings fundamentally abide in the equality of Buddhahood.

Although cause and effect are both manifested, when cause and effect are perfectly integrated, they merge with the ultimate reality; transcending the distinctions between the holy and the ordinary, who then constitutes an assembly?
Those who are currently unattached do not rely upon the Śrāvakas. Therefore, by means of the unsurpassed, wondrous...
Because he realized the great causes and conditions, he elucidated this point. This sentence explains why he does not rely upon the Śrāvakas.

Together with the preceding section, the "Section on the Summer Retreat" (*varṣā*) of the sutra is completed. With the previous establishment of the "Section on the Fixed Period for Retreat," its inclusion within the "Section on the Marking of the Dharma" is concluded. Second, the conclusion of the title.
"Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). After the three-month period has passed, one may go wherever one wishes without hindrance.
This section consists of three phrases as a concluding title: "Good son," [one phrase]; "this is called... [one phrase];
and "after the three [months] have passed... [one phrase]. "This" refers back to the aforementioned method. "Manifestation of the retreat" refers to the Bodhisattva.

Because every causal practice is nothing other than the salvation of sentient beings, it is called "manifestation. This phrase reveals that the secret fruit of the Bodhisattva is practiced through causes. Regarding "passing the period of three phases":
this means that the cultivation during the initial, middle, and final phases has been completed. "Proceeding everywhere without obstruction" means being pervasive and compliant.
This phrase reveals the accomplishment of unobstructed cultivation. The preceding sections on the combined explanation of characteristics together constitute [this chapter].

The detailed exposition of the section on limited cultivation is concluded. The combined examples showing the inclusion within the section on constant cultivation and the subordination to the section on the self-nature of awakening through cultivation are concluded.
Second, the realm beyond names and words.
Good son, if those sentient beings practicing in the final age who seek the Bodhisattva path and enter the three periods of time do not...
All objects of experience heard by him can ultimately not be grasped.
Regarding the text, there are three phrases that transcend the realm of names and words. Good son, one phrase is "if it is such-and-such," and another phrase is "it is not such-and-such.
If that phrase designates a practitioner who cultivates the Mahāyāna, it is not something heard by him.

As for this: the realm of Perfect Enlightenment transcends the path of language; what, then, could be heard? Regarding "all realms," these are the various phenomena of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
ultimately, they cannot be grasped. This is so that one may avoid giving rise to delusive confusion and instead be made to understand the distinct causes in order to sever non-resultant states.
This phrase demonstrates the severing of ignorance and afflictions. This concludes the section on the cultivation of the self-nature of awakening.
The section on the preparatory methods for entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*) is concluded. This answers the question: "How does one practice awakening during the rains retreat?

Second, the preparatory methods for cultivating contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are divided into two parts. First, the demonstration of the cultivation [of contemplation] is divided into three parts. First, the cultivation of *śamatha* is divided into two parts.
First, the cultivation of the awakening of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bodhi*) is divided into two parts. The first is the practice of awakening in accordance with reality.
"Good son, if sentient beings practice śamatha, they first grasp at ultimate stillness and do not give rise to thoughts.
When stillness reaches its peak, they become aware. Thus, from this initial stillness, it extends from one body to one world; awareness is likewise."
The six phrases of the first section correspond to the practice of awakening. "Good son" (one phrase); "If there are... (one phrase); "First grasping... (one phrase);
"When stillness reaches its limit, one then awakens" (one phrase); "In this way... (one phrase); "Awakening is also like this" (one phrase).
These various phrases indicate that which is cultivated. "First grasping the ultimate stillness" means relying on non-arising.
"Extinguishing the mind so that no thoughts arise" means relying on the profound stillness to turn away from false discrimination; this phrase indicates that concentration arises from awakening.

"When stillness reaches its ultimate limit" means being forever free from discrimination. "Thoughts become quiescent and non-arising, and one suddenly awakens" means attaining perfect, luminous awakening;
this phrase shows that concentration culminates in the manifestation of awakening. Thus, "initial stillness" constitutes the beginning of concentration, proceeding from the One.
As for the body, it has no characteristic of a self-body. As for reaching a single world-system, there is no characteristic of a world-system.

This phrase demonstrates that the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are established. "Awakening (*bodhi*) is also like this" means that awakening manifests a single body and extends to manifest a single world-system.

That which is called "stillness" (*śānta*) is the meaning of illumination within stillness; that which is called "awakening" is the meaning of stillness within illumination. Therefore, it is said: "Stillness..."

The polar lights penetrate everywhere; silent illumination encompasses empty space. This phrase combines awakening with the manifestation of concentration. Next, the characteristics of awakening are revealed:
"Good son, if awakening pervades a single world-system, and within that world-system there arises a single sentient being..."
One can know them all in a single thought-moment; it is likewise for hundreds of thousands of worlds.
Regarding the text, three phrases will now sequentially reveal the characteristics of awakening: "Good son" is one phrase; "if one awakens... and so forth is another phrase.

The phrase "hundreds of thousands," and so forth, indicates that if one awakens to the fact that a single phrase reveals the characteristic of pervasive awakening, then those sentient beings within the world who are capable of giving rise to such a thought are known to be, in all worlds, like images appearing in a mirror—the single meaning within the Tathāgata’s mind.
Likewise, the hundred thousand phrases that reveal the measure of accomplished meditative concentration are also thus; as if [one could...]

One knows the arising of a thought in a single sentient being within a single world-system. This concludes the preceding section on the combined text, completing the section on Cultivating the Awakening of Self-Nature.
Second, the realm free from names and words.
It is not that all objects heard by them can ultimately be grasped;
rather, even a single phrase of the text must transcend the realm of names and words. The commentary follows the previous method.

The preceding section on cultivating the nature of awakening, combined with the section on cultivating *śamatha*, is now complete. Second, the section on cultivating *samāpatti* is divided into two parts: first, cultivation...
The awakening to intrinsic nature opens into two. First is awakening based on the illusion of observation and contemplation.

Good son, if sentient beings practice *samāpatti*, they should first bring to mind the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions, relying upon various gateways to gradually practice the samādhi of diligent effort.
Regarding the four phrases of the text based on the illusion of *vitarka* (initial thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought): "Good son, one phrase" refers to the first phrase;
"if all [phenomena]... refers to the second phrase; "first one should... refers to the third phrase; and "based on the seeds... refers to the fourth phrase.

If these various phrases indicate that which is cultivated—namely, the preliminary recollection and contemplation—it gives rise to the mind that contemplates illusion. As for the "Tathāgatas of the ten directions," they pervade the awakened mind. Ten...
The "ten directions" refers to the pervasive nature of awakening. "All bodhisattvas" refers to the pervasive practice of awakening.
This phrase demonstrates that one contemplates the essence, characteristics, and function of awakening as neither identical to nor separate from it, thereby observing the root of illusion.
"Relying on various gateways" means giving rise to all illusory phenomena. "Gradual cultivation" means the accomplishment of illusory transformations. "Diligent exertion" refers to...

Regarding the function of delivering sentient beings: "Samādhi" refers to being capable of endurance and remaining unmoving. This phrase demonstrates that from essence, characteristic, and function, all illusions are produced;
by contemplating the function of illusion, one secondly gives rise to illusions through the arousal of vows.
Extensively issuing great vows, one spontaneously perfumes [the mind] to form seeds.
Regarding "extensively issuing great vows": these are the pure great vows of a Bodhisattva to deliver sentient beings.
Regarding "spontaneously perfuming to form seeds": through compassion, wisdom arises, manifesting illusions to benefit living beings. This accords with the preceding text.
The section on the collective accomplishment of the cultivation of the self-nature of awakening is concluded.
Second, regarding the realm beyond names and words: none of those realms heard by others can ever be grasped.

The interpretation of the phrases follows the previous example. This combines with the preceding section on the collective accomplishment of the cultivation of the self-nature of awakening to complete the section on the cultivation of *samāpatti*.
[The preceding section] concludes. Third, the cultivation of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) opens into two [parts]. First, the cultivation of the awakening to self-nature opens into two.
First is the contemplation of body, mind, and consciousness. "Good son, if sentient beings cultivate *dhyāna*, they first take up the method of counting (*gaṇanā*).

Within the mind, they clearly understand the divisions and counts of the moments of arising, abiding, and ceasing. In this way, throughout all four postures, they distinguish and count these moments. There is no [further text].
Not fully understanding, one should contemplate the body, mind, and consciousness according to the four phrases of the text. "Good son," is one phrase; "If there are various...
is one phrase; "First grasping... is one phrase; and "Thus... is one phrase. These various phrases indicate that which is practiced. First...

Regarding the "gate of counting": it refers to taking up the gate of counting breaths to discern the number of the arising of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) within the realm of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
"Discerning within the mind" means that the pure, awakening, illuminating mind fundamentally and clearly knows [this]. "The thoughts of arising, abiding, and ceasing" refers to...

The three subtle aspects of ignorance within the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses are associated with arising (*utpāda*) in the case of the karma-aspect (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), and with abiding (*sthiti*) in the cases of the transformation-aspect (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) and the manifestation-aspect (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*).

The six coarse aspects of ignorance are associated with differentiation (*viśeṣa*) in the case of the wisdom-aspect (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the term "differentiation" applied to wisdom: it means that wisdom is more clearly manifest than karma, transformation, and manifestation.
The cessation of the continuity of succession. Regarding the phrase "cessation of succession," it is because this succession is extinguished through [the presence of] cessation.
In the text, the word "different" (*anya*) is omitted within the term "cessation" (*nirodha*), because the former is different and the latter is cessation.

These [characteristics of] arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing are the deluded mind of ignorance; therefore, they are called "thoughts" (*smṛti*). As for "limit" (*pramāṇa*), it refers to the boundary of the thoughts of arising, abiding, and ceasing. "Head" (*mūrdhan*)...
Regarding "numbering": it is the manifestation of the moments of arising, abiding, and ceasing. However, these must be distinguished without confusion before the count becomes manifest;
this constitutes clarity. This phrase refers to knowing the number of mental cognitions (*vijñāna*). Regarding the expression "thus pervasively," and so forth:
it means that through such awareness of the moments of arising, abiding, and ceasing, one pervasively knows the body.

The enumerations of conceptual thoughts associated with the four modes of deportment. Regarding these enumerations of conceptual thoughts: they are the grasping and the imputation of names arising from bodily characteristics;

they are the karma, the suffering of karma, and the deluded mind-consciousness; they are the mental factors of ignorance belonging to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eight consciousnesses.
There is nothing that is not clearly known; this refers to the clear and distinct understanding of their specific categories and numerical counts.
This is knowledge. This phrase refers to knowing the number of body-consciousnesses.

Through the contemplation of the consciousnesses of the two worlds, one gradually progresses until one attains knowledge such that even a single drop of rain from hundreds of thousands of worlds is perceived as clearly as an object directly before one's eyes.
Regarding the two phrases for the contemplation of world-consciousness (*loka-vijñāna*), one gradually advances from a single phrase up to the phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*).
As for "gradually advancing": it means that from knowing the body and mind, one gradually comes to know the world;
and from knowing one world, one gradually comes to know many worlds. This phrase demonstrates the extent of the consciousness of the mind, until one attains knowledge of "and so forth."
"Thus, the three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. For what reason is the world established? From whence do all phenomena arise and perish?
Even if one were to count the drops of rain falling upon hundreds of thousands of worlds, there would be none that are not simply the number of ignorant mental conceptions.
Therefore, it is known with certainty. 'It is like... and so forth—this uses the near to illustrate the far, thereby elucidating the object [of realization].
It is known. This is not a knowledge derived from conceptual speculation; rather, it is a knowledge of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that is perfectly luminous.
This phrase indicates the knowledge of the numerical characteristics of consciousness. Together with the preceding section, this completes the chapter on Cultivating the Awareness of Self-Nature.
Second, the realm free from names and words.
It is not that all objects heard by them can ultimately be grasped.

The interpretation of the phrasing follows the previous examples. The preceding section on the cultivation of the self-nature of awakening, together with the section on the cultivation of *dhyāna*, is hereby concluded.
The combined section on the cultivation of *samāpatti* and *śamatha*, which was subsumed under the section on demonstrating cultivation, is now complete. Second, the conclusion of the names.
This is called the initial expedient means (*upāya*) for the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

To provide a summary title according to the text: "Three" refers to the contemplations; "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) signifies that concentration (*samādhi*) achieves the illumination of stillness, while wisdom (*prajñā*) achieves the contemplation of illusions, within which awakening consciousness is realized—all of which accord with the universal illumination of the *Perfect Enlightenment* (*Samantabhadra-bodhi*) and constitute the practice of the pure nature. "Initial" (*ādi*) refers to the beginning of the cultivation of these contemplations.

First, regarding the preliminary practices (*upāya*): from the stage of withdrawing into stillness, one takes up mental recollection and counting to accomplish the cultivation of the three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*).

This concludes the section on the combined demonstration of the stages of cultivation, which together complete the section on the preliminary practices for cultivating the contemplations. This answers the question of what serves as the primary focus for the three contemplations.
By linking this with the section on the preliminary practices for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), it completes the general demonstration of the section on the preliminary practices for instruction.
Second, showing the benefits of cultivation, which is divided into two parts. First, perfect cultivation and sudden realization:
if sentient beings universally cultivate these three types of diligent application of energy (*vīrya*), this is called the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
The two phrases "When... indicate the perfect cultivation and sudden realization. The phrase "If various... and so forth refers to the single phrase "That which is named...

and so forth. "Universal cultivation" means perfect cultivation. "Diligent practice" means the mind-moment after mind-moment is perfectly illuminated. "Vigorous effort" means thought after thought is perfectly quiescent.

This phrase demonstrates the practice of perfect cultivation. The phrase "That which is named Tathāgata... and so forth refers to the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
One attains the same quiescence as that of the Tathāgata and accords with the practice of pure awakening;

therefore, this is precisely the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world, and not the possession of the thirty-two marks that constitutes a Tathāgata. This phrase demonstrates the realization of sudden enlightenment.
Second, regarding the gradual realization through successive cultivation, two stages are opened: first, the severing of deluded karma.

If, in the final age, sentient beings of dull faculties desire to seek the Way but fail to achieve success due to karmic obstacles from the past, they should diligently practice repentance and constantly give rise to hope.
First, they must sever hatred and love, jealousy and envy, flattery and crookedness, and cultivate a mind that seeks the supreme and sublime.
Regarding the four phrases of the passage, the first three sever deluded karma. If one subsequently considers the phrase "if [one says] 'and so forth,'" it refers to the mind's desire;

the phrase "should diligently [practice] 'and so forth'" refers to severing [delusions] first. The first phrase indicates the root; the second phrase shows the obstacles; the third phrase shows the repentance.
"Constantly giving rise to hope" means hoping for the severance of obstacles and the accomplishment of the Path. There is...
One should hope for this and exert oneself even more in repentance so that it may arise constantly. The four lines [of verse] sever karmic activity.

For those who seek the superior mind, there is the mind of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), which combines hatred and attachment; these constitute the six fundamental ignorances (*mūla-avidyā*). Next, one should practice accordingly.

One should study one matter according to the three types of pure contemplations (*śubha-vipaśyanā*). Once this contemplation has been attained, one must not again practice that [previous] contemplation. Without letting the mind abandon it, one should gradually seek realization.
Regarding the text, there are three phrases; the phrase "the three types... and so forth is one, and the phrase "this contemplation... and so forth is one.
The phrase: "The mind does not engage in discursive proliferation" constitutes one sentence. The first sentence refers to single cultivation; the second sentence refers to combined cultivation.

"Not attaining" means not yet attaining entry into the realization of awakening. The third sentence refers to circular cultivation. "Gradually seeking realization" means gradually cultivating contemplation to seek the realization of pure awakening.
This concludes the preceding section on the benefits of cultivation and practice. [End of] the previous synthesis.
The section on "Demonstrating the Expedient Means" and its sub-sections are concluded. This concludes the section on "Continuing with the Formal Answer.

Together with the initial section on "Preface, Praise, and Permission," this completes the total long-line arrangement of the "Demonstration" section. Second, the "Verses in Summary" opens into two parts: first, the preface expressing the desire to proclaim [the teaching] once more.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

The method for explaining the verses follows the previous examples. Part Two: The Exposition of the Verses, which is divided into two sections. First: Summarizing the Essential Points to Reveal the Expedient Means, which is further divided into two.
First: Summarizing the Essential Points Regarding the Expedient Means of Dwellings.
"Perfect Enlightenment, you should know: all sentient beings who wish to seek the unsurpassed path must first establish a three-period retreat to repent for their karma from beginningless time.
After passing twenty-one days, they may then engage in right contemplation. That which is not the realm of what is heard cannot ultimately be grasped."
Second, the expedient means for cultivating contemplation according to the essential intent:
Śamatha is ultimate stillness; Samādhi is correct mindfulness and retention; Dhyāna is clarity regarding the gates of counting— These are called the three pure contemplations.
II. Summarizing the Essential Meaning to Show the Benefits of Cultivation, which is divided into two parts: 1. Summarizing the Essential Meaning of Perfect Cultivation and Sudden Realization:
"If one can diligently practice cultivation, This is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
2. Summarizing the Essential Meaning of Following Cultivation and Gradual Realization.
Those of dull faculties who have not yet attained accomplishment should always diligently repent with a sincere mind.
When all sins and obstacles from beginningless time are extinguished, the realm of the Buddha will immediately manifest before one.
The verse section is concluded. Together with the preceding prose, this completes the introductory narration and the section on the World-Honored One’s response. [The connection follows.]
The combined introductory section describing the Bodhisattva’s formulation of questions and the categorization of the stages leading to the fruit of pure contemplation are hereby concluded.
This connects to the section on the thorough penetration of causes, the severance of afflictions, and the realization of purity; thus the general main body of the text is completed.

The third section, "Circulation and Dissemination," is divided into two parts. The first part, "Detailed Question and Answer," is further divided into two. The first subsection, "Preface Describing the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry," is divided into two.
The first item is the "Preface Setting the Sequence of the Inquiry."
Thus, this introduction,

which clarifies how the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and the eleven other bodhisattvas each posed their questions, has concluded its exposition of the principles of the Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-bodhi),
encompassing both cause and fruit. What remains is solely the upholding and dissemination [of this teaching] for the benefit of future generations.
Regarding what the sentient beings of the world ought to know: the names of the sūtra teachings and the cultivation of merit;

as well as the protection and upholding of those who transmit the sūtras and the dissemination of the teaching-ground; and the posing of questions, the accomplishment of upholding, and the circulation [of the Dharma].

This consists of two parts: the introductory sequence of questions and the threefold opening of the two [sections]. Within the first part, the description of the ritual and sounds, there is a further division into two: the first part describes the questions on majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Then the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

The explanation of the phrases follows the previous examples. Second, the description of requesting instruction and receiving benefit is divided into two parts. First, celebrating the previous hearing of the Dharma:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes and for the sake of sentient beings in the末代 (final age), you have extensively opened up and awakened us to such inconceivable matters."

The first two phrases of the opening section celebrate the previous hearing of the Dharma. "The World-Honored One of Great Compassion" constitutes one phrase, and "extensively for [the sake of sentient beings]" and so forth constitutes another.
Regarding "inconceivable matters," these refer to the realm of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), which cannot be known through discursive thought or intellectual measurement.
Second, the request for four matters:
"World-Honored One, what is the name of this Mahāyāna teaching, and how should it be upheld? What merit do sentient beings obtain by practicing it?
How may I protect those who uphold the sutra? To what extent shall this teaching be disseminated?"
The text consists of five phrases requesting four matters: one phrase for the World-Honored One; one phrase for the name "This Great [Cloud]" and so forth, for upholding it;
one phrase for sentient beings and so forth, for the cultivation of merit; one phrase for "How" and so forth, for protecting those who uphold the sutra;
and one phrase for "Spreading" and so forth, for the ground where the teaching is disseminated. These are combined according to the preceding classification.

The section on "Concluding the Request for Instruction" is finished. The preceding combined section on "Preface and Inquiry into Dignified Conduct" is subsumed under the section "Preface, Description, and Pronunciation of Rituals," which is now concluded.
Second, the conclusion of the preface regarding the beginning and end.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.

The explanation of the phrases follows the previous pattern. This concludes the three sections of the Preface—namely, the Combined Preface, the Description of the Ritual, and the Phonology and Categories—which together complete the "Preface" and "Questions" sections.
The general introduction, consisting of the questions and the sequential sections, is concluded. Second, the introduction describing the World-Honored One’s response, which is divided into two parts.
First, the introduction praising and granting permission, which is further divided into two. The first is the praise for that which was requested.
