At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, you are truly able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the merits and the names of such a teaching as this."
The praise for what is requested consists of three phrases; the general rule consists of two phrases. The single phrase "You all...

briefly praises the former two [phrases] while encompassing the latter two. Regarding the two [sections of] permission, response, entrustment, and reception: first is the entrustment to listen attentively.
"Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
The interpretation of the phrases follows the previous pattern. The two disciples accepted the instruction and remained silent.
Then, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
The examples for the phrase-by-phrase commentary are as before. The combined text, categorized above, completes the section on "Consent, Response, and Entrustment.

The continuous combination with the section on "Praising the Request" concludes the first part: the section on "Praise, Consent, and Entrustment" within the Preface. Next, the formal response is set forth, divided into four parts.
First, regarding the upholding of the name, there are two parts. First, to reveal the essence of the sutra:
"Good son, this sutra has been spoken by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, it is the refuge for Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and it is the pure eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures."
The five phrases at the beginning clarify the essence of the sutra: "Good son" (one phrase); "this sutra... (one phrase);

"the three periods of time... (one phrase); "the ten directions... (one phrase); and "the twelve [links of dependent origination]... (one phrase). Regarding the phrase "that which has been taught by all Buddhas":
Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*) is the ocean of all Buddhas; it is that which all Buddhas have received as their cause, and they have all clearly expounded this Perfect Enlightenment.
"The Tathāgatas of the three periods" refers to those protected by the three periods of past, present, and future. The Tathāgatas of the past have entered the *parinirvāṇa* of perfect enlightenment;
the Tathāgatas of the present expound perfect enlightenment to manifest its excellence; and the Tathāgatas of the future take perfect enlightenment as the basis for their arising.
Of these two phrases, one concerns the benefit of others by all Buddhas, and the other concerns the self-benefit of all Buddhas.
The Buddhas constitute the Jewel of the Buddha. Those bodhisattvas who take refuge [in them] follow the teaching of Perfect Enlightenment; this phrase constitutes the Jewel of the Noble Saṅgha.
As for the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*): first, the *sūtra*, which refers to the prose sections of the various scriptures;
second, the *geya*, which refers to the verses repeated within the various scriptures—those that restate what was spoken in prose, also called "verses corresponding to prose" (*anugīta*).

1. *Geya* (Verses): Those passages consisting of verses (*gāthā*). 2. *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecies): Among the various sūtras, those that bestow the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) of future buddhahood upon bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and others.
3. *Gāthā-sūtra* (Verse Sūtras): The independent verses (*udāna*) found within various sūtras that are neither *geya* nor *gāthā* following a prose section;
these are also called *bhāṣita*. 4. *Udāna* (Inspired Utterances): Those passages within various sūtras spoken spontaneously without being questioned. 5. *Nidāna* (Causes/Origins).
1. *Nidāna-sūtra*: Among the various sūtras, those that contain explanations given in response to questions. 2. *Jātaka-sūtra*:
Among the various sūtras, those in which the Tathāgata speaks of the causes and origins of his own past deeds. 3. *Itivṛttaka-sūtra*:

Among the various sūtras, those that speak of things done by others in previous lives. 4. *Vaipulya-sūtra*: Among the various sūtras, those that encompass the rules of conduct and the practice of the path.

10. *Nidāna* (Causes and Conditions): These are the sūtras that explain the causes and conditions for the arising of various phenomena. 11. *Itivṛttaka* (Thus It Was Said): These are the sūtras that record the past lives and deeds of the Tathāgata. 12. *Jātaka* (Birth Stories): These are the sūtras that recount the various births of the Bodhisattva throughout his successive lifetimes. 13. *Vaipulya* (Extensive Teachings): These are the sūtras that extensively expound upon the profound principles of the Mahāyāna. 14. *Adbhutadharma* (Marvelous Events): These are the sūtras that describe the extremely rare and wondrous events concerning the Three Jewels and other such phenomena, as well as the disciples’ praises of the Tathāgata’s marvelous virtues.

15. *Avadāna* (Parables): These are the sūtras that establish parables within the teachings to clarify their underlying intent. 16. *Upadeśa* (Expository Treatises): These are the sūtras consisting of formal discussions and analyses.
Regarding the detailed analysis of the meanings explained throughout the various sutras, presented here as questions and answers for clear exposition and extensive interpretation:

this serves as a general outline of the twelve gateways of all the Tathāgata’s teachings. As for the "pure eye," it refers to how the Tathāgata’s entire lifetime of temporal teachings collectively reveals *perfect enlightenment* (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) to sentient beings; once perfect enlightenment is clearly realized, it is like a person who...
The Eye. The radiance of the sun illuminates so that all things may be seen; it is the root of the myriad practices. This phrase constitutes the Jewel of the Sublime Dharma (*Saddharmaratna*).
Following this, the title of the sutra is listed:
this sutra is titled *Mahāvaipulya-bodhimaṇḍa-dhāraṇī*. It is also titled *Sūtra-nītārtha*. It is also titled...
This Secret King Samādhi is also called the Definitive Realm of the Tathāgata, and it is also called the Distinctive Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. You should uphold it.
Following the six phrases of the prose section, the names of the sūtras are listed. "Sūtra" consists of five phrases; "you should uphold it" is one phrase.

The first phrase is the general retention (*dhāraṇī*); the second phrase transcends all verbal expression. The remaining explanations follow the previous pattern. The third phrase refers to the Great Samādhi.
Regarding "the secret": it is not an object of conceptual thought. Regarding "the King of Samādhis": it is the king of samādhis and the foremost of all concentrations. The fourth phrase is [not...].

"Different. Regarding "the determined realm": the original Buddha-enlightenment remains unchanging while following conditions; thus, the five phrases are not identical. Regarding "the differentiation of self-nature":
it is like the nature of the Dharma-realm, which is unchanging yet follows conditions. "You should uphold this" means that knowing the substance of name-and-consciousness is what is to be upheld.
This concludes the section on "Upholding by Name," which, together with the preceding category, completes the text.
Second, the stage of the dissemination of the teaching is divided into two. First, the ultimate fruit, the ocean of Buddhas.
"Good son, this sutra reveals exclusively the realm of the Tathāgata; only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, can fully proclaim it.
If bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this to practice, they will gradually advance until they reach the stage of Buddhahood."
When the four phrases of the text reach the ultimate fruit of the ocean of Buddhas: "Good son," one phrase; "this sutra," and so forth, one phrase;
"only the Buddha," and so forth, one phrase; and "if all," and so forth, one phrase—these phrases of the sutra are the fundamental principle, while the phrase "only the Buddha" is the Teacher.
If all the phrases proceed as practice, they are fundamentally based upon the Teacher, who is none other than the Tathāgata. There is no [other].
Because he possesses both subject and object, he practices and progresses until reaching the stage of Buddhahood. These two causes pervade the Dharma-realm.

Good son, this sutra is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna; sentient beings with sudden faculties attain awakening through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice gradually.
It is like the great ocean, which does not reject even small streams, down to those from mosquitoes and gadflies.
Those asuras who drink its water all obtain full satisfaction.
These four lines of verse should pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Good son, this single phrase—this scripture, and so forth—is a single phrase.
The phrase "also includes... and the phrase "for example... clarify the primary meaning of this sutra passage. The phrase "also includes" indicates what is secondary. As for why it is secondary:
although one practices the Mahāyāna, until one enters ultimate awakening, there are no lack of distinctions regarding the fruits and realizations of the mind.
The phrase "for example" serves as a metaphor to clarify this secondary meaning. "Not yielding to the small stream" means not yielding to its...

The benefit of its moistening and nourishing is such that even mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras can drink from it and attain full satisfaction. This is because the ocean of right view does not reject even the smallest streams.
Mosquitoes and gadflies, with their small bellies, are metaphors for sentient beings with small roots; the asuras, with their large bellies, are metaphors for sentient beings with great roots.
Indeed, while mosquitoes and gadflies find sufficient fulfillment by drinking from small streams, they likewise drink from the currents of the ocean.
Water is never such that it cannot be taken until it is sufficient and full. The asuras drink from the flowing waters of the ocean and take their fill until they are full;
however, when drinking from small streams, there are times when they cannot take their fill or reach fullness.

Therefore, these are used together as metaphors to show that one should look toward the great ocean, being able to yield to the small stream, while the small stream cannot help but yield to the great ocean. Just so...
The Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*) is able to encompass gradual cultivation (*jian-xiu*), whereas gradual cultivation cannot encompass the Sudden Teaching.

This concludes the section on the "Teaching Ground of Universal Dissemination" (*liu-fu jiao-di*), which together with the preceding section forms the combined text. Third, the "Cultivation of Merit" (*xiu-xi gong-de*) is divided into two parts.
First, "Manifesting the Inferior to Reveal the Superior," which is further divided into two. First, the superiority and inferiority of causes and fruits.
Good son, suppose there were someone who filled the trichiliocosm entirely with the seven precious treasures and used them for giving as an act of charity;
this would not equal the merit of someone who hears the name of this sutra or even a single phrase of its meaning.
The three phrases of the main text distinguish between superiority and inferiority according to their causes. "Good son," one phrase; "even if," and so forth, one phrase;
"not as good as," and so forth, one phrase. "Even if" (*jāsu*) is a term used for comparison. "Pure" (*chun yi*) means not mixed with other things.
"Seven treasures" (*saptaratna*) are: first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal; fifth, mother-of-pearl; sixth, agate; [seventh, coral].
Agate and seven kinds of pearls fill [the space], reaching a vertical height and extending horizontally throughout the trichiliocosm.

A "small thousand-world system" consists of a world-system with one thousand suns and moons and one thousand Mount Sumerus. One thousand such small thousand-world systems constitute a single [medium] world-system;
again, one thousand such [medium] world-systems constitute a medium thousand-world system. Such medium thousand-world systems...
One world, and again a thousand worlds, constitute one great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
That is to say, there are a thousand small worlds, a thousand small-thousand-worlds, and a thousand middle-thousand-worlds; these three thousand worlds together form one great trichiliocosm.
It contains ten billion suns, moons, Mount Sumerus, and four continents, which collectively are named the Sahā world-system.
It is a realm (*dhātu*). One who practices giving performs the *dānapāramitā*. Yet, although one might accumulate and give away treasures as numerous as atoms, these are all external objects;
they cannot fulfill the perfection of giving. This [former] form of giving is inferior. However, one who hears the name of this sutra attains its essence through the name;
and one who understands the meaning of even a single phrase realizes the mind through the meaning. Both are able to achieve fulfillment.
Regarding the *prajñā*, one fulfills bodhi; this phrase refers to the excellence of wisdom. Regarding the excellence or inferiority of the two fruits of realization:
suppose there were someone who taught as many sentient beings as the sands of a hundred Ganges rivers to attain the fruit of arhatship;
this would not equal someone who proclaims even half a verse of this sutra with analytical discernment.

The two lines of the first section demonstrate the superiority and inferiority of the fruits of realization. The phrase "even if... and so forth is not equal to the phrase "rather than... and so forth.
The fruits of realization of the Two Vehicles are characterized by ignorance, whereas the teaching of Perfect Enlightenment reveals the pure nature.

Therefore, although there are many teachings and proofs like those [of the Two Vehicles], they do not compare to this concise proclamation. This is because such a proclamation represents the very self-nature of the Buddha-fruit; thus it is so.
Regarding the "Excellence of the Half-Verse": taking up a single verse, one analyzes its half;

all such principles, combined with the preceding sections of the text, complete the section titled "Manifesting the Inferior and Revealing the Superior. Second, the "Supremely Excellent Manifestation of Superiority."
"Good son, if there is another person who hears the name of this sutra and their faith is not confused,

you should know that such a person has planted roots of merit and wisdom not under just one or two Buddhas. Thus, they have planted various roots of goodness under as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River upon hearing the teachings of this sutra."
The three phrases of the first section most excellently manifest superiority. "Good son" constitutes one phrase; "if again... constitutes one phrase;

and "it should be known that... constitutes one phrase. Regarding "one whose faith is unconfused": upon hearing the name of the *Sūtra* as *Perfect Enlightenment*, they immediately believe it to be their own original mind, which is entirely pure, and without further doubt, they accord with it in practice. This phrase manifests the aspect of hearing.
"One Buddha or two Buddhas" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* Buddhas.

"Planting various roots of merit and wisdom" means that those who fully provide for and draw near to the Tathāgata through the two wheels of merit and wisdom inevitably plant all such roots of merit and wisdom.

"Those who have planted various roots of goodness under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" refers to those who enter the ocean of the nature of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*, drawing near to and making offerings to it, thereby fulfilling perfect enlightenment.
"Awakened Tathāgata"—this phrase reveals its excellence. For even to be able to personally approach and make offerings to a single Buddha-Tathāgata is beyond comparison with other merits;
yet here, one directly surpasses the merit and wisdom cultivated under one or two Buddhas by speaking of the roots of goodness planted under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This supreme merit is not something that can be contained within the scope of thought. [The preceding section] was a synthesis.

The section on "Manifesting the Inferior and Revealing the Superior" and the section on "The Merit of Cultivation" are hereby concluded. Fourth, regarding the protection of those who uphold this sutra, two parts are opened:
first, the entrustment and instruction for protection:
"O son of good family, you should protect these practitioners in the末法 (mofa / final age), ensuring that no evil Māras or heterodox teachers [harm them]."
This vexes their body and mind, causing them to give rise to despondency and retreat.
The passage consists of three phrases as an instruction on how to provide protection: "You, son of good family" (one phrase); "You should protect...
and so forth (one phrase); and "Do not allow... and so forth (one phrase). As for the address "You, son of good family," it is not merely a call to the specific recipient; rather, it is...
I directly entrust this to all those present in this assembly. This phrase is the entrustment to the multitude. "Practitioners" refers to those who cultivate Perfect Enlightenment;
this phrase is the instruction for their protection. "Evil Māras" are those who delight in birth and death. "Heterodox teachers" are those who cling to false views.
"Distressing their bodies and minds" means that through supernatural powers, Māra causes the body to be restless and the mind to be obscured.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthika), by means of their conceptual grasping, cause attachment to the body and delusion in the mental continuum, leading to despondency.

"Despondency" means a lack of diligence; "despair" means losing the path of the Buddha. This phrase indicates protection. Regarding the two groups who receive and uphold this protection, there are two divisions.
First, the assembly at the site of practice (maṇḍala) is divided into two: first, receiving the instructions on dignified deportment (īryāpatha).
At that time, within the assembly were Vajra Fire-Head, Vajra Destroyer, Vajra Nīlabha, Vajra, and others—
eighty thousand vajras together with their retinues. They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The three phrases beginning with "At that time" describe the reception of the command and the majestic deportment.

The phrase beginning with "At that time," the phrase beginning with "Eighty thousand," and the phrase beginning with "Immediately from" [constitute these sections]. Regarding "those in the assembly at that time":

because the Dharma-assembly of Perfect Enlightenment is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the multitude of the practice site and the multitude of the world-systems are all included within the assembly. As for "Fire-head," it is so called because there is fire upon his head.
Jvalana. Furthermore, it is said that this Malla attained the Way by contemplating the nature of fire; thus he was given this name. He transformed his excessive lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.

Because he had made a vow in the past to personally serve as a Malla to subdue the demonic enemies when the Buddhas attained enlightenment, *Vajra*—the name of the precious mallet he wields—is used to denote his spiritual power. Nīla...
Lamba is a Sanskrit term; its meaning is translated as "Fierce and Powerful" (*caṇḍa*) and also as "Free from Bonds" (*vigata-bandhana*).
Because of his courageous progress, he is able to leave behind all fetters and bonds. This phrase introduces the name of the leading deity.

Regarding the eighty thousand phrases that introduce the numerous leading members of the retinue, they are explained by analogy with the preceding section on the ritual of salutation. Second, the formal expression of protection and maintenance.
"Bhagavān, if in the future final age there are any sentient beings who are able to uphold this definitive Mahāyāna, we shall protect them as we would our own eyes.
Even unto the site of the place of awakening and wherever they practice, we Vajrapāṇis, leading our own retinues, will protect them morning and evening so that they do not fall back.
Their households shall forever be free from calamities, obstacles, pestilences, and epidemics."
Wealth and treasures shall be extinguished [of misfortune] and always remain abundant and never lacking.
One should recite these five phrases of expression for protection: "The World-Honored One" (one phrase); "If hereafter... (one phrase); "I shall...
(one phrase); "...even unto... (one phrase); and "In that household... (one phrase). There is one who is able...

"To uphold this" is a term of congratulation. "To resolve upon the Mahāyāna" refers to the practice of the ultimate, pure definitive meaning of the Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).
This phrase celebrates the fortunate encounter with its sublime cultivation. "Like protecting one's eyes":

those who cultivate Perfect Enlightenment take the wisdom-eye of the fundamental Dharma-realm as their own. Just as the blind rely on a guide, they protect it with such earnestness as if protecting their own eyes.

This phrase concerns the protection and support of those who practice; "guarding the site of enlightenment so that they do not regress" refers to the protection and support of the dwelling place, for even an unstable dwelling causes one to regress, and thus it must be protected. The phrase concerning the household refers to the protection and support of the family members and all necessary requisites;
this encompasses the assembly of lay practitioners. As for "calamities and obstacles," these are the deeds of Māra. "Epidemics" refers to... [text ends]
Illnesses are caused by spirits. As for "abundant wealth," this explains the meaning of being fully provided with the four requisites and never lacking anything.
Since one's retinue and necessities—whether through encountering calamities, illness, or scarcity—can all disturb and disrupt the cultivation of the mind, they must all be protected and maintained.
This, together with the preceding section of the text, constitutes the various rules for the *maṇḍala*.

[The preceding section] concluded. The assembly of the two worlds is divided into two parts. First, the protection and assistance of the various devas, which is further divided into two. First, their reception of the command and their dignified demeanor:

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the twenty-eight heavenly kings, Sumeruśvara, the Heavenly King who Protects the Nation, and others, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The first section consists of two phrases concerning the reception of the command and the majestic deportment. At that time... [one phrase]. Immediately from... [one phrase].
"The Great Brahmā King" refers to the sovereign of the Sahā world. "The Kings of the Twenty-eight Heavens" collectively enumerates the celestial kings of the three realms:
six in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), eighteen in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), totaling twenty-eight.
Each of the eighteen heavens has its own king. The King of Mount Sumeru is the Lord of the Desire Realm who dwells upon the earth;
he is Śakra. The Kings of the Guardian Devas are the Four Great Kings of the first heaven of the Desire Realm who protect the boundaries of the world.
This phrase enumerates the kings of the three realms, all of whom provide protection and sustenance. Among them are Mahābrahmā and Śakra.

Regarding the specific designation of the Four Kings: because they exercise authority over the world as lords of the mundane realm, the subsequent phrases concerning their respectful salutation and dignified demeanor are explained by analogy with what preceded.
Second is the presentation of their words of protection and maintenance.
“World-Honored One, I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra, constantly ensuring they are at peace and their minds do not regress.

Regarding the two phrases of the text, ‘I shall also... and ‘constantly ensure they are at peace,’ [the former] means ‘I shall also speak thus,’ and [the latter] means ‘constantly ensure they are at peace,’ which is to say, ‘well-protect and sustain them.
Together with the preceding section, these constitute the chapter on the protection and sustenance by all the devas.”
[The preceding section] concluded. II. The various ghosts break their protection and open [the gates]. A. Receiving the command and observing the proper decorum.

At that time, there was a great powerful ghost-king named Kumbhāṇḍa, together with one hundred thousand ghost-kings, who immediately rose from their seats, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The first section consists of two phrases concerning the reception of the command and the majestic deportment. At that time... [one phrase]. Immediately from... [one phrase].
As for the *kumbhāṇḍa*, it is also called *gūbhāṇḍa*; this is translated as "jar-shaped.
He is a *yātudhāna* (sorcery-demon) whose form is fearsome and who possesses manifold powers of transformation. Dwelling in forests and wilds, he leads a host of spirits; he is thus the chief leader.

Therefore, he is titled "King. As for his being among the hundred thousand ghost-kings, he is likewise a leader. This phrase serves as an example for the protection and support provided by all ghost-kings;
the manner of their respectful salutation and deportment is explained by analogy with what precedes. Second, the expression of words regarding protection and support.
“World-Honored One, I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra, attending to them morning and evening so that they do not fall back or become discouraged.
If, within a distance of one yojana of where such a person dwells, there are spirits or ghosts who invade their domain, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust.”
The three phrases of the introductory text serve as a protective recitation. "The World-Honored One" constitutes one phrase; "I too [say]" and so forth constitutes one phrase;
"that person" and so forth constitutes one phrase. This is intended for those who do not retreat or yield, because there will be no obstacles or hindrances.
These phrases protect the practitioner within a distance of one *yojana*, which is a boundary of forty *li*. To encroach upon this domain means to enter within those forty *li*.
"Abiding and wandering within, [reducing them] to fragments like fine dust" refers to subduing through majestic power. This phrase subdues malevolent spirits.

Combined with the preceding section, this completes the "Section on Subduing and Protecting All Spirits. The preceding combination of the "Section on the Protection and Aid of All Devas" concludes the "Section on the Multitude of the World.
Together with the combined "Section on the Multitude of the Ritual Site," these are governed by the "General Section on Receiving Protection."
The section on "Holding" is concluded. This connects to the section on "Entrustment and Instruction for Protection," which concludes within the section on "Protecting Those Who Recite the Sutra.

The three sections—on "The Flow of Merit from Cultivation," "Names for the Grounds of Teaching Dissemination," and "Receiving and Holding"—are unified and collectively lead into the subsequent description of the main response, which is now concluded.
This integrates with the initial section on "Praise and Permission in the Preface," which extracts from the preface the account of the World-Honored One’s bestowed response.

The section on the classification is concluded. This includes the combined introduction and narration, the section on the Bodhisattvas posing questions, and the detailed section on the questions and answers according to the general and specific categories; this concludes the section.
Second, the general conclusion on faith and acceptance:
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, all the Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of spirits and their retinues, as well as the various devas...
The King, Brahmā, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
Regarding the structure of the text, there are three sentences that collectively conclude the section on belief and acceptance: "When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra" (one sentence);
"All the Bodhisattvas... (one sentence); and "The entire great assembly... (one sentence). This concludes the detailed analysis of the section on questions and answers, both general and specific.
The entry into the general section on circulation is completed.
*The Commentary on the Words of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment: The Definitive Meaning*, Volume Lower-Lower (End).
Epilogue to the *Commentary on the Words of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*.
In the past, while serving as a scribe and holding the military banner during my campaigns in the regions of Zhen and Shao, I had the honor of paying my respects to Master Luofeng at Mount Rizhen.
There, I was fortunate to receive the Master’s compassionate pity for one mired in delusion; he guided me through manifold means.

A single word, hitting the mark, suddenly cleared the path of my mind. Since that time, even when facing the blade on the battlefield, I have felt as if I were seeing clearly—all this is due to the Master.

This is the wondrous power of compassionate instruction. How short a time has passed since the Master entered parinirvāṇa! Yet, while my worldly ties have not yet been severed, I was beset by the duties of a naval expedition;
thus, I lacked the means to sweep his stupa. Alas! The clouds of compassion have drifted far away, yet the rain of Dharma continues to nourish in secret.

The four sensory objects of the floating faculties remain, as ever, defiled obstructions. Coincidentally, while in the city of Sui, I met the master’s senior disciple, the Head Seat Zongfu, and inquired about the master’s bequeathed Dharma.
The Head Seat said, "The Master’s commentaries fill his baskets. Among those that have not yet been circulated is the *Verse-by-Verse Explanation of the Complete Enlightenment Sutra*.

This is where our teacher uniquely exerted his insight and skill, grasping the essential veins of the teaching to point directly at people face-to-face, as if [drawing them forth] from the ten directions."
These two Bodhisattvas personally received the oral instructions from the assembly; it was as if they were overturning the case of Guifeng, yet they obtained something unprecedented.

I received and read them; the handwriting was still vividly present. Having encountered the Master’s face-to-face instruction, before I had even finished opening the scroll, my sense-bases and objects were completely cleared away.
Unconsciously, I leaped up and prostrated myself on the ground, saying: "Excellent! This is precisely what the Master has used to propagate Cao..."
This is one who carries on the tradition of the Caodong school. How could it be merely that the First Patriarch manifested the Buddha-mind school through the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*?
As the patriarchal temple enters its autumnal twilight and the teachings decline, many people are lost as to the pointing finger, let alone the moon itself.

Now, this Master strikes like a thunderclap in a clear sky, wishing to cause all to awaken suddenly and fully. It is most fitting that he propagate this widely to benefit those who come to study. May there be an assembly!
The Venerable Xilai was a close friend of Master Zuo; they were of the same source and shared the same stream, their minds and eyes being as one regarding the profound purport of this sutra.
Having previously examined and verified it face-to-face, I have now, during the intervals of my meditative contemplation, carefully compared and edited it.
Truly, this is like playing the lute with joined hands; its sound is profound and its tuning transcendent. To obtain this profound resonance, one must first attain perfect hearing.

Once it falls into the pit of conceptual thought, the sword has long since departed. Now that the work is complete, I have contributed gold to purchase nearly three hundred sheets of pearwood, entrusting them to the carvers to print and disseminate [this text], so that every person throughout the great earth may uphold it and each realize the Dharma-practice of the Tathāgata’s stages of cultivation.
This is one instance of fulfilling the compassionate vow of our Master. The Buddha spoke it; my Master Xuan interpreted it; the Master compared and refined it;
his senior disciple, the Master Zong, preserved it; Tonghuo carved it into woodblocks and circulated it; and the multitudes throughout the Dharma-realm have obtained and upheld it.
They all return to the Great Perfect Enlightenment. Respectfully written as a postscript.
Humbly recorded by the disciple of the precepts from Xin’an, Tonghuo Jiangqilong, with prostrations. *The Pearl-String Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*.
Authored by Yuan’an Lingting Jingting;
as it is included among the fifth of the twelve types of scriptures he compiled for review, it is not recorded here.
